When I became the first executive director of the country’s oldest statewide tobacco control coalition in 1999, conversations were already underway about how Colorado should spend its share of funds distributed to states from the landmark tobacco settlement.
Unsurprisingly, interest groups from across our state came forward to argue why their priorities deserved a portion of Colorado’s share of settlement dollars. While policymakers considered how to spend the state’s portion of the settlement, my job was to go to communities across Colorado and explain why a significant portion of the funds should go to tobacco prevention and education programs, rather than unrelated, even if deserving, programs.
I’ve been thinking about that experience in the wake of the $18 billion legal settlement between almost all states and social media giant Meta. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser and others have noted parallels between the two. As states make plans, it’s worth reflecting on lessons learned from the tobacco settlement nearly three decades ago.
The 1998 tobacco settlement numbers were monumental: States would receive $200 billion to resolve lawsuits against Big Tobacco for its history of harm. States had to determine where their share of the money should go.
Before 1999, I had only a basic understanding of what led up to the tobacco settlement — beyond the now-historic clips of tobacco industry executives testifying under oath before the U.S. Congress and saying, one after another, that they believed nicotine was not addictive.
I did know, however, that the tobacco settlement would be a game-changer, and in many ways, it was. It directed hundreds of millions of dollars to states to fund programs. It restricted tobacco marketing that targeted youth, like the cartoon character Joe Camel, and funded the Truth Initiative, a tobacco prevention organization that still exists.
It also led to the release of millions of industry documents, which provided explicit detail about the companies’ exploitative efforts to addict various populations and fight public health protections. The easily searchable online database offered a treasure trove of material for researchers and journalists, confirming some of our worst suspicions about the industry.
But in other areas, the tobacco settlement fell short of its goals. These missteps offer insights for the Meta settlement spending.
For one, the tobacco settlement didn’t specify how states could spend the funds, so it was open season for anyone searching for funding for unrelated projects. While some states spent money to fill budget holes or (in the Carolinas) even subsidize tobacco producers, Colorado appropriated most of its money to health-related programs, though almost all have no direct nexus to tobacco.
As a result, according to the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, tobacco prevention is chronically shortchanged to this day: In fiscal year 2026, “total state funding for these programs amounts to just 3.4% of the $21.7 billion in revenue the states will collect from tobacco settlement payments and tobacco taxes.”
Meanwhile, the shape-shifting tobacco industry continued to innovate new methods to hook new and young users, with teen-friendly sweet and fruity flavors leading to a surge in teen vaping and, more recently, highly potent oral nicotine products like Zyn. From the legislature to city halls, tobacco industry lobbyists and dollars remain omnipresent today, fighting efforts to restrict flavored products, for example.
On the positive side, the tobacco settlement spurred prevention programs to work together to address tobacco and other public health issues. The early 2000s brought a strong focus on educating communities about the harms of secondhand smoke and successful policies to restrict smoking in public places.
There were also successful campaigns in Colorado and other states to increase the price of tobacco, a policy move proven to reduce smoking in adults and youth and fund prevention and cessation efforts. These and other efforts built on the experience and trust forged through decades of policy battles, including the tobacco settlement, even if the dollars weren’t involved.
If I could speak directly to the people now in charge of distributing funds from the Meta settlement, I’d like to offer them three pieces of advice.
First, don’t rely on the industry to protect youth when its business model depends on hooking new customers and keeping them using their product. As the saying goes, fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. Whether it’s nicotine or algorithms, the result is the same: reinforcing a behavior that is harmful to users. Policymakers and advocates need to promote laws and regulations to protect youth, following the evidence of what’s proven to halt cycles of addiction.
Second, use settlement dollars to emphasize youth prevention and support initiatives with generation-spanning benefits. While addressing immediate harm is key, research related to substance use, for example, shows long-term prevention provides the highest return on investment.
Finally, consider that the movement to protect kids from these harms is just beginning and will require constant evolution and vigilance to adapt to emerging threats. Since the tobacco industry promised to change its ways, it has continually innovated new ways to deliver nicotine to users, with increased potency and efficiency. The breakneck pace of the evolution — or devolution — of technology will only accelerate, and we have learned we cannot trust tech companies to police themselves.
When companies won’t do the right thing themselves, litigation has proven effective at checking their excesses. However, legal solutions aren’t enough without forward-looking policy and sustained accountability.
Susan Morrisey headed the Colorado Tobacco Education and Prevention Alliance in the late 1990s and is now a principal with SE2, a behavior-change marketing agency that has worked on tobacco prevention for three decades.

British woman abducted in Malawi, police say
- Published
Police in Malawi are investigating the kidnapping of a British national who was abducted in the southern African nation's main city, Blantyre.
Nusrat Osman, 47, was seized at around 12:30 local time on Friday by four men who had been travelling in a grey Nissan Dualis, according to a police statement.
The authorities have offered a reward of more than $17,000 (£12,600) for "credible information" that could lead to the rescue of the mother of two young children and the prosecution of the perpetrators.
Osman was reported to have been working for a local auditing firm.
A Malawi news outlet reported that Osman's husband was in anguish about the disappearance.
"I don't know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor and I have no issues with anyone," he was quoted by Nyasa Times as saying.
Police said the motive behind the abduction was unknown and that so far the kidnappers have not contacted the victim's family or the authorities.
The UK Foreign Office told the BBC that it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities.
Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.

Srinagar, Sep 15: Minister for Agriculture Production, Rural Development and Panchayati Raj, Cooperative and Election Department, Javid Ahmad Dar, today chaired a detailed review meeting to assess the progress of ongoing Forest and PMGSY road projects in Rafiabad constituency.
The meeting was attended by Chief Conservator of Forests, Kashmir; Chief Engineer, PMGSY, Kashmir; Conservator of Forests, North Kashmir; Superintending Engineer, PMGSY; DFOs Langate and Baramulla, besides other concerned officers.
During the meeting, the Minister took a detailed review of the status of ongoing road connectivity projects being executed under PMGSY and other Capex-funded schemes in Rafiabad and adjoining areas. He sought project-wise updates from the concerned officers, with focus on the pace of execution, completion timelines and issues hampering the progress of works.
Emphasizing the importance of road connectivity in accelerating development, Javid Dar said that effective implementation of public welfare and development projects is closely linked with reliable connectivity, particularly in rural and far-flung areas. He directed the concerned officers to ensure the timely completion of all ongoing road projects under PMGSY and other Capex funds within the stipulated timelines while maintaining quality standards and ensuring judicious utilization of public funds.
The Minister called for greater coordination among the concerned departments to address bottlenecks, streamline the execution process and ensure that the benefits of developmental schemes reach the people without delays.
Highlighting the considerable tourism potential of Rafiabad and its adjoining areas, Javid Dar stressed the need to create and upgrade infrastructure to facilitate tourism-related activities and promote local economic opportunities.
He underscored that infrastructure development in the region must be pursued in a balanced and sustainable manner, ensuring that the ecological balance, natural beauty and forest identity of the area are preserved.
“Development and environmental conservation must go hand in hand. Our endeavour should be to create modern infrastructure while protecting the rich natural resources and forest wealth of the region,” the Minister maintained.
He called for coordinated planning and execution of road and other infrastructure projects so that developmental needs are met without compromising environmental sustainability.
The Minister directed the concerned officers to examine the pending issues on priority and ensure that all necessary clearances are processed expeditiously to avoid delays in the execution of important public infrastructure projects. He called for close coordination between the Forest and PMGSY departments to resolve inter-departmental issues, accelerate ongoing works and improve road connectivity in Rafiabad and adjoining areas.

KYIV/LONDON – In early July, Ukraine’s military invited a large group of producers to test a new generation of interceptors developed to counter the jet-powered attack drones Russia has used to devastating effect in recent months.
According to two sources familiar with the exercise, it did not go to plan.
Many of the interceptor drones proved difficult to control at speeds sometimes exceeding 400 kilometers per hour. Some crashed into nearby fields and forests, the sources said.

Calgary man accused of threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney
YouTube account linked to suspect had posted a death threat, RCMP say
A Calgary man has been arrested and charged in connection with allegations he threatened to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Jamie Dacosta, 31, faces one count of uttering threats.
According to RCMP, its National Security Enforcement Team (INSET) received information in July that a YouTube account had posted a death threat against the prime minister.
Court records show the date of the alleged offence against Carney was between July 25 and July 26, 2026.
Dacosta facing other charges
On Tuesday, Dacosta appeared in a Calgary courtroom over CCTV from the Calgary Remand Centre where he is being held.
He also has several other, unrelated charges before the courts, including extortion, three counts of uttering threats and wearing a disguise with intent, all connected to allegations involving an automotive business.
Defence lawyer Adriano Iovinelli noted that his client was denied bail last week on all charges by Justice Clarissa Pearce.
Iovinelli asked that the case return Friday to determine whether the Crown’s specialized prosecution unit would take over all of Dacosta’s files.

Investors on the libertarian fringe of the biotech industry are making their dream of wide-ranging access to experimental drugs a reality in Montana.
Last year, they helped draft a state law to expand access to drugs that no regulator has deemed safe and effective. Now, Montana is relying on a privately run board to decide which treatments to offer — raising concerns about conflicts of interest and, in an industry rife with unfounded claims, whether patients will get value for their money.
The company in charge works with biotech firms in a zone off the coast of Honduras that has no drug regulator. Last month, the board authorized its first treatment: Patients seeking a cure for hearing loss will take a daily antihistamine and listen to a Denver company's proprietary sound mix for 60 minutes a day.
The treatment hasn't been cleared by the Food and Drug Administration, and it wasn't reviewed by the state. It was approved by a privately run review board created by a biotech investor named Niklas Anzinger.
Anzinger is a key figure in Próspera, a private city on a Caribbean island, where anti-aging startups can administer experimental treatments without government oversight or evidence that they are safe.
Próspera, whose investors include Peter Thiel and Marc Andreessen, gained attention last year when longevity influencer Bryan Johnson was filmed receiving a $25,000 gene therapy treatment there in the widely watched Netflix documentary, "Don't Die."
Now, players in the booming global longevity industry want to make Montana into a similar medical tourism hub.
More than 40 US states have adopted measures designed to increase patients' access to therapies not approved by the FDA, and two federal programs also allow some patients to access unapproved treatments.
Montana's "right-to-try" law allows a much broader swath of patients, including those who don't have life-threatening illnesses, to access experimental treatments.
Anzinger argues that small biotechs can't compete in a market regulated through large, expensive clinical trials and that they need a system like Montana's to finance and develop therapies that patients would otherwise never get. He says that Montana's system will cut costs and provide a top-tier clinical space for Americans who now travel abroad for everything from psychedelic drugs in Mexico to cutting-edge hair replacement in Turkey and stem cells in Switzerland.
"This is really kind of a potential paradigm change in how we do science instead of top down, more bottom up, but still in a controlled way with oversight and everything," Anzinger said on a recent podcast.
The Montana experiment hinges on whether the Trump administration's FDA chooses to take enforcement action against companies that participate. The biotech industry has reason to hope: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has pledged to increase access to longevity treatments that purport to extend life like stem cell therapies, peptides and chelation. Last year, he said he had traveled to Antigua to receive a non-FDA-approved stem cell treatment for a neurological condition that affects his voice.
The Alliance for Longevity Initiatives, a Virginia-based biotech industry group, helped draft Montana's latest right-to-try legislation, along with Anzinger, who is a member of the alliance, according to the alliance and the bill's sponsor, the Republican state senator Kenneth Bogner.
Anzinger, a 37-year-old German, is the founder of Infinita City Inc., which helped create a hub for biotech companies in Próspera, an autonomous city in Honduras. Anzinger's venture-capital fund, Infinita VC, has invested in longevity startups there, including Minicircle, which sells a gene therapy intended to increase muscle mass, and Unlimited Bio, which is testing a gene therapy for circulation, endurance, and hair growth.
Próspera is part of a movement among bitcoin millionaires, startup founders, and libertarians to create autonomous private cities. Anzinger has been promoting Montana in Próspera. In a co-working space for startups there earlier this year, tables and doors were decked with stickers that said: "SB535. Montana's Longevity Law."
Anzinger said Bogner, the state Senate president pro tempore, invited him to Montana and "basically asked me, 'Well, what else do we need to do? How does the law need to look like to bring you and the biotech companies that you're talking to?'"
"Anzinger took action," Bogner said in an interview. "He came out to Montana to learn how to make Montana a future home." The senator said the state's "longevity law" is a test case that he hopes will "spur changes to the U.S. health care system that, in my opinion, isn't sustainable."
The industry's role in administering the program has raised concerns about ethics and conflicts of interest.
Arthur Caplan, former head of the division of medical ethics at New York University Grossman School of Medicine calls it a "risky endeavor."
"This thing they set up in Montana is really a program to facilitate access to anybody and everybody who wants it, to novel experimental interventions for anything," he said.
He said Montana's program is closer to a prediction market than medical research.
"It's like, you want to gamble? OK, go ahead," he said.
The Montana law barely got through the state legislature last year amid intense opposition. It set parameters for licensed treatment centers where experimental therapies could be administered with the approval of privately run review boards.
Montana now allows people to access therapies that have passed small, Phase 1 clinical trials that establish that the product probably won't kill patients, not that it works. FDA rules limit experimental treatments to people with serious conditions. Montana, by contrast, requires that patients give informed consent and have the money to pay and a provider's recommendation.
Anzinger has set up the only review board so far, the five-member Montana Experimental Treatment Review Board, operated by a private company owned by Infinita City. It charges a $12,500 application fee to companies interested in selling experimental treatments in the state.
The board approved its first treatment last month, giving the green light to Parley Neurotech, a biotech company that seeks to reverse hearing loss with a 30-day treatment of sound therapy, in combination with an off-label, FDA-approved antihistamine. Patients can't yet receive it because Montana hasn't yet issued a license to an experimental treatment center. Two applications for a center are pending completion, the state health department said.
Sam Budoff, Parley's CEO, said sales through the Montana program would help the company fund future clinical trials and allow access for patients who wouldn't qualify for those trials. He declined to share the cost of treatment but said it would reflect out-of-pocket prices in the hearing aid market. He said the law was the "right balance of regulation," and said he felt confident that the Phase 1 requirement and the review board structure would keep out bad actors.
Under Montana's rules, which took effect in July, any experimental review board with five members — including a Montana-licensed physician, a researcher with expertise in clinical outcome data, and an ethicist — can approve treatments.
Unlike similarly structured Institutional Review Boards used by pharmaceutical companies and academic medical centers to approve clinical trials, those in Montana are not supervised by the FDA.
The chair of the review board is longevity scientist Matt Kaeberlein. Kaeberlein also serves on the board of directors of the Alliance for Longevity Initiatives, a volunteer role from which he said he planned to resign soon, citing other commitments.
Dylan Livingston, founder of the alliance, said that his group has no financial stake in any review board or treatment center. Alliance board members are unpaid, and their outside roles are independent of their work on the alliance, he said.
Kaeberlein said the Montana review board "has no financial incentive in whether a determination is yes or no."
"The existing federal right-to-try, while on paper, can work, the reality is many companies are hesitant to use it, and so it's not happening," Kaeberlein said. "Is this the perfect solution? Maybe. Probably not perfect. Is it a possible improvement? I think it is."
Anzinger told Business Insider that none of Infinita VC's portfolio companies have submitted an application to the review board or have indicated plans to do so. The fund has no plans for further investments, he said.
Stephen Martin, who leads US initiatives at Infinita and handles intake for the Montana review board, said the board provided the credentials of its board members to the state. Board members must disclose conflicts every time they review an application, he said. No conflicts have occurred yet, he added. Infinita cannot direct or overrule board decisions, according to the board's rules.
He said other companies could set up review boards as well.
"If you think we are not doing a good job at oversight, come compete against us, do it better, and put us out of business," Martin said.
Montana's law requires some oversight. The board must make a public report of treatment approvals and safety outcomes at least once a year. The state's health department will confirm that each experimental treatment center contracts with a review board that complies with Montana's rules.
In interviews, some members of Infinita's review board said they wanted to open up access to investigational drugs, beyond one-off compassionate use cases. Other board members said they wanted to help bring rigor to a field plagued by risky, unproven longevity treatments. As injectable peptides have soared in popularity, for example, so have peptide injuries.
"The field of longevity is plagued right now by snake oil," said board member Felipe Sierra, a former director of the Division of Aging Biology at the National Institute on Aging, a federal agency. Trials in experimental treatment clinics could help generate data on the efficacy of antiaging therapies, he said. Those trials could be challenging to administer through the FDA's normal clinical trial pipelines, since the agency considers aging a natural process, not a disease with defined clinical endpoints, like cancer or heart disease.
Jamie Justice, who holds a PhD in neurophysiology and the physiology of aging, and is executive director of a competition that awards money for longevity startups, said she joined the review board because she wanted to help Montana's initiative succeed, and for there to be "some adults at the table" when ethically thorny questions arose.
"There are a million ways that this could fail and only a few that could go right," Justice said. "And so I think part of it really is taking our job seriously and thinking about the safety."
Some biotech companies say they are wary of offering experimental treatments in Montana because doing so could spark an enforcement action by the FDA. In June, a group that included Infinita, patient advocates, and biotech companies met with FDA officials to ask for a guarantee that the agency wouldn't take action against them in Montana. They said they have not received a direct answer.
An FDA spokesperson declined to comment.
To approve a treatment, the FDA typically requires three phases of clinical trials, including assessments of efficacy, dosage and adverse events. Under its compassionate-use program, the FDA grants requests for unapproved treatments for patients with severe or life-threatening diseases. Such patients can also bypass the FDA and access unapproved treatments under the federal right-to-try law enacted in Trump's first term, although few drugs have been used through the program and critics have noted that companies don't have an incentive to provide treatments outside of clinical trials. Companies aren't allowed to make a profit under either program.
Infinita and the Alliance for Longevity Initiatives are now pushing for legislation similar to Montana's in New Hampshire.
Without assurance that the FDA will allow companies to participate in Montana's program, some patients say they may still have to look abroad for experimental treatment.
"We don't want to get anybody in trouble…But if the FDA won't support us, what else can we do?" said Kris DeVault, a parent of a 3-year-old son diagnosed with an ultra-rare genetic disease that has no treatment. DeVault wants to go to Montana to receive an experimental treatment for his son, but the manufacturer is wary because of the possibility the FDA could shut it down.
He is now exploring going to Próspera.
Correction: September 15, 2026 — An earlier version of this story misspelled Felipe Sierra's first name.
Update: September 15, 2026 — This story has been updated to clarify that Próspera has no drug regulator.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

Kennedy Center board votes to close after judge again blocks efforts to add Trump name to it
Judge rules no one can add memorials for Trump or anyone else without Congressional approval
The board of the Kennedy Center voted on Tuesday to close over financial issues and a dispute over putting President Donald Trump's name on the iconic performing arts venue, the president confirmed on social media Tuesday.
"The closing will take place immediately," he wrote, "however the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name."
He adds that if the ruling is "a negative one," the renovation will not take place.
Trump's post followed an earlier ruling by a federal judge who blocked the Kennedy Center from returning Trump's name to the performing arts venue, saying it would violate an earlier ruling that his name was illegally added to the building when an inscription on the facade was approved that acknowledged his role in renovating and restoring the building.
Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that, "Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing."
The Trump-aligned board at the Kennedy Center voted in August to inscribe the president's name on the venue's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts restored and renovated by President Donald J. Trump."
And if the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million US, it had voted for another inscription to be added reading: "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."
The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would have also been renamed in Trump's honour, as part of the board's vote.
Months-long saga
Cooper ruled in May that only Congress can approve changes to the Kennedy Center's name. In an emergency hearing on the matter in August, the administration argued it was no longer attempting to rename the building and that the vote was simply a recognition of Trump's effort to secure money for much-needed renovations.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose wife sits on the Kennedy Center board, compared the move to the way hospitals and colleges recognize high-dollar donors.
But a lawyer for U.S. Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, argued the changes amounted to "déja vu" and violated Cooper's earlier ruling.
"The law is extremely clear: The John F. Kennedy Center is named for President Kennedy — and no one else," Beatty said in a statement Tuesday.
"But President Trump is holding the Kennedy Center hostage unless he can put his name on this sacred memorial. The court just rejected this proposal for the second time. This unlawfulness is as breathtaking as it is wrong, and it needs to stop."
Tuesday's ruling is the latest twist in a months-old naming saga that first saw the board installing Trump's name above Kennedy's. After Cooper shot down that move, an elevated tarp was erected, which obscures Trump's name and most of Kennedy's.
A more recent board proposal floated multiple options for getting Trump's name on the grounds, including inscriptions such as, "Renovation and endowment overseen by President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund." Another option: "With gratitude for support from President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."
'Turn down the temperature,' judge asks
The proposed board resolution was submitted to the court by Beatty as part of her effort to prevent the board from proceeding with the planned closure. It flatly states that "without such appropriate recognition," it's unlikely that Trump will financially support what the board says are desperately needed renovations.
Cooper, in his Tuesday ruling, tartly notes "the government plays word games."
In a scheduling hearing Tuesday morning, prior to the release of his ruling, Cooper appealed to lawyers for both sides to find a mediated solution to the fate of the performing arts centre. The centre's board has claimed the building is in desperate physical shape and the institution is desperately close to insolvency.
"Is it possible to turn down the temperature a little bit?" Cooper asked. "I'm not ordering you to do it, but there is a larger public interest here."

Are older MacBooks still worth buying in 2026?
You'll probably want to avoid Intel-powered MacBooks, but Apple Silicon models are solid.
If you're looking to save some money by buying an older, used MacBook, your main question shouldn't be how cheap it is — it should be whether its performance and software will justify the cost. An older MacBook is a solid way to save some money in 2026, especially given the price explosion for anything with RAM and storage. A MacBook with an M-series chip will more than cover basic computing needs and, more importantly, continue to receive macOS releases. Apple's macOS 27 compatibility list includes MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models with Apple silicon dating back to 2020.
Intel-based MacBooks, however, are a different story. Apple started transitioning to its own silicon in 2020 and hasn't sold Intel-based MacBooks since 2021. And the upcoming macOS 27 Golden Gate won't work on Intel Macs at all. For those still rocking MacBooks released prior to M-Series, you can expect additional security patches for the final supported version of macOS and little more.
A barebones M1 MacBook Air is still a solid option for browsing, streaming and most of the basic things you can do on a laptop. You can still find them at a reasonable price, especially renewed or refurbished models from a trustworthy retailer.
Software support and security are more important than age
Software support should be the biggest determining factor in your choice of an older computer. Apple is still releasing security updates for several versions of macOS. As of August 26, Apple's recent updates include macOS Tahoe 26, Sequoia 15 and Sonoma 14, but the macOS 27 Golden Gate release will be the first update restricted to Apple silicon.
With that being said, purchasing a MacBook that's already excluded from the newest version of macOS is risky, unless you plan on keeping things very simple. In time, however, newer apps will gradually require a more recent version. If you're savvy with Linux and can get around the T2 security chip in 2018 to 2020 Intel-based MacBooks, you can get more life out of a pre-M-Series MacBook more so than if you stick to macOS.
For most buyers, the safest option is an Apple Silicon MacBook, so you essentially have a 6-year window of options that include the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models all the way back to 2020. Of course, before buying any used MacBook, always confirm its exact model identifier and check the macOS compatibility list. Also inspect the battery's cycle count and service recommendations. Test out the keyboard, display, ports, camera, Wi-Fi and speakers (assuming you aren't purchasing online).
Buy refurbished when possible and match the model to your needs
Generally speaking, buyers get the most value out of previous-generation models instead of going with the cheapest one on the market. An older MacBook Air with Apple silicon will cover most basic working needs. It will cost less than a new model while retaining enough juice to cover most tasks. For demanding work, a lightly used MacBook Pro with more memory, storage and a stronger M-series processor will save hundreds of dollars while offering the best performance.
It's always a good idea to choose a model that's Apple Certified Refurbished or from a reputable retailer that clearly lists the condition and return period/warranty. According to Apple, its certified refurbished products include a standard one-year warranty and can save up to 15 percent versus new models. Private listings potentially save more, but the risk is obviously higher. When it's practical, meet locally so you can fully inspect the MacBook and verify the serial number and configuration.
In short, an M1 MacBook or newer is worth buying if the price is right. Intel-based models are pushing it and should only be on the list if intended use is limited or short-term.

The Poplar tree in Minecraft is one of the headline additions associated with the Wilderness Bound game drop. These are introduced alongside the Dappled Forest biome, giving the area a distinctly autumnal look filled with red, orange, and yellow foliage. So, if you’re curious about how to find the Minecraft Poplar tree and what wooden blocks you craft, go through this detailed guide below to learn all about it.
Where to Find Poplar Trees in Minecraft
If you’re searching for Poplar Trees, there’s only a single biome where these generate: the Dappled Forest in Minecraft. Now, this information leads to the question: how to find a Dappled Forest in Minecraft?
Well, you need to look out for the surrounding areas of colder biomes in Minecraft. So, make sure that you check the outskirts of the following areas:
- Plains
- Sunflower Plains
- Ice Spikes
- Cherry Groves
- Cold Oceans
- Frozen Peaks
- Windswept Gravely Hills
Since the Dappled Forest biome is designed to naturally fit the transition between two different environments, the above-mentioned regions are the best places to search. Spotting a Dappled Forest biome is the key to finding the Poplar trees in the Minecraft Wilderness Bound update, since these are the only form of timber available here.
How to Find Poplar Saplings in Minecraft
Poplar Saplings are obtained in two ways: firstly, by breaking Poplar leaves, and secondly, from the Wandering Traders in Minecraft. Naturally, the first way doesn’t cost you anything.
However, you need to offer 5x Emeralds to the Wandering Trader to receive a Poplar Sapling in return. Since the Trader only has a handful of items in its stock at a time, you might need to keep returning to get the item.
How to Use a Poplar Sapling to Grow a Poplar Tree
Now, this is where the tree’s unusual mechanic is important to understand. There isn’t a separate Poplar sapling that can grow into a specific red, orange, or yellow Poplar tree.
Instead, Poplar trees use a single sapling type that can randomly produce any of the three tree variants when grown. You can definitely speed up tree growth by using Bone Meal in Minecraft. However, note that you might get red in one attempt, yellow in another, or orange the third time.
While a Poplar Sapling grows into a tree, it also has a small chance of growing a Minecraft Shelf Mushroom on its trunk.
Minecraft Poplar Tree Wood Uses
One of the biggest attractions of the Poplar trees is that all three variants have retained the same wood color. The Poplar wood has a neutral, muted, grayish appearance that makes it quite different from the available wood types. It can pair up well with the Pale Oak wood in Minecraft and act as a neutral background material.
So, here are all the Poplar wood sets introduced in the Minecraft 26.3 update:
- Stripped Poplar Log: Interact with the Poplar logs using an axe.

- Stripped Poplar Wood: Use an axe on the Poplar wood.

- Poplar Hanging Sign: Fill two rows with stripped Poplar Logs and put two chains on top of them.
- Poplar Button: Place one Poplar plank in the crafting UI to get a button
- Pressure Plate: Put two Poplar wood beside each other to get this item.
- Poplar Boat: Craft it using 5 Poplar wood planks in a U-shape
- Poplar Boat With a Chest: Combine a Poplar boat with a regular chest.
Best Poplar Tree Seeds in Minecraft

- -178173658087667925: For a more traditional survival challenge, this seed is a good fit because you can find a little island with a small patch of Dappled Forest providing the only set of Poplar trees.

An investigation is underway into reports that a Russian oligarch paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the wedding celebrations of President Donald Trump's son earlier this year.
Umar Kremlev, a Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association, paid for two lavish parties for Donald Jr and his wife, Bettina, in the Bahamas in May.
What's next?
Robert Garcia, the senior Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, is expected to lead a deeper investigation if his party wins a majority in the US House of Representatives in November's midterm elections.
Democrats in the US Congress have launched an investigation into reports that a Russian oligarch paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the wedding celebrations of President Donald Trump's son earlier this year.
The Democrats' move comes on the heels of an article revealing that the wedding festivities of Donald Trump Jr were funded by a wealthy Russian businessman with strong ties to President Vladimir Putin and the Russian government.
ProPublica reported that Umar Kremlev, a wealthy Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association (IBA), paid for lavish wedding festivities in the Bahamas in May.
"Why is a Russian oligarch and friend of Vladimir Putin financially supporting the president's son?" US representative Robert Garcia wrote in a social media post on Tuesday, local time.
"What does Umar Kremlev expect in return for funding this three-day wedding in the Bahamas?"
Mr Garcia is the senior Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
He is expected to chair the panel if Democrats win a majority in the House of Representatives in November's midterm elections.
A representative for Mr Trump Jr declined to comment.
His wife, Bettina Trump, said in an Instagram post on Monday, local time, Mr Kremlev was a friend who had extended an "extraordinarily generous wedding gift," stressing that Mr Kremlev had paid for two after-parties, not the wedding itself.
Mr Kremlev and the IBA did not respond to requests for comment on Tuesday, local time.
He added that the wedding controversy was "not a big deal!"
US Attorney-General Todd Blanche also brushed aside the potential conflict of interest when asked about it, saying he would not investigate.

he said.

Flash floods at the Nepal-Tibet border have killed at least 543 people and more than 1,500 are missing. Hundreds were foreigners in the area to work, take guided treks or make pilgrimages.
Thousands have been rescued, with some of the injured taken to hospitals in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. The number of missing may vary because of progress in the ongoing rescue efforts and differences in how data has been collected and verified among agencies.
Here is how different countries have been affected.
Nepal
Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday the death toll in that country had risen to 538, with 977 people missing. The authority said 3,253 people had been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 of the injured were taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.
Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Centre as saying on Thursday that the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 personnel from the army and police, 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.
China
State media reported on Friday that at least five people had died and 558 were missing in Gyirong County, Tibet. The state broadcaster CCTV reported that 260 of the 558 missing people were foreigners. In addition, nearly 100 Chinese citizens were missing on the Nepal side, China’s foreign ministry said.
India
India’s foreign ministry said 288 Indian nationals remained uncontactable, including 73 people who were working on a power project. Nepali officials said many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.
US
The US state department said 90 of its citizens were unaccounted for in China and Nepal, but that it was not aware of any US deaths. Three Americans have been rescued.
Malaysia
Officials said 51 Malaysians were missing.
Ukraine
Ukraine’s foreign ministry said 55 Ukrainians were missing. The number includes two tourist groups, of 47 and seven people respectively, in addition to one Ukrainian woman travelling with a foreign tour group.
Australia
The Australian government said 39 Australians were missing.
Britain
Officials said 33 of the missing were from Britain.
Canada
The Nepal tourism board (NTB) said 25 of the missing were from Canada.
South Korea
South Korean government officials said nine citizens working on the construction of a hydropower plant in Nepal were missing.
Singapore
Eight Singaporeans were missing, according to the NTB.
Germany
The NTB said eight tourists from Germany were missing.
Russia
The Russian embassy in Nepal said eight of its citizens were missing.
South Africa
The NTB said six South Africans were missing.
Latvia
The NTB said six tourists from Latvia were missing.
Japan
Japanese media said five Japanese tourists were missing, made up of a couple and their children.
New Zealand
Five people from New Zealand were missing, the NTB said.
France
The NTB said four French citizens were missing.
Belgium
The NTB said three people from Belgium were missing.
Spain
The NTB said three visitors from Spain were missing.
Others
The NTB said two people each from Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland and the Netherlands were missing. It said 10 others – one each from Belarus, Finland, Hungary, Israel, Lithuania, the Philippines, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Serbia and Sweden – were also missing.

For some people, particularly youngsters, an AI chatbot is becoming the first place they turn to when they are distressed. It has its advantages: it is available at any hour, does not appear to judge them and can respond instantly. But when conversations involve thoughts of suicide, the limits of this interaction become consequential. Every conversation with an AI chatbot may not be harmful, but an apparently empathetic response could reinforce hopelessness, prolong rumination, or delay professional help in some people already at risk, say experts.
What the evidence shows
AI use for mental health support is now common. A U.S. survey of 1,009 people aged 12 to 21, published in JAMA Pediatrics found that 19.2% had used AI chatbots for mental health advice in 2025. Nearly 43% of these users did so at least monthly, while 5.8% used them daily or almost daily. Nearly two-thirds had not told anyone about this.
Another analysis of more than 620,000 publicly available ChatGPT conversations found that 4.9% could be classified broadly as involving mental health, although only 0.21% met a stricter definition involving an identifiable person explicitly seeking mental health help.
Studies have also found that chatbots are generally better at recognising very low- and very high-risk scenarios, but struggle to distinguish between intermediate levels of suicide risk. This is particularly concerning for psychiatrists, as suicidal distress is rarely expressed in a single, explicit statement and often emerges through a combination of subtle or changing cues.
When reassurance becomes a loop
“Suicidal distress is not always direct; people may hint, use humour or gradually disclose their thoughts,” said Mithun Prasad, consultant, psychiatry, SIMS Hospital, Chennai. Keyword recognition alone, he said, is therefore inadequate; the context and consistency of a conversation matter.
Sabaresh Pandiyan, consultant, psychiatry, Rela Hospital, Chennai, pointed to another issue: the ‘internal loop’, particularly among younger users, who may derive comfort from the empathetic part of an AI response, while ignoring advice to seek professional help. Repeated reassurance can also make suicidal thinking seem less urgent. “Talking about suicide or venting about suicide is not the problem, reinforcing hopelessness is,” he said.
Nithya M., consultant psychiatrist, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, Vanagaram, Chennai, emphasised that AI could amplify existing distress, prolong rumination or substitute validation for intervention.
In clinical practice, psychiatrists see patients use AI to discuss relationships, workplace problems and other personal concerns before speaking to family or friends. Dr. Pandiyan said around 60-70% of patients in his setting discuss such matters with AI first. For some, this may help them recognise a problem and seek care earlier. Others may spend months trying to manage difficulties themselves before consulting a professional.
Dr. Nithya said warning signs can include patients quoting AI responses verbatim, withdrawing from human confidants, resisting professional help or developing a rigid view of themselves or their relationships based on chatbot responses.
Not a substitute for care
There may be limited situations in which patients use AI alongside clinical care. Dr. Prasad said some patients use chatbots between appointments to record medication effects or organise their thoughts, and later bring a summary to their psychiatrist. This can provide the clinician with information about what happened between consultations.
But such use does not make AI a substitute for psychiatric assessment. A chatbot does not have access to a person’s psychiatric history, personality, psychological defences, adverse life experiences, protective factors or current mental state. It may validate an emotion without recognising when urgent assessment is needed. This is particularly concerning when a person has psychosis, mania or distorted beliefs.
Need for safety checks
Psychiatrists call for mandatory safety audits, independent clinical assessments and clearer liability frameworks. Companies should be required to investigate and report serious safety incidents. . Public education should also explain where AI is and is not appropriate.
Experts add that any response must also address the stigma that prevents people from seeking mental healthcare. Families and communities need to create safer spaces for people to talk about distress and seek help.
When a person is in a mental health crisis, experts said, the priority should remain timely human assessment and support. AI cannot take the place of that care.

The Bengaluru City Police have launched ‘Project Khushi’, a structured health and wellness programme aimed at supporting the long-term physical and mental well-being of police personnel, Home Minister Priyank Kharge said on Tuesday.
The programme will initially be implemented in the Electronics City police division, covering around 600 police personnel. Each batch will undergo a three-month programme comprising health check-ups, expert-led guidance sessions, and digital engagement activities.
The initiative will focus on preventive healthcare, nutrition, physical activity, quality sleep, and stress management, besides other lifestyle factors crucial for the long-term well-being of police personnel.
Pilot programme shows encouraging results
According to the Home Minister, an earlier pilot programme conducted as part of Project Khushi produced encouraging results. Around 61% of participants recorded a reduction in blood sugar levels, while 70% corrected Vitamin B12 deficiencies. In addition, 59% of participants reduced their body weight.
Mr. Kharge said that the results demonstrate that sustained and scientifically designed health interventions can have a positive impact on the well-being of police personnel.
Partnership with health and corporate organisations
“Our police personnel work every day in challenging and stressful conditions to ensure the safety of our communities. It is essential to pay continuous attention to their health. Healthy police personnel are the backbone of an effective and resilient policing system,” Mr Kharge said.
He added that equal importance must be given to mental well-being, a healthy lifestyle, and stress management, along with physical health.

Judge blocks DHS from acting against a man over a harsh email to an ICE official
A Tuesday court ruling means David Streever of Rochester, New York no longer has to worry that federal officers may threaten him over a harsh email he sent to the former acting director of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this year.
Streever filed a lawsuit in July arguing ICE agents had violated his First Amendment rights when they tried to track him down at his home, an airport and a hotel to confront him about the email and serve him with a warning notice that said he may have violated the law.
Streever's email compared ICE's former acting director, Todd Lyons, to a Nazi, called him a "monstrous human being" and predicted he would be tormented by his own conscience. Streever told NPR he sent the email after federal immigration officers fatally shot two observers in Minneapolis in January.
The warning notice agents left at Streever's home said "YOU MAY BE IN VIOLATION OF FEDERAL LAW" and lists federal laws that make it a crime to threaten federal officials. "Receipt of this Notice will be taken into consideration, should you continue to be involved in any criminal activities described above," reads the bottom of the form.
Streever, who is represented by the nonprofit free speech group, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), argued the federal agents' actions violated the First Amendment and caused him to self-censor his views.
"Mr. Streever's injury is the loss of his freedom to engage in political speech now because the threat of such an investigation or prosecution looms over him like the sword of Damocles, and he is forced to self-censor under that threat," Contreras wrote in his ruling.
He wrote that because it was likely the federal government had already infringed on Streever's First Amendment rights, he was issuing a preliminary injunction while the case continued so that Streever could continue to speak freely.
The court order blocks DHS and ICE from, "taking further steps in reliance on the Warning Notice…and from issuing any substantially similar threats to [Streever] aimed at his protected expression during the course of this matter."
In a statement, Streever said, "I'm deeply relieved that the court affirmed what I knew all along: that I am permitted to speak my conscience in the United States of America, including when I criticize government officials."
He added, "While I wish this ordeal hadn't happened, hopefully this incident will serve as a reminder that the First Amendment protects us all."
DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In court filings, DHS defended its investigation of Streever by citing an increase in threats of violence against public officials. The federal government had argued Streever's case should be dismissed and had said the investigation into Streever was closed in late June, before he filed his lawsuit.
The federal government's filing did not assert that Streever's email was a violent threat that could be prosecuted.
In his ruling, Contreras asked the government to turn over the report that closed its investigation of Streever.
"ICE knowingly pursued an American citizen for criticizing his government — speech that is at the heart of the First Amendment," said FIRE Senior Attorney Adam Steinbaugh. "Ominous letters warning people their speech might land them in prison are meant to coerce people into silence, and that's not how the First Amendment works."

Bangladesh national caught smuggling gold from Saudi inside undergarments at Delhi airport
Officials said the passenger landed at Delhi Airport's Terminal 3 from Jeddah and was caught trying to smuggle gold.
A Bangladeshi national was caught at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport on Monday. The passenger, as per customs officials, was caught smuggling gold from Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.
In an official statement, officials said the passenger landed at Delhi Airport's Terminal 3 after his flight landed from Jeddah. The passenger was then scheduled to board a flight for Dhaka, but was intercepted.
Officials added that a total of 1,596 grams of gold was found on the passenger, which was smuggled and concealed in his undergarments.
"The passenger was intercepted by the Central Industrial Security Force (Ministry of Home Affairs), IGI Airport, New Delhi-37, in the international transit area. While intensive checking by central industrial security force officers, three brownish-white, oval-shaped capsules, suspected to contain gold in chemical paste form, weighing 1596 grams approx. (including packing material) was recovered from the passenger, who had concealed it inside his undergarment," the official statement added.
Customs officials added that the passenger admitted to smuggling the gold from Jeddah to Delhi. The Bangladeshi national added that he had been asked to drop off the gold with someone in the transit area at Delhi airport.

A Diagnosis for Social Conflict That Gets Lost Along the Way
A new book suggests that arguing isn’t about winning but seems preoccupied with it anyway.
Weddings, famously, create conflict. Before I got married, my parents and I fought over the guest list. A friend of mine struggled with adding some of her husband’s Protestant traditions to their otherwise Jewish ceremony. Another friend had to decode, and then manage, complicated tensions among her future aunts- and uncles-in-law.
All of these issues got resolved, and according to the conflict-resolution facilitator Priya Parker, the process of figuring them out made our weddings more successful expressions of our values. Parker explored the group creation of meaning in her 2018 best seller, The Art of Gathering. In her new book, The Art of Fighting, she writes that arguments are crucial to a group’s ability to do just that. What’s more, in American society—which Parker describes as both conflict averse and low on big rituals—high-stakes events such as weddings are among the “last remaining collective mechanisms to help us have the fights we need to have to figure out who we are now.”
The Art of Fighting is predicated on Parker’s conviction that without confrontation, no group can work well. “Fighting,” she writes in her prologue, “is not the death of community. It is its lifeblood.” Parker considers Americans far too willing to focus on themselves rather than their communities, in large part due to a widespread fear of confrontation. A lot of loneliness, in her view, originates from the all-too-common decision to exit a challenging situation instead of dealing with its simmering disagreements. It’s a smart diagnosis, one that’s as relevant to small-bore social scenarios as it is to interactions within religious organizations, schools, and workplaces. The choice to hide from conflict is, to Parker, in many situations, a choice to be alone.
Parker’s idea that conflict is inherently a social good is intriguing and counterintuitive. But The Art of Fighting is not nearly as communitarian a book as its setup would suggest. Although its more abstract passages describe healthy confrontation as helpful and worthy, its examples tell another story. Parker presents The Art of Fighting as a “group-help book” but tends to take a side in her case studies—and in most instances, her side wins.
Her own life serves as illustration, too, and often provides the book’s most revealing moments. By way of arguing that everyone needs to get comfortable with disagreement, she mentions a clash she and her father had after the latter got upset that Parker hadn’t invited her stepbrother’s wife to her baby shower. As Parker relates it, their discussion of her reasoning—she and her stepsister-in-law just aren’t close—ends not with compromise or reconciliation but with the blunt lines: “He wasn’t getting it. And that was OK.” Such a one-sided resolution suggests a disinterest in compromise and an interpretation of fighting as an individualistic act. Facing conflict may very well be a social good—I believe it is—but her book more often seems to urge readers to wade into arguments to get what they want.
The Art of Fighting is full of stories of conflict. Some appear only once, and some are threaded throughout the book. The quarreling groups that Parker features, many of which she worked with in her role as a facilitator, range in size from an extended family to a percussion ensemble to a large architecture firm. Parker uses every case to ask a variation of her central question: “How do you fight with those to whom you want to belong?”
In the book’s most moving example, she writes about a church that, in the mid-1990s, deliberated about and then voted on whether it would perform and recognize gay marriages. Its pastor, Martin Copenhaver, understood that they couldn’t make a decision that might lead to division if his church were to survive. “In the political arena,” he tells Parker, “if you win by one vote, you win. In this arena, you win by one vote, you don’t win.”
Hoping to forge meaningful consensus, he hosted four meetings to discuss the subject; only those who attended were allowed to vote. After the election—the church decided, not unanimously but with “no great division,” to allow gay marriage—he asked everyone to reconcile in person with someone who voted differently. In essence, Copenhaver organized the entire conflict to prioritize congregants’ investment in the church, not to lead them toward a certain outcome.
I wanted to learn more about how other sorts of disputes, especially less orchestrated ones, might bolster a sense of community. But Parker is surprisingly blurry about the variety of incentives for confronting or ignoring tension that exist in one setting or another. Some strategies for managing conflict—waiting to engage until no one has steam pouring from their ears; ensuring that the arguing parties’ grievances and goals are clear; creating the right conditions for a tough conversation—may apply to all kinds of groups.
But the book doesn’t do enough to acknowledge that different sorts of conflicts have different stakes. Starting a fight for the good of the group may be wise among relatives but foolish if doing so could also mean losing your job. And a values-based argument may not be worthwhile in a corporate context where the overall goal is to maximize profit. One of Parker’s recurring examples is a debate that took place within a law firm about whether the TV in its common space should show World Cup games played in Qatar. It begins with an intern objecting, on Slack, to the “human rights abuses of workers in the lead up to the World Cup and the horrific status of rights for LGBTQ people and women in Qatar.” The managing partners invited employees to what Parker characterizes as a too-wide conversation about the World Cup. It was, she writes, “the wrong fight with the wrong assemblage of people in the wrong room.”
Parker uses this argument to underscore good and bad ways to navigate conflicts, especially ones that arise online—certainly an important issue in our screen-heavy times. But missing from this analysis is any real engagement on Parker’s part with the substance of the conflict itself. Readers never learn how the issue was resolved: Did the World Cup get shown or not? Was there ever a meaningful discussion about the objections the intern had raised? The book uses this example to describe strategies for handling internal dissent, focusing on how the managing partners could best have reestablished peace among their employees. It becomes a story about conflict management rather than conflict as a potential social good.
Some of Parker’s personal anecdotes more vividly illustrate her not-quite-communitarian approach to fighting. In one, she describes enrolling her children and their cousin in a small soccer camp one summer. Initially, the kids report hating camp and getting bullied by their counselors. Parker speaks with the camp director, who talks with his employees and establishes that Parker’s children and niece, who started on the eighth week of camp, are unfamiliar with both the established cohort’s “teasing culture” and the basic rules of soccer. Parker suggests that the camp’s coaches “give our kids a Week One experience, orient them, do the things you did with all the other kids when they were new.” They comply, and the camp—which Parker needs for child care—works out.
Parker’s reaction to the situation is entirely reasonable; what parent wouldn’t try to help a kid who’s being picked on, or scramble to rescue a child-care setup that seems about to fail? It is not, however, an illustration of confrontation as community service. She shows herself engaging in conflict to get her kids special treatment rather than nudging the kids to advocate for themselves or asking how the camp might better help them settle in despite their latecomer status. Another way to put this is that no compromise is on offer here, and we get no sense of a group working together. Parker, as the customer, gets to be right.
Throughout The Art of Fighting, individuals prevail in this way. A woman named Rebekah, exhausted by attending her family’s Passover seders—too much cooking, too much disruption to routine, too much airtime for her right-wing uncle—gives them up. But Parker never writes about what Rebekah’s parents, siblings, or children might lose when she and her nuclear family stop coming, or how her continued, if conflicted, attendance might have led her relatives to create more sustainable traditions. Just as some therapists prioritize clients over the other people in their lives, Parker prioritizes the subjects of her anecdotes over those with whom they fight.
What these stories add up to, ultimately, is a much less surprising take on conflict than the book tries to lay out. Parker provides a useful guide to having arguments in good faith without hurting anyone’s feelings unnecessarily or creating a corporate crisis. But arguments can be so much more than that. Alone in the book, the story of Copenhaver’s church demonstrates that even enduring and loaded disagreements can, if handled with enough care and respect, strengthen the bonds between parties—in other words, they can be productive, not just nondestructive. Many readers will have experienced this in intimate relationships. I, for one, have grown closer to some friends after air-clearing arguments and have drifted from others who weren’t willing or able to talk through issues when they arose.
But as Parker points out, public life in the United States isn’t set up for healthy conflict. Meaningful group fights are rare experiences. Aside from my wedding planning, I haven’t been part of one. I believe, in theory, that such a dispute could be transformational for both a community and its individual members. But in order for Parker’s book to have taught me how to navigate one, she would have had to truly let go of the old idea that the reason to fight is to win.
