AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for Congress to act
- Published
When President Donald Trump responded to mounting calls for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence (AI) on Monday, he was unequivocal.
"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," he wrote on social media. He earlier argued that "the only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs" is a "strong and smart" president.
Trump's view, unsurprisingly, is not shared by senior Democrats in Congress. It is also opposed by leading figures in the AI sector, who have in recent days issued stark safety warnings and made the case for government regulation.
In the US, however, new safety legislation on AI is unlikely anytime soon.
Any bill would have to pass in both the House of Representatives and the Senate to become law. Trump's staunch opposition to new guardrails on AI means the Republican Party, which has a majority in both chambers, is unlikely to break from him and back restrictions or government controls.
And even if they did, whatever bill is passed would most likely require the president's signature to take effect. Trump's dismissal of the need for regulations on Monday effectively hit pause on any hope for executive action.
- AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder tells BBC 
  - Published7 hours ago
- UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI 
  - Published3 days ago
Beyond this, a more immediate obstacle to any movement in Congress is the clock.
The House is set to enter recess at the end of the week until after the midterm elections in early November. Some leading Democrats are calling for that recess to be delayed until AI safeguards can be passed in the chamber.
"Congress should not leave town until something is done decisively to protect the safety and the wellbeing of the American people," Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters on Monday.
A group of House Democrats calling for Congress to be given more time to debate the issue have also written a letter to Republican Speaker Mike Johnson, who would ultimately decide on delaying the recess.
"Reasonable minds may disagree about precisely how Congress should regulate this rapidly evolving technology," the group said. "We cannot disagree about the imperative for Congress to act."
Over the weekend, Republican congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna suggested on X that "Congress SHOULD convene a special session" on the issue.
But it is highly unlikely the recess will be delayed or a special session convened in the coming days. Speaker Johnson, who on Monday faced a barrage of questions about AI from reporters in the halls of Congress, gave no sign he intended to move quickly this week.
When asked if the House would take action on AI concerns before breaking for the midterms, he replied: "This is a very complex issue."
He said Trump would hold a meeting at the White House soon with AI executives to discuss "the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety and what role, if any, the government has to play in that".
"We want to emphasise the necessity of [AI companies] providing safe products and self-regulating," Johnson said, before adding: "There is also a role potentially for Congress to play."
What that role could look like is unclear - and is a contested question among those in Congress.
No consensus and competing bills
While Democrats are pushing for more time to address AI safety, they are themselves divided on how best to regulate AI.
Even if the party were to win control of both chambers of Congress in November's elections, there are no guarantees of swift action as it would have to unite behind one proposal.
And there are numerous legislative proposals already on Capitol Hill that are designed to address AI safety, ranging from independent reviews, to a federal "kill switch", to a total moratorium on data centres proposed by Senator Bernie Sanders.
These diverging proposals point to a lack of consensus in Congress - but also an urgency among some lawmakers to take action.
Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune and his Democratic colleague Amy Klobuchar are working on a bill that would force some AI companies to submit to federal oversight.
"You don't want to stifle innovation," Thune said on Monday, "but I think you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated."
Democratic congresswoman Lori Trahan, meanwhile, has spent months working on a different bipartisan proposal in the House that would give the government the power to halt the use of an AI model if officials find there is an "imminent catastrophic risk".
"The federal government needs to put guardrails in place," she told the BBC, warning that the technology would eventually impact every aspect of society. "I don't think we have any more time to wait. This is all hands on deck."
Trahan has worked on her proposed legislation, the Frontier Act, jointly with Republican Jay Obernolte and, among other things, it would require independent audits of AI research labs.
But Trahan recognised that any movement this week was unlikely.
Calls for self-regulation
Some leading Republicans, including Speaker Johnson, have often referred to "self-regulation" when discussing government action and called on the companies to take responsibility for AI safety.
One of Trump's top AI advisers, David Sacks, told the BBC's US partner CBS News on Monday that some of the existential warnings by insiders had been overblown. "I think this is becoming a panic," he said.
"First and foremost, it is on them to make their products safe," Sacks said. "They should tell us how they should do that. If they can't do that, they should step aside for people who can do that."
"Why are you acting like this is something that you can't control?" he said, referring to Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei, who has called for a slowdown in development. "If you can't control it, then don't do it."
Some experts share the view that, in the short-term at least, it is up to the AI companies to regulate themselves responsibly.
"You might want an act of Congress, and I would love a congressionally mandated regime that requires safety and testing and bias testing," said Asad Ramzanali, the director of AI & Technology Policy at Vanderbilt University.
"But absent that action, the companies have autonomy."
Others have expressed scepticism at the recent flurry of warnings by AI staffers.
Trevor Traina, a tech executive who was a diplomat during Trump's first term, said: "I don't think the typical citizen has encountered anything scary or really problematic with AI."
"We're relying on the tweets of a half-dozen people who are all vying for perceived supremacy," he said. "The cynic in me thinks, 'Are they are really concerned, or are they trying to prove which model is the most awesome?'"
Alexandra Reeve Givens, who previously worked in government and now leads the US non-profit the Center for Democracy and Technology, said she did not think meaningful federal AI regulation would pass in the foreseeable future.
While the Trump administration has set up an entirely voluntary framework for AI companies to submit their models and tools for government assessment, Givens noted that the framework itself remains a secret.
"There's no clear standard to make sure that the approach is even grounded in the rule of law," she said.
Appeals from various groups to release the framework have so far gone ignored.
The White House approach, combined with a lack of political will and consensus, makes passing laws around AI difficult.
"There is no question that federal legislation is challenging in this climate, but Congress also has to grapple with which of the many types of AI risk need to be addressed," Givens said.
"It's not that AI is ungovernable, it's that each risk needs a tailored approach."

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s (WHO) South-East Asia Region head and daughter of ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, resigned on Wednesday (September 10, 2026) following fraud investigations by the U.N. agency and Bangladeshi authorities, according to sources.
The WHO placed Ms. Wazed, who took office in early 2024 for a five-year term, on unpaid administrative leave late last year. She was first sent on leave in July 2025, in a move that followed Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filing cases for fraud, forgery, and misuse of power against.
The WHO accused Ms. Wazed of “committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China” and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a separate letter from her lawyers to the WHO on July 3, 2026. She has denied the allegations.
The WHO also alleged she had illegally acquired a plot of land in Bangladesh, according to her resignation letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
What Saima Wazed said in her reisgnation letter
Ms. Wazed said she acquired the land before she joined the WHO and was entitled to it under a Bangladeshi law that covered the families of the country’s independence leader, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, osuted PM Hasina’s father. “I was elected to the position of Regional Director in order to serve the countries in my region, which I had sincerely done,” Ms. Wazed said in her resignation letter to Mr. Tedros sent late on Wednesday (September 10, 2026).
“Since you continue to prevent me from effectively carrying out my duties, I have lost all trust and confidence in your leadership of WHO,” she wrote. “Moreover, after nearly one year without any remuneration following your decision to place me on unpaid leave, my financial situation has become untenable. In these circumstances, I am choosing to step aside.” She declined to comment further.
Saima Wazed | Rise of the daughter
The role of WHO regional head
In the role of South-East Asia regional director, Ms. Wazed was mandated to direct international health work in 11 countries, an area with a population of over two billion people. She is a licensed school psychologist, nationally certified in the U.S.
Ms. Wazed’s appointment as Regional Director had also been under the scanner, with charges of having used her mother’s influence during the campaign, and of providing false information on her academic record during in her candidature for the post, allegedly violating Section 468 of the Bangladesh Penal Code (forgery for the purpose of cheating), and Section 471 (forging a document).
Regional directors are among the world’s most influential health policy officials, with their duties including responses to outbreaks and emergencies and adapting WHO policies to local conditions. They are elected every five years by member states, which include Bangladesh and India in the South-East Asia region.
Two sources told Reuters earlier that the U.N. agency was planning to formally remove Wazed. One of them said the WHO would announce nominations for the role on October 12, vet applications in December and hold elections on January 24. The sources declined to be named given the sensitivity of the matter.

A maiden ODI century by Matt Renshaw and Nathan Ellis’ five-wicket haul powered Australia to a 59-run win over Zimbabwe at the Harare Sports Club on Tuesday.
With the win, the Mitchell Marsh-led side took a 1-0 lead in the three-match ODI series, with the second ODI scheduled to take place on Friday at the same venue.
Batting first, Australia managed to score 294/8, led by Renshaw’s century (109 off 94 balls) and a half-century from Cooper Connolly (51 off 46 balls).
For the host, Newham Nyamhuri impressed with a five-wicket haul (5/62), while Brad Evans chipped in with two wickets (2/51).
In the chase, Zimbabwe was rocked early as it lost opener Ben Curran for a duck. The Sikandar Raza led-side lost three more wickets in relatively quick succession, with Ellis contributing for two of the victims.
Then, Zimbabwe staged a brief resistance as Craig Ervine (59 off 60 balls) and Raza (57 off 76 balls) albeit well below the asking rate.
Once Ervine and Raza fell, the Australian bowling unit dismissed the rest of the batting lineup without wasting much time to secure a comfortable victory.
Renshaw, who scored his first international ton in ten years, was adjudged the player of the match.
“I just tried to rebuild the innings. We lost a few wickets (after) the boys started really well,” the opener said after the match.
“I did not feel under any scoring pressure. It was really nice. Pitch was nice. Ten years between international hundreds was not something I was expecting.”

Treasury secretary backs Trump’s $5,000 checks but refuses to say how the country will pay for it
Trump has faced bribery accusations after promising Americans $5,000 if voters help Republicans keep control of Congress during the midterm elections
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has backed the $5,000 checks Donald Trump wants to give Americans after the midterm elections, but has refused to say how the country would pay for them.
During the Republican convention held in Dallas last week to get out the vote for GOP candidates in the midterms, the president promised that his administration would pay a “Trump Dividend” to each American adult if voters help Republicans keep control of Congress.
“So if the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” Trump said in his keynote speech Wednesday.
The idea sparked backlash, with critics accusing the president of bribery and others questioning where the money would come from. And Bessent did little to quell skeptics' concerns during a hearing before the House Financial Services Committee Tuesday.
When asked by Representative Juan Vargas, a California Democrat, if the $5,000 checks would increase the nation‘s $40 trillion debt, Bessent said, “I believe there are ways to do it without increasing the debt.”
Vargas then asked Bessent to elaborate, but Bessent just said the Treasury Department is in the process of figuring out how to pay for the checks without increasing the national debt.
“I’m not ready to discuss it at present, but at Treasury we’ve been working on it for quite a while,” Bessent said.
The Independent has reached out to the Treasury Department for comment.
Trump quickly said after he first announced the $5,000 checks that he didn’t think he needed approval from Congress, known for having the power of the purse.
“I think they will do it if we needed it, but we think not,” Trump told CBS News.
When asked about the “Trump Dividend” on Meet the Press Sunday, House Speaker Mike Johnson said he’d “work with the president hand in hand” on the matter but did not commit to being able to deliver on the checks.
The Independent’s Eric Garcia asked Johnson at a press conference Tuesday, “How is communism any different from what President Trump is doing getting equity stakes in tech and promising $5,000 checks to Americans and having equity in steel?”
Johnson and other Republicans have baselessly accused the Democratic Party of embracing communist candidates in the midterms.
Johnson sidestepped Garcia’s question, telling reporters that the president “comes up with creative ideas all the time” and that Republicans in Congress are "processing" the “Trump Dividend” proposal.
“What he is trying to articulate…if you want more money in your pockets, you gotta keep Republicans in charge,” Johnson said. “We have done that.”
But a majority of Americans don’t think Trump is doing a good job on the economy as they struggle to pay for everyday necessities like groceries and gas, partly due to the president’s war in Iran driving up energy costs.
Just 34 percent of Americans approve of the way Trump is handling the economy, compared to 66 percent who disapprove, according to a new CBS News poll.

LeBron the star as Angola aims to cash in on E1 racing
- Published
It is difficult to imagine an electric powerboat racing series capturing the attention of an Angolan audience for whom football and basketball is king, but the presence of NBA royalty LeBron James certainly helped.
The 41-year-old was among the A-listers in Luanda as the E1 World Championship rolled into southern Africa for the first time at the weekend, having made its debut on the continent last year in Lagos, Nigeria.
"It's not a short trip, but he [LeBron] is here because he believes in what we're doing," E1 chief executive Jamie Copas told BBC Sport Africa in the Angolan capital.
"You can't underestimate the value of it. They [the celebrity owners] come with huge followings."
James, like fellow sport stars Rafa Nadal, Tom Brady, Didier Drogba and Virat Kohli and actor Will Smith, is an E1 team owner after buying into the series.
Similar to Formula E on land, it aims to blend sport with strong messaging around sustainability and green technology.
James said Angola had made his first trip to the country "super welcoming" after visiting the National Museum of Slavery.
"Obviously there is a lot of history here," the new signing for the Philadelphia 76ers told local media.
"A lot of history that not only is here in the country but also [crosses] over to America."
Angola's men are reigning African basketball champions, securing a record-extending 12th continental title on home soil last year, and unsurprisingly spectators of the E1 racing at the Clube Naval de Luanda clamoured for a glimpse of one of basketball's biggest icons.
Journalist Omar Prata, covering the race for the Jornal de Angola, admitted that E1 was not on his radar until Hollywood star Smith, whose Westbrook Racing team is sponsored by Visit Angola, announced in March that a deal had been agreed to race in Luanda for the next three years.
"I see the potential it could bring to project the city at a time when the government is trying to work on tourism," Prata said.
"And of course it means a lot to have LeBron James here. Angolans have seen him on television, they try to emulate him on the street courts, they have his posters."
Boosting Angola long-term
The star power of E1's owners is helping to bring eyeballs to what is a traditionally niche sport where powerboat pilots skim and bounce around tight courses at speeds close to 100kmph.
Yet, on a calendar that features traditional celebrity haunts like Miami, Monaco and Lake Como, Luanda's name seems an outlier.
Among those taking in the action from the fanzone was local resident Edson Cabeta.
"It is the first time I have seen anything like this," he said.
"Today it is foreigners doing this; tomorrow, perhaps we could have an Angolan team."
The aspiration is that hosting an E1 race will help Angola boost visitor numbers, with minister for tourism Marcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel saying enhanced foreign awareness of the country is the "first step" in a long-term plan.
"Our ambition is not simply to make Angola famous," Daniel told the BBC.
"It is to make Angola more desirable to visit, invest in and do business in."
Angola has not been afraid to speculate to accumulate in the past, bringing Lionel Messi's Argentina side to Luanda for a football friendly last November to celebrate 50 years of the nation's independence.
Daniel said it would be "premature" to assess the economic impact of this weekend's race in Luanda.
"An event of this scale generates demand across several sectors and it creates opportunities," he added.
"We want to turn the international attention generated by E1 into future trips, stays, private investment and jobs. That is the real return we are looking for."
Sustainability challenges
Beyond the spectacle and waterfront backdrops, E1 aims to transcend motorsport.
Sustainability has been one cornerstone, and marine conservation efforts around the race in Angola included mangrove restoration.
Putting sustainability front and centre inevitably invites scrutiny - particularly when races have taken place in Saudi Arabia, the United States, Nigeria and now Angola, all major oil-producing nations.
"The world's on a journey," Copas said.
"We're welcomed in places that do have a lot of fossil-fuel infrastructure.
"Each one of those markets is conscious of it and wants to be doing more from a green point of view. If we can help, why wouldn't we?"
Copas told BBC Sport Africa that E1 would only consider air freight as a last resort for transporting its teams and that they aim to showcase their technology on each stop, persuading people that electric charging is a viable alternative to diesel even on water.
But as the global series expanded to 10 teams and seven races in 2025, its own emissions rose from 1,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in its first season to 4,049 tonnes in its second, according to E1's own annual sustainability report.
"We need to travel to meet new people, to tell our stories, which we would hope would be of greater benefit than the carbon footprint that we have," Copas explained.
"We work really hard to offset our carbon and to make sure every stage of our logistics journey is done in the most sustainable way.
"It would be crazy for us to say we're not going to travel and we're not going to race, because then we can't do the job that we're here to do."
There is an acknowledgement within E1 that the work is unfinished and that more active reductions are needed.
'Continuing the story'
E1 was due to return to Lagos in October, but Nigeria's race was cancelled earlier this month, perhaps showing how the series is still working to establish itself.
It means its longer-term impact in Africa will take time to judge, but the effect of its celebrity owners was obvious around the paddock in Luanda.
After visiting his pilots, Will Smith stopped for selfies and handshakes with fans, telling the crowd it was "great to be here".
On the water, however, there was no fairytale result as Westbrook Racing's hopes of victory were ended by a mechanical fault, with Team Brady taking the inaugural Luanda title.
Smith could have used the help of Kianda, the mermaid-like Angolan water spirit traditionally regarded as a protector of fishermen.
It will take one of her miraculous interventions if electric powerboat racing is to usurp football or basketball in Angolan affections, but Copas hopes E1 can leave a different legacy.
"I think it's for us to help tell Angola stories, and for Angola to help tell ours.
"We will be back next year, we will be back the year after. It's not just about what we're doing in the few days we're here.
"We'd love to see the journey they're on develop even more, and us playing a part in that."

The semicolon, a punctuation mark often used while writing, signifies a pause -- one that is longer than a comma but shorter than a period. It signifies a break and not the end. And sometimes, such a pause might just be what a person needs -- to ensure that the end can stay away, if not forever, at least for the time being. This is what prompted Amy Bleuel to use the punctuation mark as the symbol for the movement that she founded to raise awareness on suicide prevention and mental health.
Today, the semicolon tattoo is one of the most recognised symbols of mental health awareness in the world. But how and when did it all begin?
Project Semicolon was founded in 2013 by Bleuel, a suicide prevention and mental health advocate, to honour her father, who died by suicide ten years ago. The intention was to create a space for people to talk about mental health openly and without any shame. According to the project’s website, the semicolon became a symbol for the movement as it “is used when an author could’ve ended a sentence but chose not to… the semicolon became a symbol for anyone who could’ve ended their own life but chose to keep going.” The movement caught the attention of people worldwide and so did the semicolon tattoo.
People began tattooing the semicolon on their bodies, either as a standalone or by adding it as an element within other hybrid tattoos. These tattoos were used by survivors to honour their personal mental health battles. People have also embraced the tattoo as tributes to their loved ones who had died by suicide, while others don their tattoos as an expression of solidarity to the movement and raise awareness about mental health and suicide prevention. “For many, it’s a daily reminder to keep fighting, to keep writing, to keep living,” reads a quote on their site.
The placement of the tattoo is a matter of choice and people sport them on various parts of their body including on visible locations such as the neck, wrists, etc., while others place it in more intimate areas. The tattoos are not just meant to express but also serve as a means of personal affirmation.
The project deals with spreading awareness not just on suicide prevention but also on various other aspects of mental health including depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), and various other struggles. “What started as one woman’s act of hope has grown into a global movement — one inked semicolon at a time,” says the project’s website.
In 2017, Selena Gomez, Alisha Boe and Tommy Dorfman got the semicolon tattooed on their wrists to commemorate the premiere of their Netflix series 13 Reasons Why. The web series deals with themes of suicide and mental health and it was reported that the stars got the tattoo as a tribute to the show’s handling of the theme as well as the death of Bleuel, a victim of trauma, child abuse and rape.
Various regional organisations, projects, campaigns, etc., inspired by the semicolon project have come up in various parts of the world. India has also not shied away from embracing the movement. Semicolon (;) The Mental Health Awareness Project – India is one such initiative.
Founded by the Medical Students Association of India (MSAI) under the International Federation of Medical Students’ Associations (IFMSA), it was designed as a campaign model that could be leveraged by other local chapters. The project aims to create awareness regarding mental health and tackle the stigma associated with the same, among high school students from classes eighth to 10th.

Telangana is exploring a proposal to make six months of robotic surgery training mandatory for postgraduate medical students, as the State looks to build a trained workforce to expand advanced robotic procedures across its government hospitals.
Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha said the government would approach the National Medical Commission (NMC) for permission to introduce the dedicated training period as part of the three-year postgraduate programme.
Speaking at the ‘State Level Multi-Specialty Robotic Surgery Workshop’ at the Marri Chenna Reddy Telangana Institute of Medical Sciences (MCR TIMS), Sanathnagar in Hyderabad, the Minister said training would be central to Telangana’s plans to expand robotic surgery, whether through a hub-and-spoke model or dedicated robotic surgery facilities at the district level.
The proposal comes as Telangana is already attempting to build a statewide pool of surgeons trained in robotic procedures.
MCR TIMS Director Dr A. Narendra Kumar said surgeons from 35 medical colleges and 47 hospitals, excluding speciality hospitals, are being trained in robotic surgery at two government institutions, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS) and MNJ Cancer Institute.
Also read: Adyar Cancer Institute enables wider access to robotic cancer surgeries
“The idea is to ensure that robotic surgery does not remain concentrated in a handful of premier institutions in Hyderabad,” he added.
Robotic surgery expert Dr. Sudhir Srivastava said such a model could allow specialist expertise to reach patients without requiring them to travel to major cities. He pointed to the financial and emotional burden faced by families from rural and smaller communities when they have to leave their homes to access specialised treatment.
Former NIMS Director Dr N. Bheerappa said NIMS had recently completed nearly 1,000 robotic surgeries and that the government was bearing the cost of such procedures for eligible patients through the Rajiv Aarogyasri health scheme.
Director of Medical Education (DME) Dr N. Vani said government medical colleges had a dual responsibility of providing patient care while training the next generation of doctors. Introducing young surgeons to newer technologies, she said, could have a multiplier effect across the government healthcare system.
She also stressed that young surgeons should not rely solely on the technology, but must combine it with clinical judgement, human touch and compassion.
Experts at the workshop also cautioned that expanding robotic surgery is about considerably more than installing machines. Government Medical College Nagpur Dean Dr. Raj Gajbhiye said robotic surgery was no longer merely a technology available at a few high-end private institutions.
For government hospitals, however, he said “the real objective should be equitable access to advanced surgical technology. “Success of robotics is not about purchasing a robot,” Dr. Gajbhiye said, pointing instead to the need for appropriate infrastructure, trained faculty, structured protocols, multidisciplinary teamwork and institutional support.

Abbott Laboratories will pay $385 million to resolve claims tied to an investigation of contamination at a baby formula factory in Sturgis, Michigan, the largest in the country, which led to the supply shortages in 2022.
Problems at the facility prompted a lawsuit by the Justice Department and recall of powdered infant formula at the facility.
The recall covered several infant formula brands, including Similac, and squeezed inventory that had already been strained by supply chain disruptions and stockpiling during Covid-19 shutdowns.
The settlement, which Abbott says does not represent any finding of fault or liability, also pertains to lawsuits filed by certain relators and the Attorneys General of several states.
Abbott said on Monday that tests by government regulators of unopened product from the homes of the infants under investigation at the time of the 2022 recall were negative for Cronobacter sakazakii, a bacterium that can cause illness in infants. The company also said that no unopened, distributed Abbott infant formulas have ever tested positive for Cronobacter sakazakii.
The Justice Department under President Donald Trump closed its criminal investigation into the matter.
The Biden administration eased import rules for foreign manufacturers, airlifted formula from Europe and invoked federal emergency rules to prioritize U.S. production during the supply shortage.
Abbott closed the Sturgis facility in February 2022 after the Food and Drug Administration began an investigation. The plant was reopened by June of that year.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

The safety and privacy concerns of storing your driver's license in a digital wallet
They can reveal less information than a physical card, but privacy protections don’t necessarily follow your data after you share it.
Putting your driver's license in a digital wallet doesn't mean storing a picture of the plastic card on your phone. A standards-based mobile driver's license, or mDL, contains digitally signed information that lets a compatible reader verify it came from the issuing authority.
That design can make some interactions more private than showing a physical card, while also protecting access to the ID with your phone's security features. But moving identification onto a smart device raises a different set of questions about tracking, data retention and what happens if the phone becomes unavailable.
Why a digital driver's license can reveal less than a physical one
Handing over a physical driver's license exposes everything printed on it to the person checking it. If someone only needs to confirm that you're over 21, for example, they may also see your exact birth date, home address and license number. An mDL can be more selective. The standard supports broad age statements such as whether someone is over 21, allowing a compatible verifier to request that answer rather than seeing the person's complete date of birth.
Apple and Google add their own protections as well. Apple says you can review requested information before sharing it, and in-person presentation requires authentication with Face ID, Touch ID or an applicable accessibility method. Driver's license and ID data is encrypted, and you don't need to hand your phone to the verifier or unlock it.
Google says its US driver's licenses and state IDs are encrypted and stored locally on the phone rather than in your Google Account. Google Wallet also shows the requested information before it's shared and requires you to authenticate.
Those controls don't make a digital license automatically safer than a physical one, but they can give you more control over what you reveal.
Can a digital driver's license track where you use it?
The 2021 ISO/IEC 18013-5 standard supports two ways to provide a digital license. With device retrieval, the information is sent directly from your phone to the reader. With server retrieval, the reader gets the information from the authority that issued the license instead. Privacy advocates object to that second method because the issuer could potentially learn when or where the ID is being used.
The Center for Democracy & Technology calls this the "phone home" problem and argues that a digital ID shouldn't be able to report every use back to the agency that issued it. That doesn't mean Apple Wallet or Google Wallet work that way. The concern is about what server retrieval could allow if it were used.
There has also been an important change recently. The American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators (AAMVA), which sets implementation guidance for motor vehicle agencies across North America, prohibited server retrieval in 2025. Its current Mobile Driver License Implementation Guidelines, published in July 2026, continue that prohibition. That doesn't make every digital ID system untraceable, though; privacy still depends on the standard, regional rules and the wallet's own design.
What happens to your digital ID information after you share it?
Controlling what leaves your phone is only part of the privacy question. Once an organization receives information from your ID, the digital wallet can't necessarily control what that company does with it afterward.
That makes data retention an important part of the transaction. Before you approve a share, Apple Wallet tells you what information is being requested and, where applicable, whether the requester intends to retain it. Google Wallet also lets a requester indicate whether it plans to keep particular pieces of information before you approve the request.
The legal protections can also vary by location. New Jersey's digital ID law includes specific privacy safeguards: an organization can't require someone to hand over their device when presenting a digital ID, and presenting one doesn't amount to consent to search other information on the phone.
There's a broader concern about where digital identification might eventually be requested. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) argues that easier access to government-backed digital IDs could encourage more online services to demand identity or age checks in situations where people can currently browse anonymously. That's an argument about how the infrastructure could be used as adoption grows, not evidence that current digital licenses are tracking people's web activity.
That debate is becoming more concrete as Google expands Wallet's digital ID and age-verification features in parts of the European Union, including ways to confirm someone's age without sharing their name, address or full birth date.
What if your phone is lost, dead or unavailable?
Losing a phone containing your digital driver's license isn't quite the same as dropping the physical card. Someone who finds a plastic license can immediately read everything printed on it. Apple Wallet requires you to have biometric security on your device to add a digital ID, and you must confirm this before viewing the info. Google Wallet requires you to have screen lock protection and has you authenticate this before sharing ID details. Thus, as long as your PIN is strong, someone who finds your phone can't access your ID details.
There are remote options if you can't recover your phone. Apple users can erase a lost device through Find My, which removes its Wallet cards and passes, including a driver's license or ID. For Android, you can remotely remove a driver's license or state ID through your Google account. Our guide to disabling your digital wallet after losing your phone covers the core steps for both iPhone and Android.
A dead, damaged or unsupported phone creates a simpler problem: you may not be able to present the digital credential at all. For now, a digital driver's license is thus best treated as a companion to the physical card, not a replacement. It can limit what you reveal and protect access with device authentication, but once information leaves the wallet, the recipient's retention practices and the laws governing them matter just as much.

Zimbabwe’s Brendan Taylor broke Sachin Tendulkar’s long-standing record when he took the field in the first ODI against Australia at the Harare Sports Club on Tuesday.
Wicketkeeper-batter Taylor is playing his 208th ODI, 22 years after making his debut against Sri Lanka at the same venue.
Taylor’s ODI career now spans 22 years and four months, overtaking Tendulkar, who retired from the 50-overs format in 2012 after playing for 22 years and three months.
Tendulkar remains the top run-scorer in the format with 18,426 in 463 appearances. Taylor has scored 6704 runs heading into the game, which includes 11 centuries and 39 fifties.
Taylor retired in 2021 and was banned for three and a half years in 2022 for breaching the ICC’s Anti-Corruption and Anti-Doping codes.
After the suspension, he came out of retirement in 2025 with Zimbabwe gearing up to co-host next year’s ODI World Cup with South Africa and Namibia.

Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash
- Published
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving on a motorway after he crashed a Lamborghini into a metal gate in May.
The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.
Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May.
Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.
The former England winger pleaded guilty to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road before he crashed.
The court heard he strayed into the central reservation of the motorway and crashed into a metal gate in a layby on the A327.
He was in possession of six canisters of nitrous oxide, a Class C drug.
Hampshire Police previously said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision near the M3 southbound, near the Minley interchange.
The force said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.
Sterling most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, having left Chelsea in January, but made just eight appearances in the Netherlands.
In four years at Chelsea - including a season-long loan at Arsenal - he made 59 league appearances after signing from Manchester City in 2022.
With City he won four Premier League titles, having started his senior career with Liverpool before moving to Manchester in 2015.
He is currently without a club.
In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport.
Sterling will appear in court on 25 November for sentencing, and has been disqualified from driving in the interim.

Anthropic sold corporate giants on Claude. Now the AI company is in an all-out blitz for the mom-and-pops.
In May, Anthropic launched an AI tool specifically for small businesses. Since then, it says it's garnered 900,000 installations for the Claude for Small Business plugin and is angling to expand the tool's reach. It's planning a new slate of workshops to boost its adoption, and training people to spread the Claude gospel.
As Anthropic prepares for its initial public offering, small businesses present a major opportunity for mass adoption: In the US, they employ more than 45% of the private sector's workers and account for around 44% of the country's GDP, according to data from the US Small Business Administration. And the share of small businesses that use generative AI jumped from 23% in 2023 to 58% in 2025, according to a survey by the Chamber of Commerce.
Unlike Anthropic's coding clientele, small businesses have small budgets — and different demands and anxieties. Small firms are caught between AI sales pitches on one side and backlash against the technology on the other. Business owners told Business Insider they've faced concerns from customers for using AI and also found helpful ways to use the technology behind the scenes.
The Claude for Small Business tool handles a range of tasks for small businesses, such as reconciling finances through a company's QuickBooks account. On Tuesday, Anthropic added new plugins from companies like Shopify, Stripe, and Zoom. Lina Ochman, Anthropic's head of US small and medium businesses, called the tool "an agentic starter pack."
Now, Anthropic is creating a cascade of AI-focused workshops and quasi-influencers of the tool. It held its first sessions in San Francisco and New York last week to train people to become "Approved Claude SMB Trainers," who have to commit to hosting five workshops for small- and medium-sized businesses by the end of the year.
Anthropic's biggest rival, OpenAI, also introduced a program for small businesses this year, as these labs compete for their share of mom-and-pop shops.
Small businesses say they've gotten some backlash for using AI
This spring, Ochman traveled the country talking up Claude's potential for small businesses, hitting Chicago, Baton Rouge, San Jose, and a slate of other cities. Around 100 business owners attended each of the stops' half-day workshops.
Ochman said she found that most business owners fell in the camp of chatting with AI tools and not yet letting them automate large chunks of their business. They worried about AI's accuracy, asked if they risked getting hacked, and told her they didn't know where to start.
Business Insider also spoke with small businesses using AI tools from both Anthropic and OpenAI. Some say they've gotten backlash from customers. Steve Zumoff, who runs a tiki bar in Pittsburgh called Spork Island Trading Co., said he got several one-star reviews on his bar's Google page because he'd posted an AI-designed sign out front. He said he expects people to get more comfortable with AI over time, adding that he'd used ChatGPT in figuring out the bar's interior design.
"I have a bag of tools with an electric drill, and that's taken away a job from a carpenter, probably," Zumoff said. "I need to research something, I use Google; that takes a job away from a librarian."
Likewise, a coffee shop owner previously told Business Insider about how she got social media backlash for using ChatGPT to create a menu poster.
Monz Islam, the director of the café Zenchai in Fleet, a town in the UK, posted a photo on the café's Instagram proclaiming that it wouldn't use generative AI for posters. He said he'd made the post after younger customers had complained about other cafés' AI artwork. It feels more "authentic" to have a human-made design, even if they used Canva, Islam said.
Ochman said she doesn't encourage business owners to use Claude for tasks like banking and legal functions.
"Claude will get you 95% of the way there, but the human and the expert stays in the loop," she said.
AI-vangelizing Claude
Anthropic is now spinning up a network to hype Claude's uses for small businesses. It will run more workshops of its own, is promoting sessions held by its partners, and has kicked off a program to train new evangelists with events in San Francisco and New York.
Kelsey Flood, the chief program officer at the California workplace training nonprofit Digital NEST, attended the San Francisco session last week. She told Business Insider she's hoping to run the AI literacy workshops for other nonprofits, small businesses, and students, and keep them agnostic on which AI model to use. Flood said that, given the vast diversity of small businesses, AI labs need to build these relationships to sell their tools.
"The only way I think for Anthropic to be able to do that at scale is to partner," Flood said.
Ochman said she wants to see more small businesses become comfortable with AI.
"If they end up choosing somebody else first, that's OK for me, because a rising tide lifts all ships," she said.

Police say it could take months to identify Philippine ferry fire victims
- Published
Philippine authorities said it could take weeks or months to identify victims of a ferry fire that killed 76 people last week.
"Most of them are already in a charred condition," Richard Allan Mangalip, a forensic specialist from the Philippine National Police, told reporters on Sunday. Family members have been asked to help identify victims with personal items or DNA samples.
The MV June Aster was heading from Manila to Coron in Palawan province, a popular holiday destination, when a fire started in its cargo hold and spread rapidly throughout the vessel.
Forty-three people survived the disaster, while 13 people remain unaccounted for, authorities said.
Mangalip said they were "trying [their] best to collect the possible identifying marks" from victims' remains.
But it was hard to give a clear timeline on how long the identification process would take because of the volume of specimens, he said, adding, "It could be weeks, or it could be months."
A coast guard official said on Saturday that the priority was identifying victims and determining the cause of the blaze.
The fire continued burning for more than a day, releasing heat and toxic fumes that impeded search and rescue operations. It took more than 40 hours before rescuers could board the ship in search of survivors.
The MV June Aster had set off last Tuesday from Manila to Coron, a popular destination among both local and foreign tourists, known for its beaches and WW2 shipwreck diving sites.
Besides tourists, there were also passengers on the ferry who had been travelling to Coron for work or to visit family.
Survivors recall hearing a loud explosion before seeing smoke and fire. When fire engulfed the ship, chaos erupted on board, they said.
One told the BBC that he had been trampled after falling on the floor. He jumped off the boat into the sea before being rescued hours later.
But many burned to death on the ship. Mangalip said at the press conference on Sunday that some victims' remains were found clustered together in parts of the vessel.
"Our thoughts are also with the survivors and families still waiting for news of their loved ones," the Philippine Coast Guard said in a statement on Sunday. "We recognise the pain and uncertainty they continue to endure as recovery and identification efforts remain underway."

NBC’s telecast of the 78th Emmy Awards hit 6.7 million viewers on Monday night, per Nielsen.
That total marks a 9% decrease from last year’s ceremony on CBS, which brought in 7.4 million viewers — the award show’s best performance since 2021.
It should be noted, though, that the 2025 ceremony took place on a Sunday, making it easier for viewers to sit down for a three-hour telecast. Compared to the most recent Monday night Emmys — televised by Fox in 2024 — NBC accomplished a 41% increase. But since that telecast, which hit only a meager 4.4 million viewers, was the first in Emmys history to air with fierce competition from an NFL playoff game, the most accurate comparison is perhaps to NBC’s own Monday night Emmys in 2022. In those terms, the network’s latest Emmy efforts made a 10% improvement, up from 5.9 million viewers.
Hosted by “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star Mariska Hargitay, the Emmys did air against an NFL game between the Kansas City Chiefs and the Denver Broncos. Even with that competition, it drew enough viewers to rank as the the most-watched non-sports, non-news Monday telecast of 2026, both overall and among adults age 18-49. Hargitay referenced the football game in a pre-recorded sketch featuring a cameo from Taylor Swift, musing that the pop star wouldn’t be able to attend the show because she’d be supporting her husband, Chiefs player Travis Kelce.
Popular on Variety
According to NBCUniversal, the Emmys generated 133 million social views, counted across Facebook, Instagram, X and YouTube. The company touts that that marks a 90% increase from 2025.
It appears that this was the Emmys’ last year on a traditional broadcaster. After 31 years of rotating between NBC, CBS, Fox and ABC, the TV Academy is now in talks with Amazon Prime Video.

Japan loses contact with a surveillance drone off the country's northwestern coast
Japan's air force has lost contact with one of its surveillance drones during a flight off the northwestern coast
TOKYO -- Japan's air force lost contact on Tuesday with one of its long-distance surveillance drones after it went missing during a flight off the country's northwestern coast.
There was no immediate information as to what the mission of the uncrewed RQ-4B aircraft, also known as Global Hawk, was.
The Air Self-Defense Force said the drone disappeared from the radar and was last seen 50 kilometers (31 miles) off the coast of Tottori earlier in the afternoon.
The drone is one of three Global Hawks owned by the air force and deployed at its Misawa Air Base in the northern prefecture of Aomori.
The drones are considered valuable because they can conduct long-range missions and are able to fly at a height of about 60,000 feet (18.3 kilometers) and can fly continuously for up to 36 hours. They allow Japan to easily monitor areas on the Asian mainland, including North Korea and China.
Japan is trying to adapt to changing times and develop defense strategies that use drones, including those for combat, artificial intelligence and new methods of warfare. Under its five-year plan established in 2022, the country has doubled its defense spending to about 2% of its gross domestic product to build up its Self-Defense Forces’ offensive role to counter China’s growing assertiveness.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government is now preparing new security and defense strategies, expected to be unveiled later this year.
Beijing has criticized Japan’s defense buildup as “new militarism.”

Since the days immediately following the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, U.S. President Donald Trump, a native of New York City, has made numerous claims about what he saw that day and his involvement in the recovery efforts.
One such claim Trump has repeatedly made is his assertion that he was at Ground Zero within days of 9/11 and that he sent workers to the recovery effort at the site of the World Trade Center.
In September 2026, multiple X users debated the veracity of the claim. For example, one user (archived) wrote, "There's no proof Trump sent a large group of construction workers to Ground Zero."
Other popular (archived) posts (archived) said there was no evidence Trump, himself, went to Ground Zero and helped with recovery efforts.
Another X post (archived) alternatively claimed, "President Trump is dropping VIDEO PROOF for every Fake News outlet lying to millions that he was nowhere near Ground Zero after 9/11."
(X)
Many Snopes readers searched the site to find out if Trump's claims were true.
A couple of days after the Sept. 11 attacks, Trump told multiple news media outlets that he sent at least 100 workers to Ground Zero to help pull people and bodies out of the rubble, with 125 to 150 more on the way. However, Snopes has never been able to identify any public evidence that crews he hired helped in the immediate recovery of the 9/11 attacks. Since we cannot independently confirm with certainty whether Trump had crews on site somewhere, we are leaving this claim unrated.
Footage of interviews Trump conducted in the immediate days after 9/11 placed him within blocks of Ground Zero. Trump said in those interviews that he visited Ground Zero to encourage the workers he said he brought to assist with clearing rubble at the site. It was not possible to find evidence showing Trump helped clear the pile of debris at Ground Zero, as some posts disputed.
In a phone call with a local news media station immediately after the planes crashed into the Twin Towers, Trump said he watched the towers fall from the window of one of his buildings.
Trump's September 2026 remarks
On Sept. 8, 2026, in a post on Truth Social (archived), Trump continued to maintain that he was at Ground Zero with construction workers after 9/11, clarifying that it was "obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter":
The Failing New York Magazine wrote a story that I wasn't down at the World Trade Center after the Tragedy of September 11th, because nobody saw me there. Well, I don't think I would be the first thing on anyone's mind but, I was there, obviously not on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter, with a large group of Construction Workers.
He then added he "was there as soon as the Law allowed."
The president was referencing a New York Magazine article disputing his comments about where he was on the day of, and the days following, the attacks.
Trump also made this claim (archived) in a Fox News interview two days prior, in which he added the additional context that he was constructing a new building in New York City. This is the reason, according to Trump at a 9/11 anniversary event on Sept. 8, why he had workers who he could bring to the rubble of the World Trade Center:
I was building a big building in New York and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened and they had no hesitation. Everybody went down with me. We went down as a big group of people. It wasn't too much we could do, I'll be honest.
What Trump told the media in 2001
Trump spoke to the media multiple times a few days after 9/11. On Sept. 13, he told a German news channel, that he had more than 100 men down at the site of the World Trade Center and more than 125 on their way. According to the German-speaking reporter, the interview was conducted a few blocks from Ground Zero.
That same day, NBC News interviewed Trump at what appeared to be the same location as his interview with the German news channel. Trump said he had "hundreds of men inside working right now" and was bringing down another 125.
PBS has a recording of another Trump interview from Sept. 13, in which Trump said he had 100 workers helping to dig people and bodies out of the rubble at the World Trade Center, with another 100 to 150 workers "coming." He told PBS that those workers were "digging out" at the site.
In another interview from that day, Trump told reporters his workers had been at Ground Zero "for about a day and a half." He said they were men from his company and that a couple had gotten hurt while working at the site. He also said he was just down at Ground Zero and was there to support them.
The evidence
When Snopes first researched this claim in 2018, we spoke to Richard Alles, a retired deputy chief with the New York City Fire Department, who later served as director of 9/11 community affairs for the law firm Barasch McGarry Salzman and Penson. Alles said that in all his time he spent at Ground Zero as a New York City Fire Department battalion chief, starting 20 minutes after the buildings collapsed, he never saw a large group of workers whom Trump had hired at the site assisting with search and rescue efforts. "This is the first I'm hearing of it," Alles said via phone call. "There would have been no need for that. Between police, fire and the construction crews, we had it all covered."
Alles added that the construction crews he saw at Ground Zero helping rescue workers were from the trade unions and were not hired by Trump.
John Feal, founder of the 9/11 first responder health advocacy nonprofit the FealGood Foundation, told Snopes at the time that he responded to Ground Zero on Sept. 12, 2001, as a construction demolitions expert and that he didn't see evidence of hundreds of workers hired by Trump at the site.
The Trump Organization was building in New York City in 2001, according to the Skyscraper Center database on skyscrapers. In fact, it finished a series of residential buildings in the city at Trump Place between 1998 and 2004. He was also building the Trump World Tower residential building near the United Nations Headquarters that year.
However, it was not possible to find verifiable information about how many people, either directly employed by Trump or contracted to work on one of the Trump Organization's projects, were working on these buildings and in New York City at the time.
A New York Times fact-check from July 2019 referenced Timothy O'Brien, the author of "TrumpNation: The Art of Being the Donald," who reportedly said the Trump Organization numbered "a little bit over a dozen people" at the time of the attacks, making it impossible to send as many workers to the relief effort as Trump claimed.
Neither the White House nor the Trump Organization responded to Snopes' requests for corroborating evidence in 2018. This lack of response is consistent with past attempts by Politifact, The Washington Post, The New York Times and Politifact again to reach out to the White House and/or the Trump Organization to corroborate evidence of Trump's claims.

WASHINGTON — The Food and Drug Administration is opening applications for a pilot program designed to shorten the amount of time it takes for drugmakers to begin testing their products in humans, the agency announced Tuesday.
The pilot was first announced in June as part of Operation TrialBlazer, the Department of Health and Human Services initiative that pledged to shorten the FDA’s drug approval timelines and help the U.S. compete with the rapidly accelerating biotechnology industries in countries like China and Australia.
“Too often, the U.S. pathway can be measured in years, while other countries’ pathways are measured in months,” the department wrote in the TrialBlazer roadmap.
