When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.
However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in South Africa.
After Trump’s February 2025 executive order announcing the resettlement programme, which was expanded to include members of a “racial minority”, the first group of 68 white South Africans arrived in the US that May. The US also shut down the refugee programme for anyone else fleeing war and persecution.
Since then, more than 13,000 have moved to the US, according to state department figures. Arrivals are also accelerating, with more than 2,600 admitted in August.
Afrikaners, descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime repressed the black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.
Since the end of apartheid more than 30 years ago, affirmative action policies have helped to create a black elite and middle class. But about 38% of black South Africans are unemployed, compared with 9% of white South Africans, according to official data.
Meanwhile, the “black economic empowerment” policies, along with high crime rates that affect everyone, have fostered a feeling among some white South Africans that they are now the victims of racial discrimination.
The racist far right has also long highlighted brutal murders of white South African farmers, claiming them as evidence of white people being targeted. Official crime data does not show farmers or white people experiencing crime at higher rates. That has not stopped Trump amplifying these claims, in the face of the South African government’s furious rebuttals.
On 30 June, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for prospective and successful refugee applicants began to light up with news that people had begun to receive rejection letters.
“We are writing to inform you that, following review, USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] found your application to be ineligible for continued processing for resettlement to the United States at this time. This cannot be appealed,” the letters said, according to multiple rejections seen by the Guardian.
It is unclear how many have been found ineligible. USCIS did not provide data on the total number of refugee applications and rejections. One WhatsApp group set up to support rejects, called Hope beyond the Letter, had 311 members as of 10 September, according to one of the administrators, who noted that the membership fluctuated.
While the ineligibility letters did not give reasons for rejection, some applicants were given more information after making Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. The WhatsApp group administrator, a 64-year-old freelance TV professional, who did not want his identity disclosed, found that his case was initially “recommended for approval”. However, the recommendation was reversed because his ex-girlfriend, whom he had applied with, had a marijuana conviction.
“I cried like a baby,” he said, of receiving the rejection letter on 30 June, having finished the screening process in November. “It was something I actually believed was attainable. I believed the hype.”
Pieter and Liesl (not their real names) were told they were “conditionally approved” as refugees Last November. Both are Afrikaners who had a grandparent killed on a farm and were managing a farm when they applied to become refugees.
Pieter said he was convicted of trespassing in 2014, for which he said he paid a fine and did not go to court. He was granted multiple temporary visas to work on farms in the US between 2011 and 2024.
The couple’s youngest daughter was born in the US and is a US citizen. In the response to their FoI request, they noticed that USCIS had recorded her nationality as South African and incorrectly said that she would be left behind if they moved to the US as refugees.
They had already sold their house, car and many of their possessions when they received a rejection letter on 24 July. “We have to start all over again,” Pieter said.
Another applicant blamed not being able to speak in his native Afrikaans for what he claimed were misunderstandings that led to him and his wife being rejected. The reasons given in response to their FoI request were “crime involving moral turpitude” and “commission of acts of torture or extra judicial killing”.
The 67-year-old had admitted to shooting at least one black person when working as a security guard in 1995, but said it was in self-defence while responding to the mass break-in of an alcohol shop. “I was thoroughly investigated by the authorities,” he said. “I was not charged, because I did not break the law.”
In an emailed response that did not address specific cases, the USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said: “The Department of Homeland Security is committed to resettling Afrikaner refugees who are being persecuted by the South African government.
“[USCIS] reviews each refugee application on a case-by-case basis … [and] notifies aliens found ineligible for continued processing through the US Refugee Admissions Program, including those found ineligible for public safety concerns or criminal histories. This cannot be appealed. This administration will always prioritize the safety and welfare of the American people.”

ChatGPT has a feature to help those in crisis. But where can you find it?
Note to reader: this story discusses people grappling with thoughts of suicide.
More than a million weekly users of the chatbot ChatGPT discuss suicide and self-harm, according to NPR estimates of data released by OpenAI last fall. But suicide prevention experts say human connection is critical to preventing suicide. So, back in May, the company started an optional feature called Trusted Contact to connect those struggling with thoughts of suicide and self harm to someone they can turn to in times of emotional crises.
NPR first reported about Trusted Contact in August as part of a story about a young woman who died by suicide in 2024 after using an older version of ChatGPT as a therapist. At the time, OpenAI spokesperson Gaby Raila told NPR in an email that ChatGPT is trained to recognize signs that someone may be at risk — including indirect cues or warning signs that emerge over time. If the chatbot detects a serious safety risk in a user, it will alert their Trusted Contact — if they have one listed.
Raila said that the company has seen "good adoption" of the feature, but didn't provide actual numbers.
NPR wanted to see how ChatGPT tells users about the new optional feature — so they can sign up right away, before any crisis — like people listing an emergency contact at a doctor's office.
"Maybe you're thinking of another app?"
I'm a ChatGPT user, but I'd never been alerted about Trusted Contact. Neither had my editor, nor several other users we checked with.
So, I wondered if the bot alerts new users. My colleague Megan Lim, a producer at NPR's All Things Considered, had never used the chatbot before and volunteered to give it a try.
"Welcome to ChatGPT," the words popped on Megan's screen once she clicked on the app on her phone. Then the app prompted her to set up an account, which she did. Still, no mention of Trusted Contact or why one should consider setting it up.
The bot did ask Megan to pick a voice. She chose a soothing female voice. "It's lovely to meet you," the bot said in a British accent. "What would you like to chat about today?"
When it still didn't mention Trusted Contact, Megan asked about it directly.
Megan
Do you have a Trusted Contact feature for people with mental health issues? Under what circumstances do you offer it to people?
ChatGPT 
I'm not seeing a general Trusted Contact feature for that scenario. Maybe you’re thinking of another app that has a Trusted Contact option?
Rhitu
No. It is OpenAI’s ChatGPT.
ChatGPT
You're right. It does have a Trusted Contact feature in chat now. It's for serious safety concerns, not for general stress.
It said that a user can sign up for it on their own through the app's settings, in order for the app to notify the contact.
Rhitu
But what if the user does not know about the trusted contact feature?
ChatGPT
Hang on. If they haven't set it up, then nothing happens. It's an opt-in feature. You have to set it in Settings first. And if someone is in a serious risk situation and doesn't have it set up, ChatGPT can't notify anyone for them.
"It only works if it's set up in advance," it added, "but ChatGPT can still respond supportively if you're feeling distressed." That support includes urging the user to reach out to a loved one or contact the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, 9-8-8.
OpenAI spokesperson Raila told NPR in an email that this feature isn't available on ChatGPT voice, but that the company is working on it. But when someone is typing with the bot, and the bot detects that they are struggling with suicidal thoughts and significant emotional distress, Raila said, the bot "may" tell them to set up Trusted Contact.
Mixed reaction from mental health professionals
Suicide prevention experts say there could be some benefits to the feature, but also have some reservations.
"It would be ideal to offer it to all users when they are not yet in an emergency," Holly Wilcox, director of the Center for Suicide Prevention at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, said in an email.
Psychologist Ursula Whiteside gave the feature a try. "The steps actually were quite simple and the language, and then the words were easy to follow for the most part," said Whiteside, the CEO of a suicide prevention non-profit called Now Matters Now. "Now, if I was super duper upset, it might have been harder for me to follow the process but overall I felt okay." Whiteside and her colleagues run peer support groups for individuals who are struggling with suicidal thoughts or have already survived suicide attempts, and in need of ongoing support. Many of those people now occasionally turn to chatbots in addition to their human sources of support, so they are familiar with the technology's pros and cons.
Earlier this year, Whiteside and her colleagues did focus groups with these individuals asking them about their chatbot use and how the technology could be improved to help them.
"What they thought would be helpful for them in the future would be to have this trusted contact option where they could set up in advance while they were thinking clearly, somebody that they could reach out to when they were under a lot of stress, or when suicidal thoughts became really overwhelming," says Whiteside.
She thinks the feature could be helpful for some, especially for people like those in her peer support groups who already understand how helpful human connection can be during moments of crisis.
People who have never opened up about their suicidal thoughts to anyone may be more reluctant to respond to a chatbot's nudge to sign up for Trusted Contact, says psychologist Jennifer Lockman, who runs the suicide prevention clinic at the University of Alabama.
"We know that people who are seriously thinking about suicide believe that they are a burden on others," says Lockman. "They really have come to a place where they believe that others would be better off without them."
She says she's not sure if a bot can help a person overcome their own internal barriers to reaching out to others in their life. "It doesn't and can't simulate or replicate the process that you would go through with a mental health provider that's trained in identifying who those contacts should be," she adds.
Still, Lockman says, the new optional feature can be "another opportunity to provide human support and connection" to those thinking about suicide. "We know from research that human connection belonging is a huge protective factor to help people when they're thinking about suicide. So in some ways, anything that we can do to promote connection to real people, in theory, that's a good protective thing."
The company is also continuing to iterate when and how ChatGPT proactively offers the Trusted Contact feature to users experiencing distress, Raila wrote to NPR, and that it's doing this work in collaboration with psychologists and researchers. She also said that this new feature is not their only safeguard for self-harm and suicide — they have other safeguards like telling users to take a break periodically from the app and telling users about crisis hotlines, like 988.
Lockman is hopeful that the new ChatGPT feature will help some suicidal individuals, but she wants to see research on its impact before she believes it's helping save lives.
If you or someone you know is in crisis or if you're thinking about hurting yourself, you can call or text the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. It's 988.

Turkish habit of stashing gold "under the pillow' hurts economy, government says
Turks often hold onto gold as a hedge against inflation. It may be hurting Turkey’s financial future
ISTANBUL — In Turkey, gold is far more than a decorative accessory. It is gifted throughout life's major milestones and stashed safely at home—a time-honored practice designed to protect savings against frequent currency devaluations and a volatile national economy.
However, Turkish officials and economists warn that this culture of gold hoarding is actively undermining the country's financial future.
At the bustling Mahmutpaşa Yokuşu market in the heart of Istanbul, store owners call out their wares while shoppers dart between stalls, snapping up everything from kitchen gadgets and blankets to elaborate wedding dresses.
Among them is Nefise Asker, a 23-year-old bride-to-be searching for the perfect outfit for her upcoming wedding photoshoot—one of six outfits she plans to wear over a multi-day celebration this September. Like many Turkish brides, Asker is eager to receive the traditional staple of Turkish wedding gifts: gold.
"We'll share the gold as a couple to support our new life together," Asker says.
Historically, gifted gold used to serve as financial insurance for wives who did not work outside the home.
"If everything goes south, you still have your gold that is gifted to you during your wedding, and that will be your lifetime savings," explains Selva Demiralp, an economist at Istanbul's Koç University and a former economist for the Turkish Federal Reserve.
That mindset extends far beyond newlyweds. In Turkey, the practice of holding wealth as physical gold or foreign currency outside the formal banking system—known locally as yastık altı, or "under the pillow"—is sometimes dismissed as an outdated habit. However, Demiralp emphasizes that this behavior is a logical defense against chronic instability.
"Once you look at why people do this, it stops looking irrational actually, and it's a very rational response to a long history of high and unpredictable inflation, a few banking crises people still remember, and a general sense that the lira just doesn't hold its value the way gold does," Demiralp explains.
In Istanbul's historic Grand Bazaar, Mehmet Yıldırımtürk sits in his cramped, stuffy shop counting gold coins on a glass countertop as a small fan circulates the warm air. Yıldırımtürk, who has worked as a currency exchanger and gold seller for over 50 years, views gold as an essential line of defense.
"Gold is a vital tool for Turks," Yıldırımtürk says. "It helps protect them, especially from inflation."
Inflation remains a chronic crisis in Turkey, hovering around 31% annually—one of the highest rates in the world. As the Turkish lira continues to weaken, daily living costs have skyrocketed. Gold, by contrast, offers stability, with prices hovering near all-time highs. Stashing physical gold at home provides Turkish families with a reliable financial cushion.
According to the Turkish finance ministry, Turkish households currently store roughly 5,000 tons of gold. At current prices, that hidden wealth amounts to approximately $600 billion, according to the head of the Turkish Central Bank.
Trust Gap
Beyond hedging against price increases, keeping savings hidden reflects a systemic distrust in official institutions. Demiralp's research at Koç University highlights how severe this disconnect has become.
"We asked people directly how much they trust the country's key economic institutions on a 0 to 10 scale, and nearly four in 10 rated their trust in commercial banks close to zero," Demiralp notes.
Trust in the statistical agency was even lower, she said. Over half the respondents in her survey put it in the same near-zero range. So when people choose gold over a lira account, they are reacting to a broader credibility gap in institutions meant to manage and report on the economy.
Demiralp said that public mistrust of Turkish commercial banks is rooted in a combination of historical economic trauma, persistent inflation, and a broader credibility gap in institutions. Turkish households still carry memories of past banking crises, which creates a hesitation to leave their savings inside the formal banking sector.
This, she said, is further fueled by the stark reality of chronic inflation and negative real interest rates. When households see prices on daily goods rising at a higher rate than official inflation figures suggest, it erodes their faith in the government's numbers. Therefore, holding money in the bank feels like an automatic loss of purchasing power compared to physical gold.
As Demiralp points out, "If you think inflation is going to run nearly 50% and the deposit rate you are being offered doesn't come close to compensating for that, then gold looks like a safer bet in real terms. When we ask people directly what they plan to do with their savings going forward, gold is by a wide margin the single most popular answer."
Wider Economy
Yet economists warn that keeping such a vast sum idle creates severe headwinds for the broader economy.
"It's not being lent out to businesses," Demiralp says. "And a good chunk of the gold has to be imported every year, which adds to the current account deficit. So it's capital that's parked rather than working."
Demiralp notes that if hoarded gold were deposited into the formal banking system it would allow economic authorities to keep track of exact liquidity volumes, observe account behaviors, and design effective, targeted macroeconomic policies based on real data rather than rough estimates. It would restore the central bank's ability to influence economic demand, making monetary policy tools effective again—a necessary step toward achieving price stability, attracting foreign investment, and reducing unemployment.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has repeatedly urged citizens to bring their gold out from under their mattresses, launching various government incentives and banking programs aimed at converting physical gold into bank deposits.
"This brings no benefit to either my people themselves or to my state," Erdoğan declared in a 2023 Cabinet speech.
Despite these initiatives, the government's efforts have largely failed. Critics point to Erdoğan's unorthodox economic policies and heavy-handed control over financial institutions—including firing six bank heads over seven years—as key factors fueling public skepticism.
"The gold just isn't coming out from under their pillows," Yıldırımtürk says. "The government just hasn't been able to provide that confidence yet."
And bride-to-be Nefise Asker agrees. She has no intention of depositing her wedding gold into a bank account.
"I'll probably not put it under my pillow like in the olden days," Asker says with a smile. "But for sure, I'll hide it in a box at home."

Locked offices and millions in donations: Inside India's little-known political parties
- Published
There was little to suggest that the locked flat in Anand, in the western Indian state of Gujarat, was the headquarters of a political party.
There was no signboard, campaign poster or obvious trace of political activity. But on paper, the Satyawadi Rakshak Party had recently received an extraordinary amount of money.
In the financial year ending in March 2024, official records show the Gujarat-based party received more than 3.3bn rupees (approx $35m; £25m) in donations. A few months later, when India held the world's largest general election, it fielded a single candidate, who lost his deposit.
Its accounts say that 84.8m rupees went towards election campaigning, while more than 3.16bn rupees were listed as spending on "public welfare".
"We have spent the money on charity but have not maintained records," said Swati Ben Patel, the party's president, who lives in the same residential complex as its registered office.
The party is one of more than 2,800 Registered Unrecognised Political Parties, or RUPPs - a vast but little-known tier of Indian politics. These parties are legally registered but have not won enough votes or seats to be recognised at the state or national level.
Some contest elections only sporadically or field a handful of candidates. Yet, like larger parties, they can receive donations and claim tax exemptions. Donors can also reduce their taxable income through eligible contributions.
The rules are intended to support political activity, but tax officials say they can be misused.
A months-long BBC investigation examined six RUPPs that reported some of the largest donations in 2023-24. Together, they received about 17bn rupees, despite fielding just 15 candidates in the 2024 election. None came close to winning.
The gap between the money some parties receive and their limited electoral presence has drawn increasing scrutiny from India's tax authorities.
An internal Income Tax department document reviewed by the BBC shows that officials have been investigating suspected misuse of RUPPs since at least 2022.
It identifies 55.91bn rupees in suspected bogus political donations made by taxpayers seeking tax benefits, as well as 6.65bn rupees in foreign transactions. It also notes possible violations of tax, foreign-funding and election laws.
None of the six parties examined by the BBC has been publicly named in these wider inquiries. The BBC has not established that any of them committed financial wrongdoing.
But in several cases, it found a striking gap between the way the organisations were described in their records and what reporters encountered on the ground.
Some registered offices were closed or appeared inactive. Party officials sometimes said they did not control their organisations' finances or could not explain how large sums had been spent.
The BBC found signs that the political presence of some of these parties was limited. Although their websites sometimes carried photographs of door-to-door canvassing, one candidate, Indradevi Hiralal of the Garib Kalyan Party, said she had not visited her constituency to campaign in 2024. She showed a single poster printed for the election.
There were also signs of scrutiny from the authorities. Three parties said they or their officials had faced action by the Income Tax department. At a fourth, a relative of a party official said the family home had been searched. The other two denied facing such action.
Tax authorities in Bihar, Gujarat and Delhi, as well as the Central Board of Direct Taxes, did not respond to questions about whether any of the six parties had been investigated or subjected to searches.
Of the six parties, Aam Janmat Party reported receiving the most money.
Founded in Patna in 2020, it reported no individual donations above 20,000 rupees - the threshold at which donors must be identified to the Election Commission - during its first two years.
Then its finances changed dramatically.
Aam Janmat Party reported 2.16bn rupees in donations in 2022-23. The following year, the figure nearly tripled to more than 6.2bn rupees - more than twice the roughly 2.8bn rupees received by the Indian National Congress, the country's main opposition party.
Aam Janmat Party officials could not explain the sudden rise.
Aam Janmat Party party fielded just one candidate in the 2024 general election. He received a tiny share of the vote and lost his deposit.
The BBC traced its founding president, Anamika Paswan, to Patna city in Bihar state. Paswan, now a vice-president of the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the state, said she had resigned from Aam Janmat in 2022.
When reporters later sought documents relating to her departure, Paswan was not present. Her husband produced what he said was her resignation letter and another document stating that the party had moved hundreds of miles west to Ahmedabad in Gujarat state with Gaurav Mishra as its president.
But the office at its registered address there was shut.
Its treasurer, Dharmendra Vaishnav, said by telephone that Aam Janmat had "shut operations". He said he knew nothing about its finances and directed questions to Mishra, who did not respond to repeated calls and messages.
The party's listed bank account, however, could still receive money. The BBC transferred a small donation and the payment went through.
The registered office of the Garib Kalyan Party was also closed.
It reported receiving 1.38bn rupees in donations in 2023-24, but fielded just three candidates in the general election.
At the home of its president Neeraj Kumar Kshatriya, his mother said she knew little about the party. But she recalled Income Tax department officials searching the family home, although she did not know why.
Researchers who track political finance say the pattern raises questions about what these parties do with the money they receive.
"These parties are not electorally active, yet they are getting such huge funds and they are spending the money as well," said Shelly Mahajan, a researcher at the Association for Democratic Reforms, an election watchdog.
But tracing such transactions can be difficult. Tax officials told the BBC that money can pass through a web of taxpayers, political parties and intermediaries, obscuring where it came from and where it ultimately went.
The BBC could not establish that any donations to the six parties had been returned in this way.
It did, however, trace two people listed as donors to the New India United Party who said they had claimed tax benefits on their contributions.
One Ahmedabad resident confirmed donating 500,000 rupees. The other said he had donated on a friend's advice. "I did it as a way to save tax, and have declared the same," he said, adding that the authorities had not contacted him.
Three tax officials in Ahmedabad, Delhi and Patna, speaking on condition of anonymity, said chartered accountants and other middlemen can connect taxpayers seeking deductions with parties willing to receive donations.
In some cases, they said, intermediaries can also exercise considerable control over party finances.
Surender Tiwari said that was what happened at his Swatantrata Abhivyakti Party, which reported receiving 2.19bn rupees in donations in 2023-24.
Although he was its president, Tiwari said he did not control the party's money. Its chartered accountant handled the finances and gave him campaign funds, he said.
"The chartered accountant gave me some money for the election campaign," Tiwari said. "He would then show videos of the campaign to clients who wanted to get tax relief through donations."
Tiwari said the party received a notice from the Income Tax department in July and accused its chartered accountant Mayur Singh of keeping him "in the dark".
Singh denied wrongdoing. He said his role was limited to preparing audit reports that parties must submit to the Election Commission, although he acknowledged working for several examined by the BBC.
"Try to understand, it's the same people behind these parties," he said, without elaborating.
Concerns surrounding India's little-known parties extend beyond their finances. The Election Commission has also been trying to remove inactive parties from its official list.
Last year, it delisted more than 800 RUPPs that had not fielded a candidate in six years. But it cannot cancel a party's legal registration, limiting the effect of such action.
The BBC asked the commission whether tax authorities had shared information about suspected financial irregularities involving RUPPs, including the six examined. It did not respond.
As scrutiny grows, the challenge for authorities will be to establish who controls these parties, where their money comes from and how it is ultimately spent.

Greater dialogue as AI, outer space rivalries grow; bigger security role by major powers: China's defence chief
Dong Jun was speaking on Wednesday (Sep 16) at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing which was attended by delegates from nearly 100 countries and regions, including Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing and North Korea’s Vice Defence Minister Kim Kang-il.
Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun has called for greater security dialogue and rule-making in emerging domains including artificial intelligence (AI) and outer space - areas of growing Sino-US rivalry as their leaders prepare to meet.
“(Countries should also) strengthen risk assessment, experience-sharing and rule-making, so that emerging technologies can better benefit all of humanity,” Dong said in a speech on Wednesday (Sep 16) at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing.
Major powers should take the lead in shouldering responsibility for global security governance, he also said.
His remarks come a week before an expected meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and United States counterpart Donald Trump in Washington.
Xi is set to visit the US and meet with Trump on Sep 24 in their second summit this year as the two sides try to steady ties amid tensions over trade, technology and security. China has yet to confirm the trip.
Launched in 2006, the Xiangshan Forum is seen as China’s counterpart to major regional security meetings such as the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore.
Themed “Build Consensus on Stability, Advance Security Governance Together”, this year’s gathering from Sep 15 to 17 is attended by delegates from nearly 100 countries and regions, including Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing and North Korea’s Vice Defence Minister Kim Kang-il.
RISKS IN EMERGING DOMAINS
In his roughly 30-minute speech, Dong warned of risks including the militarisation and misuse of emerging technologies, as well as risks spilling across different domains.
“Countries should … actively engage in security dialogue in areas including artificial intelligence, outer space and the deep sea,” he said.
Chinese Vice President Han Zheng made a similar appeal at Tuesday’s Xiangshan Forum welcome dinner, calling for faster development of governance rules for such emerging domains as well as greater international cooperation.
The calls come as AI becomes an increasingly important area of competition - and potential cooperation - between China and the US, with it widely expected to be on the agenda when Xi meets with Trump.
The US has accused top Chinese AI labs of stealing the capabilities of American models through “industrial-scale knowledge distillation campaigns". Distillation is where an AI model is trained to mimic the output of a larger, more capable one.
Beijing has rejected the claims and accused Washington of using national security to suppress Chinese companies.
Outer space has similarly become an increasingly important area of strategic and military competition.
China’s Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday it opposes any arms race in outer space and warned against turning it into a “warzone”, after the US revealed that the Pentagon is operating weapons in Earth's orbit.
The US delegation to this year’s Xiangshan Forum is led by Brigadier General Stacy Kihara, a senior defence official at the US embassy in Beijing.
The Pentagon had initially planned to send Cynthia Carras, its principal director for China, Taiwan and Mongolia, but she pulled out days before the forum, according to the South China Morning Post.
MAJOR POWERS SHOULD “TAKE THE LEAD”
In his Wednesday speech, Dong also called on major powers to take the lead in maintaining “global strategic stability”.
Major powers should take the lead in shouldering responsibility, while small and medium-sized countries should actively contribute and the United Nations should play its due role,” he said.
He said a “fair, reasonable, balanced and effective” security governance system was needed to keep risks in check and uphold international fairness and justice.
Dong also called for “dialogue rather than confrontation, partnership rather than alliance, and win-win cooperation rather than zero-sum competition”.
He said conflicts ought to be resolved through dialogue, adding that military force could not address their root causes and coercive pressure would only deepen division.
“Dialogue and consultation is the only correct path,” he said, accusing some countries of “forming cliques” and “adding fuel to the fire”.
While Dong did not directly mention the US in his speech, his remarks come amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
During a visit to Egypt earlier this month, Xi called for a new Middle East security framework and said China was ready to help safeguard key shipping routes.
Dong said China’s military would deepen cooperation with other countries, including through joint exercises and training, personnel training, equipment and technology.
He also called for deeper cooperation on peacekeeping, naval escorts and counter-terrorism, citing global challenges including energy, food and shipping-lane security.

Honorable Mentions
Sonos Beam Gen 2 for $499: The Sonos Beam Gen 2 is an excellent compact soundbar options, especially if you have other Sonos speakers in your home. Bluesound Pulse Cinema for $1,499: Bluesound is better known for its small, high-res audio speakers, but this 47-inch-long soundbar sounds stunning for music too. While Dolby Atmos support is good, playing dream-like synth rock tracks like “I Will Wait” by Phoebe Bridgers reveals a truly amazing spatial audio experience. The mix seems to emulate all around the room. On “Walk Walk” by Maggie Rogers, the driving bass and drums sound ultra-realistic. This is a pricey soundbar, though, and others like the Sonos Arc Ultra sound more realistic, especially its upfiring drivers.
Polk Audio Signa S4 for $449: Former WIRED senior editor Parker Hall says that, despite its age, the Polk Signa S4 is an excellent-sounding soundbar, especially for the price. It’s simple to use, easy to setup, has a few modes to choose from (Movie, Music, and Night), and versatile 3.1.2-channel Atmos-enables speakers. It’s a little dated, though, and doesn’t have Wi-Fi connectivity. You can learn more in his Polk Signa S4 review.
KEF XIO for $2,500: For a true audiophile experience, consider the Kef XIO. Music and movies sound incredibly balanced, clear, and loud, which makes sense—Kef is known for its high quality stereo speakers. Compared to lesser soundbars, you’ll notice the uptick in quality right away, which is expected at this $2,500 price point.
Bose Lifestyle Ultra for $1,099: During my testing, I kept going back to the Bose Lifestyle Ultra to play music. While the Focal and Sonos models have more of a bone-crunching bass and slightly better Dolby Atmos sound effects, for music, this Bose soundbar filled the room better. A nice bonus is that the Atmos support worked for albums like Rumors by Fleetwood Mac on TIDAL, which plays in surround sound.
Samsung Q990H for $2,000: An updated version of their flagship soundbar (the Samsung Q990D), the Samsung Q990H uses a new Sound Elevation feature to enhance dialogue. Not hearing what people say is annoying and one reason some of us enable subtitles, but the Q990H alleviated that pain point somewhat. Samsung also added new software optimizations for sound leveling and more distinct audio at lower frequencies.
Why would you want to expand with more speakers?
Several soundbars like the Sonos Arc Ultra and the Klipsch Flexus Core 300 allow you to add extra speakers and even a sub (or two!) to the standalone soundbar. While this might seem like overkill since the soundbar itself is capable of simulating surround sound effects, adding more speakers will help with realism. Spaceships will sound like they are flying from the back of the room and gunfire will ricochet from the left to the right.
Why is Dolby Atmos so important?
Dolby Atmos is the gold standard for surround sound audio, competing with the less common DTS:X specification. Soundbars use upfiring speakers to give you the impression that music and movie audio is coming from above you or from the sides. Note that Dolby Atmos is often only available at the premium tier level of streaming apps like Prime Video and Netflix.
What is room calibration?
Audio tends to bounce all around the room, echo down hallways, and escape through open windows. If you are in a tiny space, the sound won’t have anywhere to go. Room calibration is one way to compensate for room size and unusual architectural features. A soundbar like the Sonos Arc Ultra has a calibrate feature, where it emits a tone and then listens on its microphone, adjusting its audio for that particular room. Having tested many soundbars, good calibration can make a huge difference.

"In terms of where we are today, we are not currently contemplating a returning member program like the one you saw in January," Rolapp said.
Brooks Koepka took a deal that brought him back to the US tour at the start of the year but the arrangement was rejected by DeChambeau, Rahm and Smith.

Rory McIIroy says he is not worried that a deal with the DP World Tour has yet to be concluded, but he warned that cards being made available for the lower Challenger Series would be less attractive.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
Now a 19-year-old Kimi is dominating this year's F1 championship in only his second season.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he got into, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments - Antonelli out-qualified Russell at the second race of the season on the high-speed Jeddah street circuit and stuck it on pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He has taken the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli has taken six poles and six wins in 11 races and heads into the second half of the season, starting at the Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, with a 50-point lead in the championship, and well on course for his first world title. If it had not been for dodgy reliability, he could be even further ahead.
The extent of this turnaround has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
- Antonelli-Russell contrast could hardly be more stark 
  - Published7 June
- Antonelli says he still has questions to answer 
  - Published11 June
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says. "We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said: "Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Trump’s Warning Signs Are Coming to the Smithsonian
In a letter, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said that visitors “should know” about a museum director’s ideological bias.
Donald Trump has not forgotten his midsummer promise to publicly shame the Smithsonian. The Trump administration is currently preparing temporary signs that will accuse the National Museum of American History of ideological bias, according to a letter I obtained sent by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. The September 3 letter, which Burgum sent to Senator Jeff Merkley, says that the National Park Service is planning to add about a dozen signs outside the museum at an estimated cost of $84,000. Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, and Senator Lisa Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, requested information about the initiative after Trump signed an executive order in July calling for the signs to be added.
A person familiar with the plans described some of the preparations to me. Although the Park Service has an idea of the physical structure of the signs, what the signs will actually say and who is writing the text remains a mystery to people in the agency working on them, said the person, who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record. The letter from Burgum says that the signs are not finalized, but it offers a preview of what they might look like, describing a number of things “visitors should know” before they enter the museum. Burgum, whose department includes the Park Service, extensively quotes the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and criticizes outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, seeking to frame both as ideologues. The letter also calls out exhibitions and materials that have touched on groups the administration has gone after, such as undocumented immigrants and transgender Americans.
“The informational signage therefore will provide visitors with important context about the exhibits they are about to encounter and the personal viewpoints that the curators of the exhibits are seeking to advance,” the letter says. It goes on to justify the move, echoing a 162-page report on the museum released by the White House and asserting that the museum is pushing “ideologies that distract from a coherent and accurate presentation of America’s story.” Burgum adds, “This may be the first instance in which executive branch intervention of this nature has become Necessary.”
The Smithsonian, which is partially federally funded, has historically operated independently, has its own governing body, and is regarded in the wider museum world as measured in its approach. The institution has been heading off threats and criticism from the Trump administration since March 2025. Recently, the administration’s attention has turned to the American-history museum, which Trump made a number of curatorial demands of on social media this past Friday, including insisting that it remove an abstract sculpture and erect a 30-foot-tall George Washington statue in its place. Although the Trump administration has accused the Smithsonian, and specifically the American-history museum, of not being patriotic enough, the museum’s leadership has pointed to the abundance of patriotic material on display inside—368 objects and 340 labels on the founding era; 54 George Washington mentions, according to Hartig—and has maintained that telling the American story in its full complexity is a crucial part of its role.
“Our work is governed by the Smithsonian’s standards of scholarship, accuracy, independence, and nonpartisanship,” Hartig told two House committees this summer. “The museum does not take sides in America’s political debates. We preserve and document the evidence of American life in all its breadth, so that the public can encounter the past and draw their own conclusions.”
Trump’s executive order calling for the displays also ordered the Park Service to direct visitors to White House–approved resources on history and include a temporary exhibit about the signers of the Declaration of Independence. The order was unprecedented, pitting two prominent American institutions against each other.
Before this presidency, few might have imagined a showdown between park rangers and history curators on the National Mall. But the White House has had to get creative in trying to control the Smithsonian. Unlike the Park Service, the museum complex is insulated from the executive branch’s whims. The signs will attempt to put a frame around the Smithsonian’s work before visitors even reach the door.
The Burgum letter suggests that the signs will be direct in their criticism of Smithsonian leadership and materials. It points to comments Hartig has made during her tenure on topics such as the scope of U.S. history, whether the museum should have an “America First” mentality, and the acknowledgment of Native American lands—and suggests that these comments are necessary information for museum visitors. The letter says, “A commitment to public transparency means that visitors should be informed about Director Hartig’s and other Smithsonian leaders’ history of racial focus” and quotes Hartig acknowledging white privilege in a November 2020 lecture during the height of the Black Lives Matter movement. The letter further asserts that visitors should be informed about “Secretary Lonnie Bunch’s history of invidious discrimination and anti-white animus,” quoting from a 2000 essay the secretary wrote discussing racial discrimination in the museum profession.
The letter goes on to call out a handful of exhibits mentioned in Trump’s report, including three that touched on transgender themes. It also mentions resources that discuss why educators should use terms such as undocumented immigrant instead of illegal alien.
After the announcement about the signs this summer, I was curious to know who might be working on the text for the displays and contacted some of the Trump administration’s go-to history experts. PragerU and Hillsdale College both helped create the Freedom Truck mobile museums touring the country this year as part of Trump’s Freedom 250 celebrations, but a PragerU spokesperson told me that the right-leaning edutainment nonprofit is not working on the Smithsonian signs, and a Hillsdale spokesperson told me that the conservative college is not “institutionally” involved. “When the College works with the administration on educational projects (the Story of America video series, for instance), we’re glad to say so,” a spokesperson wrote to me in an email.
Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation who was called by Republicans to testify about the Smithsonian at the hearings this summer, declined to comment on any involvement, writing to me that “any conversation I have with any level of government, from local dog catcher to the top of the federal level is private and confidential. Otherwise, why would they trust me?” He added, “And, no, you shouldn’t take that as a confirmation of anything.” He told me by phone that he thinks the signs are clever and that “at best, it’s a medium-term solution or a short-term solution.”
Even under pressure, the Smithsonian has continued to tell the American story. On a recent afternoon at the National Museum of American History, staff sat in a small room behind tables dotted with objects from 9/11 and spoke directly with visitors. Some museumgoers left the exhibit moved to tears, staff told me.There was no descriptive wall text, no glass, just the museum in its purest form—a conversation between historians and the public.

Welsh actor Matthew Rhys makes Emmy Awards history with double win
- Published
Welsh actor Matthew Rhys has made history at the Emmy Awards, becoming the first person to win two lead acting prizes in one night.
Rhys was recognised at the prestigious US ceremony for his roles in supernatural TV comedy Widow's Bay and psychological thriller The Beast In Me.
On stage, Rhys dedicated his second award "to the great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurture as anyone else".
"We are a small but mighty nation. This is incredible," he said, adding "Diolch yn fawr iawn" - which means "thank you very much" in Welsh.
Other winners of the coveted US TV awards included Jean Smart, Allison Janney and Stephen Colbert, while there was an emotional tribute to Dolly Parton and a special humanitarian award for Michael J Fox.
Proud Rhys flies the flag
Rhys was named best lead actor in a limited series for The Beast In Me, then won best lead actor in a comedy for Widow's Bay.
A small number of actors, including Alan Alda, Sally Field, John Goodman, Elisabeth Moss and Ted Danson, have previously been nominated for two lead acting prizes in the same year, but Rhys is the first to score a double win.
Backstage, he said: "I'm from a small country, and I'm glad we get moments to kind of put our flag on the map and say, 'we punch higher than our weight sometimes'."
The Beast In Me follows a grieving author, played by Claire Danes, who becomes obsessed with a mysterious new neighbour suspected of murder.
Rhys said it was a "real shock" to win the award, and told Danes: "Thank you for letting me join the mystery machine and bringing out the beast, you are an intimidating scene partner, but I'm grateful for all this."
Later in the night, accepting the comedy actor prize for playing the mayor in Widow's Bay, he thanked the family, friends and colleagues who supported his career, including his parents who "kicked me on to the stage at a very early age".
A win for 'Lancashire lass'
His Widow's Bay co-star Kate O'Flynn was among the other British winners, being named best supporting comedy actress for playing Patricia in the show about a fictional island beset by a centuries-old curse.
"I want to thank our mayor and all the residents of Widow's Bay, in front and behind the camera," said O'Flynn, from Bury in Greater Manchester.
She added: "This is the role of a lifetime... Thank you for trusting this Lancashire lass to play a sassy broad like Patricia."
Smart and Janney equal Emmys record
Elsewhere, Jean Smart won best comedy actress for her role in the fifth and final series of Hacks.
It is the fifth Emmy she has won for the Hollywood satire. "What a ride this has been," Smart reflected, and joked that the audience only gave her a standing ovation "because I'm old".
It was Smart's eighth Emmy win in total, and The Diplomat's Allison Janney also picked up the eighth Emmy of her career, scoring best supporting actress in a drama series.
Smart and Janney have both now equalled the record for the most acting wins ever, shared with Cloris Leachman and Julia Louis-Dreyfus.
Despite her past success, Janney was a surprise winner on Monday and said she was "genuinely shocked" to see off competition from four stars of hospital drama The Pitt, among others.
Meanwhile, Rhea Seehorn won the first Emmy of her career for best lead actress in a drama series for Pluribus, the Apple TV show about a woman who discovers almost everyone else in the world has been taken over by a mysterious mind virus.
The Pitt scores top prize
The Pitt won best drama, traditionally seen as the most prestigious award of the night.
And the show's leading star Noah Wyle also picked up the trophy for best lead actor in a drama series for the second year in a row.
"I'm a Hollywood kid. I was raised on a television, and movie theaters were my place of worship," Wyle told the audience. "This is all I've ever wanted to do and this is the only club I've ever wanted to join. Thank you for accepting me."
The former ER star praised all of his fellow nominees, but singled out veteran British star Sir Gary Oldman, who was nominated for Slow Horses.
Wyle said he was inspired by Sir Gary's performance as Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious in 1986 film Sid and Nancy, recalling how at the time he thought it was "the benchmark that I want to hit one day in my career".
Hero's welcome for Michael J Fox
Michael J Fox was given a standing ovation as he received the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award for his campaigning for support for Parkinson's disease.
The Back to the Future star, 65, who founded the Michael J Fox Foundation in 2000, said: "When it starts getting tough, you show up, you help, and if you get a little joy while you're doing it, that's even better."
Appearing in a wheelchair, he told the audience he initially kept his condition secret after being diagnosed at the age of 29.
"I worried that it would affect my work and my relationships with audiences when they laughed if they knew I was sick," he said.
But he added: "Eventually, I understood that accepting Parkinson's didn't mean I had to surrender to it. It just meant doing what I could for everyone living with this disease. So I set out to advocate for patients' needs and raise money, and to propel us towards a cure."

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

A rumor circulated online in September 2026 that U.S. President Donald Trump shared a social media post threatening to turn off the water to Niagara Falls, a natural landmark famously shared by the U.S. and Canada, unless Canada agreed to pay a "100% tariff."
People on social media shared a purported screenshot of a Truth Social post that appeared to show Trump complaining about trade relations with Canada. The text read (emphasis ours):
NO MORE FREE NIAGARA FALLS FOR CANADA! For far too long, Canada has been enjoying our water, our views, our tourists, and our great American waterfall — NIAGARA FALLS! They get the Canadian side, they take the mist, the water, and billions of dollars from tourism, all while treating the United States unfairly on trade, lumber, energy, and so many other things. It's a total disgrace! Effective immediately, unless Canada agrees to pay a 100% TARIFF on Niagara Falls, we will be turning off the tap to the falls. That's right — NO WATER FOR CANADA! We have the control. We have the valves. We can reduce the flow, or shut it down completely, and we will if necessary. Canada has been taking advantage of the United States for decades, getting a world-famous natural resource basically for free while insulting our country and making it harder for American businesses. That ends now! If they want the water, the mist, the tourism, and the beauty of Niagara Falls, they must pay 100% or they don't get it. No more free rides, no more unfair treatment, and no more taking advantage of the United States. AMERICA FIRST! KEEP OUR WATER IN AMERICA! Thank you for your attention to this matter.
President DONALD J. TRUMP
The alleged post circulated online as Trump escalated an ongoing trade war with Canada, leading many Snopes readers to ask us whether it was real.
(@CoffinItUp on X)
The post was fake. Searches of the president's Truth Social and X accounts, as well as an online archive of Trump's Truth Social posts, revealed no such post.
Addtionally, searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo returned no relevant results from reputable news outlets. If the president had really said he planned on "turning off the tap to the falls," journalists with reputable news outlets such as The Associated Press or Reuters would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. That was not the case.
A reverse image search of the screenshot in question found only other social media accounts posting the same fake image.
The fake screenshot included a watermark for Real America's Voice, a conservative media outlet that highlights community contributions. However, a search of ARV's social media accounts and website revealed no mention of a Trump post discussing Niagara Falls.
The fake post circulated amid the United States' trade war with Canada, which has led to tit-for-tat tariffs on goods from both countries.
It appeared the fake post was created to poke fun at these events, including a real social media post from Trump about renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America."
Snopes could not determine the origin of the fake post or whether it was intended as satire, but its tone and relevance to current events matched the style of other fake Trump posts with satirical origins.
Trump couldn't unilaterally "turn off the tap" for Niagara Falls, as its water is managed by the 1950 Niagara Treaty, which established a committee that "oversees the water flow over the Niagara Falls for display purposes" and "determines the amount of water available for generating power."
The committee reports to both the U.S. and Canadian governments "and is comprised of government and private sector interests, such as Ontario Power Generation," according to the Government of Canada's website.
For further reading, we fact-checked a claim that Trump posted an animated video of himself repeatedly hitting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney with a hockey stick.

Delhi doc killed help for ‘prioritising his wife’s tasks’ over cleaning clinic: New revelations in June murder
The police filed a charge sheet, rejecting his mental health defense, citing circumstantial evidence and witness testimonies.
A 50-year-old dermatologist allegedly killed his domestic help after becoming enraged that she only prioritised his wife’s instructions over his demands that she clean his clinic, the Delhi Police said in a charge sheet filed on Monday in the June murder in southeast Delhi’s Kailash Hills, rejecting his initial defence of a “mental-health history”.
The 340-page charge sheet was filed before Saket judicial magistrate first class Deepika Thakran, with the matter fixed for consideration of cognisance on September 18.
Manish Gupta, who ran a dermatology clinic adjoining his flat at Mount Kailash Apartments, was arrested on June 18 for allegedly beating and murdering his 45-year-old domestic help, Meena Haldar. The chargesheet, a copy of which has been seen by HT, said Gupta had been unhappy with Haldar for some time and had repeatedly asked his wife to remove her from employment.
“... accused felt Haldar refused to listen to him and only gave preference to his wife’s instructions,” police said.

To substantiate this allegation, police recorded the statement of Haldar’s son, who allegedly told investigators that “his mother had complained that Gupta was frequently dissatisfied with her work and often scolded her”.
Police reject mental-health defence
The charge sheet also addresses the defence raised by Gupta and his family that he had been undergoing treatment for mental-health issues and had taken antidepressants for several years.
“Psychiatric evaluation of accused was conducted and past medical records and prescriptions were examined. No concrete proof of any recent behavioural change was found,” the charge sheet said.
Gupta had told investigators that he was distressed over his son’s studies, but police said no conclusive evidence had emerged linking it to the offence.

‘Dirty clinic’ trigger
According to the police, Haldar had worked for Gupta’s family for around 16 years and came to their home for routine work at around 10.30am on June 18. Gupta’s wife, police said, had left for work at 10am at her Ayurvedic clinic in Karol Bagh while their 18-year-old son was asleep in his room.
Police alleged Gupta asked Haldar to clean his adjoining dermatology clinic as customers were expected to arrive by 11am. When he returned a few minutes later and found the clinic unclean, he allegedly became furious and reprimanded her.
The charge sheet said Gupta then asked Haldar to clean the terrace storeroom. When Haldar entered, Gupta allegedly struck her on the head with the bat. “When she managed to flee the room, Gupta allegedly followed her onto the terrace and stabbed her six times in the neck,” the charge sheet said.
Police said the weapons had not been procured specifically for the murder.

At around 11.40am, a neighbour allegedly spotted Haldar lying in a pool of blood on the terrace and made the first PCR call. Gupta was subsequently arrested from his apartment.
The charge sheet names 43 witnesses and relies substantially on circumstantial evidence. Among the key witnesses is a neighbour who allegedly saw the attack from the ninth floor of the building.
Police also alleged that blood recovered from Gupta’s clothes matched Haldar’s blood. Gupta remains in judicial custody.
Gupta’s counsel, advocate Kamal Nayan Tiwari, told HT, “The police had earlier alleged black magic and now the theory of a dispute of Gupta with his wife over employment of the domestic help has come up. These are false theories by the police and the reality is that they are not able to trace the actual culprit.”
He added that there are multiple entries and exit points at the terrace where the body was found and “no eyewitness has said that Gupta had committed the murder”.
