It’s about 10 pm in Delhi, at the end of a long working weekday, when Mihir Ranjan sits down at his computer at home. Nothing particularly unusual about that. The IIM Ahmedabad graduate works at McKinsey & Company and spends much of his day in front of a screen, surrounded by the familiar rhythms of corporate life. There are meetings, presentations, spreadsheets, deadlines.
But now, late at night, the 25-year-old has got something else to look forward to.
“Now my second life begins,” he tells Sportstar.
He slips into something comfortable, closes the door to his room and keeps his phone on silent, so he won’t be disturbed. He puts on his headset and joins his teammates online on the League of Legends server. He’s not Mihir Ranjan anymore but ‘ Lotus’.
Joining in from Kochi is Akshaj ‘Kat Bot’ Shenoy, the team’s 24-year-old captain who is preparing for his MBA while helping run his father’s sanitaryware businesses. From Greater Noida, cloud engineering intern Aakash ‘ Infi’ Shandilya logs in. In Aligarh, Ahmed Shahid Israr, ‘ Nero’ to his teammates, is getting ready at the end of a day he’s spent studying to be a chemical engineer. Sanindhya ‘ Deadcorporal’ Malik will join from Mauritius, where he’s working to build the island’s telecommunications infrastructure. Rahul ‘ Bob’ Bisht, a product designer and entrepreneur from Bengaluru, is there as well.
Six men with entirely different lives, separated by thousands of kilometres and, in one case, an entire country, are about to become one team. But they aren’t just playing for fun. They are preparing for the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, where they will be representing India in League of Legends.
For most Indian athletes heading to the Asian Games, preparation for a major multi-sport event involves the familiar rituals of elite sport: camps, coaches, physiotherapists, strength and conditioning sessions, teammates living together, training facilities and months spent in one another’s company.
For India’s League of Legends team, preparation can look very different.
None of them makes their living from the game. Everyone is squeezing in practice time at night around their work and study commitments. Their training ground is not an academy or a national camp but the internet. Their meeting room is on Discord. They’ve never hung out together outside of competitions, where games are played over LAN (Local Area Network). The only time they’ll actually play together in person will be when they reach Nagoya in a few weeks’ time.
They do all of this while operating in an Indian esports ecosystem that is still tiny compared with those of the countries they are trying to compete against.
League of Legends is a multiplayer online battle arena, or MOBA. Five players work together to destroy the opposing team’s base, with each player taking on a different role. They have to make decisions individually and collectively, often in fractions of a second.
A player’s ability to control his champion — what players call “micro” — is only the foundation. The larger question is what five players do together: where they move, when they fight, which objectives they pursue and how they respond to the opposition.
“You can’t just play with the person if he’s just good. You have to have similar goals,” says Shenoy.
That distinction matters.
At the highest level, League is as much about how five people function together as how well any one of them can play. And building that understanding has been particularly difficult for India’s players because they have never had the infrastructure that exists in the game’s strongest countries.
Yet the team exists because one of its players decided that India’s best individuals should stop playing separately.
Akshaj had watched good Indian players become scattered across different teams, often playing alongside friends rather than the strongest players available. If the pool of elite players in India was small, his thinking went, why not put as many of them as possible on one team?
So in 2022 he started reaching out.
There was no national scouting programme identifying the players. No academy had developed them. No centralised system had brought them together.
They found one another online.
The team that eventually emerged became one of the strongest in the Indian League of Legends scene. And when League of Legends was introduced as a medal sport at the Asian Games, the same group would go on to qualify for the Games and compete in Hangzhou, where they eventually finished fifth.
Akshaj knows all too well just how different his team is.
“At the last Asian Games in Hangzhou, we were at the Games village food court when one of the Indian track and field athletes came up to us and said, ‘You guys are from the esports team, right?’” Akshaj recalls.
“I was like, ‘How did you guess?’ And he told me it was because we were the only team that came in different shapes and sizes. That was pretty funny, but it was also very accurate.”
The players don’t look, live or train like what most people imagine an athlete should.
But the Games have given them something the domestic ecosystem could not: a reason to see themselves as athletes representing their country. Games that had been played in bedrooms, offices and university rooms suddenly had a national-team consequence.
For some, it also provided the first real evidence to their families that this was more than a hobby.
Mihir’s parents, for example, had long struggled to understand exactly how serious his gaming was. That changed in a particularly strange way when officials from the National Anti-Doping Agency turned up at their house before the 2023 Asian Games. “I had been informed that I would probably be tested at some point, but still it was startling when officials arrived at my home in Delhi and told me I had to pee in a cup while they watched,” he recalls.
But what was initially a bit startling turned into a flex.
“My parents were at home when all this happened. Until that point, they were always having this bit of disbelief over how real my gaming was. I think they thought I was making some of it up and I’m not really going to the Asian Games,” he recalls.
The dope test changed that. His parents began questioning the official about where he was from and whether he was from the government. “For them, it was probably a weird matter of pride. The fact that I was drug tested actually gave some legitimacy to the whole thing,” he recalls.
There is a certain irony in the story of India’s League team. The players are legitimate enough to be subjected to the same anti-doping protocols as other athletes at a major multi-sport event. But they aren’t yet playing in an ecosystem capable of making all of them full-time professionals.
The team’s choice of practice time, late into the night, makes complete sense when you realise that’s the only time they all have to spare.
Mihir has made a deliberate choice not to become a full-time League player. It is not because he lacks the mentality of a professional athlete. Quite the opposite.
“I do consider myself a professional sports person, from a mentality perspective,” he says.
He has been playing the game for 13 years. He still loves it. He’s even convinced his girlfriend to play. And when he faces a better team, the competitive instinct kicks in. “I have a drive and a passion in me that I want to get as good as these guys, and I want to beat them someday,” he says.
But passion and economics are different things.
For Mihir, becoming a full-time League player in India did not make financial sense. The Indian ecosystem was not developed enough to support the sort of professional life he wanted.
“If I were to do this full time, how much can I really not even like, how much money can I make? I don’t think anyone does sports for money; you do it for the love of the game,” he says. “At that point, it was just becoming a bit apparent to me that I will not be able to sustain the kind of lifestyle I want. In this game at least.”
That decision reflects the reality of the Indian game.
They have players good enough to represent their country at the Asian Games, but they do not yet have an ecosystem capable of making all of them full-time professional athletes.
So they work and study. And then they play. Then they get back to working.
Rahul Bisht’s life is another example.
A BITS Pilani computer science graduate, Rahul is the oldest member of the squad at 29. He has spent eight to 10 years as a product designer and says he has worked with multiple companies. One of his projects was the initial design of the Paytm card machine in 2017 and 2018.
“I think that’s probably something that’s had much more of an impact than anything else I’ve done,” he says.
He has since moved on to other things and is now running his own technology startup. He has also tried his hand at other businesses, including a conventional haircutting salon, which he eventually sold.
Gaming, though, has been the one constant in his life. But even so, he has to prioritise.
“There’s no other time in which to practise other than late at night. That’s when we are all free. We’ll practise together until about 12 am. After that I’ll play a few personal games. Then I’ll work for the next few hours. I probably sleep for about four or five hours a night,” he says.
Sanindhya’s situation takes that contradiction to an almost comic extreme.
He works for Telecommunications Consultants India Ltd. (TCIL), a Government of India company. He is currently based in Mauritius, working on telecommunications infrastructure. He gets up around 7 a.m., goes to work and returns home before logging into League with his teammates.
His day job is maintaining telecommunications infrastructure in another country. His second job, effectively, is using that infrastructure to prepare for the Asian Games in Japan.
But sometimes even that connection fails.
Late last year, a submarine fibre optic cable serving Mauritius was damaged, leaving the internet operational but too slow for Sanindhya to play properly. For about a month, he couldn’t practise at the level he needed.
“All that is frustrating. And when I have my regular job to do, it gets really tiring to play after that. But when you have a goal, when you have passion, it doesn’t matter. You just do it. I don’t get tired when I log in and practise with my team. The tiredness just goes away,” he says.
Ahmed has had his own problems, though not quite on that scale. He admits he’s lost games for his team a couple of times after losing the Wi-Fi signal in Aligarh.
But for Ahmed, the youngest member of the team, the problem has sometimes been explaining to people that there is even a sport to prepare for.
When he applied to his university for a no-objection certificate because he would miss classes for the Asian Games, he had to explain what esports was, what game he played and why it qualified as a sporting event.
“They wanted to know if I even counted as an athlete, and I had to tell them yes, I do count as an athlete. It’s a medal event,” he says.
Things are starting to change, even if the pace is incremental.
Mihir noticed it at the last Asian Games itself. The other athletes they met did not necessarily know that esports was an event, but they were curious.
“A lot of athletes were a lot more open-minded than I expected,” he says. He thinks it’s because the Games coincided with the boom in mobile games such as PUBG.
“When you play something like that, you kind of realise, like, okay, there is even within something traditionally called a video game, there are levels,” he says.
“And the moment you establish that, you can have respect for anyone who has that level of skill or mastery or proficiency in anything.”
But both Ahmed and Mihir know these questions would have been easier to answer had India possessed the kind of League ecosystem that exists elsewhere.
It doesn’t.
Officially launched in 2009, League of Legends has a huge global player base, with an estimated eight million players competing simultaneously at its peak. India provides only a fraction of that. Akshaj estimates that the official Indian League community has around 4,000 to 5,000 members, with perhaps 1,000 active players. “We have probably one thousandth or one ten thousandth of the player base that South Korea has,” he says.
And there is a more immediate disadvantage.
India does not have a dedicated League of Legends server.
The players therefore use the Singapore server. At home, they experience relatively high latency of about 80-90 milliseconds, the time their inputs take to travel to the server and back. In the strongest League ecosystems, players can operate at dramatically lower latency.
At the Asian Games, where the game is played on a local server, the delay can fall to almost zero.
For a player who has spent years compensating for the delay, that creates a peculiar problem: the conditions suddenly become better, but the player isn’t necessarily immediately better in them.
“Playing at high ping is like playing with a weighted vest. The player becomes accustomed to the extra resistance, unconsciously compensating for the delay. At a tournament, the vest comes off, and suddenly everything is faster,” Mihir says.
That is one reason why the team’s preparation for Nagoya is so complicated. They are trying to train themselves to compete at a level they cannot fully reproduce at home.
But the server is only part of the problem.
The very depth of the competition in India is different.
Every League player can reach the highest rank on his own server, but those rankings do not necessarily mean the same thing across regions.
“A player who is Challenger (mathematically limited to the top 200 players or about 0.01 per cent of the players of any given server) on the Singapore server may actually be in Diamond (top 1-2 per cent) on the Korean server. The competition there is much deeper,” says Mihir.
India’s players can therefore dominate the ecosystem available to them without necessarily being tested against the best players in the world.
Hangzhou, where the team eventually finished fifth, provided the most painful demonstration of what that means.
India came through the group stage but ran into Vietnam in the quarterfinals.
The two matches lasted less than 20 minutes each. Games between equally matched opponents usually last between 30 and 35 minutes.
“Vietnam destroyed us,” Mihir admits.
It was not simply that Vietnam had better players. The Indian players realised they were operating in a fundamentally different system.
The Vietnamese team had players who had been playing professionally for years. They were salaried. They had competed at the World Championship. Their matches and careers were documented and easily available to study.
Although India now has an official team, with the players competing under the banner of S8UL, an esports and content creation platform in India, there’s still very much a gap between them and the top teams in the world.
Against Vietnam, the Indians discovered that some of the things they believed were possible limits of the game were not limits at all. Players could make mechanical plays that they simply had not encountered often enough in domestic competition to expect.
“They were doing things that we didn’t know were possible,” says Mihir.
The result forced them to rethink what “good” meant.
They had known they were strong.
They discovered they had not been strong enough.
Ahead of the 2026 Games, the team has done what it can to close that gap. Two players, Ahmed and Rahul, were brought in earlier this year to strengthen the outfit. They have set up scrims with top teams from South and West Asia. They don’t just play. They analyse results and plays, much in the way other sports teams might conduct post-match video analysis.
There is a lot of work that happens before they even enter a game.
And then, after all the analysis, they still have to play.
The players also reject the idea that because the sport is played sitting down, the body does not matter.
Aakash’s physique wouldn’t look out of place in a weightlifting squad. He’s a regular at the gym. Akshaj goes to the gym and sometimes plays badminton. Other members of the team make an effort to walk, exercise or simply get away from their desks between sessions.
The reason is partly performance and partly survival.
“They spend hours sitting. Their backs hurt. Their wrists take punishment. Their concentration has to remain high for extended periods,” says Aakash.
“The more physically fit we are, the better we play. It is about being able to sit down at a computer for hours and still have a functioning body and a sharp mind at the end of it.”
As much as they try, the players know there is a limit to how much they can improve under their current circumstances.
Some of it, like the lack of a country server, is out of their hands.
There is also the question of whether they could become a better team if they lived and trained together, as the very best teams do.
Probably.
But for now, even that is unrealistic.
“If we sit together and train for six months without doing anything else, we probably would be better, but right now even if you put us in the same city it wouldn’t work out,” says Sanindhya. “We all have our own lives to live, and we would probably still be playing out of our homes.”
Despite the challenges, there are moments when everything comes together.
To qualify for the Asian Games this time, India had to come from behind against Jordan. They were thousands of gold behind and down on objectives, with their qualification hopes at stake.
They recovered and won.
“That was a really hype moment,” says Aakash.
It is that sort of comeback that has kept the team going through the less glamorous parts of the job, the late-night practice sessions, the day jobs, the university commitments and the hours spent playing on a server outside the country.
There is also the simple pleasure of being around the people whose careers they once followed from a distance.
In Hangzhou, Aakash met Neeraj Chopra as well as other athletes from the Indian contingent. But he was far more excited when he met Lee Sang-hyeok, better known as Faker, the legendary Korean League player he had grown up watching online.
“He was always the guy I grew up watching on streams or in World Championships. It’s like if you got to meet Sachin [Tendulkar] or [Lionel] Messi,” Aakash says.
For a League of Legends player, Faker occupies a place in the sporting imagination that is difficult to explain to someone who has never played the game.
For Aakash, meeting him was one of the highlights of the Games.
But perhaps most special of all is simply getting the chance to represent the country.
Folded away in Mihir’s cupboard is a reminder of what all those late nights are for. It’s a couple of blue T-shirts with India written on them, his kit from Hangzhou.
“It’s basically passion that’s driving all of us. It’s not like we make a living out of this. I’m not someone who likes to show off my accomplishments. I don’t go and tell people about the fact that I’ve played for India at the Asian Games.
“But I don’t think there’s anything as special as getting the opportunity to wear the India jersey. I gave one set to my grandparents, and it was one of the most sentimental moments of my life.
“It didn’t matter what kind of sportsperson I was. It was the India jersey. And when you wear it, everything we do seems to be worth it,” he says.

The weather forecast might still be screaming “summer,” but the calendar betrays the truth: The holidays are going to be here before you know it. What’s usually billed as a jolly time of year can inspire dread — all the planning, all the spending, all the gathering can be exhausting, especially if you have a large family. Of course you’d like to put that off for as long as possible, right? Surely these conversations can wait until after Halloween.
Why you should start planning for the holidays now. Yes — in September.
Holiday planning can feel like a second, unpaid job. Here’s how to make it less stressful and more meaningful.
But waiting too long can actually make the holidays more stressful — and can put undue stress on the women in your life, who often shoulder the burden of organizing and planning. One lollygagger who delays in committing to a plan can prevent the rest of the family from booking flights or buying necessary supplies. What can seem like an annoying text from your sister reminding you to RSVP for Thanksgiving in early October only adds to her mental load in planning a dinner for 20 people.
“There can be an enormous amount of invisible labor involved in making the holiday magic happen, and that labor falls disproportionately on women and caregivers,” Jamila E. Holcomb, a licensed marriage and family therapist and associate teaching professor at Florida State University, told Vox. “If one person is coordinating everyone’s flights, planning meals, buying gifts, arranging childcare, communicating schedules, and managing family conflict, this can cause significant stress. It also makes one person responsible for everyone else’s experience, which is an unequal division of labor.”
The pressure to plan the “perfect” holiday isn’t merely logistical. In our hyper-connected and visible culture, people may feel pressured to orchestrate a high-stakes production that somehow is meaningful, memorable, and Instagram-worthy. In other words, planning for the holidays can be its own form of labor these days. To help make the whole ordeal more manageable for everyone — not just the hosts or Type A family members — five experts offered their advice on sharing responsibilities and actually enjoying the season.
Getting ahead of this coordination can help minimize the stress on everyone in a few months. So even though end-of-year celebrations might be the furthest thing from your mind, the ideal time to start planning them is, I’m sorry to say, right now. Here’s why early fall is the ideal time to start bugging the family group chat about the holidays.
Planning early will save you money
Prices on many goods, from flights to groceries, have increased over the last year. Getting ahead of these purchases before holiday crunch time can help you secure the best price and budget. While there’s no exact date for when to find the cheapest flights, travelers shouldn’t wait to book their tickets believing the price of gas will come down, travel expert Katy Nastro told Vox. In general, Nastro suggested locking in domestic travel between three and seven months ahead of time and between four and 10 months before international flights. “If you can get everything set… by the end of September for Thanksgiving, you’re going to be in a better place than most people,” Nastro said.
The same goes for rental cars: reserve them now. Unlike flights, you don’t need to pay for them in advance, so you can always cancel the reservation if your plans change. Nastro recommends the platform AutoSlash, which aggregates prices from multiple rental companies. “With rental cars, there’s only so much inventory and you want to even make sure that you have that option if you need it,” she said.
Early fall is also a great time to start shopping for presents, especially if you’re on a tight budget or coordinating a group gift with multiple people. Content creator and actor Rachel Ann Thomas and her eight siblings begin brainstorming ideas for their parents’ holiday gift in September or October every year. When holiday and event planner Lance “Mr. Christmas” Devereux decided to buy his loved ones matching Christmas pajamas, he started tracking down everyone’s sizes and placed the order before November. The earlier you nail down your shopping list, the sooner you can start looking for sales and slowly making purchases to save your bank account in December and avoid the stress of paying express shipping on last-minute gifts.
You need time to create new traditions and to split the labor of creating them
The holidays tend to be a period of nostalgia, and some families may heavily rely on time-honored traditions. But if you’ve outgrown them or just want to try something different, now is the best time to determine what would be meaningful, fun, and low-stress. Maybe that’s changing the location of a celebration from a grandparent’s home to a cousin’s; maybe that’s going on a fabulous vacation. The sooner you start thinking about it (and then commit to it), the easier everything else will be.
Holcomb, the therapist, suggested asking your loved ones now what they want the holiday to feel like, what traditions or events matter most, and what they realistically have the capacity for. You can also ask if there’s anything new or different they’d like to incorporate this year. Then you can come up with a game plan for how to share planning responsibilities. “Our cultural expectations around the holidays can make it easy to confuse a ‘successful’ holiday with a highly productive one,” Holcomb said. “Making time to ask these questions is especially important because we can disrupt traditional relational patterns and roles that we have taken for granted as normal.”
Both Holcomb and Thomas recommend creating a shared calendar or spreadsheet to keep track of logistics and divide responsibilities. In Thomas’s family, it’s called the Thomas Christmas Itinerary, and her mother starts it every September. “It basically lays out what the itinerary is for the whole Christmas time,” Thomas said. “What activities we’re doing, when we’re going over to grandparents’ houses, even down to what our dinner menus are.”
A spreadsheet can also be helpful for assigning and delegating tasks so that one person doesn’t end up managing everything by default as things come together at the last minute. So once you’ve committed to a general plan with your family, start breaking things down further — and proactively ask people to take ownership of different events and tasks (e.g., choosing a movie to take all the kids to see together, buying the snacks, and figuring out who is driving everyone). “If you’re hosting, you don’t have to simultaneously be the chef, activities director, chauffeur, mediator, and person responsible for everyone’s enjoyment,” Holcomb said.
Advance planning allows for the downtime everyone craves
When you are able to take a broad view of the holidays without the time crunch, you can be more deliberate with the itinerary and build in breaks. Events can be planned with intention, not obligation, and you’ll be able to zoom out and see that your calendar is getting overloaded before you’re completely underwater. “Another priority should be adding rest into the schedule before you need it,” Emily Barry, the senior vice president of holiday planning at online stationery and art marketplace Minted, told Vox. “Protect mornings or evenings when nothing is planned. Give yourself permission to stay inside instead of attending another event.”
“Don’t try to make the schedule perfect — make it meaningful,” Barry said. “Pick the one or two moments that are most important for everyone to be together, and build the rest of the holiday around those anchors.”
Slow planning over the course of a month or two ultimately makes it easier to offer flexibility to family members who may have traveled a considerable distance, have young kids, or are juggling multiple celebrations, Barry said — and to be realistic about what you personally can handle. “The goal is to spend meaningful time together, not create an itinerary that everyone has to execute perfectly,” she said.

South African president vows justice as more women's bodies found near Johannesburg
- Published
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings of several women in and around the town of Kempton Park, north-east of Johannesburg, over the last two months.
Another body was discovered on Tuesday morning and police say their investigation now includes the deaths of seven women most of whom have been found either partially or fully naked.
"These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," the president said.
Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings.
"[It] could be that it's a copycat crime that is happening right here but so far, no linkages as yet," police spokesperson Brig Athlenda Mathe said.
One arrest has been made in connection with the discovery of the first body. The person is still in police custody.
So far only two of the seven women have been identified.

On Monday, police said that one of them was Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a runner whose disappearance last week sparked a frantic and public search for her.
President Ramaphosa said he had directed that the cases be prioritised: "Our law enforcement agencies are working urgently to establish the facts, keep communities safe and bring the perpetrator or perpetrators to justice."
South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women.
The discoveries of the bodies have sparked outrage and fear across the country, with many criticising the authorities for failing to adequately protect women.
Moselakgomo was identified by her relatives on Monday after her body was discovered on Saturday. It was the 38-year-old's young daughter who raised the alarm about her disappearance after she failed to return from her daily run last Wednesday.
The body of the first woman was found in mid-July, the second in late August - the others were discovered this month, two in the last two days.
On Tuesday, police said that the body of woman found on 7 September in a town nearby Kempton Park was also being included - bringing the total number of bodies being investigated to seven.
"After noticing that there are bodies being picked up, we went back to our police stations… and unfortunately it came to light that a body of a female in her late 20s was observed in a river next to a mall," Maj-Gen Fred Kekana, acting police chief for Gauteng province, said at a briefing.
Police have urged women in the Kempton Park area - which is by South Africa's main international airport - to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".
South Africa's Commission for Gender Equality urged residents of Kempton Park to work with the police to find the perpetrators.
"These deaths are indicative that women in South Africa continue to face environments in which their ordinary freedom of movement can become a matter of life and death," it said.
"Women should be able to run, walk to work, use public transport, return home, visit friends and participate in community life without having to calculate whether an ordinary activity could place their lives at risk."

Iran war reshapes Brics ties but also exposes divisions
- Published
This weekend, some of the most powerful people in the world gathered in Delhi around a vast circular table.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that together, the leaders next to him should increasingly become "rule-shapers", not "rule-takers".
Among those listening were members of the Brics group, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.
These are hardly natural allies. They have histories of border disputes and even military confrontations.
India and China engaged in a deadly clash along their disputed border in 2020. Iran and the UAE have been on opposing ends of the war in the Middle East, with Tehran launching missiles and drones at its fellow Brics member as the conflict sent shockwaves across global economies.
The fact that India was able to gather these leaders together in person is a feat in and of itself and testament to its diplomatic reach. The weekend also provided a platform for countries to reassess their relationships in light of the Iran war.
But agreeing on what a new global order should look like and achieving clear, tangible outcomes was a much harder task, and that tension ran through this weekend's summit.
A counterweight to Western influence
For members such as China, Russia and Iran, Brics offers a vehicle to dilute the influence of the US and western Europe.
But India has been reluctant to cast Brics as an anti-Western bloc. Modi himself said at the summit that the group is "not against anyone".
That distinction matters for Delhi, which wants to preserve its relationships with nations at odds with each other.
"There are countries in the grouping which would like it to become anti-western, but it is not that," says Anil Trigunayat, a veteran Indian diplomat and former ambassador. What India has achieved, in his view, is a push for "strategic autonomy in an era of war" and initiatives to "enhance greater collaboration amongst themselves".
Inside the joint declaration
The summit succeeded in delivering a joint declaration when divisions among members have rarely been so glaring.
Twice earlier this year, meetings between Brics ministers had failed to produce a joint statement. This time a consensus was reached, but by side-stepping issues that members sharply disagree on, with few solutions.
The "New Delhi Declaration" was adopted on the first day of the summit. But what is striking is what it doesn't say.
On the war in the Middle East, the declaration urges "maximum restraint". It also condemns "attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities" but assigns no blame.
It reiterates support for a two-state solution, opposes forced displacement of Palestinians or actions that could "legitimise or prolong occupation", framing it carefully around existing UN resolutions.
It makes no mention at all of Russia's war in Ukraine, a departure from previous Brics declarations.
There is similar caution on trade. It lists concerns over "indiscriminate rising tariffs" and condemns unilateral sanctions but stops short of naming the US, and is likely to avoid Washington's ire.
Several Brics members would have been loath to draw President Donald Trump's anger, as he has previously called the group's proposals, including potentially linking central-bank digital currencies for cross-border trade, "anti-American".
"Not mentioning any country by name, even as they condemned the conflict in the Middle East, bears the hallmark of India," says Praveen Donthi, senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.
"I was pleasantly surprised that there was a strong reference to tariffs, because India could have wanted to be less direct about it, but perhaps this was a chance to convey their displeasure," he added.
Beyond the summit
In the wake of Trump's trade threats and the shock of the war in the Middle East, reshaping the global order has become a vital need for many member economies.
What the summit did provide is a platform for meetings that seemed hard to imagine just a few months ago.
Iran's Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince sat down for talks together - the highest-level face-to-face meeting known between the two countries since the war began.
This weekend offered Tehran a chance to show that it does not stand alone amid the US and Israel's military attacks and economic pressure.
As Iran tries to withstand US sanctions, Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast" and a naval blockade on its ports, Pezeshkian pressed for deeper economic ties with Brics members, including Malaysia, India and Ethiopia.
As for China, this was President Xi's first visit to Delhi in seven years. There has been deep mistrust between China and India since the 2020 border dispute, but those tensions have eased. There is also a large trade imbalance, with a deficit tilting heavily in China's favour.
There was a cordial handshake between Xi and Modi, not the latter's signature hug. Xi also stayed for less than 24 hours, skipping the gala dinner hosted by Modi on Saturday night.
But the weekend was still a big moment for two countries with such a difficult relationship. According to official readouts, the two leaders agreed to strengthen business ties and transport links and address barriers to trade.
Trigunayat believes this is part of a gradual warming of relations in recent years, and that there is a will on both sides to work together. But whether it will produce substantial progress remains to be seen.
"I always say we have to trust, but verify first," he says.
What comes next?
The summit showed that Brics can create space for rivals to talk and manoeuvre outside Western-dominated institutions.
The harder question is what happens next. It's clear that members agree they need a new global order more than ever, but what exactly should replace it and how to get there is far more challenging to answer.

FDA suspends licence of Mumbai’s Cafe Mondegar for food safety violations
FDA allegedly found that the drainage system near the food preparation area was inadequate and created a risk of cross-contamination
The Food and Drugs Administration (FDA) has suspended the licence of Mumbai’s iconic restaurant Cafe Mondegar at Colaba following alleged deficiencies relating to food safety and hygiene, an official statement said.
During its inspection on September 12, the FDA found that the drainage system near the food preparation area was inadequate and created a risk of cross-contamination. It also found that the equipment was not being properly cleaned and sanitised, and its flooring was damaged due to dampness.
Besides, the team also found deficiencies in the maintaining temperatures for its food items. It said hot food items were not being stored at the requisite temperature of above 60°C, and that cold storage was not being maintained at the required temperature of below 5°C. Improper thawing of food items and failure to rapidly cool cooked food items as required were also found.
Cafe Mondegar was started in 1932 as an Irani Cafe but was converted into a restaurant in the 1990s. It was the first restaurant in the city to introduce a jukebox in the mid-90’s and was particularly known for cartoonist Mario Miranda’s murals on its walls and ceiling.
HT attempted to contact managing partner Hoshang Yazdegardi, but he did not respond.

The FDA also suspended the licence of Maharashtra Biryani Center at Hanuman Nagar, Kandivli (E), following violations on Sep 11, and those of three other food outlets from Mumbai apart from two others in Pune.
Besides, FDA teams have also seized 30 litres of milk and 4,139 kg of dairy and sweets stock (khoya, paneer, ghee, peda, halwa, shrikhand, butter, milk powder, etc.) valid at over ₹15.5 lakh.
As part of its drive between September 11 and 14, FDA inspected 38 food establishments and collected 47 food samples such as milk, khoya, ghee, sweets, etc for testing.

For a long time, fungal infections have meant itchy skin, discoloured nails and sometimes hair loss.
These symptoms are collectively called dermatophytosis and are caused by a group of fungi called dermatophytes.
‘’Unfortunately, immunocompromised patients can get lesions all over their body. The itchiness and the lesions can get so severe that people even get suicidal thoughts,” said Shivaprakash Rudramurthy, professor of medical mycology at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh.
Global warming
Dermatophytes are molds: fungi that grow in long strands. The other common category of fungi is yeast, which are single, oval-shaped cells. Among the yeasts, Candida auris is rapidly emerging as a multidrug resistant pathogen in ICU facilities. It enters the blood stream and causes severe infections, most of which are untreatable by the available antifungals. According to Prof. Rudramurthy, those infected suffer a 30-40% mortality rate.
C. auris has become a menace only in the last two decades. The first report was in 2009 in Japan. Several other fungal species have become more pathogenic only in recent times. The cause of this rise remains unresolved but scientists and medical doctors have some ideas.
Fungi grow best in damp places below 30° C, so they can grow on our skin, especially in moist areas of the body, like armpits and the genital area. However, bloodstream infections in humans were rare because they could not survive in the body’s 37° C temperature.
“Fungal infections are common in cold-blooded animals with lower body temperatures,” Sriram Varahan, a mycologist at CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad, said.
“But global warming puts a selective pressure on fungi such that only the more heat-tolerant ones survive. These ones can survive inside our bodies too, if they gain access to it. This is called the fungal infection — mammalian selection hypothesis.”
Clinical samples
Today, roughly 20% of infections reported in hospitals are fungal in nature — yet most hospitals in India lack the capabilities and infrastructure to identify fungal pathogens, Prof Rudramurthy said.
This prompted PGIMER to begin storing fungal pathogens some 25 years ago. Today, the institute holds a stock of 15,000 clinical fungal isolates across India and helps other medical centres and clinicians identify and culture them for study, free of cost.
The C. auris isolates from PGIMER’s repository have come handy for Kaustuv Sanyal and his research associate Aswathy Narayanan, both at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru. They study how fungal pathogens divide and their genomes evolve.
In a recent study published in Nature Communications, they characterised the clinical isolates of C. auris found across India. Their focus was the pathogen’s ability to resist antifungals. They were able to establish their findings in patient samples and go beyond earlier studies in model systems.
“More than 90% clinical isolates of C. auris are resistant to common azole-based antifungals, such as fluconazole,” Prof. Sanyal said. Some “30% of them are resistant to another class of antifungals called the polyenes. They mostly respond to a different class of antifungals called the echinocandins.”
A drug may not work on a pathogen for many reasons, including the drug’s target becoming mutated or the drug’s effect being negated by the pathogen’s own biomolecules. Dr. Narayanan and her collaborators at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram, found significant changes in drug-resistant C. auris genomes that could explain why Indian clinical isolates were able to resist azoles and echinocandins.
Susceptibility tests
A fungal cell has two protective layers surrounding it. The outermost is the cell wall and the inner one is the cell membrane. Azole and polyene antifungals target a fat called ergosterol that is enriched in the cell membrane. Echinocandins target the cell wall.
“When we grow C. auris isolates in the presence of fluconazole, the pathogen fights back by making extra copies of the Erg 11 gene. This in turn helps in higher production of ergosterol, thereby eliminating the effect of the azole drug,” Dr Narayanan said.
The study found parts in the C. auris genome where additional copies of the Erg11 gene were present.
With echinocandin drugs such as caspofungin, the team found mutations in the Fks1 gene that allowed the pathogen to resist the drug’s action. The team also found genetic changes promoting higher tolerance of echinocandins.
“Fks1 mutations can enable C. auris to survive even caspofungin doses up to 16 ug/ml. That means a patient with such a pathogen will need the drug at a concentration higher than 16 ug/ml,” Prof. Sanyal said. “Today, clinicians would not know that because they test the pathogen’s ability to survive only until 2 µg/mL of caspofungin — as defined by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and followed globally.”
The logical thing for clinicians would be to look for mutations like in the Fks1 gene and decide the limits for tests to decide the antifungal dose for patients. But due to associated costs, a more practical way is to increase the limits of susceptibility tests for caspofungin to higher than 16 ug/ml, Prof. Sanyal added.
C. auris, without any specific gene mutation or gene duplication, still responds to high concentrations of caspofungin in unexpected ways. While the pathogen dies at lower concentrations of the drug, at exceptionally high ones, it survives. This is paradoxical.
“This is because caspofungin at high doses activates compensatory pathways in the fungus,” Prof. Sanyal explained. “The fungus starts producing chitin, the raw material of the fungal cell wall, in large quantities. Any damage that caspofungin brings about on the cell wall is compensated by the extra chitin production. And thus the cell wall remains intact despite the antifungal.”
Such examples of paradoxical growth are called the Eagle effect, named for the U.S. pathologist Harry Eagle.
Beyond the arms race
The studies underline the importance of clinicians conducting more nuanced susceptibility tests to decide the antifungal doses. They show that fungi are protected from antifungals by genetic mutations as well as by making more copies of protective genes.
Prof. Sanyal also stressed on the need for a combination of therapies to target cellular compensatory pathways, keeping the major antifungals effective against drug-tolerant species.
However, Dr. Varahan said he believed scientists and doctors need to think of gentler alternatives: “When we target [a molecule] without which an organism cannot live at all, evolution ensures that its population survives with a changed molecule. So instead of participating in an arms race, it is perhaps better to target the less critical molecular pathways, inhibition of which will allow the pathogen to still survive but not cause a disease.”
It seems the idea of dousing fungal pathogens with antifungals is nearing its end. The next-generation of antifungals will need more planning.

Rise and shine, everyone, another busy day is on the way. And it is getting off to a pleasant start here on the Pharmalot campus, where clear blue skies and comfy breezes are greeting us. A Bigoted Outburst Against Texas Sports Fans
Bo French’s xenophobia should force Republicans to confront the prejudice in their ranks.
On Saturday night, college-football fans in Texas were blessed with a moment of collective ecstasy. Their Longhorns were playing Ohio State, the nation’s No. 1 team, and trailed by 20 points. Then they improbably scored three touchdowns in the fourth quarter. A frenzy shook the stadium as more than 100,000 people, most in team colors, celebrated the stunning comeback. But Bo French, the Republican nominee for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, was upset by what he saw in the crowd.
“I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” he wrote yesterday on X, where he posted an image of a cluster of fans at the stadium who appeared to be of South Asian ancestry. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” Dispelling any doubts about his meaning, he continued: “I weep for the families in Texas who can’t get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans.” He added, “Like body-cams exposed criminals, social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners.”
In reality, there is no reason to assume that the students in the photograph are foreigners, and Texas does not prioritize foreigners over Texans. Quite the contrary. Ninety percent of slots for first-year students at UT Austin are reserved for Texas residents. Foreign students even pay higher tuition, which effectively acts as a subsidy for Texas residents at the college. But some people are so psychologically distressed by diversity and difference that their reactions have little to do with the facts on the ground.
Some prominent Republicans have objected to the latest––but not the only––bigoted remarks from French. Senator John Cornyn of Texas, who has held office since 2002, posted on X, “Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized.” He warned, “This is how great political parties self destruct.”
But others seemed more incensed by Cornyn’s critique than they were by French’s remarks. A Republican state legislator from North Dakota wrote, “Eat shit you fucking loser.” John Doyle, who has a show for the populist-right outlet Blaze Media, wrote, “For now we can ignore how unqualified you are to speak on behalf of ‘The Republican Party’ as someone who reflexively embraces liberal moralizing about ‘racism’ and ‘intolerance’ in response to a Patriot acknowledging that Texans didn’t ask for their state to become a playground for the third world.”
Changes to content moderation on X under Elon Musk’s ownership––not to mention rhetoric and actions within the federal government––have made clear how common bigoted identitarianism is in the GOP coalition. Republicans who believe in the values of Christianity, the creed of the Declaration of Independence, or the moral imperative to judge people as individuals need to confront the prejudice in their ranks.
The identitarian right’s rise has lessons for progressives too. First, seeking to raise the salience of race and ethnicity in American politics and culture was a mistake––as ought to have been clear by 2016, when Donald Trump exploited that heightened salience for his own ends. As the political scientist Karen Stenner argued in her 2005 book, causing people who are uncomfortable with difference to perceive it as a threat to social cohesion can activate a latent predisposition toward intolerance.
Second, not only was embracing race as a factor in university admissions unpopular with voters, so much so that it lost ballot initiatives even in left-leaning California; colleges’ discrimination against white people and Asians also stoked racial resentment by putting identity groups in a zero-sum competition.
And third, once the left began to treat mere departures from left-identitarian shibboleths as racist, it became harder to stigmatize actual racism or xenophobia, as surely as crying wolf at every shih tzu, tabby cat, and hamster would make it harder to warn against actual wolves on the hunt.
The Republican and Democratic Parties could do well in future elections to revive a straightforward, morally sound position: Judge others by the content of their character, not by the color of their skin. That ethos needn’t foreclose all disagreements about immigration. And one needn’t pretend not to notice racial and ethnic diversity. But insofar as a diverse crowd cheering for a Longhorn victory implies anything about past or present immigration and its effects, it is this: People of all races and ethnicities have already assimilated into the quasi-religion of Texas football, one of America’s most distinctive cultural phenomena.
If, heaven forbid, this great multiethnic nation is ever invaded by a foreign power, there is evidence that the people in that Texas stadium could unite in common cause without regard to race or ancestry. Bo French, who feels distress at seeing his neighbors come together, may lack that ability––a weakness that makes him unfit for office in America.

Brazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest crisis since the return of democracy in the 1980s, as two rival judges lock horns on the eve of the presidential election with unpredictable consequences for Latin America’s largest democracy.
The politically charged dispute exploded into public view on Tuesday as judges traded insults and accusations during a heated supreme court hearing that was livestreamed into millions of Brazilian homes.
During one of the most ferocious exchanges, one of the judges at the eye of the storm, Alexandre de Moraes, berated his rival, André Mendonça: “You’re at the service of a political group that tried to launch a coup in this country!”
“It’s a lie!” Mendonça cried back.
Minutes later, a third judge, Gilmar Mendes, angrily accused Mendonça of weaponizing the court’s work to cause political chaos and influence October’s presidential election.
“Don’t point your finger at me, Minister Gilmar! Don’t point your finger! You’re not talking to any old person! Show some respect to this court!” Mendonça warned Mendes, who shot back: “Respect is earned, not given.”
The courtroom drama – in many ways a proxy for the electoral battle between the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro – pits Moraes, a pugnacious shaven-headed martial arts practitioner, against Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who is the only openly evangelical member of the 11-seat court.
Moraes was appointed almost a decade ago by rightwing president Michel Temer. But the 57-year-old judge is widely associated with Lula thanks to his successful prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for plotting a botched coup after losing the 2022 election to the leftwing veteran.
Mendonça, meanwhile, was named during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018-23 presidency and leftwingers widely view him as a stooge for the disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his failed power grab.
With less than three weeks to go until the election, the two judges have gone to war, as Brazil’s biggest-ever banking scandal has snowballed into a judicial and political crisis of similarly shocking proportions.
The Banco Master scandal began last November when the playboy owner of that collapsed bank, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested by federal police as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta.
Investigations uncovered apparent links between the jailed banker and an astonishing panoply of figures from Brazil’s political and judicial elite, foremost among them Flávio Bolsonaro and Moraes. Other members of the supreme court and their relatives have also been linked to Vorcaro.
Mendonça has been accused of deliberately fast-tracking the investigation into Moraes, while stalling the inquiry into Vorcaro’s ties to the Bolsonaros and the banker’s bankrolling of a film about Jair Bolsonaro.
Earlier this month, Mendonça unsealed an explosive police dossier relating to the Banco Master investigation that contained compromising WhatsApp exchanges apparently between Vorcaro and Moraes as well as a copy of a $25m contract between Banco Master and the law firm of Moraes’s wife. In one text message, sent two days before his arrest, Vorcaro asked Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?”
Moraes hit back on the eve of Tuesday’s hearing, claiming he was being smeared with politically-motivated “criminal lies” as part of a revenge attack by the rightwing forces behind the coup attempt that culminated in the January 2023 riots in Brasília. Moraes also alleged that the attacks on him involved “external actors” and were part of a possible foreign attempt to interfere in Brazil’s election.
The Moraes/Mendonça tussle reached a crescendo on Tuesday as supreme court judges convened in Brasília to decide whether an investigation should be opened into Moraes’s conduct. Moraes has demanded an investigation into Mendonça.
The judicial scandal has exploded just as Brazil’s election campaign is coming to a head, with polls suggesting a dead heat between Lula and Bolsonaro, who are likely to face off in a second-round run-off on 25 October.
“The timing is awful. We are just a few weeks away from elections that already look to be challenging for a democracy that has been struggling to deal with extremist and anti-democratic groups that continue to be an important political force in the country. So I think we have a perfect storm here,” said Eloísa Machado, a constitutional law professor who follows the supreme court.
Machado said Lula had “absolutely nothing to do” with the scandal engulfing Moraes and the supreme court, noting how the leftwing president had not appointed the judge.
Even so, the crisis looks likely to hurt Lula’s chances of winning a historic fourth term, given the widespread public association between him and Moraes because of the judge’s involvement in Jair Bolsonaro’s jailing.
In a social media video posted as Tuesday’s hearing played out, Flávio Bolsonaro blamed the judicial scandal on Lula’s administration but made no mention of his own alleged ties to Vorcaro.
“This [is happening] because the current government ... is part of this decaying system and we are now seeing this rotten system reveal itself before the eyes of the entire nation,” Bolsonaro said, claiming Lula had “shared power” with Moraes.
Thomas Traumann, a political analyst, predicted the scandal would accelerate the election campaign’s descent into a carnival of mudslinging, as both sides battled to convince voters of their rival’s sins.
“This campaign is going to get dirtier much faster than we had expected,” he said.

The story so far: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) summoned Meta officials for a hearing on Wednesday (September 9, 2026) as a part of an inquiry on child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) on Instagram. An investigation by British public broadcaster BBC threw up many ads that linked out to CSEAM on other platforms. The IT Ministry has also summoned the company on the issue.
What did the BBC investigation show?
In July, BBC reported that the organisation saw dozens of ads promoting CSEAM on Instagram with a test account. CSEAM is banned around the world, and attracts strict criminal penalties. Meta said in a statement, “Before these cases were brought to our attention, our enforcement systems had already identified and disabled several of the violating ads and the accounts behind them.”
The company said that it automatically removes millions of CSAM posting accounts each year, but that “no system is perfect and that determined criminals will continue to try to exploit our platform”. This month, the Tech Transparency Project reported that it found hundreds of CSAM ads on Facebook and Instagram, including some that were served to India.
Why are CSEAM ads appearing on Instagram?
While social media platforms prohibit CSEAM, automatic moderation systems, that use some AI to detect unlawful media, are not able to catch all violative submissions. The Tech Transparency Project, a US-based nonprofit, said that what Meta was doing was not enough even within the scope of what it could. The nonprofit said that even in cases where Meta was taking down CSEAM, it was tagging the ads as adult sexual content, and so “may be undercounting instances of child sexual abuse”.
While the firm revised this information for ads reported by TTP, “did not fix the flow of child exploitation content in its advertising system,” and continued to show CSEAM ads to certain audiences, the nonprofit said. One of the ads appeared to feature an unidentified “underaged European royal,” TTP said.
Amusing or addictive? The algorithms powering our social feeds
Many such ads were placed by “resellers” for ad spots on Meta’s platforms based in China, who account for billions of dollars of ad revenue. TTP pointed to a Reuters report that indicated that ads going through this channel were subject to a more relaxed enforcement regime, where the platform earned $18 billion in 2024. This channel is intended for Chinese firms who want to advertise to overseas customers.
Even with a human reporting CSEAM posts, action was not guaranteed, TTP found. “With 57% (73) of the CSAM ads reported to Meta, the company sent back a message that said, “We’ve taken a look and found that this ad doesn’t go against our Advertising Standards”,”, TTP said.
What was NCPCR’s reaction to the report?
NCPCR issued a notice on July 3, the same day the BBC report came out, demanding an explanation from the company. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) also sought an explanation from the company.
Shortly after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s July 23 video message to Indian youth was briefly removed from Facebook due to an “error,” MeitY summoned Meta’s global public affairs director Joel Kaplan to demand an explanation on that removal. In that meeting, the BBC reporting was also discussed. The summoning came as the government sent a massive volume of takedown notices for Instagram posts on the Jantar Mantar protests, and footage from the protests and the ensuing police crackdown went viral.
Meta provided written responses to both MeitY and NCPCR. The latter declined a Right to Information request by The Hindu for a copy of the company’s response, arguing that providing this information would impede its investigation.
After the written response, Meta officials were summoned by NCPCR this month. Neither side provided a description of the meeting.
What powers does NCPCR have to conduct an inquiry like this?
Like the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the NCPCR’s founding law, the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, gives the body the powers of a civil court under the Criminal Procedure Code (replaced recently by the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita Bill, 2023).
As such, it has the statutory power to demand explanations on issues of child safety from private organisations and can demand reports from law enforcement.
NCPCR’s remit includes “matters relating to children in need of special care and protection including children in distress,marginalized and disadvantaged children, children in conflict with law, juveniles, children without family and children of prisoners and recommend appropriate remedial measures,” and to “[i]nquire into complaints [relating to] non implementation of laws providing for protection and development of children,” the commission said.
NCPCR has in the past issued notices to firms like Netflix in response to the show Bombay Begums, and to Bourn Vita maker Mondelez over sugar content in their malt powder.
