Colombian ex-foreign minister charged over nanny's lie detector test
- Published
Prosecutors in Colombia have accused former foreign minister Laura Sarabia of abusing her power after she made her nanny take a lie detector test.
The scandal erupted in 2023, when Colombian news weekly Semana reported that a woman Sarabia had employed to look after her son had been hooked up to a polygraph and questioned over the alleged disappearance of a case full of cash from Sarabia's flat.
Sarabia, who was the chief of staff for President Gustavo Petro at the time, resigned in June 2023 but was later appointed as foreign minister and, following her resignation from that post, as Colombia's ambassador to the United Kingdom.
She has denied any wrongdoing.
The 32-year-old was one of the closest advisers of Gustavo Petro, Colombia's first left-wing president, who governed from 2022 to August this year.
Prosecutors said Sarabia abused her position as his chief of staff by ordering police to question her nanny, Marelbys Meza, over the alleged disappearance of the cash, which was said to amount to several thousands of dollars.
Meza told Semana that she was taken by Sarabia's driver to an official building opposite the presidential palace, saying it felt like "a kidnapping".
Police officers then attached her to a polygraph machine and questioned her about the alleged disappearance of the money.
Meza denied having stolen any money during the test, and has consistently denied any wrongdoing in media interviews since.
Prosecutors allege that in ordering police to question Meza, Sarabia improperly used state resources to investigate a matter which was not related to her official post.
Sarabia rejected the accusation during a hearing, without going into further details.
She had earlier said in a social media post that her lawyers were dealing with the issue and that she respected the judicial authorities and trusted their decisions.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

One person has died and more than 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the country’s government says.
The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail with more than 40 passengers and crew on Friday from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.
“Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones,” Vanuatu prime minister Jotham Napat’s office said in a statement on Sunday.
“Search and rescue operations are continuing.”
Fifteen of those onboard have been “accounted for alive” and one body has been recovered, the statement said.
“Over 30 people remain missing at sea,” it said.
“To the survivors, we pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of those missing and those we have lost, please know that the nation stands with you in this time of grief.”
An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.
“This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement added.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in New Caledonia said it was assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday morning.
The centre said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.
Matai Seremaiah, the member of parliament for Luganville who is assisting in the search, said efforts would concentrate on the south-east coast where currents may have carried survivors.

Police detain dozens at an Istanbul courthouse protest over LGBTQ+ crackdown
Police have detained dozens of demonstrators outside a courthouse in Istanbul
ISTANBUL -- Police on Tuesday detained dozens of demonstrators who staged a protest outside a courthouse in Istanbul to demand the release of LGBTQ+ activists taken into custody during a sweeping crackdown days earlier.
Police surrounded the demonstrators outside the Caglayan courthouse before detaining them.
On Sunday, Turkish authorities cracked down on multiple LGBTQ+ groups and individuals, detaining dozens of members, breaking into association offices and raiding popular hangouts. The organizations’ websites were also blocked.
The crackdown aimed to “protect children, the institution of the family, and public order,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said. He said the operation, dubbed “My Family is Safe,” targeted 162 suspects, nine associations and 13 businesses.
On Tuesday, Michael O’Flaherty, the Strasbourg, France-based Council of Europe’s Commissioner for Human Rights, expressed concerns over the raids and detentions, saying “mere references to ‘family values’ or ‘protection of children’ cannot serve as legal justification for human rights restrictions.”
“I call on the Turkish authorities to release anyone detained for engaging in human rights or civil society work,” he said in a statement, adding that he would continue to monitor the situation.
Outside the courthouse, demonstrators carried banners reading: “Being LGBT+ and organizing is not a crime” and chanted slogans in support of LGBTQ+ rights before police intervened.
“We are going through a period where there is an attempt by the ruling power to portray LGBT+ people as the cause of every problem in this society,” 36-year old Banu Aslan, one of the protesters, told The Associated Press.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling party, which has roots in Turkey’s Islamic movement, has been increasingly vocal against LGBTQ+ groups in a bid to consolidate the more conservative elements of its base. In 2015, it banned Istanbul Pride, which had tens of thousands of attendees in previous years. Since then, authorities have violently dispersed any attempted gatherings for Pride.
This summer, an LGBTQ+ cruise ship that tours the Mediterranean and has docked in Turkey multiple times in the past was refused permission to dock there.

The US House of Representatives on Tuesday advanced a bill that could allow US President Donald Trump to impose 100 per cent tariffs on India and other major buyers of Russian oil and gas, bringing the measure closer to becoming law. The bill also seeks to extend sanctions on Russia and Iran.
The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 cleared a key procedural vote by 214-211, with two Democrats joining Republicans in backing the measure. The House is expected to hold a final vote on the bill on Wednesday.
For India, the bill is significant because it could give Trump the authority to impose punitive tariffs on countries that continue buying Russian energy. India is among Russia's major oil buyers and has sharply increased its purchases of discounted Russian crude since the Ukraine war began.
The Senate had already passed the bill on August 7 by an overwhelming 86-11 vote. The Senate version does not specifically name India or China. Instead, it refers to the five largest importers of Russian oil and gas by volume.
If the House passes the bill, it will have to be sent to Trump for his signature before it can become law.
What the bill means for India
The proposed measure could expose Indian exports to the US to tariffs of up to 100 per cent if Trump uses the authority against countries buying Russian energy.
The bill is aimed at putting further economic pressure on Moscow by targeting countries that continue to trade in Russian oil and gas. The US has argued that revenue from Russia's crude oil trade helps fund its war against Ukraine.
The measure would also target Russia's leadership and energy sector, along with the "shadow fleet" of vessels used to transport Russian oil and evade sanctions.
The potential tariff threat comes as India continues to balance its energy needs and its ties with both Russia and the US.
House vote shocks Democrats
The procedural vote was approved 214-211 after two Democratic lawmakers broke ranks and voted with Republicans, a move that reportedly shocked House Democratic leadership.
Democratic Congressman Gregory Meeks, the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, had opposed the legislation on Monday. He argued that it would give Trump broad powers to impose tariffs without sufficient safeguards.
The bill is now expected to face a final House vote on Wednesday.
The timing is also significant as pro-Ukraine groups have intensified lobbying efforts in Washington.
The Ukraine Action Summit, organised by the American Coalition for Ukraine, is currently being held in Washington to lobby US lawmakers for continued support for Kyiv.
What happens next
The House is due to break for an early recess on Thursday and is expected to reconvene on November 9 after the US midterm elections.
The immediate focus is therefore on Wednesday's vote. If the House approves the legislation, it will move to the next stage of the lawmaking process and could eventually reach Trump's desk.

Iran denounces Austria for blocking its nuclear chief from a meeting in Vienna
Iran has condemned the exclusion of its Atomic Energy Organization head from the UN nuclear agency's meeting in Vienna
VIENNA -- Iran on Monday condemned the exclusion of the head of its Atomic Energy Organization from the annual gathering of the United Nations nuclear agency in Vienna saying that it constitutes “a serious breach” of Tehran's rights as a member nation.
“By obstructing our full and effective participation, the denial of access contravenes both the letter and the spirit of the legal framework” governing attendance at meetings of the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran’s ambassador to the agency, Reza Najafi, told delegates at its general conference.
Najafi criticized Austria, the host country of the IAEA and other U.N. organizations, saying that Vienna’s decision not to grant a visa to Mohammad Eslami “violates the host country’s obligation.”
The Russian ambassador to the U.N. in Vienna, Mikhail Ulyanov, echoed Iran’s remarks, saying that Austria had “grossly violated” its obligations as host nation of the IAEA.
Western nations had “unleashed a genuine campaign of visa-related abuses so as to settle scores with countries they deem to be undesirable,” he said.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei on Monday likewise condemned Austria’s refusal to issue a visa to Eslami.
Baghaei said Tehran protested the decision and summoned the Austrian chargé d’affaires, saying Austria was obligated as the host country to issue the visas.
Austria responded by saying a U.N. Security Council committee had rejected Austria’s request to exempt Eslami from the travel ban.
“As a consequence, Austria was obliged to deny one member of the Iranian delegation the entry into its territory,” said Christian Ebner, Austria’s ambassador to the IAEA.
As the host of international organizations, Austria can request exemptions from travel bans to enable sanctioned officials to attend international conferences at the U.N. in Vienna.
The decision whether to grant the waiver rests with the U.N. Security Council’s sanctions committee.
The committee is responsible for overseeing the punitive measures reimposed last year after France, Britain and Germany triggered the so-called snapback mechanism that automatically reinstated all United Nations sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program.
The reinstated sanctions include a travel ban, a conventional arms embargo, restrictions on ballistic missile development, asset freezes and a ban on producing nuclear-related technology.
Iran, Russia and China reject the legality of the sanctions reimposed under the snapback mechanism.
The U.S. ambassador to the U.N. in Vienna, Preston Wells Griffith, said Austria's exemption request was denied after Washington lodged an objection with the committee.
“While we are focused on a diplomatic solution to the challenges posed by Iran’s nuclear program, we could not allow a U.N. designated official to travel … without any meaningful cooperation on nuclear safeguards,” he said.
Since Israel and the U.S. struck Iran’s nuclear sites during the 12-day war in June 2025, Iran hasn’t given IAEA inspectors access to the affected sites — even though Tehran is legally obliged to cooperate with the watchdog under the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty.
The IAEA has also been unable to verify the status of a stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the June bombing. According to the IAEA, Iran maintains a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
The U.N. atomic watchdog’s board earlier this month adopted a resolution reporting Iran to the U.N. Security Council for the first time in 20 years because of its failure to cooperate citing in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites.
Western officials suspect that the traces could provide evidence that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons program until 2003. Iran says that it’s not pursuing nuclear weapons, and that its program is entirely peaceful.

- The claim that Donald Trump was rescued by firefighters in or around the United States Steel Building (also known as One Liberty Plaza) after 9/11 in Manhattan is unproven.
- According to some versions of the claim, Trump said firefighters pulled him from the rubble at Ground Zero. That was a misrepresentation of his actual words.
- The rumor stems from a speech Trump made on Sept. 8, 2026, while commemorating the 25th anniversary of 9/11. In it, he said the United States Steel Building was "creaking" a lot and "we thought it was going to fall down" when two firefighters "grabbed [him] under the arms" and got him out of there.
- Video interviews of Trump place him a few blocks from the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan in the days following the attack. However, there is no concrete evidence that Trump was inside or around One Liberty Plaza and no firefighters have come forward to corroborate his account. We also know that the building itself was not in danger of collapse in the days after 9/11, despite rumors at the time.
- We reached out to the White House, which did not respond to questions about Trump's whereabouts and actions in the wake of 9/11. A spokesperson called the speculation from the media a "disgrace."
In 2026, the U.S. marked the 25th anniversary of the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. As U.S. President Donald Trump commemorated the occasion in a speech on Sept. 8, he claimed that he was rescued by firefighters in New York City just after the attack.
Snopes readers asked us to confirm if Trump was indeed rescued by firefighters from the possible collapse of the United States Steel Building, a historic name for the building now 
Other readers claimed Trump said firefighters pulled "him from the rubble at 9/11."
Posts sharing versions of the rumor appeared on platforms including Facebook and X.
Some posts incorrectly claimed Trump said the firefighters pulled him from the rubble at Ground Zero. That was a misrepresentation or misunderstanding of what Trump actually said.
On Sept. 8, 2026, Trump recounted his purported rescue by two firefighters during a speech (emphasis ours):
I was building a big building in New York, and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened.
And they were -- they had no hesitation. Everybody went down with me; we went down as a big group of people. Wasn't too much we could do, I'll be honest. It was raw; nobody had seen anything like it ever. We had other buildings -- the United States Steel Building was creaking, really creaking, and we thought it was going to fall down. The truth is, it creaked a lot; it creaked, it still creaks, but it never came down. And I'll never forget two firemen -- we thought it was coming down on top of us and two firemen, big, strong guys -- and I'm not the smallest guy in the world. They grabbed me under the arms, said got to get out of here, and they literally lifted me up. This is not easy to do, I'm big.
They lifted me up and they started running with me. I said fellas, I can run myself. But they were amazing, but they thought it was coming down; it didn't come down, US steel.
Trump made several claims in this part of the speech: first, he said he "took the whole crew down" to Ground Zero to help after the attack. Second, he claimed that the "United States Steel Building was creaking" and in danger of collapsing on him. Third, he claimed he was saved by two firefighters.
We investigated Trump's claim that he went to Ground Zero with a group of workers immediately after the 9/11 attacks in a 
We have no evidence to support Trump's claim that he was rescued by two firefighters at One Liberty Plaza, though television interviews place him in the vicinity in the aftermath of 9/11. As such, we leave this claim unrated until more information becomes available.
We reached out to the White House to ask about Trump's location after the attack, the identity of the firefighters and more. The White House did not answer our questions and sent us the following statement from spokesperson Davis Ingle over email:
President Trump spent the morning yesterday paying tribute to the heroic first responders who laid down their lives in service to others in the September 11th attacks and honoring their incredible families. The President was relaying his experience of a city reeling immediately after and in the days and weeks after the horrific attacks - and the fact that the failing legacy media is using this to try to attack him is a disgrace and yet another reason why Americans' trust in the media is at an all-time low.
Below, we address the claims Trump made about being at One Liberty Plaza and his alleged rescue by firefighters.
Was Trump at One Liberty Plaza?
There is video evidence that Trump was near Ground Zero in the days after the attack, but we found no proof that he was actually inside the nearby One Liberty Plaza. Trump's remarks are not clear about where he was standing when the building was supposedly creaking.
The White House did not respond to our request for photo or video evidence of Trump's proximity to One Liberty Plaza specifically.
Trump's claim that the building was in danger of collapse was incorrect. Right after the attack, many reportedly expressed concerns that the building would collapse, but officials at the Department of Buildings debunked the claims. According to an October 2001 New York Times report, the building remained structurally sound even on Sept. 12:
''There are no structural concerns with this building,'' said Ilyse Fink, the director of communications for the city's Department of Buildings, reinforcing a message she has delivered almost daily since Sept. 12. ''It is not and was not in danger of collapse. The building is structurally sound.''
Did firefighters save Trump from a potential building collapse?
Given that we do not know exactly where Trump was around One Liberty Plaza, and that we know the building was never in danger of collapse, it is not clear which building and which firefighters Trump was referring to in his Sept. 8 speech.
The White House also did not respond to our question about the identity of the firefighters. Without any firefighters corroborating Trump's account, this claim remains unproven.
In sum, while we know Trump was in the vicinity of Ground Zero in the days after the attack, we do not have evidence that he was in One Liberty Plaza, nor that he was rescued by firefighters. We also know that the building was not in danger of collapse. Trump did not mention other buildings in his remarks.
Snopes has fact-checked many of Trump's claims in the aftermath of 9/11.

Why Pietersen will add unfiltered challenge that England need - Finn
- Published
I was as surprised as most that Kevin Pietersen has joined the England coaching ranks as a mentor in the build-up to the 50-over World Cup in South Africa next autumn.
Not only was his last interaction with the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) sitting in the offices at Lord's being told he wouldn't play for England again in 2014, but the success of his YouTube channel, The Switch, and the time it takes to commit to something like that made it seem inconceivable that it could work.
However, when I took a step back to remember what it was like to share a dressing room with him at the beginning of my England career, I remembered a number of occasions that lead me to believe this can only be a good thing for all parties.
Kevin can be blunt and forthright, but dressing rooms need that in order to function properly. They can't be an echo chamber.
On the white-ball tour of India last year, while working for the host broadcaster, he was bemoaning the lack of practice, external that England's players had opted for in the build-up to games.
His practice was always intense and with purpose. Usually, he would come up to me as he was walking into the net and say he was going to smash me everywhere and not get out. That would usually rile me up to try to bowl quicker in order to not let him have it his way.
He wanted to make sure the practice had that bit more on it, something that is important when steeling your mind and reactions to go out and play at the highest level.
I used to enjoy the battles in the nets and it made me a better bowler by having competitive nets against one of the best players in the world.
We'd constantly be arguing about what angle the fielders were when he was deciding how many runs he'd scored off that ball, or whether I thought it could have gone to hand when he hit it in the air.
England v Sri Lanka, first T20
Tuesday, 15 September at 18:30 BST
Follow ball-by-ball commentary on BBC Sounds, BBC Radio 5 Sports and the BBC Sport website and app. Live text updates and in-play video clips on the website and app. Extended highlights on BBC Two and BBC iPlayer from 23:05 BST.
Kev was ahead of his time with both his mindset and skills. The inventor of the switch hit, and the most ardent supporter of the IPL before it became mainstream.
The flamingo flicks through mid-wicket in Test matches and hitting Glenn McGrath back over his head for six at Lord's in 2005.
None of which would look out of place now in 2026.
But, he never thought he'd cracked the game.
In 2012 when we were in Sri Lanka, I remember turning up for training at the SSC in Colombo to play a warm-up game and Kev had already been there for an hour facing local left-arm spin bowlers in order to try to correct his technique (ironically overseen by Andy Flower) that had been a problem for him intermittently.
As a result of that hard work he scored the most remarkable 151 against Rangana Herath in the second Test, hitting him to all parts, and backed it up later that year against India away to seal a historic red-ball series victory where his runs, particularly in Mumbai, formed the bedrock of the win.
Those runs and the manner with which they were scored, wouldn't have been possible without those long practice sessions while people weren't watching.
It wasn't just about him improving too. In Perth during the 2013-14 Ashes, when Mitchell Johnson and his moustache were running amok, it wouldn't be out of place to see a tailender looking shellshocked at the prospect of having to go and face him in the corner of the dressing room.
I vividly remember KP coming over to me (even though I wasn't in the starting XI), and saying 'let's go practice facing the short ball in the nets'. He threw bouncers at my head and helped me figure out a technique to be able to play (mainly evade) the short-pitched bowling.
I don't know whether at that stage of the tour he just wanted to be out of the dressing room rather than in it, but it helped me.
I can see him doing similar things with players he sees areas of improvement with in his role as mentor.
Kevin was never shy of letting the dressing room know his thoughts when debriefing a match, or when discussing the team's approach.
I saw this first hand with his dissent towards a fitness fielding session in the build-up to the 2014 Sydney Test match, among others.
Some may argue that bringing this into an environment that is clearly working and improving may be a bad thing.
However, I believe McCullum has learned from the way the Test team turned a corner as soon as everything seemed in order.
Pietersen comes from an era where there was no substitute for hard work and your main way of making a decent living from the game was by playing Test cricket - where you needed to work hard on a fundamental technique in order to firstly survive, but then to build and expand upon to be good at other formats.
The balance has clearly shifted now and the power lies with the players able to globetrot and play franchise tournaments.
In my eyes the 50-over format is now closer to the pace of modern Test cricket than T20 cricket, helping players with the fundamentals, married up with a strong work ethic can only be a good thing when looking to excel in the format, especially in conditions where there will be passages where the bowlers may be on top.
But, I believe he will bring this attitude to the dressing room for the next 14 months leading up to that World Cup.
There is no better time to introduce a voice of challenge than now, as it means that the team will not be able to simply maraud on as they have been without checks and balances.
Pietersen will provide this, unfiltered.

The intelligence services of the Russian Federation are plotting to carry out targeted killings in the United States and in European nations supporting Ukraine, federal authorities said on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) as they announced charges against five people who remain at large.
An indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court said a network of the intelligence services has paid and attempted to pay individuals in the United States and in other countries to surveil targets to be killed with plans to then kill them.
The associates recruited in the network also have been solicited to carry out acts of terrorism against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries that are perceived to be aligned with Ukraine, the indictment said.
James C. Barnacle, Jr., head of New York's FBI office, said the FBI disrupted the plans “through relentless work” as members of the Russian Intelligence Services and their affiliates "conspired to intimidate, threaten, or murder people on U.S. soil and around the world.”
Darren B. Cox, head of the Washington, D.C., office of the FBI, cited “extraordinary work by multiple FBI field offices, components, and partner agencies that collectively disrupted Russia's attempts to conduct violent acts in our nation's capital and throughout the United States.”
He said in a release that when the threat was first identified, the FBI's Washington field office and its partners “moved quickly to disrupt the plot and hold the Russian government accountable for its actions.”
According to the release, a network of people working for the Russian Federation's intelligence services had, since at least 2024, conspired to conduct and had conducted attacks and murders around the world, including within the United States.
It called the Russian intelligence services network “one arm” of the Russian Federation's apparatus designed to carry out external attacks, including murder, around the world.
Previously, the release said, the network had focused on Russian dissidents and defectors but most recently had targeted nations perceived to be allies of Ukraine.
Recently, it said, members of the network have tried to recruit multiple people in the United States.
Authorities said the network this summer recruited an individual based in the United States to surveil and murder a prominent Russian dissident it believed to be residing in the United States.
The indictment said a person identified only as “U.S. Resident-1” was sent to two locations associated with the targeted victim and was given “explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance” while being promised $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the work.
After conducting the surveillance and providing multiple photographs and videos of locations associated with the intended victim to one of the men charged in the indictment, the U.S. resident turned down the $40,000 that was offered to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target through murder.
When the offer was rejected, the member of the intelligence services who made it tried to recruit multiple other people within the United States to finish the job by offering them substantial amounts of money, the indictment said.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Wildfires in Indonesia are sweeping through a critical research site for Bornean orangutans and are now threatening a celebrated research camp, home to one of the world’s longest-running studies of wild apes.
In the past few days, the fires have burned within 200 metres of Rangkong research station, a satellite of Cabang Panti research station, which lies about four miles north in Gunung Palung national park.
Hundreds of Bornean orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus), one of three orangutan species, live in the direct vicinity of the research stations, with more than 2,500 thought to inhabit the park, many areas of which are now on fire. All three orangutan species are considered critically endangered.
“Orangutans are fleeing from these forests. It’s just horrible,” said Prof Cheryl Knott, a biological anthropologist at Boston University who has been leading scientific research on orangutans at Cabang Panti for 32 years.
In most cases, the fires were intentionally set to clear land, as is done every year on the island. But an extremely strong El Niño – a warming of sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean that disrupts global weather patterns – has fuelled exceptionally hot and dry conditions across the country, with fires easily escaping control as a result. In West Kalimantan province, some areas have gone months with little to no rainfall.
Scientists at Cabang Panti have collected decades’ worth of data on wild orangutans and their life histories, following some of the same individuals from birth to grandmotherhood. Research carried out at the site has helped to establish the orangutan reproduction cycle, finding that the apes only give birth once every eight years – the longest cycle of any mammal. “The long-term nature of this database and the detailed nature of the database is unparalleled,” Knott said.
But the fires threaten to undo such continuous observations. At the rate the flames are moving, without intervention or large firebreaks, the fires will reach Cabang Panti in 20 days’ time, scientists said.
“[Cabang Panti] protects what has been, until now, one of the only truly ecologically intact tracts of lowland tropical rainforest in Borneo,” said Prof Andrew Marshall, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan who ran an orangutan research project at the site from 2000 to 2020. “Without long-term, continuously collected field data, we cannot understand how tropical ecosystems are adapting to or suffering from global climate shifts.”
In a desperate effort to save Rangkong research station, a team of more than 40 people – mostly field assistants, staff and local villagers – are fighting day and night to stave off the encroaching inferno. Recently, they constructed a firebreak and an improvised sprinkler system using a punctured hose line around the station to saturate the surrounding peat.
Once fire reaches a peat swamp, it can smoulder underground for months – even after surface flames have been extinguished. Keeping the peat wet is therefore a key defence.
“The issue has surpassed any local organisation’s capacity,” said Caitlin O’Connell, deputy director of the Gunung Palung orangutan conservation programme. “We need large-scale water bombing and skilled firefighters.”
Even if they manage to save the research station, it may be for nothing if the orangutans lose their home.
“The orangutans need the forest,” Knott said. “If all we have left is the building, what are we studying if the orangutans are all gone, and the food they have is all gone? They can’t survive without that forest.”
As solitary animals, orangutans require large ranges and live at low population densities. “You can’t just shove them all together in what remains of the forest,” Knott said.
Those leading the on-the-ground fire response have already witnessed the impact on the apes. “Five orangutans from our long-term study population were observed fleeing the fire, some only metres from the flames,” said Wahyu Susanto, research director for Yayasan Palung, an Indonesian NGO that protects Bornean orangutans. “These are individuals that we have followed and studied for years.”
Indonesian meteorologists predict an intense fire season persisting through October as climate forecasts point to a strengthening El Niño.
“The hotspots are everywhere,” O’Connell said. “I don’t think it’s hyperbolic to say that what we thought couldn’t burn could actually completely disappear if we’re looking at these dry conditions going on for months.”

Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.
On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”
Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.
The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.
The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”
In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.
“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”
The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.
“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”
Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

Gas Prices Could Cost Republicans the Midterms
Many voters understand that the president isn’t directly responsible for the price of oil. Except this time, he is.
One might expect Donald Trump to be concerned about gas prices. Less than two months out from the midterms, gas costs 37 percent more than it did a year ago. Home-heating oil was up 52 percent as of August, and diesel is up a staggering 69 percent. None of those numbers is likely to go down significantly as long as the Iran war drags on. Meanwhile, just last week, a Saudi oil pipeline that carries about 4 percent of the global oil supply shut down after being bombed. (No one has claimed credit for the attack.)
But Trump says he isn’t worried. Speaking with reporters last week, he insisted that the United States, not Iran, is in control of the Strait of Hormuz. “Right after the election,” he said, “oil prices are going to be tumbling downward.”
Even if that prediction were based on anything resembling fact, the timing would be too late to do Trump much good. Political scientists tend to agree that gas prices influence voter behavior. Although many voters no doubt understand that the president isn’t usually directly responsible for the price of oil, this time, he is. In fact, the oil shock related to Trump’s war of choice with Iran is the only reason the U.S. has any inflation to speak of. Inflation in all non-energy consumer purchases is at just 2 percent over the past year. If Democrats manage to take back the House and Senate in November despite an inhospitable electoral map, the Trump effect on gas prices may well be the reason.
Voters hate inflation, and gas prices are especially hard to tune out. Juan Felipe Riaño, an economist who has studied inflation’s political consequences, told me that voters understand that price increases translate into lower real wages. The more they drive, the more pronounced the effect. People who live in rural areas and exurbs have the most to lose, because they have the longest commutes. These are the reddest parts of the country, meaning that they are home to millions of voters whom Democrats are trying to persuade to vote blue. According to a Brookings Institution analysis, the average voter in a Republican-held district drives 26 percent more miles than their counterpart in a Democratic district. Other research has found that those with longer drive times are more likely to hold the president accountable for increases in gas prices.
These Trump-friendly areas are exactly where Democrats need to make inroads. They can’t take the Senate without winning multiple states that Trump won by more than 10 points in 2024. Meanwhile, although gerrymandering has created more red districts, it has done so by spreading the Republican advantage more thinly across districts. This has created more places where Democrats could win in a wave election. Currently, Democrats lead Republicans on generic congressional polls by about seven points. In a plus-seven election, their best recruits could pick up seats even in districts that went heavily for Trump in 2024.
Perhaps the best thing Trump could do to avoid that outcome would be to bring gas prices down before Election Day. His approval rating has been declining almost continuously since he took office a second time, and since August, it has hovered around 38 percent, according to Silver Bulletin. Voters say that their top issue is the cost of living, and only 25 percent approve of how Trump has handled it. That’s a decline of nine points since the war with Iran began.
As for Republican candidates in competitive races, their best bet for avoiding the gas-price backlash might be to distance themselves from the president. But Trump has made that extremely difficult. Last week, Republicans gathered in Dallas for an unusual midterm convention devoted to celebrating Trump’s greatness. At one point, he asked the crowd to repeat a “pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States.”
And if Trump’s goal is to remind Republican candidates that their voters’ first loyalty is to him, not them, he seems to be succeeding. Only a tiny handful of congressional Republicans have publicly denounced the Iran war. Several vulnerable Republicans have refused to allow daylight between themselves and Trump, even when doing so would seem to be tactically wise. Michael Whatley, Mike Collins, and Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominees in the swing states of North Carolina, Georgia, and Michigan, respectively, all spoke at the convention. So, too, did Jon Husted and Ken Paxton, who are running in Ohio and Texas, two states Trump won by more than 10 points in 2024, but where polls suggest that Democrats have a chance to pick up Senate seats.
Even when voters believe that the president is to blame for painful gas-price increases, they may be unsure about how aligned their local House or Senate candidate is with the White House. Heading into the midterms, Trump is going out of his way to make sure no such uncertainty exists.

Trump’s Kennedy Center Shakedown
The only appropriate response is to refuse to accede to his demands.
The saga of Donald Trump’s repeated attempts to slap his name onto the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts will not go away. In May, Trump lost in court and was ordered to remove his name from the building. But now—according to a 57-page presentation by Trump’s hand-picked executive board obtained by The Washington Post—the Kennedy Center is warning that it will likely go bankrupt. Unless, that is, Trump gets to put his name back on the wall next to that of his slain predecessor.
The Post reports:
Trump’s support hinges on getting public credit for his involvement. The financial resolution says Trump has offered to “raise the necessary funds to keep the Center from bankruptcy” while the building undergoes a sweeping renovation. But it says Trump is unlikely to provide “fundamental oversight” of that project or lead a financial rescue without “appropriate recognition” of his role.
That’s not an offer of help; it’s a shakedown—or, in more direct terms, political blackmail. Two lawyers who have been fighting the Trump administration, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, said in a statement: “Trump is taking the Center hostage and threatening to in effect kill it unless he gets his way.” The president is counting on the board’s civic spirit and affection for the institution—neither of which he evidently possesses—to strong-arm it into giving him what the law and courts would not allow.
Even more galling than Trump’s attempt to pressure the trustees is that his offer is a response to a crisis mostly of his own creation. It’s true that the Kennedy Center, opened more than a half century ago, needs investment and repairs. But the plummeting ticket sales are a result of Trump’s hostile takeover. Performers and patrons alike did not want to legitimize the obscenity of placing Trump’s name on an institution meant to honor Kennedy, and they voted with their feet and their dollars. This very public repudiation of Trump by a slice of the American cultural elite appears to have been an embarrassment to the president; Trump then claimed that he needed to close the center for two years (ostensibly for a complete reconstruction) rather than suffer further humiliation.
(Trump, apparently, could not submit to the public indignity of having his name removed from the building in June. He—or someone seeking to please him—ordered workers to cover the building’s wall with tarps at 3 o’clock in the morning so that no one would see the removal. The tarps remain in place.)
The only way to avert letting the center go bankrupt, according to the executive board, is to let Trump raise money—and heaven knows what kind of ethical issues that effort would entail—and then to add his name to thank him. The presentation to the board suggests 10 possible statements to place on the building, including “Renovation Restoration and Endowment overseen by President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Putting Trump’s name in front of Kennedy’s is an especially offensive touch, and would enshrine the idea that the center would no longer be named solely for Kennedy.
The American people do not support Trump’s mania for renaming things, of which the Kennedy Center is just one example. (The White House itself has become a public exhibit of Trump’s garish taste, including gold script identifying The Oval Office, as if it’s a function room at one of his resorts that needs to be labeled in case a tipsy wedding guest gets lost.) All of this architectural bombast and glitz are expressions both of ego and of insecurity: Trump wants to leave his mark—and his name—on a city that has never accepted him and that will almost certainly try to scrub away his influence when he is gone.
The president admitted as much recently, when the writer Ben Terris asked him whether he is building monuments to himself because he is worried that no one else will build them when he’s gone. “That’s true,” Trump said. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will.”
The president’s admission suggests a way to deal with his attempted shakedown of the Kennedy Center board: take his dare.
The center’s top officials, the people who were supposed to be entrusted with the future of this cultural icon, have admitted their failure. They acknowledge that Trump will not support the institution unless his name is on it. Well, so be it. The trustees should let the center close, declare bankruptcy, and come to a sad end—all on Trump’s watch. Allow the Kennedy Center to fail in full view of the American public, and let them decide whether such things matter.
Otherwise, Trump will plow ahead and do something no one wants, because no one bothered to stop him.
The Kennedy Center can always be rebuilt and reopened. Indeed, the restoration of the center could be one of the items on the next president’s to-do list. Scrap the czarist-style ballroom. Rebuild the East Wing of the White House. Halt the fascist-flavored victory arch that will dishonor nearby Arlington Cemetery. Fix the Reflecting Pool. Chisel Trump’s name off the U.S. Institute of Peace. (If the president wants to land at Donald J. Trump International Airport in Palm Beach when he leaves office, that’s between him and the people of Florida.) Painful as it would be to see the Kennedy Center go bankrupt, it would be more painful to cave to Trump’s deeply cynical refusal to save a national treasure unless he gets his name on it.
In a famous 1911 poem that gave the world another name for blackmail—danegeld, a reference to the protection money that medieval English villages paid, often in vain, to Danish raiders—Rudyard Kipling warned powerful countries against caving to extortionary threats. The Kennedy Center board, and the American people, should heed Kipling’s advice:
We never pay any-one Dane-geld,
No matter how trifling the cost;
For the end of that game is oppression and shame,
And the nation that plays it is lost!

Police registered an FIR against northwest Delhi’s Mundka BJP MLA Gajender Drall and others under the SC/ST Act on Tuesday (September 15, 2026), five days after a Dalit party worker, Sunil Kumar, alleged that he was severely beaten and subjected to casteist slurs at a party office, police said.
The FIR was registered at the Kanjhawala police station. A senior police official said that the FIR included provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, the Arms Act, and other relevant sections. A counter-complaint from Mr. Drall has also been received and is being investigated, the official said.
According to the FIR, the alleged assault took place on September 10 when Mr. Drall called Kanjhawala Mandal president Mr. Kumar to the party office in the evening on the pretext of discussing voter lists, and along with others workers, allegedly confined him and physically assaulted him through the night with pipes, belts and sticks. He also alleged that Mr. Drall and others used caste-related slurs against him, adding that he was allowed to go on the morning of September 11 and was threatened not to approach the police. Mr. Kumar, later, got admitted to the Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital and contacted the police.
Several videos of Mr. Kumar, shared by his friends and family, went viral, purportedly showing his body covered in bruises.
Party action
Meanwhile, Delhi BJP president Harsh Malhotra said on Tuesday that the state wing has taken cognisance of matter and referred it to the State disciplinary committee, adding that further action will be taken based on its report.
“After speaking with the concerned Member of Parliament and the District President, we issued a letter on Monday evening to the concerned MLA and the Mandal President, asking them to submit their explanation to the Delhi BJP Disciplinary Committee by 3:00 p.m. on September 16,” he said.
He added that while both parties are free to seek police or legal action, the party will take appropriate disciplinary action as per its organisational rules.
Political backlash
The incident has triggered a sharp political backlash from opposition Aam Aadmi Party and Congress.
AAP MLA from Kondli, Kuldeep Kumar, said that he accompanied Mr. Kumar to the DCP (Rohini) office at 10 a.m. on Tuesday and helped him register a case. “After nearly 6 hours of continuous struggle and demands for justice, Sunil Kumar’s FIR was finally registered,” he wrote on X.
He demanded the immediate arrest of the MLA and his associates, and security for the victim and his family, and a fair investigation.
Meanwhile, on September 13, Congress leader and former MP Udit Raj also visited the victim at the hospital along with members of the Dalit community.
Dr. Raj alleged that when around 50-60 people went to a police station on September 11 evening seeking registration of an FIR, the police did not act on the complaint. He accused the police of putting pressure on the victim not to pursue the case. In a post on X on Tuesday, Mr. Raj said, “After a four-day struggle, finally today, Sunil Kumar Valmiki’s FIR was registered at the Kanjhawala police station.”

- The claim that an image shows U.S. President Donald Trump kissing White House aide Natalie Harp on a golf course remains under investigation.
- The rumor stems from two versions of the image shared on social media in mid-September 2026. The higher-resolution version had telltale signs of artificial intelligence, such as hands with too many fingers, as well as a watermark confirming it was created or edited using OpenAI's generative AI tools. The lower-resolution image did not have an OpenAI watermark and was too blurry for telltale anomalies to be apparent.
- The White House declined to provide Snopes with legitimate photos of Trump and Harp golfing that could be compared to the images shared online. A spokesperson said the image was "clearly a fake."
- Hany Farid, co-founder of deepfake detection company GetReal, told Snopes the higher-resolution image was AI-generated and was clearly derived from the lower-quality version. While he said the lower-resolution version's quality itself was "a bit of a red flag," he said he considered its authenticity inconclusive.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces.
In summer 2026, many people scrutinized White House aide Natalie Harp following news reports of what appeared to be an unusually close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump.
In September, following a Trump visit to Ireland during which he took time to golf at his Trump Organization-owned course, people started sharing multiple versions of an image that appeared to show Trump kissing Harp, whose back is turned toward the camera, while on the golf course.
For example, one X post (archived) shared a low-resolution version of the image. Another popular X post (archived) shared a higher resolution version with crisper colors.
Users also widely posted the image on Threads (archived) and Instagram (archived). Snopes readers emailed us to ask whether the image was real.
Snopes could find no credible evidence or source supporting the authenticity of the image, but we were able to find multiple red flags indicating the higher-resolution version was generated or edited with artificial intelligence tools. The lower-resolution version did not have those same red flags, in part because of its poor quality. Therefore, we've left this claim unrated until more evidence comes to light.
We used Google Lens to run a reverse image search on both versions of the image. The oldest example that turned up was a thumbnail image for a Sept. 14 YouTube video uploaded by political commentator Keith Edwards. We've fact-checked images originating from Edwards' thumbnails twice before. In one of those fact checks, Edwards confirmed he had used an AI tool to generate the image.
Snopes reached out to Edwards by email to confirm the origin of the image of Trump kissing Harp. He responded:
My thumbnail team found the image online. We did not create or alter the underlying image, but we also did not independently verify its original source or that the woman pictured is Natalie Harp. Given that only the back of her head is visible, I don't think her identity can be confirmed from this image alone.
Following this, Snopes used the thumbnail to conduct another reverse image search. While it failed to unearth any older versions of the image, the results (archived) included a wider shot of the subjects than any other we could find. That version, which included the "wtf" text on Edwards' thumbnail, linked to the same Edwards video.
None of the reverse image searches turned up links to credible news sources or even less-credible tabloids sharing the image. Considering the reporting already scrutinizing Trump's relationship with Harp, it's unlikely, if the image were real, that not a single credible news source would report on it. The image also did not appear among photos kept by credible photo repositories, such as Getty Images and The Associated Press.
Although there was no photographer, date or location listed for any version of the image, the timing of its spread suggested it was likely meant to depict something that took place while Trump was visiting his golf course in Ireland on Sept. 13, an activity listed on his calendar as "Executive Time." Photos of that golf course and Google Maps satellite view don't show any trees, in contrast to the image of Trump and Harp kissing.
Snopes reached out to the White House by email to ask if any photos of Trump and/or Harp at the golf course over the weekend exist in order to compare what either was wearing in those images with what they supposedly wore in the image of the kiss. The White House did not send or confirm the requested images, but a White House official said the image shared online was "clearly a fake photo."
While many of those who spread the photo presumed the woman was Harp, there's no way to confirm that considering the subject's face isn't visible.
Some people online claimed the image was actually a 2017 photo of Trump exchanging a cheek-kiss with Norwegian golfer Suzann Pettersen as a greeting. This is false. That kiss was not actually on the golf course, Pettersen was in a different outfit than that of the woman in the recent image and Trump was also dressed differently, as shown in images capturing the moment from 2017.
AI evidence
A tool by OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, detected a watermark in the higher-resolution version image consistent with those generated or edited using the company's AI tools. Moreover, the image depicts Harp holding her golf club with six fingers.
The lower-resolution version of the image was too blurry to clearly identify AI tells such as an excessive number of fingers on either person's hands. While OpenAI's tool didn't identify a watermark within the lower-resolution image shared across X and Threads, the tool did detect OpenAI watermarks on the thumbnail for Edwards' video.
Separately, Snopes tested what the tool would find on a real photo where a small portion had then been edited by AI. OpenAI's tool detected the watermark on such an image, even when the photo was cropped to remove the part that had been edited.
Hany Farid, co-founder of deepfake detection company GetReal and a professor at Drexel University, told Snopes over email that "the high-resolution version was clearly derived from the lower-resolution version and has a SynthID watermark. As for the lower-resolution version, there is not a lot to go on here given the quality and resolution."
"While there are no obvious visual anomalies, the low quality/resolution is a bit of a red flag. In particular, given the apparent narrow depth of focus, this does not appear to photographed with a mobile device and is more likely taken with a DSLR that would afford this type of narrow depth of focus," Farid continued. "Assuming this to be the case, I would expect the image quality to be better. At this point, I'd say the authenticity is inconclusive."

Despite the Indian teams’ mixed performances at the recently concluded World Cups, with the men finishing eighth and the women placing a commendable fifth, the men’s side will enter the Asian Games as the overwhelming favourite for the gold.
Craig Fulton’s India has been the undisputed king of the continent for the last four years. Since 2023, the men have won every continental competition they have contested, including two Asian Champions Trophy titles, the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, without losing a single game.
However, a second successive gold medal, a feat no team has achieved since 2006, will be anything but straightforward. India’s challenge will begin in Kakamigahara in less than a week’s time, with the team still reeling from its disastrous World Cup campaign. The Asian Games will now serve as a make-or-break competition for Fulton and several senior players in this side.
Defenders Amit Rohidas, Jarmanpreet Singh, Sumit, Jugraj Singh, Yashdeep Siwach, Sanjay Rana and Harmanpreet Singh all had forgettable outings as India shipped 19 goals, the tournament’s fifth-worst defensive record. Even Pakistan scored three, aided by sloppy handling of possession.
Almost every department, from goalkeeping to the forward line, had a tournament to forget, with Harmanpreet’s dragflicks from Penalty Corners (PC) the notable exception. Despite a crocked back, his world-class finishing from short corners repeatedly dragged India into contests when it struggled to find goals from open play.
Harmanpreet’s heroics will need to be backed up in field play by his attackers. Since the 2023 Asian Games, only Abhishek Nain has remained a threat, notching up 30 goals in 86 appearances, while senior forward Manpreet Singh’s returns have dwindled to just 11 goals in 69.
Fulton lamented his side’s struggles to maintain its standards across all four quarters, but will breathe a little easier knowing the continent’s contenders might not have the sustained quality to punish its lapses. With an LA 2028 Olympic berth up for grabs, Fulton has opted for more experience in the squad, with Aditya Lalage making way for Raj Kumar Pal, who was part of the travelling group at the World Cup.
Early tests against host nation Japan and South Korea in the group phase will help assess if India has learnt from its misadventures in the World Cup, before likely coming up against Pakistan or Malaysia in the knockout stages.
Aiming to reign supreme
In the women’s section, Sjoerd Marijne’s India will feel primed to go for gold, confident of dethroning China. There is a renewed spirit within this group, infused with a vibrant mix of youth and older heads after exceeding expectations with its disciplined World Cup showing.
India kept clean sheets against England and Australia, while conceding just six goals in matches against China, South Africa, Netherlands and Germany. Of the six opponents it faced, five were ranked higher.
Better composure on the ball against Australia might have seen this side compete in the semifinals, but the young team, which had 11 World Cup debutants, will take those learnings into the Asian Games.
Navneet Kaur and Deepika will be the biggest source of goals, both from open play and PCs, while matches in the group stage against lower-quality opposition will give the rest of the attack opportunities to contribute.
India has two strong goalkeepers, Savita Punia and Bichu Devi, whose services will likely be crucial in the medal rounds with a potential meeting against China. India showed it can match up to China in the opening match of the World Cup, earning a 2-2 draw, but inexperience in defence proved costly when Shilpi Dabas conceded a Penalty Stroke.
Senior midfielder Neha is bullish about India’s chances of ending its 44-year gold medal drought at this stage. “We have to win the gold medal. No matter what happens, we will give our best. We will win the gold medal,” said Neha.
Marijne, who is overseeing another renaissance with the women’s side, felt this group of Indian talent might be better than the group he managed during his first stint in charge. But the class of 2026 will have to earn that billing on the pitch by following up its impressive fifth-place finish at the World Cup with a rare Asian Games gold.

A Brihanmumbai Electric Supply and Transport (BEST) bus, a vehicle wet-leased by the undertaking rammed into a metro rail pillar at Goregaon on Monday evening, injuring two people, police said.
The incident occurred around 5pm at Ittbhatti Junction outside Oberoi Mall.
“While proceeding from Dindoshi Depot to Bhayander Station (East), the bus was taking a right turn beneath the Dindoshi flyover at the traffic signal opposite Oberoi Mall. During the maneuver, the bus grazed the rear right side of a private car and subsequently collided with a metro rail pillar,” a BEST spokesperson shared in a statement.
Two persons sustained injuries and were taken to Trauma Care Hospital in Jogeshwari (East) for medical attention. The injured are Rajendra Murlidhar Sonawane (58), a BEST employee, who suffered a head injury and required three stitches and Mangesh Ramchandra Modlekar (57), a passenger, who sustained injuries to his chin and head and required one stitch on the chin and five stitches on the head, said police.
Minutes after the incident, a police team was deputed to assist. The bus was towed by a BEST towing vehicle and taken to Vanrai police station. The private passenger vehicle owner lodged a complaint against the driver, whose name BEST did not reveal.
This route number 705 bus is operated by wet-lease company Mateshwari Urban Transport Solutions. Earlier this year, there were at least three reported incidents involving the same company.
On July 7, route 512 ran over a 56-year-old civic sanitation worker Jayshri Bhanaji Parmar as she was crossing the road when a signal turned green at Mulund Check Naka.
On May 13 at Andheri West, a chain collision near Amboli Naka involved multiple buses after a fallen tree, crushing and killing a Mateshwari bus conductor Shekhar Baburao Rawate who got trapped between vehicles. On May 24, two BEST buses caught fire at Pratiksha Nagar depot in Sion Depot due to suspected overheating; there were no injuries from this incident.
