LONDON -- The leaders of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland signed a pact Monday that threatens to lead to the breakup of the United Kingdom.
The first ministers of the three semiautonomous regions of the U.K. told Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government to prepare for constitutional change and that their future lies with the European Union.
“For people watching across these islands — for people watching around the world — there could be no clearer sign that Westminster’s time is coming to an end,” they said in a memorandum of understanding, referring to Parliament.
The announcement came about 48 hours after U.S. President Donald Trump waded into the waters of the politically contentious issue when he said he would “ love to see ” a reunified Ireland during a trip to visit his golf course hosting the Irish Open.
It’s the first time the leaders of all three countries are either from pro-independence parties, or pro-unification in the case of Northern Ireland, which was partitioned and remained part of the U.K. when Ireland won independence from Britain over a century ago.
Burnham's spokesperson brushed aside the threat and said the prime minister strongly believes in the union and was more focused on lowering the cost of living than dealing with constitutional debates.
“The United Kingdom is at its best when people come together around our shared values and problem-solving, rather than division,” Tom Wells said.
Nicola McEwen, director of the University of Glasgow Center for Public Policy, said the summit was symbolically important but has no legal significance.
“I don’t see the threat to the union being bigger today than it was yesterday,” McEwen said.
In the late 1990s, the U.K. passed legislative acts that decentralized government through the process of devolution, giving each country except England some level of policy independence and self-governance through their own parliaments. But tensions have remained with the U.K.-wide government in London, which retained control over national issues and those concerning England.
Scotland’s John Swinney and Northern Ireland’s Michelle O’Neill called for independence referendums in their countries, while Rhun ap Iorwerth did not provide a timetable for one in Wales.
The three leaders appeared in their political capacity, rather than their official one, possibly because O'Neill is in a power-sharing government with the Democratic Unionist Party.
Northern Ireland's Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, of the DUP, accused O’Neill, of the Sinn Fein party, of “weaponizing” the role of first minister by signing the agreement.
“I am first minister in the north of Ireland,” O'Neill replied. “This is about historic change happening all around us.”
Scotland tried unsuccessfully to break away in 2014, with voters rejecting a referendum 55% to 45%. But McEwen said support for Scottish independence has grown since Brexit, in which the U.K. formally left the European Union in January 2020, following a referendum in June 2016.
Swinney, leader of the Scottish National Party, said he believed voters would now vote for independence if the U.K. government approved a referendum.
Burnham told Parliament last week he would allow such a vote to be held if there was a “clear consensus” in Scotland, but later sent Swinney a letter saying a vote was “off limits.”
The 1998 Good Friday peace accord that ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland known as “The Troubles,” requires a vote on unification if polls there indicate it would likely pass, a threshold the U.K. government says has not been met. Ireland would also have to approve the change in a referendum.
Burnham has made devolution a major theme since taking office less than two months ago, but his focus has been on regional governments across England, a reflection of his years as mayor of Greater Manchester.
Swinney tried to turn Burnham's ideology to his advantage, saying his frequent talk of devolution “leads you to the logic of recognizing the right of the people of Scotland, in my case, to decide their own future.”
Beyond any threat of departing the union, McEwen said the greatest impact of the three joining forces could be that they agreed to cooperate with each other routinely and that could help to exert more influence on the U.K. government.
“It does keep on the agenda that question about, well, if the United Kingdom is a union based on consent, what is the pathway where it looks like that consent may no longer be there?” McEwen said. “Any U.K. government has been very reluctant to engage in that discussion.”

Why Does Donald Trump Hate This Sculpture?
The president wants the Smithsonian to add a colossal George Washington statue—and remove another work of abstract art in D.C.
The sculpture that Donald Trump wants removed from the National Mall has a reputation even among its admirers for being a bit inscrutable. Dedicated in 1967 at what is now the National Museum of American History, José de Rivera’s Infinity looks, fittingly, like an infinity symbol with an extra twist. (A bow? A pretzel?) By pairing the technical prowess required to create smooth, curved metal with the delicate spinning of a music box, the slow-turning work seems to take a different form each time you pass it. The museum’s architect, Walker O. Cain, wrote that Infinity “has the characteristic of stimulating everyone who has seen it to create his own personal imaginative interpretation.”
But the president does not appear to have been stimulated. “That strange modernist sculpture tells visitors nothing about America, inspires no one, and honors none of our Great American Heroes,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday night. Trump insisted that the Smithsonian replace Infinity with a 30-foot high “Colossus” of George Washington. In the same post, he called for the mounting of a five-year exhibition about the Founding Father to open immediately (museum shows of such magnitude typically take years to plan), and said the museum should create a “Center for American Heroes.” Trump also wrote that the institution should add another, 11-foot-tall Washington statue to the museum’s Flag Hall. That one was displayed at the Grand Prix race held in Washington, D.C., this summer as part of Trump’s Freedom 250 festivities. He’d like it dedicated at the museum this Thursday.
Trump’s latest demands might be partially understood as a test of how far he can push an institution that he does not control. They came just three days after the Smithsonian’s secretary, Lonnie Bunch, announced his upcoming retirement, following a year and a half of standing between the museum complex and the White House. In a July executive order, the president called on the National Park Service, which is part of the executive branch, to place signs outside the National Museum of American History accusing it of partisan bias.
Few would question the appropriateness of having a healthy amount of George Washington in an American-history museum, but Trump’s ask might be a little too redundant. For one thing, a Washington sculpture can already be found on the museum’s second floor. Classical in style and portraying the first president as a kind of Zeus figure, Horatio Greenough’s 1841 statue boasts chiseled muscles that rival even the machismo AI depictions Trump circulates of himself and Washington online. And when approached from the east, Rivera’s Infinity—the aspirational site of Trump’s Washington colossus—elegantly frames another abstract form: the obelisk known as the Washington Monument.
Trump’s call for changes to the museum fits a few recent patterns: He has been on a campaign to institute his preferred version of history in the national museum system. He has begun to leave his mark, and occasionally his name, across the architectural landscape of Washington, D.C. And while doing so, he appears to have indicated a distaste for abstract art. Earlier this month, the Kennedy Center, which Trump controls, took down Joel Shapiro’s playful metal sculpture Blue. When the Trump administration—addressing a controversy at the National Portrait Gallery last year—criticized a decidedly representational Amy Sherald painting of a trans woman as Lady Liberty, part of its complaint was that, in the words of the administration, “the Statue of Liberty is not an abstract canvas for political expression.” The use of abstract reads like an insult.
Trump has pushed a classical makeover in D.C.. He has issued executive orders mandating classical designs as the default for new federal buildings, for example, and remounted figurative statues that were torn down during the Black Lives Matter movement. He has mused about the White House upgrading its columns to a higher Greek order (adding more classical to the neoclassical); his most prized project, the White House ballroom, looks like a Corinthian-columned department store. In his first executive order on architecture, he said federal buildings should command respect.
When it comes to the Rivera outside the National Museum of American History, Trump’s issue with it—and with abstraction largely—might not be that the sculpture “says nothing about America,” but that it doesn’t say what he wants it to. That is, he can’t control what it says at all.
The American artist Robert Motherwell wrote in a 1951 essay celebrating abstraction that one of the most striking aspects of the approach is its “nakedness,” or the way it turns, with such decisiveness, away from the symbols we know. “How many rejections on the part of her artists! Whole worlds—the world of objects, the world of power and propaganda, the world of anecdotes, the world of fetishes and ancestor worship,” he wrote. With abstract works such as Infinity, we’re free to find our own reading—or not.
Whereas abstraction attempts to reject passed-down meanings, the image of George Washington is layered with them. Part of what is so moving about, say, getting up close to Washington’s military uniform at the National Museum of American History is the way it challenges how we’ve come to see him as an icon rather than as an actual person.
Abstraction has long been subject to right-wing attacks. During the Red Scare, for instance, George A. Dondero, a U.S. representative from Michigan, crusaded to rid American art of what he saw as communist influence. In a 1949 speech that could be ripped from Truth Social today, he framed a list of 20th-century art movements as un-American weapons for destruction: “Dadaism aims to destroy by ridicule. Expressionism aims to destroy by aping the primitive and insane,” he said. “Abstractionism aims to destroy by the creation of brainstorms.”
Sure, the unpredictable responses to abstract art—the brainstorms—can be a little intimidating. How many of us have stood, a bit clueless, before Jackson Pollock’s riotous colors or Cy Twombly’s frenetic scratches and wondered if we might need a Ph.D. for this?
But there’s also a certain joy to find in it. One National Museum of American History curator, David Shayt, embraced the compounding, shifting meanings of abstraction in a 2008 essay about the museum’s Rivera. The sculpture marked an early work of abstract art commissioned by the U.S. government, but, Shayt argues, the commission was more about the government’s belief that Rivera, a prominent abstract-expressionist sculptor known for his twisting metal forms, could capture the museum’s dual identity in its early days as the National Museum of History and Technology. Cain, the architect, had convinced the government that the sculpture would be a mechanical model of the solar system, a “twenty-first-century orrery.” But Rivera, who cited the abstractionist Piet Mondrian and the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși as among his influences, asserted no such thing. “What I make represents nothing but itself,” he said.
That didn’t stop the National Museum of American History’s staff from making their own meaning over the years, particularly as employees of a “pragmatic museum of history rather than a museum of art,” Shayt wrote. “Is it a mathematical symbol? A wisp of battlefield smoke? A tennis stroke?” he asked of Infinity. One of the sculpture’s greatest attributes, he continued, is “an expressiveness that can evolve in step with the evolution of the museum whose entrance it fronts.”
For an example of the kind of aesthetic Trump prefers, you don’t have to go far from the Rivera. A short walk brings you to Freedom Plaza, where the National Park Service has installed a pop-up exhibition for the nation’s 250th birthday. Rows of traditional, metal statues of Revolutionary War soldiers line the plaza—many, notably, represent enslaved individuals. Standing on a high plinth, meanwhile, is Caesar Rodney, a slaveholder and Declaration of Independence signer, who looms over the display. The statue had been removed in Delaware during the Black Lives Matter protests, only to be restored in Washington as some conservatives began championing him as a symbol of the left’s overreach. Trump has placed a similar style of traditional statue—direct, simple—throughout the White House Rose Garden and envisions much of the same for the Garden of American Heroes, another of his planned D.C. projects, where abstraction is explicitly forbidden. There’s very little room for interpretation in these sorts of statues. They mean what they mean.
Much of the Trump-era fight over history has boiled down to a struggle about trust. The Trump administration says the history the Smithsonian tells is not patriotic enough; the institution counters that Americans can hold patriotism and complexity at once. The National Museum of American History museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, told a congressional committee this summer: “Telling our history fully is not anti-American. It is a form of respect for the American people.” Abstraction, too, holds a kind of esteem for its viewers, trusting them to navigate its symbol-less terrain. In his essay, Motherwell wrote that the emergence of abstract art is one sign that there are still people who “know how to respect and follow their inner feelings, no matter how irrational or absurd they may first appear.”
On the west side of the museum stands another abstract piece, a massive, 40-foot Alexander Calder that the museum calls a “monument to modernity.” Its jagged black edges reach outward, conveying a sense of rupture or change. On Saturday, the area around the Calder was roped off with caution tape, surely something to do with conservation or work on the museum grounds. But it felt a little ominous, as though it were a warning not for museumgoers, but for the art itself.

Nearly two years after the last update to Boox’s smartphone-sized black-and-white e-reader, the company announced the Palma 3 with a sleek redesign, new functionality, and a handful of other small updates that may justify its significant price bump depending on how you plan to use it. While the Palma 2 launched in 2024 for $279.99, the Palma 3 will be $339.99 and is expected to be “available soon.”
The Boox Palma 3 gets stylus support and a sleek redesign
The next version of Boox’s smartphone-sized e-reader ships with Android 16.
The most obvious upgrade for the Palma 3 is the hardware itself. It still features the same 6.13-inch, 300ppi E Ink Carta screen as its predecessor (which is now quite a few years old), but it’s wrapped in a new anodized aluminum frame with a paperlike fiberglass backplate. The Palma 3 looks like a significant upgrade to the Palma line, even if under the hood you’ll find more of the same. The pocketable e-reader is powered by a Qualcomm Q-6690 octa-core processor with 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage expandable with a microSD card. It also includes a 3950mAh rechargeable battery, a 16-megapixel camera on the back, and a fingerprint reader in the power button.
The original Palma and the Palma 2 came with Android 11 and Android 13, respectively, but the new Palma 3 ships with Android 16, which is just one generation behind the latest version of the OS. That should help it feel like a more modern mobile device. And like the color screen Palma 2 Pro, the Palma 3 supports the Boox InkSense Plus active stylus so you can use the e-reader as a digital notepad with your preferred note-taking app. But it’s not included. The stylus is an optional upgrade that will add another $46 to the cost of the Palma 3, pushing it closer to the price of premium e-notes like the Remarkable Paper Pure.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink made the first public declaration Monday that the United States has placed “space control weapons” in orbit, an announcement that will surely reverberate in the power centers of Beijing and Moscow.
Space Force officials have previously expressed their interest in acquiring space-based weapons, and Pentagon leaders have become more open to discussing space warfare in recent years. Therefore, Meink’s announcement Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference near Washington, DC, was not entirely unexpected.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats, wherever they exist. This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said in prepared remarks.
Meink did not reveal any details about the weapons, but the disclosure of their existence underlines a remarkable turnaround in the Pentagon’s thinking about orbital warfare, something no senior official wanted to discuss publicly until a few years ago. Military officials recently have openly discussed orbital combat, defensive countermeasures on satellites, and a new ground-based weapon designed to disable an enemy satellite in orbit.
“There are a lot of factors that roll into how we talk about these things,” Meink said. “We spend a lot of time talking about how we’re going to talk about these things. It is important from a deterrence perspective. But on the other hand, me talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit deterrence, so we’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else.”
Meink also did not say when the Space Force deployed the space-based weapons. The development of space technology often takes years, so it is likely the weapons program, whatever it is, spanned multiple presidential administrations.
“I would just say that the space environment is critical for military and economic security, and we need to make sure that the US can operate freely there,” Meink said.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink speaks Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland.
Credit:
Craig Hudson/Air and Space Forces Association
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink speaks Monday at the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland.
Credit:
Craig Hudson/Air and Space Forces Association
Taking stock
The Pentagon’s acknowledgement Monday comes after US officials began highlighting Russia’s testing of an apparent anti-satellite weapon in orbit in 2020. Officials in the Biden administration accused Russia in 2024 of deploying operational anti-satellite weapons. Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), the former chair of the House Intelligence Committee, revealed a US government assessment the same year that Russia might put a nuclear weapon into space. A nuclear detonation in low-Earth orbit would jeopardize thousands of commercial and military spacecraft, including Starlinks, US spy satellites, Chinese satellites, and the International Space Station.
China, too, has deployed satellites that US military officials view with suspicion. Open source data indicate Chinese satellites routinely maneuver close to US military assets in orbit, likely for surveillance, similar to the way US satellites sometimes park themselves next to Chinese or Russian spacecraft.
“China continues to launch and operate highly maneuverable satellites, demonstrating an advanced level of technological and operational acumen that, if not already deployed for such purposes, could enable a formidable on-orbit counterspace arsenal,” analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies wrote in their 2025 Space Threat Assessment.
In press conference later Monday, Meink defended the US military’s deployment of space-based weapons by citing China and Russia’s own advancements in the field.
“Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?” Meink said in response to a reporter’s question. “For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space. We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment.”
Military commanders have routinely used satellites for communications, navigation, and missile warning for decades. Today, the list of applications is expanding, with space-based sensing and targeting, broadband connectivity through networks like Starlink, and perhaps soon, space-based interceptors for missile defense.
The first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared (Next-Gen OPIR) missile warning satellite, estimated to cost more than $4 billion, is likely the Space Force’s most expensive satellite since the branch was established in 2019.
Credit:
Lockheed Martin
The first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared (Next-Gen OPIR) missile warning satellite, estimated to cost more than $4 billion, is likely the Space Force’s most expensive satellite since the branch was established in 2019.
Credit:
Lockheed Martin
“With everything we’re talking about doing, from long-range fires to control of our forces, our maintaining and being able to count on those space capabilities is important,” Meink said. “It is critically important that we maintain our dominance, not only in the air but in space. So we’ve had to take steps to make sure that that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”
President Donald Trump nominated Meink for the top civilian post in the Air Force last year. Before becoming secretary, Meink served as an Air Force officer, civilian program manager, and senior intelligence official in Democratic and Republican administrations.
The categories include directed-energy, such as lasers, radio frequency jammers, and kinetic weapons capable of physically destroying a target. These types of weapons could be positioned on the ground or in space. In 2025, Gen. Chance Saltzman, until earlier month the Space Force’s chief of space operations, said other countries, presumably China and Russia, are pursuing all six categories. “We’re not pursuing all of those yet,” Saltzman said at the time.
But Saltzman argued that maybe the United States should. “There are good reasons to have all those categories,” he said.
The Space Force revealed its first acknowledged weapon system in June, when it announced the operational acceptance of a ground-based mobile satellite jammer called Meadowlands. Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation think tank, speculated that the “space control weapons” announced by Meink on Monday could be jammers placed in orbit.
“China and Russia are both thought to have space-based jammers,” Samson wrote in an email to Ars. “I’ve always thought that the US must have them, too.”
Anti-satellite tests, particularly those using direct ascent or other kinetic weapons, have been widely condemned because they generate space debris.
Anti-satellite tests, particularly those using direct ascent or other kinetic weapons, have been widely condemned because they generate space debris.
Credit:
NASA
US officials have repeatedly voiced a preference for “counterspace” weapons that do not generate space debris. A space-based kinetic weapon would leave behind a cloud of space junk jeopardizing countless satellites in orbit, including the US military’s own assets, and there’s no public indication that the United States has tested such a weapon (the US military has demonstrated a ground-based anti-satellite weapon), according to Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“Then there are non-kinetic weapons such as signal jammers and spoofers and laser dazzlers. From an under-the-hood hardware standpoint, such weapons are doppelgängers to technology already found at scale in orbit,” Swope said. “Any radio transmitter could be a jammer. Any inter-satellite optical link could be a laser dazzler. Certainly, a jammer or dazzler could be purpose-built, too.”
It is also not clear what the US military’s space weapons might target. Space control has a broad definition in US military doctrine, and term encompasses weapons that could be used against targets in space or on Earth, Swope said.
“For example, blowing up a satellite ground station to prevent an adversary from using a satellite is a space control activity,” Swope told Ars. “The fact that the weapons—plural—are on-orbit is a more significant data point and disclosure. This might be the first time a US official has spoken about the United States possessing on-orbit weapons.”
Swope said the lack of detail in Meink’s statement Monday raises questions about the Pentagon’s motivation for the disclosure.
“It is too vague to have a meaningful deterrent value,” Swope said. “Deterrence is not only about a weapon’s fact of existence but also about having an awareness of how the weapon will be used. For example, the concept of mutually assured destruction was based on the premise of how nuclear weapons would be used and not simply the fact of their existence.
“What also made deterrence work is an awareness of the destructive power of nuclear weapons,” Swope continued. “Both how and when the [space-based] weapon would be used and its destructive potential are ambiguous. Talking heads and pontificators like me are going to have a field day with the disclosure, but it’s not clear what Russia, China, and other potential adversaries are supposed to do with it.”
There was no immediate reaction Monday from the governments of China or Russia.
“Now that the United States has officially acknowledged it has those systems in space, it has opened the door for China and Russia to do the same, which people in the US will then use as justification for why we needed those systems there in the first place,” Samson said.
What is clear is there is now an arms race in orbit. The United States and China are leading the way by measures of volume and sophistication, while Russia appears to be the most aggressive in terms of tactics. But it matters less who started the arms race than how it ends.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

Ryder Cup 2027: Team Europe stars give verdict on early trip to Adare Manor and 'fresh energy' for Luke Donald's side
Team Europe enjoyed a practice round at Adare Manor on Monday ahead of the Ryder Cup being hosted there next September; Several members of Luke Donald's side discussed the benefits of the team trip in their BMW PGA Championship press conferences
Tuesday 15 September 2026 23:21, UK
It may still be a year to go until Team Europe's bid for a historic Ryder Cup threepeat, but Luke Donald has already had many of his prospective line-up together at Adare Manor.
Although not quite a full scouting mission like Donald provided ahead of previous Ryder Cup wins at Marco Simone GC and Bethpage Black, it gave many of his potential players an early experience of tackling next year's Ryder Cup venue in Ireland.
A mix of established Ryder Cup members and likely rookie contenders made the trip after the Amgen Irish Open, with a team dinner followed by 18 holes on Monday

Sixteen players joined Donald and his vice-captains for the team session ahead of travelling onto the DP World Tour's BMW PGA Championship - 10 of last year's line-up, two more with past Ryder Cup pedigree and four potential debutants.
"Any time I'm asked to go to Adare Manor, I'm going to go happily and willingly," said Jon Rahm. "It's one of the best hotel golf course experiences there is in the world.
"It was a lot of fun. It was very enjoyable. I think those days are great for all of us to see each other and just in a way remember why we do what we do.
"For those players who have never been there before, I think it's just getting those first nerves out of the way of how they may feel.
Who made the trip to Adare Manor?
Only Rory McIlroy and Rasmus Hojgaard were missing from Donald's dozen that celebrated a 15-13 victory in New York. Alex Noren - a winner in 2018 and vice-captain last year - and Nicolai Hojgaard, part of the 2023 team, also made the trip.
Alex Fitzpatrick and Kristoffer Reitan both featured after impressive rookie campaigns on the PGA Tour, while Spanish duo Eugenio Chacarra and Ángel Ayora were the other newcomers involved.
Most travelled straight from the Amgen Irish Open, with Shane Lowry a later arrival after his record-breaking 11-shot win on home soil at Trump International Golf Links.
"It was a lovely boys' day out, in the sense we got together and had a nice dinner," Justin Rose told the Sky Sports podcast. "There was some intention-setting of what it means to be on the team and what the plans are going forward.
Subscribe now on: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | Spreaker
"The round itself yesterday was very casual, very fun and just a first look at the golf course. Having Adare Manor pretty much to yourself is a pretty special experience.
"For them [rookies], it lights the fire even more in them to want to be a part of that team. It gives them the comfort to feel like they're already part of the team, in the sense of [being in] Luke's thoughts, the way of doing things and how the captain goes about it.
"It doesn't necessarily feel like a game-changing trip and 'wow, we have an advantage' or anything like that, but I think it's very important in terms of culture setting and all that."
What were course conditions like?
The European players went out in groups of four for a round in calm conditions, with some playing the course for the first time and others refamiliarizing themselves with a venue that previously hosted the JP McManus Pro-Am.
"With the good weather they've had in Europe, in Ireland, it was in as good a shape as I've ever seen it," Rahm added. "It was actually firm. They could have had it as fast as they wanted to.
"It wasn't overly fast because obviously I think they want the public to still enjoy the week. It was in perfect condition. It was immaculate."
The last two Ryder Cups in Europe have been on venues used for regular DP World Tour events, with Le Golf National (2018) a past site of the Open de France and Marco Simone GC (2023) the Open d'Italia, giving Donald a different challenge in Ireland.
"The strategy around setting up the course is very different from when they have a lot of data from the [DP World] Tour," Noren explained. "It's a very difficult task to set that up, I think, to our advantage. We'll see how they do.
"It's the course and the resources where you can set it up pretty much however you want - you can grow in the rough, you can expand, and you can use tee boxes. It's like not particularly a blank sheet of paper, but you can do whatever you want."
Who else was missing and what happens next?
PGA Championship winner Aaron Rai was invited but unable to attend due to a close friend's wedding in Portugal on Sunday, while Tom McKibbin - who played two rounds with Donald in Ireland last week - was not involved.
Ryder Cup qualification is already under way, with points only available via the Race to Dubai standings for the rest of this season before including FedExCup points in January, with Rose expecting to see some new editions in Team Europe next September.
"I think freshening it up a little bit would be a good thing," Rose admitted. "You want your team to be experienced but to have some fresh energy is always great. Whether that be ideas, style of game, pairing options - to change is up is a good thing.
"There's plenty of opportunity for guys to break through. I think the transition from Whistling Straits (2021) into Rome was fantastic and I think that only strengthened into solidifying some of those players that stepped into that role at Bethpage.
There are so many good young players, like the Højgaards [Nicolai and Rasmus], Ludvig [Åberg], even Bob [MacIntyre]. Those guys are now real stalwarts of the team. There has been a great transition in Europe, so we can afford another new batch of youngsters."
Could consistency be key again for Team Europe?
Europe carried 11 of their 12-man line-up and four of the five vice-captains from their 2023 victory to New York in 2025, with the Molinari brothers - Edoardo and Francesco - already confirmed for a third consecutive stint in Donald's backroom team.
Padraig Harrington has been added as a vice-captain on home soil, while McIlroy anticipates the bulk of Donald's last two teams to be back together again in Ireland.
"If there's ever a place to blend rookies, it is in Europe," McIlroy told Sky Sports. "The thing that I preach around the European Ryder Cup team is there's this continuity.
"I think continuity between the captain, the players, the vice captains is a big thing in a team environment. Look, inevitably there might be some new faces on that team, but I don't think there's certainly not going to be wholesale changes.
"I think the nucleus of our team will remain the nucleus. You might have a couple [new] maybe, but I'd say for the most part, as long as everyone plays well and stays injury-free, you're going to have a very similar looking team to what we've had the last couple."
The Ryder Cup will be held from September 17-19 next year, live on Sky Sports. Donald will be looking to be the first captain in history to win three consecutive Ryder Cups.

What triggered the mass migrant crossings into Ceuta?
Over the last 24 hours, the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta - home to around 83,000 people - has seen an unprecedented surge in migrant arrivals.
An estimated 60,000 people from Morocco are believed to have crossed into the North African enclave that has long been a focal point for migrant attempting to reach Europe.
Dozens of people died while trying to make the crossing.
On Friday evening, Spanish officials confirmed that more than 48,000 of the migrants had voluntarily returned to Morocco.
BBC's Sarah Rainsford explains what may have triggered the surge in crossings and what happens next.

State of U.S. democracy reaches new low, report finds
U.S. democracy has reached its lowest levels in 50 years, according to a new global report that tracks democratic performance around the world.
For several years, Dr. Seema Shah, who heads the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance's democracy assessment team, said their researchers have observed a global pattern of democratic decline: "Severe drops in scores that measure freedom of expression, freedom of the press, credible elections, effective parliament," she said.
Shah says that in the 50 years of compiling this survey, she's seen undemocratic trends like this correcting themselves.
But not this time.
"It's getting worse and worse," Shah says. "So that's really worrying, especially because we also see that people are more willing in some cases to consider non-democratic leadership or non-democratic governance."
The organization's annual Global State of Democracy report, which tracks democratic performance across 174 countries and draws on data going back to 1975, was released Tuesday. The latest report focuses on changes in democratic performance between 2020 and 2025.
And Shah says one country stood out for how far its democracy has declined. "The clearest example, unfortunately, is the United States," she says.
The report says that in 2025, "President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies. … The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing long-standing alliances and multilateral cooperation."
Shah says the U.S. has historically served as a bastion of democratic governance, with strong performance in the rule of law and judicial independence and a prominent role in promoting democracy around the world. "But that's no longer the case," says Shah.
"Inside the U.S. and outside the U.S., we're seeing in the U.S. administration policies harming domestic democracy...but also really weakening global norms and actually providing fodder for other non-democratic leaders."
Democracy, she notes, is no longer the central focus of U.S. foreign policy.
Democratic values are also no longer the basis for new alliances globally, Shah says, noting that the democratic aid the U.S. used to provide to developing countries has been dismantled.
President Trump has hinted at this himself. At a summit last year in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, he criticized previous U.S. administrations as "interventionist" and said the U.S. would no longer give other countries "lectures on how to live."
Domestically, Shah says, the U.S. has seen declines in nearly half of the 30 indicators the organization measures. She says they've hit their lowest levels in 50 years of gathering data on democracies.
And it's not just the U.S. seeing these declines.
The organization's survey shows that 57% of countries surveyed showed declines in at least one key indicator of democratic performance, with the rule of law serving as the weakest-performing area of democracy globally.
But what about countries that have seen a resurgence of democracy — places like Poland, Hungary and Syria in recent years?
"What the research shows is that, depressingly, in 90% of cases, a democracy that has suffered decline and then comes back and what's called a U-turn in 90% of the cases, they suffer another democratic decline within five years."
Shah says candidates promising change typically find that when voters give them power, they often are not able to deliver on those promises because remnants of the old guard often prevent those changes.
"And unless," she says, "you're willing to break your own democratic laws to get them out, what can you do?"

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of ₹10 Lakh on ride unicorn Rapido for misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices, unfair contract and dark patterns, where consumers are prompted to pay more before their rides are confirmed. The order, passed by a bench comprising chief commissioner Nidhi Khare and commissioner Anupam Mishra, follows a sector-wide examination of cab aggregators operating in India to understand pre-ride tipping and dynamic pricing practices in India. During the investigation, the CCPA found that Rapido’s app displayed users prompts suggesting specific top-ups of ₹10, ₹20 or ₹30 to improve their chances of getting a ride. The regulator held that Rapido's algorithm first quoted a fare, and then, once the rider had booked at that fare, asked the rider to pay more because ‘Captains’ (drivers) were supposedly not accepting the fare. That created a false impression that getting a ride quickly depends on paying extra fees. The CCPA held this to be "confirm shaming", a dark pattern listed under the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, as it creates urgency and a fear of losing the ride if the rider does not agree to pay more. Separately, the regulator examined Rapido's "set your price" slider and found its colour coding was steering pricing decisions. Raising the price surfaced a green message about a higher chance of getting a ride, while lowering it triggered a red or orange warning. This design, the CCPA held, amounted to a second dark pattern — "interface interference". A tip, as the regulator observed, is a voluntary payment made after a service has been rendered, and can not be presented as a condition for the service being provided at all. It also pointed to the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025, which require any tipping feature to be offered only after a ride is completed — not at the time of booking or during the ride. Rapido had argued that tipping on its platform is voluntary, and that the prompts simply mirrored the kind of real-time negotiation that happens offline between a rider and a driver. The CCPA rejected these submissions, holding that the timing and design of the prompts applied pressure at the moment the users seemed to be the most dependent on the platform. It also noted that Rapido had not shown any data to show that paying more actually improves a rider's chances of getting a ride, making the claim unsubstantiated and misleading. The action against Rapido is part of the CCPA's broader scrutiny of advance-tip and dark-pattern practices across ride-hailing and bike-taxi platforms. The regulator had earlier issued notices to Uber, Ola, Rapido and Namma Yatri, directing them to comply with the 2023 dark patterns guidelines and file self-declarations on compliance. Its examination of Uber and Ola is still ongoing. Besides, it also adds to the ongoing regulatory scrutiny over the advance tipping dark patterns employed by ride-hailing platforms. Earlier in August, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) directed ride-hailing aggregators to remove tipping prompts shown before or during rides, saying these violate the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025. The ministry reiterated that passengers can tip drivers only after completing a ride, with the entire amount going to the driver. Platforms also cannot suggest that tipping could improve ride confirmation, driver acceptance or service quality. The directive comes amid wider scrutiny of aggregators, including NHRC action over alleged overcharging. The 2025 guidelines also cover licensing, driver training and insurance, vehicle safety, fares and penalties, including licences of up to five years and fines of up to ₹1 Cr.

Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) spokesperson Saurav Das asserted that all schools in Uttar Pradesh's Gautam Buddha Nagar were directed to shut down after the pressure group conducted infrastructure checks at government schools as part of its nationwide 'School Thik Karo' (Fix the Schools) campaign.
“All government schools in Gautam Buddha Nagar in UP have been directed to be CLOSED immediately. This is after we inspected just ONE SCHOOL in Noida,” Das posted on X (formerly Twitter) on Tuesday.
"What is the UP government trying to hide?" he asked.
Das alleged that he and his team were denied entry to any other school after they inspected the first one. He further alleged that the principal had told them the decision was taken on the instructions of senior officials.
“We had plans to visit five schools, but we were allowed to visit only one primary school in Garhi Chaukhandi. Everywhere else, we were denied entry. The principal at the school told us that they had received an order from above not to give us access,” Das was quoted as saying by HT.
The District Inspector of Schools (DIOS) of Gautam Buddha Nagar, however, described the claims as “misleading and false.”
Speaking to Hindustan Times, an official from the DIOS office said: “All schools in the district are open as of now. There is no such notice of closure."
“All government-run schools in Gautam Buddh Nagar are being operated as per the timetable prescribed by the government and the education department, and no order has been issued regarding the closure of any school,” HT quoted the statement from his office.
During his inspection of schools in Noida, part of the CJP's ongoing school audit campaign across several parts of the country, Das urged young people to conduct similar audits of government schools in their own areas.
“Today, we’ve come to Noida. We’re going to audit some schools here as part of our 'School Theek Karo' campaign. We’ll see the conditions in which children are studying. Noida is one of the better districts in UP, so hopefully, the school conditions will be good too. Whatever the situation is, we’ll show you the reality,” Das said while talking to the media.
"We want young people from UP to go out and audit schools as well—to show what condition the schools in their neighbourhoods are in and what kind of education children are receiving. Today, we’re planning to visit schools in Noida, but we’d encourage other young people to take on this responsibility too and audit schools in their own areas..." Das added.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke launched the 'School Thik Karo' campaign last month from his native village of Santuk Pimpri in Maharashtra’s Hingoli district, calling for a nationwide social audit of government schools and improved basic facilities for students.
Dipke said the campaign would involve collecting information on basic facilities in government schools across Maharashtra and other parts of the country.
The CJP plans to provide a standardised assessment form through social media, allowing parents and residents to report deficiencies by uploading videos and other information about schools.
The proposed checklist will cover facilities such as electricity, drinking water, separate functional toilets for boys and girls, benches and the quality of midday meals.

Denmark says Russian frigate fired flares at helicopter
The helicopter was on a ‘routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate’ in the waters off Denmark’s southernmost town
Denmark and Russia were at a war of words on Tuesday after Danish authorities accused a Russian frigate of firing flares at a Danish military helicopter.
The armed forces said in a statement late on Monday that “one of the air force’s Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser”, Denmark’s southernmost town.
The frigate had fired “two flares towards the helicopter. One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter”, it added.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen on Tuesday slammed the incident as “reckless action from Russia”.

Pennsylvania health officials have confirmed two additional measles-associated deaths, bringing the total confirmed deaths in the state this year to four, and driving U.S. fatalities to the highest level in decades.
Both individuals were unvaccinated, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said in a statement on Tuesday. One lived in Jefferson County, the other lived in Mifflin County. Additional identifying details won’t be released, the department said.
The deaths are a grim milestone in the return of a disease that the U.S. once largely considered vanquished. Pennsylvania hadn’t recorded a measles-related death in 35 years before this summer; it has now reported four in a matter of weeks, as the state’s outbreak has swelled to nearly 700 cases.

The rollout of a Medicare program that uses artificial intelligence to approve or deny care was hasty and error-ridden, according to more than a thousand pages of recently released documents and data.
The pilot program, called the Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction model, or WISeR, launched in January and requires health care providers to seek approvals before they can provide certain procedures and products, like skin substitutes and epidural injections for pain management. The experiment operates in New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, and Washington and will run until 2031.
Among other issues, the documents obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit show that one WISeR vendor warned the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services that it was unrealistic to expect a working product by the time the federal agency wanted to launch the program.

5 rescued baby orangutans stable, expert panel reviews health at Odisha zoo
A specialist team examined five rescued baby orangutans in quarantine at Nandankanan after one developed fever. The review found them stable, even as Odisha agencies pursue a suspected trafficking trail.
A six-member team of experts on Tuesday examined the health of five baby orangutans being kept in quarantine at Odisha's Nandankanan Zoological Park, days after they were rescued from a forest in Balasore district. The review came after one of the infant primates developed a fever on Sunday and was put on medication, officials said.
The orangutans, a species native to the rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, were rescued on September 8, triggering an investigation into suspected wildlife trafficking. Zoo authorities said all five infants are now stable and under close observation.
In a statement, Nandankanan Zoological Park said members of a technical committee constituted by the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Wildlife), Odisha, visited the quarantine facility and assessed the health of all five orangutans.
"After further examination and discussions tomorrow, the committee will submit its observations," the zoo said.
According to a health bulletin issued by the zoo, the body temperatures of the five infant orangutans ranged between 98 and 99 degrees Fahrenheit.
"All five are apparently stable, with normal feed acceptance and improved activity," an official said.
Zoo veterinarians are monitoring the animals continuously. Authorities have also made special arrangements for their care, including mosquito nets and a temperature-controlled room.
Aditya Acharya, head of the Centre for Wildlife Health at the Odisha University of Agriculture and Technology, said elevated body temperature in orangutans is monitored in a manner similar to humans and treated accordingly. As per a diet chart prepared by experts, the animals are being fed milk every two hours, along with apple and banana fluids and boiled potatoes at regular intervals.
Following the rescue, the Odisha government constituted a five-member technical committee to oversee the orangutans' care. Meanwhile, the Odisha Police's Special Task Force and the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau are jointly investigating a suspected international wildlife smuggling network linked to the case. Officials said there has been no major breakthrough in the probe so far.

Canon announced the second-generation of its EOS R8 with a new retro-inspired redesign and the addition of in-body stabilization. That feature was one of the most notable omissions from the original R8 that launched in 2023 as a smaller, cheaper, and more accessible alternative to the Canon R6 Mark II for photographers wanting a larger full-frame shooter. While the new EOS R8 Mark II is slightly heavier than its predecessor at 1.2 pounds thanks to the additional stabilization functionality, it’s lighter and cheaper than last year’s EOS R6 Mark III.
The EOS R8 Mark II is Canon’s lightest full-frame camera with stabilization
The 24.2-megapixel camera features a retro redesign inspired by Canon’s old film cameras.
The Canon EOS R8 Mark II is expected to be available sometime in late October for $1,899 for the body only, or $2,099 bundled with a Canon 24-50mm stabilized lens. That’s more expensive than the original R8 that launched at $1,499, but more accessible than the $2,799 EOS R6 Mark III thanks to some lower specs and omitted features.
Like its predecessor, the R8 Mark II features the same 24.2-megapixel full-frame CMOS sensor as the R6 Mark II, while the R6 Mark III got a bump to a 32.5-megapixel sensor. The new R8 Mark II still exclusively uses an electronic shutter instead of an additional mechanical one, with high-speed captures maxing out at 40fps again. To ensure you’re not too late to a critical moment, a pre-continuous shooting mode captures up to an additional 20 shots before you press the shutter button.
The new five-axis in-body stabilization offers up to 7.5 stops of shake correction that can be expanded by pairing the camera with a lens featuring its own stabilization. The R8 Mark II also features Canon’s Dual Pixel CMOS AF II system with what the company describes as “more tenacious tracking” than what the R8 offered. The autofocus system can also recognize animals, vehicles, and people, with the option to register up to 10 different people by their faces and rank their priority.
Video capabilities max out at 4K/60fps, but frame rates can be boosted to up to 180fps by dropping the resolution to 1080p. As Canon is targeting the R8 Mark II as a potential full-frame option for amateur photographers, the camera includes 16 different color filters, an easy to way to increase or decrease depth of blur that handles settings like f-stop and shutter speed automatically, and creative bracketing that takes three photos with different brightness and color tones.
Following other companies drawing inspiration from older film cameras for the design of new digital shooters, the R8 Mark II eschews the curves of the original R8 for a more boxy and angular body. Canon credits the nearly 40-year-old EOS 650 and its pentaprism housing on top as the inspiration for the R8 Mark II. Other hardware upgrades include a new multi-controller joystick above the camera’s screen, which makes it easier to select focal points, and its single SD card slot repositioned on the side of the camera so it’s still accessible when using a tripod. Canon will also sell a matching $99.99 accessory that extends the R8 Mark II’s grip, making it easier to hold when using larger lenses.
In October Canon is also releasing a free new Windows app called Dual Pixel 3D Converter that leverages additional info captured by Canon’s dual-pixel autofocus system to generate 3D imagery from the 2D photos the camera takes. You can use the app to create a 3D photo with a background you can move around, a 3D model with the background completely removed, or short 3D videos demonstrating an animated perspective adjustment of close-up subjects.

Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline
- Published
Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.
The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.
The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.
New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.
The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.
It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.
The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday.
Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand.
"Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis.
Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed".
The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended.
There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen.
At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based.
The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects".
The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict.

Cate Blanchett will travel to Tokyo for the 39th edition of the Tokyo International Film Festival, where five short films backed by the Displacement Film Fund will receive their Japan premieres.
Blanchett co-founded the Displacement Film Fund, which supports displaced filmmakers and those with a demonstrated history of telling authentic stories rooted in the experiences of displaced people. The fund was announced at the International Film Festival Rotterdam in January 2025 in partnership with IFFR’s Hubert Bals Fund, which serves as managing partner. UNHCR acts as strategic partner, with additional backing from Amahoro Coalition, Master Mind, the Tamer Family Foundation, Uniqlo – a founding partner – and Droom en Daad, a Dutch cultural foundation. The SP Lohia Foundation came aboard as a major partner when the second edition of the fund was confirmed at IFFR 2026.
Blanchett said: “I am privileged to have the opportunity to share the inaugural short films supported through the Displacement Film Fund with audiences at Tokyo International Film Festival. In a world where conflict and persecution are driving displacement and division, cinematic storytelling has a vital role to play in connecting with the experiences of others. Being displaced shouldn’t mean filmmakers abandon their creativity; in fact their stories may feel even more urgent.”
Popular on Variety
Following the screening, Blanchett will participate in a Q&A alongside two of the five directors whose work is included in the program: Mohammad Rasoulof, whose “Sense of Water” centers on an Iranian writer confronting a foreign language in exile, and Shahrbanoo Sadat, director of “Super Afghan Gym,” which is set in a downtown Kabul gym during the one hour each day reserved for women.
The other three films in the selection are “Allies in Exile” (U.K./Syria), directed by Hasan Kattan, which follows two Syrian filmmakers documenting the trauma of waiting for asylum; “Rotation” (Ukraine/Turkey), directed by Maryna Er Gorbach, depicting a therapeutic hypnosis ritual experienced by a young Ukrainian woman who transitioned from civilian life to military service; and “Whispers of a Burning Scent” (Somalia/Austria/Germany), directed by Mo Harawe, in which a quiet wedding musician finds his private life drawn into public view.
Blanchett’s Tokyo visit coincides with a separate honor: she is to receive the Praemium Imperiale Award during the same week. She recently wrapped production on Alice Birch’s “Sweetsick” and is in development with Janicza Bravo on a film about Martha Stewart. Her feature “Father Mother Sister Brother” (2025), which won the Golden Lion at the 82nd Venice Film Festival, is scheduled for Japanese theatrical release on Nov. 20.
The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival is hosted by Unijapan and takes place Oct. 26 to Nov. 4.

Apple’s High-Stakes Gamble On Siri AI Two years on, Apple’s rebuilt Siri AI has now finally arrived with iOS 27. But most of its advanced AI features are limited to premium devices, feature access remains uneven and a subscription model may be on the horizon. So, will Siri AI justify the price? The Long-Awaited Siri: The new launch is Apple’s attempt to turn its voice assistant into a more personal, context-aware interface. Siri AI can draw on information across messages, email and photos, understand what is on screen and act within compatible apps. But not everyone will get to experience the full version. A Fragmented Experience? The iOS 27 update will reach a broad group of iPhones, but Apple Intelligence and Siri AI will require newer devices. Advanced features will need higher memory and have been reserved for select premium products. This creates a two-tier experience: many users can access Siri AI, but only high-end devices will be able to receive its fullest version. The India Test: Just like its US peers, Indian users will also receive broad availability for several Apple Intelligence tools. But availability does not guarantee a seamless experience. Siri AI must understand local accents, different speech patterns and multilingual habits if it is to feel truly useful in India. Early reports suggest uneven reliability in routine tasks even though users expect an assistant to be fast and dependable. The New Apple Tax: The cost question extends beyond buying an AI-ready iPhone. Apple has indicated that some server-based AI features will have usage caps, adding that higher access could carry a fee from 2027 onward. This could push Siri AI into a tiered subscription model, likely linked to iCloud+. On top of this, developers will also have to quickly build compatible apps for Siri AI. So, can Apple turn Siri AI into a must-have service rather than another expensive ecosystem lock-in? Despite 10 nominations, Shrinking came up short at the Emmys on Monday, but the Warner Bros Television produced show may be taking centerstage in court soon.
A longtime Key Second Assistant Director on the Jason Segel and Harrison Ford starring series says she was abruptly fired after a long day of shooting on July 10 by Executive Producer Kip Kroeger because of so-called “different needs of production.” In her seven claim compliant filed today in L.A. Superior Court against WBTV, Shrinking EP/director Randall Winston and others, Mindy Tessa McKoin doesn’t buy it.
As the document from attorney Avi Gholian exclaims of the industry vet’s multi-season Shrinking stint: “no performance deficiency, misconduct. or business rationale was identified then or anytime thereafter.”
Watch on Deadline
Filing earlier today with the California Civil Rights Department before going to the LASC docket, McKoin alleges the real reason she was canned was because of reporting an intentional “sexual abuse” by Winston at the June 22, 2024 Shrinking Season 2 wrap party, She says it was because of that and because of her raising a stink about of “inaccurate time records and pay statements.” Production and WBTV problems that Loot and Young Sheldon alum McKoin and her lawyers assert resulted in zero “corrective action” on the former and a lot of her Shrinking bosses not making a “big deal” about the former.
McKoin says the CAA-repped Winston subjected her “to unwelcome, severe harassment because of her sex, including by grabbing and groping her breast without her consent at a work-related function in the presence of a coworker” at the 2024 party. “Such conduct was sufficiently severe to alter the conditions of Plaintiff employment and to create a hostile, intimidating, and offensive working environment.”
An environment made all the worse by WBTV doing nothing about it, according to the plaintiff.
While the sexual harassment and sexual battery claims sit on the top of McKoin’s allegations, it is the pay and timecard tampering of sorts that takes up the bulk of Tuesday’s unspecified damages seeking filing.

The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes.
The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US.
From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought.
The US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal.
In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand.
Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades.
The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall.
The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side.
If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water.
In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companies scrambling to find alternative routes.
El Niño has severely affected Central America and northern parts of South America, where nine countries have experienced their hottest June-August period on record this year.
Fifty-two countries across all continents broke their seasonal temperature records for that period, according to an Agence France-Presse analysis of meteorological data from the European Copernicus programme.
The extreme heat has taken many forms, from unprecedented heatwaves in Europe to devastating drought in Sudan and toxic smoke in Indonesia.
More than a third of people experiencing the hottest northern summer months on record were in Africa, particularly in the Sahel and areas south of it.
Eighteen African countries broke their seasonal records for the June-August period, from Mauritania and Sierra Leone in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east.

What is IMAX Enhanced and do you really need it?
IMAX has a certification for content you view at home as well as in the cinema.
IMAX has become somewhat of a household name of late, thanks to the virality of 70mm presentations like The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three. But you may have noticed that the company has expanded its footprint beyond giant cinema screens with a designation for at home-viewing, as well. On Disney+, for instance, a growing number of movies now carry the IMAX Enhanced label.
Confusingly, however, IMAX Enhanced doesn't necessarily mean you're getting the absolute best in image or sound quality. Streaming services intentionally limit the bitrate at which content is delivered to prevent buffering, and this applies to IMAX Enhanced streams too. 4K or Ultra HD Blu-ray offers the highest bitrate, but not every movie gets the IMAX Enhanced label.
What's more, you don't need an IMAX Enhanced-certified TV or sound system (yes, those exist) to realize its benefits. This may seem confusing as many other standards like Dolby Vision actually need compatible hardware too.
So what's the deal with IMAX Enhanced and does the certification really bring anything meaningful to the table?
What does IMAX Enhanced mean?
IMAX Enhanced is a certification for content and hardware devices in your home (rather than the cinema) that promises to deliver a more premium media-watching experience. A movie with the IMAX Enhanced label indicates it has gone through a Digital Media Remastering process to improve the overall quality of the image. But more importantly, IMAX Enhanced movies appear taller than their regular counterparts.
This is because most movies have historically been presented in the wide 2.39:1 aspect ratio. Regular theater screens are designed with this wide aspect ratio in mind (pictured above), but most screens in our lives are actually much taller. TVs almost universally have a 16:9 or 1.78:1 aspect ratio, often resulting in black bars when watching movies at home.
Films shot for IMAX typically have a taller aspect ratio, though, at least for a handful of scenes. An IMAX Enhanced movie will therefore appear taller than a regular, widescreen version. You may still see small black bars since IMAX Enhanced movies on Disney+ are presented in 1.90:1, but you'll still see more of the image.
The other major image-quality component is high dynamic range, or HDR, although some movies may also receive additional remastering from IMAX. HDR significantly improves the color volume, contrast and brightness, but it's not unique to IMAX by any means.
IMAX Enhanced also claims to offer a "theater-quality" digital soundtrack. In practical terms, however, this will greatly vary depending on your audio setup. Turning on IMAX Enhanced requires your setup to support DTS:X spatial audio.
Where can I watch IMAX Enhanced content and how do I enable it?
Many movies released in 4K Blu-ray disc form offer the expanded aspect ratio we've come to associate with IMAX. The Dune series, Interstellar, and the upcoming physical release of The Odyssey use the 1.78:1 aspect ratio to fill modern TVs without any black bars. The back of some 4K Blu-ray cases, like The Dark Knight, explicitly call out "1.78:1 (IMAX sequences)", but others like Interstellar omit the IMAX mention while still acknowledging the 16:9 aspect ratio.
Disney is one of the few holdouts in this regard, though, where its physical releases typically don't get the expanded aspect ratio at all.
For example, the 4K Blu-ray copy of Avengers: Endgame lacks the IMAX label and only offers a 2:39:1 image, even though it's otherwise the highest quality version available on the market. This means you realistically have to choose between the expanded aspect ratio that's available exclusively through the IMAX Enhanced stream on Disney+ versus the excellent detail that a 4K Blu-ray disc offers.
However, few people truly care about the admittedly minimal image quality improvement that you get going from a high-bitrate 4K internet stream to a 4K Blu-ray. My family would immediately notice and appreciate the expanded aspect ratio, making the streaming version superior for them, even if I would personally prefer the Blu-ray.
Disney+ currently has the largest catalog of IMAX Enhanced films in one place. You can also find some IMAX Enhanced content on the Sony Pictures Core app, but you'll need a PS5, Xperia phone or Sony smart TV.
Do I need an IMAX Enhanced TV or sound system?
IMAX Enhanced also exists as a certification for hardware makers, and you'll see TVs and speakers with the label from brands like Sony and TCL. The logo is meant to signal that the hardware in question meets the performance standards outlined by IMAX. However, you don't actually need certified hardware to play back IMAX Enhanced content.
Most modern TVs with support for HDR standards like HDR10 and HDR10+ will be able to play IMAX Enhanced movies on Disney+ as intended. If you're shopping for a new TV, make your choice based on the display technology (like OLED or mini LED) rather than an IMAX Enhanced certification. The latter doesn't always improve your viewing experience, while an OLED display will give you excellent black levels no matter what you watch.
IMAX Enhanced certification is also not required for the expanded aspect ratio on Disney+. All supported devices can display it, even an iPhone. And if you don't want to spend hundreds of dollars on a DTS:X-capable sound system, IMAX Enhanced sound is a separate setting within Disney+ that you can disable entirely.

There is a need to reinvent engineering education, make it contemporary and tailor-made to fit the industrial need of the economy, urged Chief Secretary Shalini Rajneesh, while speaking at the Founder’s Day of the Federation of Karnataka Chambers of Commerce & Industry (FKCCI) here on Tuesday. The key talking points from Pocognoli's bold Scotland squad

Six new call-ups, seven uncapped players, a refreshed defence, a more-of-the-same midfield and an exciting, new-look attack.
The Sebastien Pocognoli Scotland era is already creating serious intrigue - and the Belgian's squad are yet to assemble for a training-ground rondo, never mind play a game.
The 39-year-old's first taste of competitive action starts with a Nations League opener in Slovenia on 26 September - live on the BBC - beginning an extended four-game international period.
In the meantime, let's dissect the talking points from a bold 28-man selection.
- McBurnie & seven uncapped players in Scotland squad 
  - Published6 hours ago
- Scotland fans allowed to buy alcohol at upcoming games 
  - Published6 hours ago
- Is Sevilla's 'all-round striker' Ure ready to lead Scotland's attack? 
  - Published23 August
Gunn to continue behind refreshed backline?
There have been no new call-ups in the goalkeeping department. Angus Gunn, now playing with San Jose Earthquakes in the MLS, has 25 caps and will be the favourite to continue between the sticks.
Pocognoli's first selection has shown that a surprise is not beyond him, though. The Belgian stressed the importance of his style in relation to his squad picks, and Falkirk's Scott Bain is a goalkeeper who can deal with the ball at his feet.
Jon McCracken is also playing regularly for Bradford City in England's League One, but Liam Kelly very much remains second choice at Rangers.
As for the backline, the new Scotland boss has predominantly played with a back three throughout his coaching career at both Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco.
He insists on his teams being aggressive in and out of possession, so will want defenders capable of picking brave passes but also with the pace to cover big distances when playing a high line.
Scott McKenna, Jack Hendry and Kieran Tierney all have experience of playing in a back three under Steve Clarke, albeit the approach will differ under Pocognoli. Captain Andy Robertson also clocked up a lot of minutes at left wing-back.
Aaron Hickey, Nathan Patterson and young Colby Donovan, who has impressed Pocognoli "but needs to improve on things like every young lad", are options for the opposite flank.
Uncapped trio Luis Binks, Stephen Welsh and Luke Graham add more depth at centre-back.
Brondby captain Binks, who qualifies for Scotland through a grandparent, has had an interesting career. "The feeling and the timing about him was right," Pocognoli said of the former Bologna and Como man.
At the age of 25, the left-footed centre-back has already played in the MLS, Serie A, English Championship and now Denmark's top tier.
Meanwhile, Stoke's Graham - also left-footed - enjoyed a breakthrough spell at Dundee last season and continues to excel in England's second division, along with Swansea's Welsh, who proved he could thrive in a possession-based Motherwell side last term.
McPake included in familiar midfield
It is much of the same in midfield, although Scott McTominay is absent following a successful heart procedure and Udinese's Lennon Miller is back after being left out of Clarke's World Cup squad.
There is a welcome return for McTominay's Napoli team-mate Billy Gilmour, who suffered a crushing injury just before the start of the finals.
Arguably Scotland's most composed midfielder and best progressive passer, many expect the 25-year-old to thrive in Pocognoli's system. Miller, 20, could also fall into that category.
Experienced campaigners John McGinn, Ryan Christie, Kenny McLean and Lewis Ferguson - the Scots' standout performer earlier this summer - are all included in a seven-man midfield selection, which also features thriving Hearts player Josh McPake.
Signed this summer from St Johnstone, it has been a remarkable rise for the 24-year-old, who has been listed as a midfielder in the squad despite featuring on the left wing for the Tynecastle side. He was a Stirling Albion player just two years ago.
How excited should fans be by new-look attack?
While Ben Gannon-Doak, Findlay Curtis and McPake offer options in attacking wide areas, there is a centre-forward spot up for grabs in the absence of injured pair Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland, plus the omission of Lyndon Dykes.
A free-scoring spell in Sweden earned Robbie Ure the number nine shirt at Sevilla, Oli McBurnie and his Hull team have made an impressive return to the Premier League and Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie scored in a win against Juventus on Sunday.
"Players who are performing well are in the new pathway," Pocognoli said when asked about Rangers academy product Ure, who is yet to score since his switch to La Liga.
"Robbie is adapting well to La Liga. He's put in some good performances, but he maybe needs to adapt to the intensity. Being selected gives him an opportunity."
On the return of McBurnie, who has received his first Scotland call-up in five years, he added: "It's regarding style of play, playing time and performance. I have to start on a new journey, a new book and it's a new opportunity for some players."
The head coach also spoke of his desire to mix youth with the "DNA and heritage" of his squad, evidenced by the inclusion of teenage James Wilson, who is showing signs of fulfilling his serious potential at Hearts.
By the end of the first week in October the Tartan Army, many of whom have been calling for what Pocognoli is preaching to deliver, will have a clearer idea of what that formula is going to look like on the grass, with a fascinating four-match window approaching.

Athletic Club forward Inaki Williams has announced his retirement from international duty with Ghana.
The 32-year-old scored two goals in 28 caps for the Black Stars after making his debut in September 2022.
