How Long Can the U.S. Escape an Atlantic Hurricane?
The government doesn’t seem ready for a major disaster.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Every president likes to take credit for good news on their watch, but most of them have at least a little shame about it. Not Donald Trump.
September 10 is typically the peak of Atlantic Ocean hurricane season. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration expected a relatively restrained year, but as the meteorologist and hurricane specialist Michael Lowry writes, the season “has never gone beyond September 11th in the reliable records (since at least 1950) without a hurricane” in the Atlantic Ocean—until this year. There aren’t even any strong prospects forming.
Amid spreading violence in the Middle East, warnings of an AI apocalypse, and high fuel prices, it’s a rare piece of good news, and Trump wants credit. Over the weekend, the White House flagged the news, commenting, “Thank you, President Trump!” This is absurd, though maybe no one should be surprised that a man who believed that marking a map with Sharpie can change a hurricane’s path would take credit for a low-key storm season. (He also reportedly once suggested attacking storms with nuclear weapons, so perhaps, as the journalist Catherine Rampell jokes, this is deterrence in action.)
Better explanations than presidential benevolence exist. As my colleague Joshua Partlow has reported, this is an unusual year for the El Niño cycle. In the Pacific Ocean, it has produced very warm water, as well as a number of hurricanes. Hawaii, which is seldom hit, has been struck by two hurricanes so far this year. At least four deaths have been attributed to the storms, and power remains out on some parts of the island of Kauai. But scientists say that El Niño also accounts for the absence of major storms, so far, in the Atlantic. “It’s really staggering, just how inhospitable the Atlantic is to anything that could form a tropical cyclone right now,” Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of atmospheric science at the University at Albany, told PBS. The lull is especially notable because last year’s hurricane season was also astonishingly mild in the United States. Although parts of the Caribbean endured hurricanes, not a single one hit the U.S. mainland.
This is great news for the Americans who are otherwise often in hurricanes’ paths, and who have been slammed by a series of storms in the past decade—including 2024’s Hurricane Helene, the deadliest to hit the mainland United States since Hurricane Katrina, in 2005. It is also great news for Trump, who must be one of the luckiest people in history. Hurricanes can help or, more often, badly hurt a president. George W. Bush’s reputation never recovered from Katrina, whereas Barack Obama’s steady hand during Hurricane Sandy seemed to bolster his reelection campaign. Trump’s handling of storms during his first term was poor; he demonstrated little human warmth and, in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria, jarring coldness.
Trump’s personal behavior aside, his administration has been especially fortunate because under his leadership, FEMA appears to be in no shape to handle a major disaster. In the first months of his second presidency, Trump and then–Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced plans to dismantle FEMA entirely, devolving responsibility for relief to states, an idea panned by most experts. In the meantime, he seemed determined to slowly strangle it, appointing interim leaders with no disaster-relief experience. First came Cameron Hamilton, who was fired after telling Congress that he did not support liquidating FEMA. Next was David Richardson, who, shortly after taking his post in May 2025, acknowledged that he had no completed plan for the impending hurricane season and would reuse the previous year’s. (FEMA employees reported that Richardson said he didn’t even realize such a season existed; a FEMA spokesperson later said he was joking.)
Because no storms have since struck the mainland, these failures ended up having much less human and economic cost. FEMA appears to be on a somewhat stronger footing now. Trump has backed off plans to eliminate FEMA, Noem and Richardson are gone, and Hamilton is back as permanent administrator—and has won some tentative praise for working to learn more about disaster relief. He inherits serious challenges, though. A federal judge ruled on Friday that an administration order to lay off half of FEMA’s workforce was illegal. “Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air,” the judge wrote of the government’s proposal, which included cutting thousands of on-call employees who rush in with aid after a disaster.
A report released last month by the Government Accountability Office was even more scathing. The GAO found that FEMA’s personnel decisions had been made “without assessing whether it had the necessary staffing capacity to meet its mission,” including what it is required to do under law, and that “FEMA is not positioned to determine whether it has the right number of people with the right skills in the right positions at the right time to meet its mission.” Furthermore, the report said, “the agency has no overall strategic direction.”
Alas, the calm before the storms won’t last indefinitely. Experts who spoke with The New York Times said that it would be premature to assume that no major Atlantic hurricanes will form this year. If the president’s political luck continues, then perhaps the East Coast won’t see a really bad storm until after the midterm elections, or maybe even next year. Given his administration’s approach to hurricane preparedness and the travails of FEMA, though, ordinary Americans along the Atlantic coast and the Gulf Coast are likely to see their weather luck run out.

OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar said that AI is reducing the need for some workers, but only repetitive ones.
In a Tuesday interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer on "Mad Money," Friar addressed AI use for efficiency at OpenAI, using her own finance department as an example.
"There is no doubt we are doing things with our own products inside of finance, for example, that do limit the number of people we need," Friar told Cramer. "But in many cases it's for jobs that I don't think of as great jobs, frankly."
Friar pointed to credit checks as one example. OpenAI's procurement operation was conducting them at an annual rate of 2,800 last year, she said.
"That credit check is a pretty mundane piece of work," Friar said. "Do you want a junior analyst doing that, or can we get a very intelligent model to do it for us?"
"I think it's actually enabling people to do more work at the edge, more work where intelligence is needed," Friar added. "And then you get a lot of the rote stuff done by the model and actually done at probably a better scale and with more accuracy, frankly."
The financial payoff was significant: Friar said the cost per check fell from $200 per check to about 17 cents.
"That is a great ROI for a CFO," Friar added.
Friar's comments come as some leading AI figures issue much starker warnings about the technology's impact on employment. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs, while Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as a "godfather of AI," recently said such predictions were "probably right."
Hinton said AI still fails at some tasks, but cautioned that the technology is improving quickly.
"We're in the very early stages," Hinton told Bernie Sanders in an interview in November 2025. "This is a new technology. It's getting better very fast."

Indigenous leader Raoni receives palliative care in Brazil after cancer diagnosis
Renowned Indigenous Chief Raoni Metuktire is receiving palliative care at home in the Brazilian heartland after being diagnosed with cancer at age 94, his institute says
SAO PAULO -- Renowned Indigenous Chief Raoni Metuktire is receiving palliative care at home in the Brazilian heartland after being diagnosed with cancer at age 94, his institute said Monday.
The Raoni Institute said the cancer diagnosis in the chief's digestive system was confirmed after he was hospitalized in Sao Paulo in June due to a severe intestinal obstruction. He underwent surgery then and returned to the region of the city of Peixoto de Azevedo, in Brazil's Mato Grosso state.
“At this moment, our priority is ensuring that Chief Raoni is well cared for, comfortable, and close to his family and his people. We wish to share this information transparently, but we also ask for respect regarding his privacy, his need for rest, and his family’s decisions,” the institute said in a statement.
Raoni, one of the most renowned advocates for the protection of the Amazon rainforest and for Indigenous rights, traveled the world for decades to raise awareness about environmental preservation.
Doctors opted for palliative care given Raoni's advanced age, overall clinical condition, and the high risks associated with aggressive oncological treatments, the institute said.
“Palliative care does not mean an absence of treatment. The goal is to control pain and other symptoms, prevent complications, and ensure nutrition, hydration, medical supervision, nursing care, physical therapy, and the best possible quality of life,” it added.
Raoni is currently resting at home, surrounded by his family, community, and specialized health teams. The care plan also incorporates intercultural and spiritual support, the institute added, which honors his Indigenous heritage and allows traditional healers alongside medical professionals.

Markets regulator SEBI has greenlit the proposed IPO of lending tech startup Fibe, formerly known as EarlySalary. According to SEBI’s latest processing status, the regulator issued its final observation on the offer documents of Fibe parent Social Worth Technologies Ltd today. In SEBI parlance, the issuance of final observations signals the regulator’s go-ahead for a company to proceed with its public issue. Fibe filed its DRHP in June this year. As per the draft documents, its public issue will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹750 Cr and an offer-for-sale (OFS) component of more than 4 Cr equity shares. The IPO will provide a major liquidity event to the startup’s investors. TPG will be the largest selling shareholder, offloading up to 1.17 Cr shares through its investment entity The Rise Fund III SF Pte Ltd. Norwest Capital and Eight Roads Ventures plan to sell up to 67.38 Lakh and 65.56 Lakh shares, respectively. Piramal Finance, TR Capital, IDG Ventures, and Chiratae Ventures are among the other investors looking to pare their stakes through the OFS. The startup plans to invest ₹562.6 Cr from the fresh issue proceeds in its NBFC subsidiary, EarlySalary Services Pvt Ltd, over the next two fiscal years. The capital infusion will be used to augment the subsidiary’s capital base and support its lending requirements. The remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes. Fibe may also consider raising up to ₹150 Cr in a pre-IPO placement. Founded in 2015 by Akshay Mehrotra and Ashish Goyal, Fibe operates a digital consumer lending platform offering personal loans and purpose-driven financing solutions. It also offers financing embedded at the point of purchase across segments such as education, insurance, healthcare, rooftop solar, travel, and ecommerce. On the financial front, Fibe’s net profit more than doubled to ₹257.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹113.7 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue grew 31% to ₹1,584.6 Cr from ₹1,208.9 Cr in FY25. The startup’s assets under management grew at a compound annual growth rate of 45.49% to ₹8,602.7 Cr as of March 31, 2026, from ₹4,064.2 Cr as of March 31, 2024. Fibe has raised close to $300 Mn to date. TPG’s The Rise Fund III is Fibe’s largest shareholder with a 23.26% stake, followed by Norwest Capital and Eight Roads Ventures with about 13% each. Cofounder and CEO Mehrotra owns 2.1%, while cofounder and CFO Goyal holds a 1.75% stake.

For most of history, menstrual blood has been dismissed as biological waste. But emerging research is now recasting this material as a goldmine for non-invasive diagnostics and regenerative medicine. Its potential applications are surprisingly broad, ranging from innovative cervical cancer screenings to advanced cartilage repair.
Much like saliva or blood plasma, menstrual fluid is rich with biological information. It is packed with immune cells, endometrial tissue, proteins, and genetic fragments.
Scientists are now digging into these biomarkers hoping to find ways to detect diseases early, and thus drop the use of invasive clinical procedures.
Stem cells
Researchers have recently reported that they had used menstrual blood to spot cancer early. Normally, medical workers have screened for cervical cancer using clinical check-ups that many people skip due to discomfort, cost, limited access to healthcare, and in fact plain embarrassment. As a result, screening rates remain low even in economically developed regions.
In 2025, a large population-based study in The BMJ by researchers from China offered a workaround. The team found that menstrual blood collected directly from sanitary pads could be tested for human papillomavirus DNA and precancerous lesions just as accurately as cervical swab samples collected by a clinician. Of course, the method excludes those who do not menstruate, but the fact that it offered a non-invasive, inexpensive, and suitable test that could begin from home is notable.
Menstrual blood is also gaining research focus thanks to stem cells derived from it. The groundwork for this was laid back in 2007 when a team from the U.S. and Canada successfully isolated menstrual stem cells from menstrual blood. These cells came from the endometrium, the uterine lining that breaks down and rebuilds itself on a monthly cycle without scarring — something other human tissue cannot do. The researchers believed the stem cells had something to do with that ability. In the lab, the menstrual-blood-derived stem cells readily divided and proved to be tough and versatile.
Researchers are already using them to grow uterine organoids — small functional models of the uterus located outside the body and used to study conditions like endometriosis. The stem cells could reveal traces of exposure to chemical compounds like phthalates and parabens, which was previously not possible to discern without an invasive examination.
Indeed, while bone marrow stem cells are still the gold standard for many therapies, extracting them is a gruelling process. It is painful, requires anaesthesia, and bears significant surgical risks. Menstrual-blood-derived stem cells however can be collected non-invasively, and sans the ethical baggage that often complicates stem-cell sourcing.
Future of regenerative medicine
As the science of these cells has matured, so have their applications. For instance, in 2025, a team in China studied the role they could play on Niemann-Pick disease type C1. This is a rare and devastating inherited condition that is caused by cholesterol and lipids build-up inside cells, leading to rapid neurological decline, loss of motor function, and dementia. The study found that menstrual-blood-derived stem cells could significantly lower neuroinflammation and cell death in experimental models of the disease. The work is still in its early stages, but for a condition whose therapeutic options are currently limited to drugs easing the clinical symptoms, a potential new advance is welcome.
A 2023 study by Iranian researchers showed that when these cells were delivered alongside their conditioned medium — the nutrient-rich fluid they had been cultured with — they helped accelerate heart recovery in rat models after a heart attack.
In hepatology, menstrual-blood-derived stem cells have been found to suppress the specific liver cells responsible for scarring and fibrosis. Because they naturally migrate towards areas of inflammation and cancer, researchers are also exploring engineering these cells to deliver therapeutic genes directly to a tumour site, sparing the rest of the body from the toxic side effects of chemotherapy.
Many experts increasingly believe extracellular vesicles (EVs) are the future of regenerative medicine. They are easier to standardise than whole stem cells — which are complete, living biological units that can divide and adapt within the body, but vary significantly from one batch to another. They also carry risks of becoming unintended tissue types. Because EVs are not whole cells, but rather clumps of proteins, lipids, RNA, and signalling molecules enclosed by membranes secreted from the parent cell, they can’t divide or differentiate into other tissues. This makes them safer, more stable alternatives and less likely to trigger immune rejection, can be engineered to evade immune detection, and can be frozen and stored just like conventional biological drugs.
Menstrual-blood-derived stem cells can be made to release these EVs when cultured in specific conditions in the lab, such as hypoxia (low oxygen) or by adding inflammatory cytokines.
Ordinary challenges
In a notable study published in Scientific Reports in February, a team from Lithuania isolated EVs from healthy donors and introduced them to human cartilage cells taken from patients who had undergone joint surgery. Within hours, the cartilage cells had absorbed the EVs and produced a new extracellular matrix, the scaffolding of healthy joints. When the team simulated joint inflammation, the vesicles reduced the release of markers associated with cartilage degradation.
Since osteoarthritis disproportionately affects women, the researchers also tracked hormone receptors. Specifically, when they examined how EVs affected receptors in the joint tissue, they found that the EVs had increased the expression of the progesterone receptor in cartilage cells, potentially restoring a hormonal signalling pathway that tends to deteriorate in women following menopause.
While most current treatments for osteoarthritis mask the pain, these findings suggest a way to actually slow or reverse the damage. Even though the research is nascent, if the findings hold up in future trials, any benefits will matter considering the number of people living with this condition, estimated to be 595 million worldwide in 2020.
Some significant hurdles remain as well. Scientists do not yet know how long these cells will survive once they are introduced into the body. There is no long-term human safety data— partly because there are no reliable markers to track the cells once they are inside a patient. Producing consistent, high-quality batches also remains a challenge, since no standardised benchmarks exist to verify the cells before use. The cells must themselves behave differently depending on the donor, varying with age, hormonal status, contraceptive history, and the conditions in which the cells were grown in the lab.
Then again, these are ordinary challenges of early-stage biomedical research rather than reasons to dismiss what has already been found.
Manjeera Gowravaram has a PhD in RNA biochemistry and works as a freelance science writer.

A shopkeeper’s alleged murder in West Bengal’s Titagarh on September 11 has triggered a controversy after Barrackpore BJP MLA Koustav Bagchi attempted to give it a communal spin by describing the victim as a ‘Sanatani’ murdered by ‘jihadis’.
In a 33-secong-long video that has now gone viral for over a week, the MLA’s claim was challenged on camera by the victim’s son, who interrupted Bagchi to say that there was nothing communal or political about his father’s murder.
The victim, Ramji Shaw, used to run a small corner shop from a portion of his home in the GC road area of Ward 18 of Barrackpore Municipality. He was allegedly killed after he refused to sell cigarettes on credit.
According to the locals, on September 11 afternoon, Shaw was trying to protect his son, who was allegedly being assaulted by three young men who were demanding to buy cigarettes from the shop without paying money on spot. As Shaw declined to sell cigarettes on credit, the men allegedly began attacking him and his son.
In the physical altercation, Shaw was pushed and heckled and lost consciousness. His family members rushed him to Barrackpore B N Bose sub-divisional hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries. According to locals, the three accused have been identified as Banti Ghosh, Sk. Sahil and Md. Nasir. Shaw’s wife had told Bengali news channel ABP Ananda that the accused had assaulted their son in the past.
Deceased’s Son Corrects MLA
As news of the alleged murder spread in the locality, Bagchi visited the deceased’s family the same day. Speaking to news channels while at Shaw’s home, he attempted to present the murder as communally motivated, specifically targeting the identity of the two accused who belong to the Muslim community.
In the viral clip, Bagchi can be heard saying (translated from Bengali), “This incident is not just related to an altercation over payment. Three Jihadis have killed a Sanatani. They wouldn’t have killed someone from their own religion.” However, even before Bagchi could finish his sentence, the deceased’s son corrected him, (translated from Bengali), “Sir, there is nothing related to religion in this case. The accused had come to my shop, looking to buy things on credit. When my father objected, they beat him up.”
The BJP MLA, seeming baffled by the interruption, responded: “I am speaking! Why are you not letting me speak!”. A few moments later, a person in purple shirt can be seen escorting the son to another room. While leaving the scene, the son stated, “This is not a matter of party politics.”
‘Politicians Inciting Locals for Electoral Gains’
Alt News visited the locality to independently verify the claims surrounding the murder and Bagchi’s allegation of a communal motive. While the bereaved wife and son both declined to speak, Shaw’s daughter Rikita confirmed to Alt News that it was indeed her brother who was seen correcting Bagchi in the viral video.
Sheikh Afroz (Ripon), who is Shaw’s immediate neighbour, said that the people in the area lived in communal harmony, as Hindus and Muslims co-existed there for generations. He added that politicians were, in fact, attempting to incite hostility between the communities. He also confirmed that Shaw’s son was seen in the video. “After the tragic incident, locals started to protest against the ‘gundagardi’ culture, and police officers had to come and pacify the situation. As the area is predominantly occupied by Muslims, most of the protesters were also Muslim. Does this not prove that this was not a communal incident?” asked Afroz.
A few metres from Shaw’s house, Md Mansoor, who runs a mobile repairing shop, said that Shaw’s shop used to have ‘ittar’ (perfume) and ‘surma’ (kohl) which were not found anywhere else in the area. “Every Eid, people from the Muslim community thronged to his shop to buy these products. Given that this was the reality which we saw every day, we don’t understand where this communal angle is coming from,” he said.
According to Mansoor, the accused youths were “known troublemakers”. “It is unfair to malign the name of an entire area and community for the wrongdoings of a select few. One of the accused is a Hindu, but the MLA still went on to claim that Shaw was murdered by Jihadis. Most of the shops in the neighbourhood, which is a predominantly Muslim area, were all shut in protest of Shaw’s murder for a few days after, only because there is no feeling of communal tension in this area,” Mansoor added.
No Communal Motive: Police
Alt News spoke to Titagrah officer-in-charge (OC) Atanu Chakraborty. The police station is located 1 km away from the crime scene. The officer confirmed that three people had been arrested in connection with the case. He said police did not find any communal motive behind the incident. The accused had pushed and beaten Shaw, following which Shaw suffered a stroke and died, he added.
“The accused are Sk Sahil, Md Nasir and Banti Ghosh. We have primarily booked them under sections pertaining to murder and further investigation is on. We couldn’t find any communal angle behind the crime,” he said, adding, the accused have been involved in public nuisance in the area in the past.
The police account, therefore, refutes Bagchi’s claims of a communal motive behind the alleged murder.
My Comments Twisted, Victim’s Son Apologised later, Claims MLA
Speaking to Alt News, Bagchi alleged, “There is no confusion. Some people are trying to do mischief with my quote. If I wanted, I could have done a lot of things over this issue, but I restrained myself considering the situation of the family. The area where this family lives are surrounded by Muslims — 90 out of 100 people living here are Muslims. The Hindu’s are constantly under a lot of pressure. So, whatever they said that day is due to fear.”
“I have a video of Ramji Shaw’s son. He had made a video and had sent it to me, clarifying their position. He also called me and apologised. Since my comments are being twisted, now I feel I have to publish the video that I have. I told his son that I can understand his emotions, his pain and fear. In the video, he also said that Hindus in that area are very few in number compared to the Muslims. However, they haven’t yet realised that the TMC government is gone and they [Hindus] are safe. I told him to be fearless,” Bagchi claimed, adding, “There definitely is a communal angle to this incident. The Muslims have kept the Hindus in that are terrorised.”
When asked about the one Hindu accused and how he could confidently claim that Shaw was murdered by ‘jihadis’, Bagchi said, “Banti Ghosh is a rowdy element and he mixes with them [the other two accused]. However, the main culprits are the two Muslims men. They have continued this for long, and you won’t find them attacking any Muslim.”
Alt News’ interactions with the locals and an observation of how they live, however, contradict Bagchi’s ‘fear of Muslims’ narrative. Shaw’s house is 550 metres from the Titagarh railway station. About 200 metres from the station, beside G C Road, stands a Muslim shrine (mazar), and next to it, a Ganesh Puja pandal has been erected. The two structures are separated only by a food stall.
A search on Google Maps of the area brought up an image from two years ago, in which a Durga Puja pandal was erected right next to the same Muslim shrine.
Further down the road, opposite to Mansoor’s shop, is Hasanjan Sporting Club, and a Hindu temple stands right next to it.
Pointing towards the narrow path beside the club, Mansoor said, “Ten families live there. Six are Muslim and four are Hindu.”

What Trump’s Bizarre Posts Are Teaching Us About AI
The president’s recent Truth Social barrage of fake images reflects the dangers—for all of us—of virtual self-aggrandizement.
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.
Here is a selective list of the dozens of images the president has recently disseminated on Truth Social: Donald Trump on a horse next to George Washington on a horse, in the body of Hulk Hogan, beating Hogan in arm wrestling, standing between General George Patton and General Douglas MacArthur in a World War II uniform, hovering menacingly with a hockey stick over the Canadian prime minister, commanding the deck of an aircraft carrier, nuking parts of Earth from space, gleefully dancing to “YMCA” as he replaces a sign for Lake Ontario with one for Lake America. Maybe most surreal (though, admittedly, kind of funny), he posted a video of a squad of “Donald Ducks” with his signature hair, armed with machine guns, waddling in formation to protect said lake.
Trump has never been shy about his proclivity for self-aggrandizement (daydreaming about having his face chiseled onto Mount Rushmore or printed on a $250 bill). But his recent spate of social-media posts—almost all products of AI—has him living in an expanded fantasyland. His supporters are likely to just giggle; more fun and trolling—so what? His critics might roll their eyes at the extravagant immaturity but almost can’t be bothered anymore (unless they’re Iceland). After a decade of Trump shenanigans, getting worked up either way is hard. Also, these images might come across as just a little sad—the projections of a man who is losing power and virility but desperately needs to see himself as powerful and virile.
The absurd cartoons are worth pondering, though, and not for the sake of getting to know Trump better (I believe that onion has been thoroughly peeled). Because what AI can do to exaggerate and aggrandize Trump, it can do to everyone. For the president, this may be just one more level up on his escalator of self-regard, but for those without Napoleonic degrees of narcissism, the mental terrain opened up by these quick-prompt chimeras is new.
When the psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan wanted to understand how the ego takes shape, he thought of mirrors. Sometime from six to 18 months of age, he theorized, a baby begins to recognize their reflection, and experiences what Lacan—abstruse French structuralist that he was—described as the “jubilant assumption of his specular image.” In plainer words, the baby realizes, That’s me! This is significant because the child at this point is otherwise a fragmented mess, experiencing the world through disconnected sensation. Lacan thought the mirror provides an idealized perception of wholeness when, really, inside it’s all a scramble, and through this illusion of coherence, a proper ego—a sense of self—begins to bud.
Lacan didn’t believe that we ever really outgrow this reliance on our reflection, whether seen above a bathroom sink or in the ways other people look at us. But the mirror he had in mind could show you only the person who stands in front of it—the image is always tethered to physical reality. The AI mirror is something else. It asks what we’d like to see and produces it.
In the past, only kings and emperors could indulge their most exalted, exaggerated picture of themselves. They could commission heroic, larger-than-life representations—though even these were limited by available materials and plausible realism. AI image-making has now democratized this kind of statue-building. I know because I just asked ChatGPT to create an image of me astride a bronze horse in the center of a city, and I’ve never looked more commanding. But AI can do so much more: The ideal self has escaped the confines of the mirror and even the gilded sculpture; it can now inflate to unimaginable dimensions.
In this new world, our insecurities are not obstacles; they are starting points. Take my modest height. I can conjure up what I would look like in Victor Wembanyama’s stretched-taffy body—though I’d settle for something one foot shorter. I’m fully aware that this is just an image, and a bizarre one, but it engraves this taller me—a version who walks into a party and looks down, not up, at everyone—into my brain. It creates a gulf between reality and such a picture. This fantasy made manifest can either delude or taunt me. It exists, and I can’t forget it. Conversely, I should say, it also reveals what I’m most self-conscious about—exactly as AI does for Trump. The puffed up, dominating, victorious man with the six-pack is what the AI mirror shows the president, because that is what he prompts it to show him. (In most cases, of course, he is reposting images prompted by supporters, who are thereby exposing their own displaced fantasies.)
To give Trump a little credit, he seems vaguely aware of the idea that AI is, like the Mirror of Erised in Harry Potter, showing us what we most want. One of his posts has Barack Obama looking into a mirror and asking: Mirror mirror on the wall who’s the greatest president of them all. No surprise, it’s Trump, who is staring back at him.
What I see in the AI mirror is greater than I could ever be—and infinitely editable. Instead of feeding a desire for coherence, as Lacan imagined, it creates a bottomless hunger for the unachievable. I can keep tweaking it with more prompts: “Give me thicker hair. Make my jaw more chiseled.” Start down this road, I’m afraid, and you’ll encounter unhappy young men using hammers to shape their actual faces so that they can come closer to the digital simulacra.
Not all people are narcissists, and certainly not all are like Trump. But we are all susceptible. Who doesn’t dream occasionally of evading reality or the truth of the body you are stuck living in? On the scale of human history, it has been only about a second since we got photography (and the inevitable selfie) to augment what for so long only a pond’s surface or a piece of glass could show us: our own face. What will come from finding, instead, Supermen, kings, popes, and Jedi staring back at us?
Without AI, Trump might be forced to look around him, perhaps at the portraits of other presidents in the White House—just like Richard Nixon did. In their book The Final Days, Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein recounted what became a famous story: As Nixon’s presidency was crashing down around him, he began talking at night to these dead former presidents. (One of his sons-in-law denied this claim.) Oliver Stone dramatized the moment in his 1995 film, Nixon: The defeated, haggard president focuses on a painting of John F. Kennedy and says, with startling self-awareness, “When they look at you, they see what they want to be. When they look at me, they see what they are.”
Fiction, I know. But this is the kind of reckoning that can happen when you have no choice but to see what is in front of you. Trump is also very aware of the presidents who came before him. In another recent post, he ranks them all in a tiered chart from Great (Lincoln, FDR, Jefferson, and so on) to Failures (Biden, Obama, Carter, and so on). And atop the entire graphic in a box roughly four times the size of all the others, Trump’s severe, unsmiling face looks out under a label that reads back to him: The Greatest.

Ash from Mount Etna grounds flights at Sicily airport
- Published
All flights have been suspended from one of Italy's busiest airports because of volcanic ash released from nearby Mount Etna.
It is the second time in recent months that Catania International Airport, on the island of Sicily, has stopped flights due to emissions from Etna, which is Europe's tallest active volcano and erupts frequently.
Airport officials said arrivals and departures, which were first halted on Monday, would be suspended until 22:00 (20:00 GMT) on Tuesday.
Ongoing activity at Etna prompted the INGV Etneo Observatory to issue a red aviation alert on Monday.
In a statement on its website on Tuesday, Catania - Italy's fifth-busiest airport by passenger traffic - said further updates would follow.
It also advised passengers due to fly from Catania to check with their airline for updates before travelling to the airport.
Catania, which usually serves about 12 million passengers each year, was closed for almost a week during the peak summer season last month because of volcanic activity.
There have been calls for the airport to shut and other facilities in Sicily to be expanded because of its proximity to Etna.
The volcano, which stands at 3,324 metres (10,906ft), is about 40km (25 miles) away from the airport.
Despite air traffic disruption, August's eruption drew large crowds of onlookers to Etna's lava flows. About 1.5 million people visit Etna every year.

Pro Ref chief Howard Webb agrees with Phil Foden red card in Manchester derby but admits Bruno Fernandes should have been booked
Pro Ref chief Howard Webb says sending Phil Foden off for violent conduct in the Manchester derby was the correct decision; Webb reveals Bruno Fernandes should have been cautioned for the "petulant" kick which sparked the incident but VAR could not intervene
Tuesday 15 September 2026 17:27, UK
Pro Ref chief Howard Webb has backed the decision to send off Phil Foden in the Manchester derby but revealed VAR could not intervene to caution Bruno Fernandes for the "petulant" kick that sparked the altercation.
Foden was sent off for violent conduct in Man City's 1-0 win at Old Trafford after kicking out at Fernandes after he was fouled by the Man Utd captain.
Fernandes escaped punishment after seemingly initiating the incident with a kick on Foden before the City forward reacted.
However, there appeared to be confusion during the VAR review of the incident as the officiating team checked for a possible Man Utd penalty after Enzo Fernandez's challenge on Youri Tielemans.

While referee Michael Oliver was brandishing the red card for Foden, VAR official Matt Donohue can be heard discussing the penalty while also saying: "Who has been sent off and for what?" shortly after.
Donohue is then alerted by his assistants to analyse Fernandes' kick on Foden, which initiated the melee between the two players.
The confusing VAR process surrounding Foden's red card
Referee: No, no. The ball, in my opinion, is played by Enzo Fernandez. Feet are side by side.
VAR: Checking possible penalty. One more angle to prove he's definitely played the ball. It looks like he's played the ball.
Phil Foden then kicks out at Bruno Fernandes after being caught by the Man Utd captain and is sent off shortly after.
Assistant VAR: Possible kick-out as well.
Referee: Has he kicked him there?
VAR: Confirm here you think that Enzo has definitely played the ball and that this is no penalty.
Assistant VAR: Possible violent conduct.
VAR: Okay and then he's gone red card. So, I would say no penalty there, he definitely plays the ball, yeah? Okay and now we need to look at the rest, okay?
So, who has been sent off here and for what?
Assistant VAR: It was for a kick-out. It looks like he's given a foul and then the legs came up.
VAR: Michael [referee], the penalty is checked and cleared. Just confirm your on-field decision in terms of discipline here, please.
Referee: Red card, Phil Foden. Kick out into the body of Bruno [Fernandes]. The foul is by Bruno on Phil. I think he's in a tangle and when they are separating, I think Phil kicks him. But they will check.
VAR: That looks like a clear red card to me. Secondary movement, watch broadcast. Okay, happy to confirm?
Red card. Happy to confirm? Confirming the red card for Manchester City 47. A kick to the midriff with two feet.
Just roll through to check that Bruno does nothing. I'm absolutely certain he doesn't. No, he kicks the ball; it's fine.
Assistant VAR: No, the other one [Bruno's first kick]. That's not what they're talking about. That is the one they're talking about.
VAR: Minimal, minimal. That's not for us; that's fine.
Assistant VAR: Yeah, I agree.
Webb: Foden decision was correct but Fernandes avoids 'petulant' yellow
Pro Ref chief operating officer Howard Webb:
"I agree with the red card for Phil Foden for violent conduct. He kicks out with force into the upper body of Bruno Fernandes. We saw a player sent off for Aston Villa, Joao Gomes, for a similar thing.
"That is seen by the referee on the field and that is the on-field decision.
"When you look at the footage, there is the petulant kick from Fernandes into the back side of Foden. It is more petulant than violent. To be violent conduct, it has to have excessive force or brutality.
"When you look at that at full speed, it does not have that element. It would be a yellow card and VAR cannot step in to give a yellow.
"If all of it was missed and nothing was given against Foden, then VAR could step in and see Foden's actions for a possible red card and capture Fernandes' yellow card action. Because the referee gave the red card, that option is not open for VAR."
Analysis: Fernandes deserved equal treatment to Foden
Sky Sports' Laura Hunter:
The review of this incident is all over the place. But the most alarming element is the reading of Bruno Fernandes's part.
Lead VAR official Matt Donohue is distracted by a previous incident in real time.
His VAR assistant leads with "possible kick out" by Foden. The immediacy of the on-field decision from Michael Oliver to send Foden off is the determining factor here. Oliver acts fast which suggests he is sure, and so VAR allows the call to stand.
The bar for intervention by VAR has been deliberately lifted higher for subjective decisions, remember, to avoid re-refereeing of games. This remains a grey area but less VAR interference is a good thing in my book.
Most can accept that Oliver's decision to dismiss Foden is not a "clear and obvious error" given where he makes contact with Fernandes. Whether it meets the threshold for "violent conduct" is of course open to interpretation.
What the VAR room failed to spot, however, is the trigger for Foden's reaction. Why is that not scrutinised in more detail?
"I'm absolutely certain he doesn't [do anything]," Donohue says of Fernandes's involvement. In reality, the Man Utd captain is the first offender and Foden's kick was retaliation for the kick he received after being fouled.
The decision not to punish Fernandes for the exact same action Foden is red-carded for is surely a huge oversight. Both deserved equal treatment in my opinion, especially important as Oliver clearly missed the first part from his position on the pitch. There is never any mention of it.
VAR's job is to alert him. Isn't that what the pitchside monitor is there for?

When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
- Published
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.
Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.
But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.
The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.
And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.
"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"
Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.
Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."
Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter.
Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months.
The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths.
Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers.
Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following.
In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after.
Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant."
But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met".
Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest".
This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart.
Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened.
"That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it."
On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says.
By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak.
At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains.
The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow.
The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak".
"We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope.
The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed.
The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall.
By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life.
But something was bothering him.
One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him.
Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night.
But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak.
Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers.
He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m.
It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong".
Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors.
"I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice.
He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once.
"Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind."
Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition.
Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back.
They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks.
But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home.
When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'".
Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated.
The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home.
Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says.
The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days.
There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot.
On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby.
With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down.
The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says.
The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away.
The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four.
Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope.
The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him.
Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall.
"They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived."
The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families.
Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain.
Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home".
This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done.
As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming.
Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him.
But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop."

US defense chiefs warn of munitions shortfall as Iran war costs hit $33bn
President Donald Trump’s ‘Operation Epic Fury’ assault on Iran has cost $33.4 billion and has resulted in a strategic missile shortage, the Department of Defense’s inspector general finds
President Donald Trump’s “Operation Epic Fury” assault on Iran cost $33.4 billion in its first four months and has resulted in a munitions shortfall, according to a report by the Department of Defense’s inspector general.
The 44-page report to Congress states that, between February 28 and June 30, the joint U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran saw the Trump administration spend $22.3 billion on munitions alone.
The onslaught “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” Inspector General Platte B Moring III concludes.
His report also lists the damage done to American military assets by Tehran’s retaliatory strikes, listing four F-15Es and and up to 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones as destroyed and one F-35A, seven KC-135 tanker aircraft and seven helicopters as damaged.
The F-35A plane is the first of its type to be compromised by enemy fire, according to CNBC, and would cost $92 million to replace. An F-15E, meanwhile, costs $31.1 million to produce, U.S. Air Force data indicates, putting the pricetag for replacing four at $124.4 million.
The U.S. also spent $79.2 million responding to emergencies arising from the conflict “such as evacuation-related expenses for State personnel and their family members, U.S. citizens, and eligible third-country nationals.”
Damage done to U.S. diplomatic premises in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the U.A.E. add another $184 million to the bill.
Even further expense was incurred by Iranian strikes on military buildings and infrastructure in the U.S.-allied Gulf states of Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan, although no cost is calculated in the report as it is not yet clear whether they will be restored and who would pay for the work.
The Independent has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.
Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies was asked by CBS News, in response to the report’s findings, whether he believed the U.S. still had a sufficient supply of munitions to call upon.
“For a war against Iran, the answer is yes,” he answered. “The problem is a war against China. We might be able to provide enough munitions for a month, but getting on to month two or month three or four, that’s a great challenge.”
Trump himself has repeatedly insisted the U.S. has no munitions supply issues but was angered when it was reported in early August that he had confronted Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the matter at Camp David in Maryland, reportedly saying he thought the problem “had been fixed.”
The president took to Truth Social in anger over the story, threatening the “leakers” who spoke to the press with jail.
Reuters reported around the same time that the U.S. Army had significantly depleted its stockpile of long-range missiles, using up “virtually all” of its crucial surface-to-surface weapons.
Trump was back on his social media platform Monday to claim: “The United States is producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History.
“They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East, and beyond. Our Defense Company Factories are moving 24/7, while at the same time building, on average, 4 to 5 largescale brand new Plants, each!
“A primary focus of this production has been Patriots, THAAD Systems, Tomahawks, and other Standard Missile Systems, of which we already have large numbers in stock.”
His unpopular war has rumbled on for another 10 weeks since the period documented by the report and shows no obvious sign of coming to an end even now, although Trump has said he is “open” to negotiations with Iran while stressing the final decision rests with him.
At least 18 U.S. soldiers have been killed and more than 750 service members injured in the conflict.

Trump’s Kennedy Center sabotage is complete
Trump can’t put his name on the building — so he’s closing it instead.
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump can’t put his name on the Kennedy Center — so he’s closing it, effective immediately.
What’s happening? On Tuesday, the board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted to close the building indefinitely, shortly after a federal judge rebuked efforts to engrave Trump’s name into the facade.
According to the board, the closure is because the center is in bad financial shape and the building itself is in a dangerous state of disrepair. Without Trump’s support, they claim, a renovation will be impossible — and Trump has made clear he won’t support it unless his name is on the building, even though Congress already approved $257 million for the project last year.
How did we get here? Trump has been obsessed with claiming the Kennedy Center — a memorial for an assassinated president — and its cultural cachet for himself ever since he returned to office last year. He quickly stacked the Kennedy Center board with his appointees, then installed himself as chair.
In December, he had his name added to the building’s facade and its official title, temporarily making it the Trump-Kennedy Center. A federal judge ordered him to undo the renaming in June, and the administration complied — but the facade has remained covered since then, obscuring the removal.
In August, Trump also threatened the center with demolition if he didn’t get his way; he sounded a similar note in a Truth Social post Tuesday, writing that “the Building is destined to doom.”
What’s the context? Trump and his handpicked board have both portrayed the Kennedy Center as a destitute, derelict institution in need of rescue. More than 100,000 people in Japan are now aged 100 or older
- Published
The number of people aged 100 or more in Japan has exceeded 100,000 for the first time, according to the health ministry.
Figures show Japan is now home to 107,677 centenarians, the highest number in the world, of whom 88% are women. The oldest woman is Kishimoto Fuyo, a 114-year-old from Kyoto City and the oldest man is Kato Hikaru, a 112-year-old from Kumamoto.
Health Minister Kenichiro Ueno said he was "delighted that so many people are living long, healthy and active lives", citing progress in medicine and technology.
But Kenichiri also warned of the challenge the country faces in maintaining a sustainable social security system.
Experts put the long lives of the Japanese down to several factors, including a healthy diet and an active lifestyle.
The island nation's cuisine predominantly consists of fish, vegetables, and rice - and less saturated fat than many Western diets.
Older people also regularly walk, use public transport, cycle and stretch.
Japan has been aging for years and sales of adult nappies have been higher than those for babies for more than a decade.
Companies have also developed new products for the older population, including a powered exoskeleton to support moving various parts of the body and eyewear that automatically adjusts its focus.
For a population to replace itself, each woman needs to give birth to 2.1 children on average. Last year Japan's total fertility rate dropped to a record low of 1.14.
The total population is estimated to drop to 87 million by 2070, representing a 30% decline from its peak of 128 million in 2008, according to data from the National Institute of Population and Social Security research.
Residents aged 65 and older currently make up around 30% of the population and are expected to make up nearly 40% by 2070.
Japanese authorities have called the trend an "existential crisis" with Prime Minister Sanae Takichi describing the decline as a "quiet emergency".
In 2025 Japan's total population decreased in all 47 prefectures but two, and the rate of decline is accelerating.
The government's many programmes and subsidies to encourage young people to have more children do not appear to be boosting birth rates.
Experts say the reasons are complex, ranging from lower marriage rates and more women joining the workforce to the increased costs of raising children.
While immigration has risen in previous years, foreigners only make up around 3% of the population and opposition to accepting more has grown.
When Japan began its centenarian survey in 1963, there were 153 people aged 100 or over. That figure rose to 1,000 in 1981 and stood at 10,000 by 1998.
The most recent figures were released ahead of Japan's annual "Respect for the Aged" public holiday, on which the government honours those turning 100 with a personal letter and traditional sake cup.
Studies have previously cast doubt on the validity of global centenarian numbers, suggesting data errors, unreliable public records and missing birth certificates may account for elevated figures.
A government audit of family registries in Japan in 2010 uncovered more than 230,000 people listed as being aged 100 or older who were unaccounted for, some having died decades previously.
The miscounting was attributed to patchy record-keeping and suspicions that some families may have tried to hide the deaths of elderly relatives in order to claim their pensions.

What to Look for When Buying a Smart Bird Feeder
The world of smart bird feeders is vast and can seem overwhelming, but there are some key features that will really make a difference in your user experience, and they may not be what you think. I've tested dozens of feeders for years from many different brands, and this is what I think you should pay attention to when comparing models.
Subscription: Most, if not all, smart bird feeders require a subscription to access all features, in order to support the company's continued investment in user experience. There are few things more disappointing than giving or receiving a smart bird feeder as a gift, only to find out it's not actually usable without shelling out an additional $70 a year. Reputable companies will note subscription requirements up front, and some even offer models that have a lifetime subscription built in. Note that if a feeder costs less than a hundred bucks, odds are it will require a subscription to capture photos, whether it says so in the marketing materials or not, so you will need to do your due diligence before buying.
Mounting options: If you live in an area with squirrels, your best bet is to pole mount your bird feeder—especially a more expensive smart feeder, which often has cords that squirrels and other rodents like to chew. Not all feeders offer a pole-mounting option, though, so this is another important detail to confirm before buying.
Wi-Fi network: The vast majority of smart feeders only work on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi frequencies. If you only use 5 GHz, you will need to look for a feeder that specifically works with a shorter transmission range, or has dual range, such as the Camojojo Hibird, above.
App: An app can make or break your smart bird feeder experience since it's where all of your bird viewing, sorting, and saving will take place. Apps with added features like useful facts, the capacity to share feeds with others, quality AI identification, and the ability to sort by bird are sometimes worth the added cost over a less-expensive feeder. Many companies use security cameras in their bird feeders that don't have a separate app—this means you'll just get a utilitarian list of image captures with no detail or context. To help buyers with their decision-making, I am currently building a rubric to grade and rank smart bird feeder apps, which I hope to add to this guide within the next couple of months.
How Does WIRED Test Bird Feeders?
I test all feeders in my rural-suburban backyard in the Pacific Northwest. I mount seed feeders on a 1-inch pole with a baffle, using the provided mounting hardware and hose clamps. If pole mounting isn't feasible, I mount on a fence or a shepherd's hook. I hang hummingbird feeders from a shepherd's hook mounted on the side of my house. I fill the seed feeders with Audubon Wild Park bird seed and the hummingbird feeders with a nectar mixture of 4-to-1 granulated sugar and water. I keep each feeder up for a minimum of four weeks, with all app notifications enabled.
I look at all app features available both with a subscription and without, seeing how often I get notifications and noting whether they are accurately picking up just birds or any type of outdoor movement, and how well the AI feature is able to distinguish bird species. I also look at connectivity, seed capacity, video quality, and how well the feeder bodies hold up to squirrels and inclement weather.
The majority of feeders I tested were provided as press samples by the company. Some are kept for longer-term testing, others are put in storage for future testing or comparison purposes, and others are donated locally via the Buy Nothing Project.
What Do I Need to Know Before Setting Up a Smart Feeder?
- Keep feeders super clean. The last thing you want to do to your feathered guests is make them ill from eating moldy seeds or spread avian diseases. Every two weeks, scrub feeders with warm, soapy water, and then either soak them in one part bleach to nine parts water or one part white vinegar to one part water—both methods are recommended by Audubon. Rinse and dry thoroughly before adding more seed (you don't want bleach residue either). Keep an eye on bird flu outbreaks and pay attention to what the birds look like at your own feeders. If you suspect something is off, you'll want to remove the feeder until things look better.
- Only get a hummingbird feeder if you're dedicated to keeping it spotless. You need to be even more diligent about cleanliness here, committing to cleaning a hummingbird feeder every two to three days. Nectar sitting in the sun harbors bacterial growth quickly, which can cause hummingbird tongues to swell and almost always end in their death. Red attracts these birds, but don't use red nectar. There are no studies conclusively proving that dye harms birds, but at best it's unnecessary and at worst might make them sick. Instead, go for feeders with red pieces to get their attention or stick to planting hummingbird-friendly flowers and skip the feeder altogether.
- Add a water source too. Birds need clean water for drinking and bathing, so you can make your backyard more of an oasis by providing it. Birdfy makes a smart birdbath, reviewed above, or you can make your own fountain out of anything—even a favorite pot, or a bucket—using a solar pump kit. I'm currently testing this one and will report back. The same cleaning technique outlined above goes for baths. You can also consider adding regular bird houses—analog or smart versions, like Birdfy's Polygon, above—for birds to nest.
- Give birds time. You likely won't see birds at your feeder on day one. Give them time to find it and trust it. If after a few weeks you still don't have visitors, it might be time to reevaluate what kind of bird seeds you're using or where you've placed the feeder.
Why Do Most Smart Feeders Only Run on 2.4 GHz?
This section was inspired by an email from a reader who installs home Wi-Fi systems and did not appreciate my recommending a feeder that has the option to run on 5 GHz. He's not wrong that this isn't the preferred band for a smart bird feeder, but I'll explain why someone might want 5 GHz below.
First off, what is 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz? In simplest terms, these are the main radio frequency bands Wi-Fi uses to send data wirelessly between your smart bird feeder and your router. One gigahertz (GHz) is 1 billion hertz, the unit of measurement for how fast radio waves oscillate. Both bands are the accepted standards for Wi-Fi, which yes, is a name brand.
It follows, then, that 2.4-GHz waves oscillate more slowly than 5-GHz waves. This also means the slower waves can travel farther and pass through walls and other obstacles more effectively. With Wi-Fi-enabled products placed outside the home, the ability to penetrate through walls, trees, and other potential barriers is more important than speed. These slower waves also result in less power consumption by devices. It makes sense that 2.4 GHz would be a preferable band for a smart bird feeder, which likely would be in or near a tree-filled area.
However, 2.4 GHz is a more crowded band and thus prone to interference from other Wi-Fi networks and devices, so it can be less stable. It also results in slower overall performance, leading to sluggish downloads and lag during streaming and video calls. Most modern routers offer both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands, but some may be configured (for whatever reason) to broadcast only 5 GHz. Other routers feature something called band steering, which automatically diverts devices to the less-crowded 5 GHz. So, really, a smart bird feeder that offers dual connectivity simply provides more options. If the bird feeder is right outside your window where the router is located, you may want the faster speed. Or maybe you just don't want to try to figure out how to turn off band steering. If you're not dialed in to your router, no pun intended, it may make sense for you to consider a bird feeder with dual-band connectivity.
What About Squirrels?
As is the case with any bird feeder, squirrels love to eat at smart bird feeders, most of which are not squirrel-proof, regardless of marketing claims. However, most of the smart feeders we’ve tested are just as sturdy, if not in some cases sturdier, than analog bird feeders. The worst-case scenario is likely the squirrel eating all the seed, chewing the edges, and covering up the camera with its fuzzy butt.
The yard where I test smart feeders year-round is lousy with the large and persistent rodents, and the squirrel damage I’ve sustained on test feeders has been minor. With the Birdfy Pro Duo, above, the animals chewed off the edges to better get at the seed supply when it was low, and the FeatherSnap Scout had its mounting bent. Top of mind is the 5-7-9 method of siting a bird feeder—at least 5 feet off the ground, at least 7 feet away from any structures, and at least 9 feet away from anything a squirrel could jump from (branches, fences, roofs). I explain this in more detail in my guide to keeping squirrels away from your bird feeder.
Another option is an aftermarket baffle added to feeders hanging on shepherd’s hooks, or a pole with a built-in baffle, like this one offered by Birdfy. Another option is using seed treated with capsaicin, or hot pepper. Birds don’t have capsaicin receptors like mammals do, so they’re not affected by the taste. That said, I’ve found capsaicin only keeps squirrels away for a couple of days, whether because they’ve gotten used to it or the pepper loses its potency when exposed to the elements. As a last resort, you could always just learn to live with the squirrels and dedicate a feeder to them, although my neighbor does this and I'm of the mind that doing so brings even more squirrels to the area.

Trump team has deported more than 170 migrants in violation of court orders: report
Immigration attorneys say DHS in such a hurry to hit targets and expel people ‘they aren’t actually looking at the legality of some of this stuff’ but department insists: ‘The law is on our side’
The Trump administration has deported more than 170 migrants in violation of court orders since last year, according to a report.
Politico reports that President Donald Trump’s raids on undocumented migrants, part of his mass deportation push, have seen instances of people wrongly removed from the U.S. “in violation of court orders, in defiance of legally mandated due process protections, or to countries from which they had sought or received protection from torture and persecution.”
The outlet offers the example of Jose Ojeda Duarte, who was picked up by ICE officers in Chicago during last fall’s Operating Midway Blitz and told he was being taken to a court date relating to a pending asylum application, only to spend seven months in Arizona detention centers.
He was then deported to Venezuela, which was later found to have been a blunder caused by a “data quality issue.”
Ojeda has since been allowed to return to the Windy City and spoken of his struggle to readjust since his ordeal, fearing he will be sent back again. “Sometimes, I get a terrible feeling, like a fear of going out,” he told The Chicago Sun-Times.
Typically, judges have responded to such errors by ordering the administration to “facilitate” the return of those removed from the country by mistake.
However, those offers have not always been accepted, as in the case of college student Any Lucia Lopez Belloza, who was detained at a Massachusetts airport late last year en route to a family Thanksgiving reunion in Texas and instead sent to Honduras, a country she had not visited since she was a child.
The administration has apologized for violating a court order in her case but she has nevertheless declined to return to the U.S. Like Ojeda, she fears being detained again, according to Politico.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told The Independent: “DHS complies with all court orders, even as radical NGOs shop for the most favorable forum and activist judges seek to thwart our work to fulfill the American people’s mandate to detain and remove criminal illegal aliens.
“As our record in the U.S. Supreme Court demonstrates, the law is on our side. When issued a court order to return a removed alien to the United States, DHS takes every reasonable step to ensure that they are safely brought back for continued immigration proceedings and to guarantee public safety. We are a nation of laws, and we follow the law, even when activist judges warp it for political purposes.
“Enforcing immigration law is not optional and is essential to protecting America’s national security, public safety, and economic strength. Operations are conducted lawfully within the authority granted to immigration officers under Title 8. Every removal of an illegal alien helps restore order and reinforce the rule of law.”
Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a Maryland-based immigration lawyer who represents Kilmar Abrego Garcia – illegally deported to El Salvador last year, provoking a national outcry – told Politico the reason for the errors was overzealous enforcement by a Trump administration keen to deliver on its targets.
“The machine is running at 110 percent,” he said, adding that he had only worked on three illegal deportation cases over the course of his 17-year career before Trump’s return. Now, his firm is now taking on three per month.
Another attorney, Javier Rivera, said: “They’re in such a hurry to kick people out and expel people from the United States that they aren’t actually looking at the legality of some of this stuff.”
Rivera represents a client who was deported to Nicaragua in August in spite of legal protections put in place to shield her from removal given that she is a victim of domestic violence. Her return has already been ordered by a federal court.
U.S. District Judge Jill Parrish of Utah attacked the administration along similar lines in a February order in which she rebuked it for adopting a “deport first, litigate later” approach to tackling illegal immigration

Multiple inmates stabbed during brawl at notorious New York jail housing Luigi Mangione and Nicolas Maduro
Several inmates’ injuries were so severe that they had to seek medical treatment outside of the jail, according to federal officials
Multiple inmates have been stabbed and slashed during a major brawl at the federal jail in New York City that is currently housing UnitedHealthcare CEO killer Luigi Mangione and disgraced former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
Federal officials confirmed to The Independent that the massive fight took place on the morning of September 6 at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, New York. The New York Daily News first reported on the brawl, which their sources said was gang-related.
Members of the Trinitarios gang fought another gang on the seventh floor of the jail’s west building, the Daily News’ sources said, adding that a total of at least 20 people had joined in the brawl.
“Several incarcerated individuals were medically assessed and treated for minor injuries at the facility, while other incarcerated individuals sustained injuries requiring outside medical treatment,” Donald Murphy, a spokesperson for the Federal Bureau of Prisons, told The Independent.
Murphy did not confirm the exact number of inmates involved in the fight and the number of those wounded remains unknown. The exact injuries that the wounded inmates sustained are also not clear.
Murphy told The Independent that jail employees were able to contain the incident without being injured themselves, adding, “At no time was the public in danger.” The incident is still under investigation.
MDC Brooklyn, as the jail is commonly referred to, is known for holding infamous inmates like Mangione and Maduro.
Mangione, 28, is currently awaiting sentencing in the jail after he admitted last month to fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on the streets of Manhattan in 2024. Thompson’s murder shocked the nation as the New York City Police Department tracked down the Ivy League graduate, with some admiring the killer for what they saw as a stance against the health insurance industry.
“I shot Mr. Thompson and he died,” Mangione said in court on August 14. “I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.”
Maduro, 63, and his wife Cilia Flores, 69, are currently awaiting trial at the jail on drug trafficking charges, following a stealth mission by American forces to capture the couple from their Caracas home in early January. Their trial is set for next June.
Both have pleaded not guilty to charges stemming from an alleged conspiracy to transport thousands of tons of cocaine to the U.S.
Maduro “and his co-conspirators have, for decades, partnered with some of the most violent and prolific drug traffickers and narco-terrorists in the world, and relied on corrupt officials throughout the region, to distribute tons of cocaine to the United States,” their indictment reads.
MDC Brooklyn has a history of violence, including the reported February 2025 stabbing of Karl Jordan Jr., who was convicted and then acquitted of the 2002 murder of New York rap star Jam Master Jay. Jordan survived the attack.
In September 2024, the Justice Department announced charges against nine inmates in five separate cases involving violence at MDC Brooklyn, including the murder of Uriel Whyte on June 7, 2024, and the murder of Edwin Cordero on July 17, 2024.
“Violence will not be tolerated in our federal jails,” Breon Peace, United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said at the time. “As the only federal pretrial facility in New York City, MDC-Brooklyn houses pretrial inmates accused of some of the most serious crimes in our region.”
“Let these charges serve as a warning to those who would engage in criminal conduct behind bars, and anyone else who facilitates those crimes: your conduct will be exposed, and you will be held accountable,’ Peace said.
