After Home Minister Amit Shah's assertion that a Uniform Civil Code will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before 2029, key NDA partners TDP and Shiv Sena on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) backed the BJP on the issue.
Another BJP ally JD(U) gave a guarded response, saying it will study the Uniform Civil Code Bill and will "not oppose it for no reason".
The support of the TDP with 16 Lok Sabha MPs, the Shiv Sena with 13 and the JD(U) with 12 is crucial for the Narendra Modi government. While the TDP is in power in Andhra Pradesh along with Jana Sena and BJP, the BJP shares power with the JD(U) in Bihar and the Shiv Sena in Maharashtra.
TDP's Andhra Pradesh president P. Srinivasa Rao said in Amaravati that it is bound by the Union Home Minister's statement on UCC as an NDA partner.
"Yes, I have seen our Union Home Minister's statement on UCC and as NDA partners we are bound to go by his statement," Mr. Rao, who represents Gajuwaka assembly constituency, said.
Though there is criticism over UCC, he noted that it "strengthens the unity of the country and doesn't show much gender bias".
"And critics, of course, some say that it (UCC) infringes on religious freedom. Our country is culturally diverse. But we always think that this UCC will strengthen and unify the country," he said.
"So, we will be going by our home minister's statement being NDA partners," he added.
CPI(M) state secretary V. Srinivas Rao, however, claimed that the BJP is resorting to UCC politics to divert the country's attention as it is "facing heat from the new generation (Gen Z) due to unemployment" and other reasons, especially in the backdrop of the recent Jantar Mantar student protest movement.
Bihar Deputy Chief Minister Vijay Kumar Chaudhary also said the JD(U) will study the Uniform Civil Code Bill and will "not oppose it for no reason" if provisions are unexceptionable.
The former state JD(U) president made the statement while addressing a press conference at the party office. He was replying to queries about the political turbulence that has ensued after Shah's assertion that UCC will be implemented "across 22 NDA-ruled states by 2029".
On Monday (September 14, 2026), senior JD(U) leader and Phulwari Sharif MLA Shyam Rajak had spoken out strongly against the UCC, claiming that he was expressing a view in line with the stand taken earlier by party supremo Nitish Kumar, who had told the Narendra Modi government at the Centre, "we will support the Bill in Parliament but are opposed to its implementation in Bihar".
Mr. Chaudhary, however, maintained that "there is no reason to make haste in the matter" and pointed out that "our national working president Sanjay Kumar Jha has said that he will hold talks on the issue with none other than the Union home minister".
"As of now, we are not aware of the details of the legislation on UCC. Let it be placed before us. If we find there is nothing objectionable, why shall we oppose it without any reason? And if there are points of concern, these will be conveyed to the Union Home Minister," he said.
Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister and Shiv Sena president Eknath Shinde backed Shah on the UCC issue, saying Sena founder late Bal Thackeray had envisioned the common law for all.
"Hinduhridaysamrat Balasaheb Thackeray's vision was 'one country, one law' with equal justice for all. Union Home Minister Amit Shah has also stated the same position on UCC," Mr. Shinde said.
He added that the Mahayuti government in Maharashtra remains positive about the Uniform Civil Code and will make a definitive decision at an appropriate time.
Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Monday (September 14, 2026) said the State government would implement the UCC once the committee preparing the draft bill submitted its report.
Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah said the BJP should introduce the UCC Bill in Parliament if it has the numbers to pass it, instead of pushing it through individual states, and claimed the BJP's allies also have reservations.
"If you have the numbers, bring it to Parliament. Why are you doing it through different states? Anyway, within their own NDA, not everyone agrees with this. According to the news, Janata Dal (United) raised their hands and said this won’t be implemented in Bihar,” Mr. Abdullah told reporters here.
The National Conference leader said the BJP should not bring the UCC “through the backdoor”. "The way their own allies are not in favour of it, I don’t think they will be able to get it passed in Parliament. That is perhaps why they are taking this route,” he added.
All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) president Asaduddin Owaisi said in Bhopal that if the NDA constituent parties such as the JD(U) and TDP have "the slightest disagreement" with the BJP's ideology, they should oppose the Uniform Civil Code.
The UCC was being introduced in various states with the aim of "targeting" India's 18 crore Muslims, and the real objective of the BJP and RSS was to "dismantle" the protections guaranteed (to religious minorities) under Articles 25, 26, and 29 of the Constitution, he alleged.
Owaisi said it would be a different matter if the NDA allies had aligned themselves completely with BJP's ideology. "But if they still have even the slightest difference with the BJP, they should oppose it (UCC)," he said.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Communauto says it was hit by data breach initiated by its own employee
Breach affected 'some thousand members' across the country, says company
The Montreal car-sharing company Communauto said it was hit by a potential data breach after one of its employees tried to access customers' personal information.
In an email sent to affected customers on Monday evening, Communauto said the incident happened during the night of Sept. 3 to 4.
"Our investigation determined that an automated script had been deployed without authorization by an employee in an attempt to access and download customer records," the email reads.
The company says police executed a search warrant the next day at the residence of the employee suspected of carrying out the breach to seize their computer equipment.
Communauto says account passwords and payment information were not affected by the breach, but that personal information, including people's names, addresses and driver's licence numbers, was. If the customer had a photograph of themselves or of their licence attached to their file, then those were downloaded as well.
In a statement to CBC, Communauto's vice-president of strategic development, Marco Viviani, said the breach affected about two per cent of its users, representing "some thousand members" Canada-wide.
"At this stage, we hope that no data was disclosed externally," he said.
"Based on the information available to us, we did not believe it was necessary for anyone to be taken into custody, but we have not received any additional details since law enforcement became involved."
Viviani says the company hired a specialized consulting firm to monitor the web and dark web for any signs of data exposure.
Communauto says those affected by the breach should "remain vigilant regarding unsolicited emails, phone calls, and text messages, particularly those requesting personal information, payment, urgent action, or encouraging you to click on a link or open an attachment."
It says customers should set up multi-factor authentication and make sure their account password is strong and unique.

How did the first Ultimate Championship go?
- Published
As poster boy Armand Duplantis performed the Ultimate Championship's official song and fireworks lit up the sky above the newly crowned winners, athletics had taken its first strides in a new direction.
Across three fast-paced evenings the inaugural event played out in Budapest, where a record $10m (£7.4m) prize pot was distributed among the sport's biggest stars.
It looked different. It felt different. And, after three successive sell-out crowds and positive feedback from the athletes, it appears it is here to stay.
"It's a good first step towards changing track and field for the better," said Usain Bolt, event ambassador and the greatest sprinter in history.
"The athletes are loving it. It's a different energy, a different vibe."
World Athletics and its president, Lord Coe, worked for three years to tackle the absence of a season-ending pinnacle event.
Rather than keeping to an established formula, the Ultimate Championship was a bold, innovative undertaking - and it is hoped it can exist as a testing ground to help shape the sport's future.
"We walked out, we came through the little starlights and we all looked at each other and said, 'this is unbelievable'," Britain's four-time global relay medallist Imani-Lara Lansiquot told BBC Sport.
"It's so rare that things really live up to the expectation, the hype. I'm so, so glad, having been in this sport for many years now, to actually see us be put on a platform and celebrated in this way."
Athletics has long grappled with the issue of maintaining the interest and excitement which it generates at the Olympics throughout the rest of those four-year cycles.
The structure of the season has not always been clear for occasional viewers, while showdowns between the world's top athletes can be inconsistent. From a storytelling perspective, that is far from ideal.
They are all issues World Athletics has sought to begin addressing with the biennial Ultimate Championship, while also compensating the athletes with record prize money.
The premise is accessible: condensed, fast-paced sessions, with the best competing against the best for a global title and significant prize money.
A striking new appearance and several innovative features ensured the Ultimate Championship provided a notably different feel to that of the sport's established global championships.
An infield painted black sought to focus attention on the illuminated live events, while the horizontal jumps were decided in a bright pink sandpit.
A new trophy waited for the winners on a plinth, with their crowning moment marked by sparklers and celebratory music.
New features for TV audiences attempted to enhance the viewer experience, with athlete headshots, win probabilities and projected finishing positions flashing up on screen.
They did so with varying success.
Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen was unimpressed by his predicted finishing position of 12th before winning the 5,000m title, while Britain's 1500m champion Josh Kerr was expected to finish last - a result of both athletes racing lightly over recent seasons.
There was a notable athlete-centric feel to the event beyond the increased financial rewards.
The world's top athletes arrived on the eve of the championship for a red carpet event featuring photoshoots.
Athlete videos were played inside the stadium before events and winners held centre-court style interviews before being escorted to a champions' enclosure, where they joined Bolt and master of ceremonies Noah Lyles.
On the videos, Britain's Georgia Hunter Bell said: "I do like the fact that it builds personality and character for, hopefully, people to connect with the athletes. That storytelling is something that's really interesting.
"If you think of superstars like Carlos Alcaraz, Serena Williams or Tadej Pogacar, obviously they're great athletes, but it's their personality coming through that makes it fun."
BBC commentator and former 1500m world champion Steve Cram said: "The key is the exposure of it. It's good for the sport. It's really good for the profile of the athletes."
But the championship did not avoid criticism - the biggest its exclusion of certain events.
World Athletics took the decision to include events based on viewer behaviour, including pulse rate and sweat response.
That meant that distance track events, including the 3,000m steeplechase and 10,000m, were omitted, while only selected field events were included. Shot-putters and discus throwers were excluded entirely.
The event format was also altered. Round progression in several field events meant increased jeopardy, with the competition whittled down to the top four athletes by the fourth and final round.
British long jumper Jazmin Sawyers told BBC Sport: "Some field events didn't get any attention because they're not here. The championship is worse off for not having them.
"It looks amazing in stadium and broadcast. It's dynamic. It's exciting. There's a place for it alongside regular championships.
"I don't think I would like to see it replace regular championships, but I like the idea that this is something that exists alone."
On the long jump competition format, she added: "I would love to see all eight [athletes] get all four jumps. It makes it more interesting.
"I was able to come from fourth to second. What if the person who was eighth could go from eighth to first? That's more exciting."
On the matter of the excluded events, Coe said the disciplines held at the Ultimate Championship were "not in tablets of stone".
Looking ahead to the next edition in 2028, the Ultimate Championship will be positioned at the end of a season which is headlined by an Olympics.
It remains to be seen how it will fit alongside the Diamond League - the sport's season-long series - in the schedule of the athletes.
Former Olympic heptathlon champion Denise Lewis told BBC Sport: "People have wanted to see something that looked different and felt like a different product. World Athletics has delivered.
"I don't think we know what it will do to the global calendar of athletics.
"The overall picture and the landscape isn't clear. There is place for this, but I do think it is unclear what yet."
Coe accepted before the weekend that there would be "no guarantee we're going get everything right" and said a "slightly different format" might be considered in future.
But, regardless, the competition was a statement of intent as the sport seeks to engage with new, bigger audiences while ensuring its star names are rewarded with prize money closer aligned to that of other sports.
Speaking after become Britain's first Ultimate champion in the 1500m, Josh Kerr said: "I welcome anything that can push this sport on to make it more entertaining for people to watch and athletes to go out and compete.
"There is one last thing that we can do to get it right and that is to let athletes wear their own brands versus their country.
"I love my country and competing for them, but we don't make money from that. We don't have the pay cheques other sports do just yet.
"My $30,000 pay cheque just came through from winning the World Indoors, so $150,000 is a huge jump and I'm massively appreciative."

Multiple spells of heavy rain lashed Bengaluru on Tuesday evening, leaving several parts of the city waterlogged and bringing traffic to a crawl, with office-goers struggling to get home.
In Domlur, a portion of the compound wall of a military campus collapsed, reportedly trapping four cows underneath. The BBMP deployed a civic team for a rescue operation. Another compound wall collapsed at Nanjamba Agrahara. No injuries were reported in either incident.
Central Bengaluru came to a standstill as waterlogging was reported at several key junctions, including Mayo Hall Court Junction, Garuda Mall Junction, Trinity Circle, Anil Kumble Junction, UB City Junction, ASC Centre (HAL) Airport Junction and Tonique Junction.
A senior traffic officer said evening traffic was affected in Central Bengaluru, with knee-level water stagnation at multiple points.
“The rain started during the evening peak hour, and many office-goers were on the road already. So, even the multiple connecting roads were gridlocked,” he said.
Commuters also struggled to get cabs and autorickshaws, while fares surged sharply. Several areas in east and southeast Bengaluru experienced power outages.
Bengaluru corporations and the Bengaluru Traffic Police reported tree falls at multiple locations, including near the Shivajinagar bus stand, near CB Road Junction towards ESI Junction, and near Hosmat Hospital towards Rajamohan Roy Road. More than three trees were also uprooted.
Waterlogging points
Flooding was witnessed at multiple locations, including Kalpana Circle near Mount Carmel College, Sankey Road near High Grounds, SJP Road, RV Teachers College, and T. Mariappa Road, all of which were cleared.
The stormwater drain on Nala Road overflowed, affecting traffic movement. In Chamrajpet, waterlogging at the K.R. Market up-ramp triggered traffic chaos along Mysuru Road.
Other waterlogged stretches included Anepalya Junction towards Mico Junction, Wilson Garden 10th Cross towards Dairy Circle, the Ayyappa Underpass in Madiwala towards Madiwala Police Station, NGO Gate towards Passport Office Junction, Koramangala Inner Ring Road towards Indiranagar 100 Feet Road, and the Peenya flyover towards the city, among others.
The severe waterlogging prompted civic agencies and the Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP) to jointly clear stagnant water at several locations, even as traffic on these stretches crawled at a snail’s pace.
Cab prices shoot up
Aisiri Srinivas, a resident of Koramangala, said travelling home from her office near Vittal Mallya Road cost her nearly twice what she usually spends.
“I usually get an autorickshaw for ₹170 to ₹190, but the fare went up to ₹250. Even then, no driver accepted the ride. I had to keep increasing the tip and finally paid nearly ₹400 to get an autorickshaw,” she said.
Nakul S., a resident of Yelahanka, said it took him nearly two hours to reach home from M.G. Road, compared with the usual 70 to 75 minutes. “Even the Hebbal ramp was waterlogged, which added to the delay, apart from the traffic chaos at Anil Kumble Junction and Tonique Junction,” he said.

London misses out to Nairobi in World Athletics bid
- Published
London has missed out to Nairobi in the bid to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships.
The decision, which means an African city will host the event for the first time, was confirmed at a World Athletics council meeting in Budapest.
World Athletics president Sebastian Coe said Nairobi had presented "a compelling and emotional bid".
"We were fortunate to have four outstanding bids for 2029 and 2031, and this was not an easy decision for the council," said Coe.
"With this decision today, we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide with the hosting of our World Athletics Championships in Asia, Africa and Europe over its next three editions.
"Nairobi presented a compelling and emotional bid, and taking the World Athletics Championships to Africa for the first time will be historic.
"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment."
The London Stadium, home of Championship club West Ham United, was the proposed host venue for the UK bid.
The stadium was also used for the 2012 Olympic Games and the yearly London Diamond League, and also when the city last hosted the Worlds in 2017.
The UK's bid was led by Athletic Ventures, which consisted of UK Athletics, London Marathon Events and the Great Run Company.
Jack Buckner, CEO of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: "We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.
"We would like to thank the Government, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, the Mayor of London and UK Sport for their fantastic support for our bid. Our thanks also to the London Stadium, West Ham United and our many stakeholders for their commitment and hard work to put the bid together.
"Our congratulations go to Nairobi and we wish the organising committee all the best for a great event in 2029."
Rome was the other city to miss out, as World Athletics also confirmed that Munich would host the 2031 event for the first time.
Nairobi, the capital city of Kenya, submitted a bid for the 2025 championships but missed out to Tokyo.
The city's Kasarani Stadium is being renovated before the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) in 2027, which strengthened its case as a host venue.
Kenya finished second in the medal table at the 2025 edition, winning seven gold medals and 11 in total.
'A painful snub for London'
This is a painful snub for London, so why did it fail?
Those behind the bid had secured £45m in public money, and were confident of replicating the commercial success of the 2017 event.
However, there had been uncertainty over whether West Ham would grant permission for the London Stadium to be used. That was finally confirmed last month, but only shortly before the bid had to be formally submitted.
Another issue may have been the fact that nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's 23,000-seater Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships last month, with some fans blaming the cost of tickets.
Lord Coe has refused to be drawn on whether either were factors in the decision, preferring instead to focus on Kenya's rich tradition in distance running, and the fact Nairobi will make history by hosting Africa's first world championships. However, the spate of doping scandals in Kenyan athletics in recent years will also lead to some scrutiny over whether it is an appropriate host.
Britain is still hosting the Grand Depart of the men's and women's Tour de France cycling races in 2027, and then the men's Euros in 2028, and is bidding for the 2035 Women's World Cup. But at a time when government is also interested in a possible Olympic bid for 2040, today's decision is undoubtedly a blow.
'That was my dream'
World indoor 400m champion and British record holder Amber Anning was in the stands as a fan for the 2017 championships, and although she expressed her disappointment to miss out on the experience of a home event as an athlete, added that Nairobi was a chance for something "really special".
"There was a lot of disappointment, honestly," Anning told BBC Sport.
"That was our dream. In 2017, I saw that we have the best crowds, the best atmosphere. So I would say it is a bit unfortunate that we weren't able to get the bid.
"But seeing how Botswana was for the World Relays this year, I think it will be really special to have it in Africa for the first time. It's going to leave a legacy, so while it was not the result we wanted, it's still a chance for another country and another generation to inspire. It's an honour."
Greg Rutherford, who memorably won Olympic gold in the long jump as part of Super Saturday at the London 2012 Games, echoed Anning's sentiments.
Rutherford said it was a "bitter pill to swallow" for London to miss out but praised the strength of Nairobi's bid and highlighted the need for change.
"We've seen over the years how well we can put on these incredible championships - 2017 was massive, record amounts of people through the doors, bums on seats watching some amazing performances," Rutherford told BBC Sport.
"We also saw that in 2012 but at the same time, we are seeing something that is going to change the lay of the land.
"Of course there is real disappointment but equally, it's going to be incredible to finally see this event in Africa.
"I think what may have harmed it [London's bid] is that we had hosted one so recently, and Nairobi's bid was a very strong one. They are looking to invest into Africa so there is more chance for their nations to have the opportunity like this going forward and I do think we need to see change at times."

Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have announced that the Ebola outbreak ravaging parts of the country has reached its peak.
For the first time since the epidemic was declared in May, the numbers of people becoming infected is slowing down, according to officials.
Stressing that strict adherence to preventive measures needed to be kept in place, Samuel Roger Kamba, the Congolese health minister, said there was a decline in transmission of the Bundibugyo variant of Ebola.
“We are fighting a very dangerous virus that is killing many of our people. Today, we can say that the outbreak is under control,” he said. “At one point, we were recording about 120 cases per day; today, we’re seeing about 80 per day. So the number of new cases is decreasing every day.
“It has been more than 22 days since 10 of the 62 health zones have reported new cases. And so we can now definitively remove six health zones from the list because they have gone more than 42 days without new cases, and we can remove four health zones that have gone more than 21 days without a new case,” Kamba said.
Last week, the Sud-Ubangi region, on the DRC’s borders with Congo-Brazzaville and Central African Republic, became the sixth province to report the disease.
The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared by Congolese authorities on 15 May and is concentrated primarily in Ituri province, where ongoing conflict has created challenging conditions for those responding to the disease. It is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in the DRC since the highly contagious disease was first identified and named in 1976.
No effective treatment for the Bundibugyo variant has been found so far but there are clinical trials in the region. The DRC received more than 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine last month, which is the only approved treatment for the more common Zaire Ebola virus.
According to the latest data from the Congolese health ministry, the number of confirmed cases stood at more than 7,200, including more than 3,475 deaths, as of 14 September.
While welcoming the progress made, Iracan Gratien de Saint-Nicolas, an MP for Bunia, warned against what he called “triumphalism” and stressed that efforts must intensify to show people that the disease was under control.
Gratien Iracan called for lessons to be learned from failures in epidemiological surveillance that contributed to the rapid spread of the disease.
The MP also expressed some scepticism over the government announcement. “Claims that an epidemic is under control must be supported by objective indicators. If the indicators show that the epidemic is indeed under control, let’s make them public. Transparency in the data will strengthen public confidence,” he said.
He warned that some indicators that showed an epidemic was under control seemed to have been omitted by the DRC authorities, such as a sustained decline in new cases (over seven to 21 days), a decrease in deaths, a reduction in areas with active transmission, the majority of new cases originating from contacts already identified, and a high rate of contact tracing, as well as dignified and safe burials.
Early last month, Jean Kaseya, the director general of the African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, visited Bunia – capital of Ituri and a centre of the current Ebola outbreak – and said then that there was no way of knowing when the peak might be reached but that containment and contact tracing were still not effective enough.
Kaseya said: “A large portion of the mortality – 60 to 70% of deaths – comes from the community. The list of contacts we have just keeps growing. Epidemiologists say we’ve reached the peak when all cases come from the list of contacts.”
In Rwampara, a town in Ituri, people are exhausted from the past few months of living with the dread of the disease. Léa Munyere, 36, a mother of four, said she was relieved that the health authorities had announced that Ebola was under control. Two of her close friends had died and she was still struggling to come to terms with the loss, she said.
“We hope the disease will soon be declared over. It has robbed us of the people we cherish so much since it was first reported,” she said. “We just want to get back to our normal lives.”

The opening ceremony of ‘Yudh Abhyas’ was held at the Auli Foreign Training Node in Uttarakhand, where Major General Amaresh Gunjan, General Officer Commanding, 14 Infantry Division, and Colonel Benjamin Jackman, Commander, 1st Infantry Brigade Combat Team, 11th Airborne Division, U.S. Army, addressed the participating contingents, according to a Union Ministry of Defence statement.
Around 600 personnel from each side are taking part in the exercise, which is being conducted simultaneously at Auli and the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan.
The exercise is aimed at enhancing the joint military capability of the two armies for the employment of integrated battle groups in mountainous and semi-mountainous terrain, with a focus on infantry-dominated operations.
A key focus of the exercise is the use of technology in battlefield operations. Participating troops will train in the employment of drones and autonomous systems for surveillance and reconnaissance, while contemporary weapon systems will be demonstrated at the Mahajan Field Firing Range.
Subject matter experts from the two armies will also exchange views on emerging technologies, and developments in multi-domain warfare, the Defence Ministry said.
The exercise will provide an opportunity for both sides to share tactics, techniques and procedures, and strengthen their ability to plan and execute coordinated military operations across varied terrain and operational environments. It is also expected to strengthen interoperability between the two forces through joint training and exchange of best operational practices.

A Night for Actor’s Actors, Not Movie Stars
This year’s Emmys ceremony celebrated versatile performers, not glitzy celebrities.
When the Widow’s Bay creator Katie Dippold accepted her Emmy for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series last night, she joked that she was so proud of her win, she intended to display her trophy as prominently as possible in her home. The award would be mounted on a rotating turntable, she explained; mirrors would be set up around the space so visitors could always see it, wherever they were. “This is going to become my entire personality now,” she warned.
This year’s Emmys essentially turned Widow’s Bay into its personality, too. The Apple TV series about a haunted island town full of eccentric inhabitants swept the field, winning six categories over the course of the evening, including Outstanding Comedy Series. The show’s star, Matthew Rhys, even made Emmys history: With his win for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series, he became the first ever nominee to score a trophy in all three lead actor categories. (Earlier in the night, he was awarded for his work in The Beast in Me, a limited series; in 2018, he won for The Americans, a drama.) His achievements helped underline how much the ceremony honored true-blue actors such as him—and how television, despite years of movie stars dominating prestige shows, remains best designed for versatile performers and textured roles.
Consider Rhys’s fellow winners from Widow’s Bay, a series that married the chill of a Stephen King novel with the goofy humor of Parks and Recreation. Kate O’Flynn, who built her career in British theater, won Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series for her spirited turn as Patricia, a lonely but resilient woman. Her co-star Stephen Root, who took home the trophy for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series, is widely regarded as an actor’s actor—the kind of performer who adds depth to any story, no matter the genre. In his speech, he underlined how unusual it was for him to be recognized, pointing out that his son was shocked that he was in the same category as Harrison Ford.
The ceremony, of course, featured plenty of the movie stars: Michelle Pfeiffer, Nicole Kidman, Tom Holland, and Zendaya were all seated close to the stage. But many of the performers who took home awards were respected TV industry veterans who have spent most of their careers disappearing into their work rather than commanding the spotlight. Noah Wyle may now be an Emmys favorite after winning two years in a row for starring in The Pitt, but he beat out Mark Ruffalo and Gary Oldman for the honor. Allison Janney (who, to be fair, is an Oscar winner) expressed her shock about winning her first Emmy in 11 years, for her arresting supporting turn as a fictional U.S. president in The Diplomat.
The night also featured several satisfying, overdue wins: Rhea Seehorn, who led six seasons of the often-nominated Better Call Saul, finally took home her first Emmy, for her jittery performance in Pluribus. Hiro Murai, a director who has helped define the cinematic look of modern television through his work on shows such as Atlanta and Barry, won his first directing Emmy, for—once again—Widow’s Bay.
The Emmys producers seemed to know that many of its winners might not be household names. The show was frontloaded with the performance categories, which meant that all of the acting awards were finished halfway into the three-hour show. That’s unusual for a Hollywood ceremony, which normally tries to keep people glued to their screens by showing as many stars for as long as possible, and boosting viewer anticipation for their speeches. But then again, the night’s host was Mariska Hargitay, one of television’s mainstays; she’s led the cast of Law & Order: SVU for 27 seasons, with another on the way. To honor a slate of experienced pros only felt right.

Donald Trump Jr and Bettina Trump say Putin ally paid for some wedding festivities as a 'gift'
- Published
Donald Trump Jr's wife, Bettina Trump, confirmed that their May wedding was paid for in part by an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
A post on her Instagram account – attributed to the couple – said that two nights of their three-day wedding festivities on a private island in the Bahamas were partially funded by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with close ties to Putin.
The statement was released Monday after investigative journalism outlet ProPublica published a story detailing that Kremlev paid "hundreds of thousands of dollars" for the celebration.
Donald Trump Jr, the president's eldest son, is a private citizen, so it is not illegal for him to accept gifts from a foreign national.
"Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," the couple said in the statement.
But ethics watchdog groups said it still presented the appearance of a conflict of interest for the president's son to accept lavish gifts from someone associated with a foreign head of state – even if he is not a US government employee.
"People don't just give hundreds of thousands of dollars to a random acquaintance without wanting something," said Jordan Libowitz, vice president of communications for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW).
"You can see how [Putin] would enjoy all this press about how people in his circle are cozying up to people in the president's circle."
According to the ProPublica article, the couple was married on a private island in the Bahamas, then held a two-day celebration on a separate island that rents for approximately $100,000 per night. Kremlev also paid other costs for the party, including a roughly $70,000 fireworks display, the report found.
Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association (IBA), an organisation funded by the state-backed Gazprom energy company. The Olympic Committee suspended the group in part over its failure to report its ties to the Russian energy giant.
Earlier this year Kremlev was part of a delegation that visited China with Putin. The Russian president also gave Kremlev the Order of Friendship, a top state honour, according to ProPublica.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr told the news outlet that the president's son and Kremlev were personal friends and did not have "a business relationship".
An ally of Trump Jr referred the BBC to the Instagram statement.
In a statement to ProPublica, Kremlev's office said "Mr. Kremlev and Mr. Trump Jr have a friendly relationship." The statement said the men met a few years ago.
Kremlev attended part of the wedding, the outlet reported. Other attendees included one of the US president's daughters, Ivanka Trump, and her husband, Jared Kushner, who has worked for the US on diplomatic negotiations with Iran, Russia and in the Middle East.
The Trump campaign and family faced controversy for potential ties to Russia during the 2016 presidential election, resulting in a special counsel investigation. During the campaign Donald Trump Jr brokered a meeting at Trump Tower with a Russian operative that was closely scrutinised during the probe.
Libowitz, of CREW, said either the president, who is a billionaire, or Trump Jr – who is worth $300 million, according to Forbes – could have paid for the full wedding to avoid a conflict of interest.
"His father is worth billions he could have picked up the tab. Clearly they just didn't want to pay for it," Libowitz said. "They don't really care about the ethical ramifications."

What is Merchant Discount Rate and how MDR will be calculated after revised UPI charges
As per the new rules, Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI payments above ₹2,000 will attract a 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR).
The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) announced on Tuesday that a 0.4% fee will be charged on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions to certain merchants when the transaction value exceeds ₹2,000. It also clarified that customers will not have to pay any fee for making UPI payments under the revised system.
As per the new rules, Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI payments above ₹2,000 will attract a 0.4 per cent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR). However, the charge will not exceed ₹300 for a single transaction.
But what is MDR?
MDR refers to the fee charged to merchants by banks and payment service providers for processing digital payments. The amount depends on factors such as the payment method, the type of merchant, the transaction value, and the agreement between the businesses involved.
In a digital payment system, a customer pays a merchant electronically, while the merchant pays a small fee to the company or bank that processes the transaction.
Although merchants are generally expected to bear this cost, some businesses may add the charge to the customer's bill. This is more common with high-value card payments, where MDR rules are different from those applicable to UPI.
Who will have to pay the MDR fee?
The 0.4% MDR will apply to Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI payments exceeding ₹2,000. For transactions of ₹75,000 or more, the charge will be limited to ₹300.
For example, a ₹1,00,000 transaction would otherwise attract a 0.4% charge of ₹400. However, because of the cap, the maximum MDR payable for that transaction will be ₹300.
Small merchants covered under the P2PM (Person-to-Person-Merchant) framework will not be charged MDR. The P2PM framework is a separate account category introduced by NPCI for small vendors who receive payments directly into their personal bank accounts.
The small vendor category includes merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month through UPI QR directly into their accounts, the NPCI said in a document. The category is designed to encourage digital payments among small businesses and vendors in the unorganised retail sector.
How will MDR fee be calculated?
The MDR is calculated according to the value of each transaction. For a purchase of ₹3,000, the 0.4% rate would mean an MDR of ₹12, which the merchant pays to its acquiring bank.
The maximum MDR is ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more, while payments below ₹2,000 will not incur any MDR.
For a ₹50,000 transaction, the same rate would result in an MDR of ₹200. However, for a payment of ₹1,00,000, the 0.4% charge would be ₹400, but the merchant would pay only ₹300 due to the cap.
| Amount paid to merchant | Applicable MDR | MDR paid by merchant | 
|---|---|---|
| ₹ 2,000 | - | ₹ 0 | 
| ₹ 3,000 | 0.40% | ₹ 12 | 
| ₹ 50,000 | 0.40% | ₹ 200 | 
| ₹ 75,000 and above | Fixed ₹ 300 | ₹ 300 | 
However, the new percentage-based MDR will not apply to all types of merchants.
Merchant categories that qualify for a flat fee
Certain categories, including railways, telecom services, insurance, and fuel, will instead be charged a fixed MDR of ₹5 per transaction for payments above ₹2,000.
In these cases, merchants will not be charged the 0.4% rate. They will pay a fixed ₹5 fee irrespective of the total transaction value.
The fixed fee helps keep costs under control for essential public services, utility payments and low-margin businesses such as fuel retailers, NPCI said.
NPCI said the MDR collected from high-value transactions will be shared among different participants in the UPI ecosystem. The move aims to help fund the expansion of UPI to more users and merchants, while also supporting spending on resilience, cybersecurity and innovation.

Thank you for joining us for our continuing coverage of the aftermath of Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods in the Himalayan mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Poor weather has hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of people missing enters its fourth day.
Nepal’s finance minister says his country will need up to $5bn to rebuild after the floods, believed to have been caused by a melting glacier high up in the mountains that set off a deadly cascade of water into the valleys below.
Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters today those figures are “just an estimate” and that “loss and damage is being assessed”.
Here’s a summary of what we know so far:
Nearly 3,000 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 626, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.
At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.
India said it is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China.
The deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border were believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse that was detected as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event by geologists. You can read this explainer to find out more about how a collapsing glacier can generate a powerful flood, and whether the climate crisis is contributing to the risk.
Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India’s Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, said: “Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbour, and also have a similar geographic situation … we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region.”
Uttarakhand is one of the most ecologically sensitive regions of India, with 1,266 glacial lakes. As glaciers melt, water can accumulate in lakes held back by natural barriers. If those barriers fail, vast volumes of water can be released suddenly, triggering devastating floods.
“We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state,” Kaushik told AFP.
‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal
The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.
Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:
Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.
“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”
Nepal’s government has appealed for financial help as it faces the daunting task of recovering from the devastating flash floods and braces for the possibility of more flooding.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross says.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the UN Children’s Fund.
The disaster comes just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s 8-9 September mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government.
Nepal is now led by prime minister Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper turned politician widely known as “Balen”. The former Kathmandu mayor swept March elections on a wave of euphoria calling for political change.
The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the devastating flood occurred earlier this week has decreased, Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 sq metres in size this morning – around the size of 14 football fields combined – having shrunk by 21,000 sq metres compared with images from Thursday.
Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.
State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, which has been monitoring the lake since Thursday, dispatched a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to gather more data about the lake.
An overflow from the lake on Friday temporarily halted rescue work before further assessment deemed the risks manageable.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Apex Legends VS Street Fighter 6 Event Release Date

The excess reliance of the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) on the State government for financial support has been brought to light once again — this time, through the State Finances Audit Report for Tamil Nadu by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG).
In the 14 years since 2013-14, the government aid, both in the form of tariff subsidy and grants, has accounted for ₹2.55 lakh crore.
If the final figures for 2024-25 are compared with those for 2013-14, the growth was a whopping 451%, as only the revised estimates for 2025-26 and 2026-27 are available.
On an average, the annual assistance is around ₹18,130 crore. Since 2021-22, the State government was mandated to absorb the losses of the power discom fully, making its financial condition shaky.
A perusal of the data reveals that the aggregate figure of tariff subsidy and grants exceeded the five-digit mark in 2016-17, when the scheme for providing free electricity of up to 100 units to domestic consumers was launched.
Five years later, the 100% absorption of the financial loss of the discom came into effect in the wake of the power utility having been sanctioned an assistance of about ₹30,230 crore in 2020 under the Central government’s COVID-19 liquidity infusion scheme.
As the gap between the average cost of supply and the average revenue realised has been narrowed down, thanks to the liberal assistance of the government, and it is likely to turn positive this year, the TNPDCL may not be getting as much aid through grants as it had been receiving in all these five years.
Yet, ₹5,000 crore has been earmarked towards grants for the current year, in addition to tariff subsidy.
Another significant feature is that out of the subsidy figure of about ₹18,860 crore this year, nearly ₹9,893 crore, accounting for 53%, is set aside for domestic consumers, who are being given free electricity of up to 200 units, subject to the overall consumption not exceeding 500 units bi-monthly.
To make matters worse for the State government, the Supreme Court’s direction last year of having to recover regulatory assets, which are akin to deferred income, requires the government to shell out as grants a sum of ₹11,800 crore per year for five years (2026-27 to 2030-31), totalling ₹59,000 crore, towards the power discom.
Alternatively, the amount can be recovered as enhanced consumption charges, as the regulatory assets cover the previously incurred losses that can be recovered from consumers in future, subject to the regulatory body’s approval.
However, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam-led government has said that that it will not go in for an upward power tariff revision. In such case, it is the State government that has to bear the additional stress.

Family income rose and poverty fell in 2025 — but safety net cuts could erase gains
The average American family made more money last year than in 2024, while the number of people living in poverty fell slightly, according to a new report from the Census Bureau.
The annual snapshot of last year's family income, poverty and health coverage comes as Americans are currently wrestling with stubborn inflation that's been rekindled by the war with Iran. Prices have been climbing faster than average wages for the last five months.
In 2025, by contrast, families saw real improvements in their purchasing power. The average family's income rose 2.6% last year, after adjusting for inflation, to $87,460. Families at the top of the income ladder saw bigger gains than those at the bottom.
Analysts say those gains could be eroded by cuts to the social safety net. In 2025, programs such as Supplemental Nutrition Assistance (SNAP) helped keep many families out of poverty, as measured by a special yardstick that includes government aid. Some of those programs are being scaled back as part of the sweeping tax cut package passed by the GOP Congress last year. Results of those cuts are likely to be reflected in future Census tallies.
Health insurance coverage held steady in 2025 but is expected to fall now that enhanced subsidies for Obamacare coverage have lapsed. Stricter work requirements for Medicaid are also set to take effect next year.
"Things like SNAP and Medicaid made a really big difference in lowering poverty and expanding health coverage," says Sharon Parrott, president of the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. "Instead of building on that improvement and recognizing the record of success of things like SNAP and Medicaid, Republican policymakers enacted very deep cuts, historically large cuts that right now are taking food assistance and health coverage away from people, putting upward pressure on poverty, increasing the ranks of the uninsured, and really taking us in the wrong direction."
The share of people living in poverty declined last year to 10.2% from 10.7% in 2024. In 2025, 34.5 million people in the country fell below the poverty line, compared to 36 million the previous year.
A supplemental measure of poverty, which accounts for taxes, government benefits and additional expenses showed somewhat higher levels of poverty — 13.1%. This figure was little changed from 2024.
While average family income rose last year, some families did better than others. Families in the top 10% of income saw gains of 1.7%, while those in the bottom 10% saw little change. On average, African American families saw the largest increase in income last year — 4.8% — but at $59,980, the median income among Black families remains far lower than for white ($91,930) or Asian ($126,300) families.
"2025 becomes a benchmark of sorts," Parrott says. "We saw these modest gains. We saw some improvement in poverty. We saw health insurance hold steady at relatively low rates. And we saw real wage gains. And on almost every measure, things are worse today."

The Boston city government abandoned Flock Safety’s license-plate reader cameras after the company shared data nationwide in violation of a contract provision, according to city officials.
“We have actually abandoned Flock,” Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said in her monthly “Ask the Mayor” segment on GBH News last week. Wu made the comment a few days before the release of Boston’s annual surveillance technology report, which said a Flock “vendor error” resulted in nationwide data sharing.
The report, which covers 2025, describes how the Boston Police Department deployed about 45 Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras in a trial with Flock from April to September last year. The unauthorized data sharing occurred during the first few days of the pilot, the report said:
Pursuant to the contract, the Flock ALPR Pilot Program was designed to restrict access to the data collected by BPD ALPR cameras exclusively to trained BPD personnel. The contract clearly noted that data sharing was to be disabled, and BPD confirmed with Flock that settings were “off” for sharing. Within three days of initiating the Pilot, BPD became aware that other law enforcement agencies were able to access license plate and vehicle information collected from BPD ALPR cameras using a nationwide lookup feature that was enabled by the vendor in error. Upon learning of the vendor error, BPD ensured that the function was immediately disabled and access to the Department’s data was no longer available without submitting a written request to BPD as described above. No further direct access was available for the duration of the Pilot.
The report didn’t say how many law enforcement agencies accessed the data. The problem with Flock didn’t stop Boston from seeking another vendor of license-plate reader technology. The police department started another license-plate reader trial with Motorola in February 2026 and a third trial with Axon in June 2026.
Boston’s report comes amid a larger privacy debate over law enforcement access to license-plate camera data. An Electronic Frontier Foundation report yesterday described how the nationwide lookup tool lets police conduct searches with little or no justification.

For the best part of a decade, abusive deepfake “pornography” websites have published thousands of nonconsensual videos depicting women, including high-profile celebrities, politicians, and public figures, into sexual situations. Now, in what is likely the largest takedown of explicit deepfake websites to date, officials in New York have seized more than a dozen of the harmful sites.
On Monday, the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office announced the seizure of 12 domains which it says have been used for “unlawfully” sharing, publishing, and selling celebrity deepfake videos. Around 1,200 people—overwhelmingly women—were depicted in nonconsensual sexual images and videos on the websites, the office says. These included social media influencers, actors, activists, athletes, musicians, and politicians.
“These horrific violations of privacy follow victims into their careers and personal lives and take an immense toll on emotional and mental well-being,” district attorney Alvin Bragg said in a statement, urging potential victims to come forward and contact his office’s cybercrime bureau. The office says its investigations into who is responsible for the websites, plus those who uploaded damaging videos of victims, are ongoing.
The seizures, carried out under New York’s criminal procedure laws, mark perhaps one of the most significant and sweeping actions against websites hosting explicit deepfake videos since the technology first emerged at the end of 2017. As artificial intelligence technology has improved, a dark industry of websites, apps, and bots has appeared: They are designed to “undress” photos of women or create graphic sexual videos that include them. The images and videos are increasingly realistic and can be generated in seconds.
While deepfake technology is widely used against non-famous women and girls—often being shared in private social media groups—celebrities have spoken out about the many harms of being depicted in the content and the challenges of getting it removed. While laws against deepfakes have been slow to emerge, the US Take It Down Act increasingly allows images to be removed, with part of the law allowing law enforcement officials to take down and seize websites.
The Manhattan District Attorney’s Office has not publicly named the websites it has seized. However, ahead of Bragg’s announcement, WIRED independently observed several of the sites’ homepages being replaced by takedown notices—“THIS DOMAIN HAS BEEN SEIZED”—late last week, with the sites now saying they have been taken over following a seizure warrant issued by a New York State Supreme Court.
“The takedowns are a significant win in the fight against synthetic nonconsensual intimate imagery (NCII),” says Leonie Oehmig, a researcher at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), who has studied the deepfake creation ecosystem. Oehmig says that enforcement of state laws shows that the harmful content can be tackled and that the seized sites don’t appear to be accessible if using VPNs to try and access them from other locations. “This shows that meaningful, coordinated enforcement is achievable even where regulation itself remains fragmented across jurisdictions.”
The websites were likely viewed millions of times. Many used names that included phrases such as “sex celebrity” or promised “real deepfakes.” They hosted false videos of some of the world’s most famous celebrities, with one saying, “various actresses’ faces are used for deepfakes.”
Videos could be several minutes in length and include fully sexually explicit scenes—often swapping the faces of celebrities or public figures into existing pornographic videos. Archived versions of the websites show some videos had been watched tens of thousands of times, with one of the websites claiming to have been online since 2018.
“Most videos took the shape of actual pornographic movies, manipulated to instead show targets’ faces instead of the original actors,” says Benjamin Shultz, the lead researcher at the American Sunlight Project, a nonprofit. Shultz, who has been documenting deepfake abuse against political figures and had come across some of the websites during this research, says that many videos appeared to be reposts of content that had originally be shared on the MrDeepFakes website, a notorious deepfake platform that was taken offline after its creators were unmasked by reporters.
“On at least two of the seized websites, elected officials were given profiles containing their name and position, along with a grid of manipulated videos hosting their likeness,” Shultz says. Through recent research, Shultz says that 56 European politicians had been mentioned or appeared on the websites, including 16 US politicians and two based in the UK.
While Oehmig, the ISD researcher, says the takedowns are encouraging, there are many other parts of the deepfake industry that are causing serious harm. “Effective intervention needs to target the ecosystem at multiple points, including the tools used for the creation of synthetic NCII, the discovery and promotion of these, the hosting and technical infrastructure that keeps them online, and the payment and affiliate systems that enable operators to monetize them,” Oehmig says.

In September 2026, an image circulated online supposedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump and the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on a boat together.
The image included a date in the bottom righthand corner: July 14, 1985. It circulated on X, Threads, Reddit (screenshot) and Facebook (screenshot).
Snopes readers contacted us to ask whether it was an authentic image or a digital creation.
This image was generated using OpenAI tools, according to the company's detection tool. The detector found a SynthID watermark, an indicator embedded in Google Gemini and OpenAI images to help differentiate them from legitimate pictures. AI detection tools Pangram and Hive Moderation also determined there is a high likelihood the image was created using AI.
(OpenAI)
Some social media users shared a higher-quality version of the fake image; we uploaded that version and similarly found a SynthID watermark.
(OpenAI)
Detection tools are fallible. However, there were other visual indicators that the image is AI-generated, including the fact that credible images of Trump and Epstein show they looked far younger in the mid-to-late 1980s than they appear in the picture circulating online. As such, we have rated it as fake.
A reverse image search could not determine the original creator of the picture. However, it did determine that no journalists from reputable news outlets had documented the existence of the image. We also did not locate the image in credible media repositories, such as Getty Images. If the image was real, news outlets would have covered it.
AI image creators — or people circulating those images and attempting to pass them off as legitimate — often add heavy filters to mask indicators of AI. A closer look of the high-quality image revealed such abnormalities, including nondescript white triangles floating in the ocean and poles that lead nowhere.
(Reddit user Hodenmumps-164)
For more on Trump and Epstein, we have compiled various rumors about the pair's relationship.

How Maresca is tackling football's impossible job
- Published
Enzo Maresca seemingly took on an impossible job in the summer when replacing the legendary Pep Guardiola at Manchester City, but is making it look an easy task in the infancy of his tenure.
Four victories in as many games has City sitting joint-top of the Premier League alongside Arsenal, and the early signs suggest those two sides will be the ones tussling for the title once more.
Maresca clinched his most significant win since taking charge with an impressive 1-0 victory against rivals Manchester United at Old Trafford on Sunday, despite playing much of the game with 10 men following Phil Foden's sending-off.
The City players, though, mirrored their manager's feelings by staying calm, and it is this type of composure which has been the most impressive aspect during these first few weeks.
- Is the Premier League already a two-team title race? 
  - Published15 hours ago
- Left in the dark - will fans ever get to hear live VAR audio? 
  - Published15 hours ago
Cool with the media & house music in training
Maresca looked back to last September when goalkeeper Robert Sanchez was dismissed after only five minutes for former side Chelsea at the same venue - a defeat which he referenced after Sunday's game.
The manager was forced into changes that evening and appeared to panic by making two substitutions in the opening seven minutes, effectively moving his side to a back five but unable to see the game out.
Fast forward one year - his decision to assess the situation before making major changes proved critical, shifting Rayan Cherki to the right, then replacing him at half-time with Iliman Ndiaye was a noteworthy tactical tweak.
"How do you say in English? Happy wife, happy life. For us, happy Erling, happy life," said a beaming Maresca after being asked about Erling Haaland's winner and his contributions this season.
Such jovial remarks from a smiling Maresca in news conferences are in contrast to predecessor Guardiola, who often looked like he would rather be anywhere else but in that chair.
In May, which transpired to be Guardiola's final month at City, the Spaniard was asked what advice he would give the next manager.
"Be themselves," was the reply - and Maresca is beginning to step out of his shadow.
While Guardiola was often leaping and screaming around his technical area during games, Maresca looks to be the opposite as he tends to stand motionless by the pitch with his arms folded.
The most eye-catching change in training has been the introduction of loud house music, which Maresca himself described as the "boom, boom, boom" type - the approach is to make the players feel "more happy" and "work better".
New captain Ruben Dias recently said in a BBC Sport interview that Maresca had introduced his own ideas, but the fundamentals remain as they were under Guardiola.
Dias said: "There's obviously many things from training sessions to some details about the way we press, details about the way we defend that make all of these Enzo's idea.
"It's still a change, of course. Many things have changed, but in some ways continuity in terms of the way we are playing, and there are details that make it different. But still, all very similar to the way we have always behaved at the club."
Guardiola comparisons 'don't put pressure on me'
Maresca's arrival began with the inevitable comparisons of when David Moyes replaced Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in 2013.
The 46-year-old referenced Ferguson and Arsene Wenger in his unveiling news conference, saying clubs "struggled a little bit" after the departures of long-serving managers.
It's almost easy to forget City started this season with a 3-0 defeat at the hands of Arsenal in the Community Shield, but the side have bounced back in style with five straight victories, including the Champions League win at Porto.
While the Old Trafford job appeared to be too much for Moyes to handle, lasting only 10 months before being sacked, Maresca seems to be embracing the "challenge" and "privilege" of succeeding Guardiola.
Maresca acknowledged to reporters in pre-season that City's former boss would be referenced on a regular basis, but batted that particular narrative away by asserting "it doesn't put pressure on me".
The former Chelsea and Leicester manager needed to hit the ground running at Etihad Stadium in order avoid questions about whether he was the right man for the job having been the only person City targeted to take over.
City made major changes in the squad during the summer and the new-look side begin their Carabao Cup defence against Norwich at the Etihad on Thursday (19:30 BST), followed by hosting Sunderland in the Premier League three days later.
Maresca dispatched rivals United on their own turf, and victory in the next two games will ensure a near-perfect start to his tenure in one of football's toughest jobs.
