The Supreme Court Recognizes the Danger of Trump’s Election Plan
A majority of justices decided not to make the coming elections needlessly more chaotic than they already are.
Neither snow, nor rain, nor heat, nor gloom of night, nor Donald Trump will stop the United States Postal Service from delivering mail-in ballots in the coming midterm elections. Tonight, the Supreme Court handed down an emergency ruling blocking the Trump administration from implementing a new policy that would have made mail-in voting so onerous as to be effectively impossible for election officials to administer. The Court’s decision spares those officials from pointless chaos—and voters from potentially widespread disenfranchisement.
In the United States, election administration is carried out by a patchwork of local officials working state by state across roughly 10,000 different jurisdictions. Usually, USPS’s role in elections is clear: The Postal Service transports mail ballots to voters from state and local election offices; if voters return their ballot by mail, USPS takes care of that too. The nature of this responsibility has evolved in recent years, particularly during the coronavirus pandemic, as many states shifted toward encouraging voting by mail. The Trump administration looked at this system, which has been popular among voters, and decided to cause havoc by imposing new and arduous criteria for election officials to meet before USPS would commit to mailing ballots.
A number of states and several nonprofits, along with the Democratic Party, quickly brought legal challenges. Before the Court resolved the matter tonight, the cases zagged madly among district and appellate courts, then up to the Supreme Court and back down again. Many judges were skeptical both of the legal basis for the rule and of the speed at which the administration was attempting to implement it, with less than two months to go before the elections.
But despite this broad agreement in the lower courts, experts were uncertain how the Supreme Court would handle the case. The Court’s past friendliness toward even the most legally dubious of Trump’s policies cast into doubt whether the justices would stand against his efforts here, especially after the Court rejected an earlier iteration of the challenge on the grounds that it was premature. “The Supreme Court has made law totally unpredictable,” the election-law expert Justin Levitt told me last week, while the country waited for the justices to rule. “In a normal world, there would be a zero percent chance” that the Court would allow the USPS rule to go into effect. Yet, he went on, “we don’t live in a normal world anymore.”
Our world is still not a normal one. But this time, a majority of the justices on the Supreme Court decided not to make it worse. In a terse, unsigned paragraph, the Court declared that the Trump administration had failed both to make its case on the law and to show that a ruling in Trump’s favor would not upend the upcoming elections. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in a brief concurrence, indicated that the Postal Service’s plan might have had firm legal grounding but that he’d agreed to block the policy because “state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections.”
That final part of his assessment is obviously correct. USPS’s plan would have required election officials to upload lists of eligible voters through a Postal Service “portal”—yet the government has given no indication that the portal is operational. USPS would also have required election officials to receive Postal Service approval for the design of their ballot envelopes, but officials have already printed their ballot envelopes and do not have the money or time to create new designs. Last week, a Tallahassee, Florida, paper reported that USPS had rejected the envelope designs submitted by Florida’s Leon County on the grounds that the return address was 0.014 inches too close to other text on the envelope—about the thickness of four sheets of paper.
Election administrators prepare to send out ballots far in advance, and if the USPS rule had gone into effect, election officials might have found themselves unable to count on the Postal Service to mail ballots at all. However conservative the Supreme Court is, “there aren’t five votes for abject chaos,” Levitt wrote to me after the ruling.
Still, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, the pair on the Court who most reliably tilt toward Trump, would have allowed the USPS plan to go forward. Alito’s dissent is strikingly unconcerned with the potential risks to the midterms if the Postal Service were to refuse to mail ballots, noting only that 12 states (all Republican-led) have “asserted that compliance at this time is practicable.” (Local election officials in some of those states disagreed with that assessment in their own court filings, but Alito does not address this.) Moreover, the federal government’s interest in detecting “election fraud” is compelling, Alito declares. As for the last-minute dash to shake up the midterms, Alito manages to blame not the government but the plaintiffs, the lower courts, and even his own colleagues on the bench for the litigation that—he claims—delayed USPS from finalizing its rule.
In a blog post, the UCLA law professor and election scholar Rick Hasen deemed Alito’s dissent “disingenuous.” Among other things, USPS continued working on the rule during the course of the litigation over the summer. And even if the Postal Service had finished the planning process earlier in the summer, state and local jurisdictions still might not have had enough time to rework their envelopes to comply.
Fortunately, officials won’t need to scramble to submit envelope designs to USPS to be measured down to fractions of an inch, or upload voter names into a portal that doesn’t exist. Election workers will likely face plenty of challenges in the month and a half before the midterms. Mailing ballots, though, will not be among them.

Snoopy and the Peanuts gang have arrived at Starbucks for the autumn season, with the coffee chain launching a new limited-edition collection inspired by the classic It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown special. The Starbucks x Peanuts collection launched on September 15 at select Starbucks coffeehouses around the world. The collaboration brings together two distinctly recognisable pieces of autumn culture: Starbucks' seasonal offerings and the Peanuts characters created by Charles M Schulz. The collaboration turns familiar Peanuts imagery into everyday Starbucks items, from cups and mugs to bags, pins and plush toys. Hyrox athlete won competition while leaking diarrhea. Was she right to push through?
Hyrox apologized after Australian Joanna Wietrzyk won Saturday's competition in Beijing
Popular indoor fitness competition Hyrox has said it has changed its protocols after allowing an Australian athlete to keep competing — and win — despite suffering from what appeared to be diarrhea.
The graphic images of world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk competing with feces running down her legs at Saturday's Hyrox in Beijing have sparked debate about the health and safety of competitors versus the mentality that a win is a win, no matter the cost.
"It's a biohazard, how they let the competition go on is beyond me," an observer wrote on Reddit.
"Think about how disgusting it is, especially when we use the exact same track," a race participant told the South China Morning Post.
Footage showed Wietrzyk continue to push through her events using communal equipment such as ropes, sandbags, rowing machines and medicine balls, and doing burpees and lunges on a shared indoor track. She was the pro women's champion with a time of 1:01:23.
"Go hard or go home … a win is a win," Wietrzyk posted — then deleted — on Instagram after the event along with a selfie in what appeared to be a hospital bed, according to multiple news outlets.
As the incident went viral, online commenters were quick to point out the health risks for other competitors, with many people saying Wietrzyk should have quit or Hyrox should have disqualified her. Others are calling on Hyrox to refund the other competitors or offer them compensation.
"Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not," co-founder Moritz Fürste wrote in an Instagram statement Monday.
"As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again," he added.
The Hyrox official rulebook already had some penalties in place for other bodily fluids, noting that spitting or clearing of nostrils onto the floor is strictly prohibited, but until this week, there was no mention of penalties for feces contaminating the race course.
As some people have pointed out in the comments on Hyrox's Instagram apology, perhaps it's "unbelievable that this even needs a rule."
"That’s not a rule. That’s basic human decency," someone commented.
So, what happened?
Hyrox, a structured indoor activity divided into eight segments, each involving a one-kilometre run followed by a fitness exercise, attracts tens of thousands of participants to its biggest events.
The event was developed in 2017 by German entrepreneur Christian Toetzke and Moritz Fürste, who won field hockey gold medals for Germany in the 2008 and 2012 Summer Olympics. It's since become a global phenomenon, was accepted as a format in World Triathlon this year (under the name Hyathlon) and has its sights set on the Olympics.

And Wietrzyk is the women's pro world record holder after her performance at the Warsaw Major in April. While she hasn't made an official statement about what happening in Beijing, several reports claim Wietrzyk was suffering from food poisoning.
A spectator at the event told the South China Morning Post that feces was visible on the track about 30 minutes after Wietrzyk started her race, causing several runners to slip.
Hyrox China, in a statement posted on the social media platform Weibo, said a competitor experienced a "sudden medical issue." The statement explained that organizers later disinfected contaminated areas, removed any contaminated equipment and replaced the carpet in the venue.
As the TaiPei Times reports, Hyrox China did not apologize, but "admitted in an earlier statement to 'shortcomings' in the regulations which had prevented judges from intervening immediately during the competition."
Wietrzyk's coach, Chris Bayens, defended her in a statement posted to Instagram Sunday, urging people not to judge her "intent, clarity, or morality."
"Sport occasionally produces moments that are imperfect and deeply human," Bayens wrote.
"What happened was an extraordinary set of circumstances that were unforeseen, rapidly evolving and almost impossible to fully comprehend in real time."
CBC News has reached out to Hyrox, Wietrzyk and her coach for comment, but not yet heard back.
Poop incidents are common
As many high-intensity athletes likely know, shit happens. Sometimes literally. There's even a term for it: runner's diarrhea, which Healthline describes as an inflammation of the colon caused by the intensity of workouts that can lead to frequent bowel movements.
According to a 2014 study, anywhere from 30 to 50 per cent of athletes report gastrointestinal problems. More recently, a 2025 literature review published in the World Journal of Gastroenterology concluded that high-intensity or prolonged exercise may contribute to symptoms such as nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.

How to improve the audio quality on your iPhone
Your iPhone sounds decent out of the box, but some tweaks can drastically improve what you hear.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Between listening to music, watching videos and taking calls, audio quality plays a big role in how you use and enjoy your iPhone. So whether you're playing sound straight from the device's speaker or through headphones, you'll of course want the audio to be as clean as possible.
Luckily, there are several ways to improve your iPhone audio experience, and your options go far beyond adjusting audio settings on AirPods. The Settings app (and individual app settings) offer a smorgasbord of options for improving audio quality, from noise cancellation to equalizers and lossless audio.
Naturally, having the right hardware for the job is important for optimizing audio quality; there isn't too much you can do with software to make an ultra-cheap speaker sound amazing. Then again, even high-quality equipment can sound better by tweaking some options, so it's wise to look at the issue from both sides of the coin.
Optimizing your settings in Apple Music and Spotify
Major streaming apps have settings that adjust the audio quality delivered to your device. For Apple Music, go to Settings > Apps > Music, then tap Audio Quality and choose your settings for mobile data, Wi-Fi and downloads. High Quality is the best balance of data and sound; as we discuss below, Lossless is only worthwhile if you have high-quality wired headphones.
Spotify offers the same setting under your profile picture at Settings and privacy > Media quality. Free users can only select from Low, Normal and High, while Premium subscribers can also choose Very high or Lossless. For Wi-Fi streaming, Very High is good for most cases.
After enabled high-quality streaming, take a look at your equalization (EQ) settings, which let you boost or reduce certain frequencies. For Apple Music, you'll find these under the same Settings > Apps > Music menu. Select EQ, then pick from the list of music types depending on what sounds best. Unfortunately, you can't create a custom EQ in Apple Music. Meanwhile, the Sound Check feature normalizes the volume level across all tracks. People are mixed on this; some claim it reduces audio quality, while others appreciate not having to adjust the volume regularly. Give it a try both on and off to see what you prefer.
For Spotify, you'll find these options by tapping your profile icon, choosing Settings and privacy and selecting Playback. Tap Equalizer to enable it, then choose a preset or drag the dots for each frequency to fine-tune the sound to your liking. The Volume normalization slider is at the bottom of this page; if you use it, don't choose Loud for best quality.
Understanding lossless audio on iPhone
The Lossless option mentioned above deserves special attention. As you saw, Apple Music and Spotify Premium subscribers can take advantage of lossless audio. This preserves all the audio's original data, producing a crisp sound that's equivalent to CD quality. In both Quality menus visited earlier, you can choose Lossless separately for Wi-Fi, mobile data and downloads as desired. Note that this will use much more data and storage space than lossy options.
Unfortunately, having the best AirPods won't help you here, as Bluetooth doesn't support lossless. The AirPods 4, AirPods Pro 3, USB-C AirPods Pro 2 and Powerbeats Pro 2 can support wireless lossless when paired with the Apple Vision Pro, though this is a niche case. Bluetooth speakers also have this limitation.
To get the best audio, you'll need one of the best DACs for Apple Music. A good DAC (digital-to-analog converter) will properly carry the quality and texture of lossless audio. The budget-friendly FiiO KA11, for instance, provides everything most people need at an affordable price. Apple Music also offers Hi-Res Lossless, which is studio-quality audio that uses even more data. Unless you have premium equipment, you probably don't need to bother with this.
Accessibility settings and speaker quality
Your iPhone's accessibility settings hold even more audio optimization potential under Settings > Accessibility > Audio & Visual. Here you can toggle Phone Noise Cancellation (only available on iPhone 12 and earlier), which removes traces of ambient noise. Use the Balance slider to adjust your audio if sound is uneven across right and left channels.
Then, while wearing supported Apple headphones, head to Headphone Accommodations, where you can adjust Frequencies (which boosts certain frequencies, similar to EQ settings) or Soft sounds to amplify quieter sounds (which makes subtle environmental sounds and phone call audio more legible). Mess around with these settings while you have your headphones in to get a sense for what sounds best to your ear.
If you're playing audio from your phone's speakers, other than fine-tuning your settings for your ears, you won't need to do much more than keeping your speakers unclogged. If you need extra help with cleaning out your speaker grills, you can use a specialized tool like cleaning putty or an air blower.

Brook likened to Pietersen in SL win - how do they compare?
- Published
First Vitality T20, Southampton
England 254-4 (20 overs): Brook 114* (49), Buttler 80 (44)
Sri Lanka 135 (19 overs): Wellalage 33 (21); Baker 3-12
England won by 119 runs
Harry Brook hit a brutal century and drew comparisons with Kevin Pietersen as England thrashed Sri Lanka by 119 runs in the first T20 in Southampton.
The sensational Brook, after a summer without a Test hundred, crashed the ball to all parts in hitting 114 not out from 49 balls to power his side to 254-4.
His 10 fours and six sixes were ferocious - reminiscent of former England batter Pietersen, the newest addition to this side's backroom staff.
His intensity and running between the wickets was equally impressive.
"I don't even think the genius of KP could come close to what Harry Brook has talent-wise," said Brook's former captain and team-mate Ben Stokes, who was watching on TV.
"You are an absolute freak, Harry."
Brook was six years old when Pietersen - a shock appointment as a mentor through to next year's World Cup - secured England the Ashes on the final day at The Oval in 2005.
He was 14, now old enough to understand, when Pietersen was controversially dumped by England after the 2013-14 Ashes defeat.
"I used to love watching him bat when I was younger," said Brook, external - then little more than a year into his international career.
"He always looked to take the attack to bowlers and put them under pressure. In that aspect, I'm quite similar."
How do Brook and Pietersen compare?
Brook is, in many ways, the TikTok generation's Pietersen.
Pietersen invented the switch hit - a shot Brook rarely plays. Brook's version is that tumbling scoop over his and the wicketkeeper's head, which was absent here.
They are most similar in the way they pick length, allowing them to pull, flat-bat or cut balls from spinners even in good areas.
Brook did so throughout his partnership of 128 with Jos Buttler, who also played superbly for his 80 from 44 balls.
And while Pietersen was educated in Pietermaritzburg, South Africa and Brook under the Cumbrian hills, they come from the same cricketing school.
"That's the way I play," Pietersen said after one aggressive shot too many during a Test in 2009.
"I got to 97 playing that way so it obviously wasn't meant to be."
Those words could easily have come from the mouth of Brook.
Such words are why Pietersen and Brook have stirred opinion among England fans more than any other batters in the modern era.
"Is it really that hard to just sit back and admire these players for what they are, on the good days and the bad days, and stop berating them for doing things that we would never, ever, ever even think of doing because we simply aren't on their level to think that way?" Stokes added on social media.
Stokes, who backed Brook to succeed him as Test skipper, has always been a Brook fan.
Picking between Brook and Pietersen may well be pub chat one day, should Brook's career turn out as many hope.
For what it is worth, there is little to choose between their records at Brook's age of 27.
Pietersen's Test average, which ended at 47.28 after his 104 Tests, stood at 49.55 at this stage. Brook's is 53.08, though Pietersen had two more centuries.
Pietersen has the edge in one-day international cricket - an average of 47.87 and six centuries to Brook's 37.43 and three - but the Yorkshireman's second T20 century, hit on the south coast, is two more than Pietersen ever managed.
Perhaps where Brook lags behind is those iconic moments.
While Brook's Test best 317 on a road in Pakistan is a mark few can match, Pietersen's 158 at The Oval won England the 2005 Ashes in his fifth Test - the first of his four Ashes series wins.
Eighteen months later he made the same score against Australia in Adelaide against Shane Warne and Glenn McGrath.
Brook's best Ashes score remains 85. He is yet to win the urn.
The world's most complete batter?
Still, Brook's latest T20 display showed the company he could one day keep. A more mature batting style in whites this summer has also been noted.
Since being promoted to number three in England's T20 side at the World Cup earlier this year, Brook averages 95.20 at a strike-rate of 200.84.
He has scored 288 runs in the format since he was last dismissed.
"Harry Brook has today cemented himself as maybe the best all-format batter in the world," said former England bowler Steven Finn.
"[Australia's] Travis Head would be up there and so would [India's] Shubman Gill.
"Brook is lacking a Test century in the last year or so but he still averages 42 in that time.
"When you see the versatility of what he did today and the tempo he has played, he's a mighty special player."
Brook also has one clear advantage in any debate for the maverick position in a fantasy England XI.
Overlooked for the Test captaincy, Brook has won 18 of his past 20 T20s as England captain. Pietersen's stint as England skipper lasted only five months.
Sri Lanka's target was always likely to be beyond them but, even without Jofra Archer or Sam Curran, England ruthlessly dismissed their opponents for 135 in Southampton.
Brook oversaw young seamer Sonny Baker's best performance in an England shirt. He took 3-12 in four overs.
"I thought the performance tonight was near perfect," he said afterwards.
England want Pietersen to help them win the 50-over World Cup next year. He will do well to improve on this.

India’s ubiquitous UPI payment system is set for a significant change from October 15, with the introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select transactions. Under the new framework, merchants will be charged an MDR of 0.4% on person to merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The charge will be capped at ₹300 for transactions worth ₹75,000 or more. The October 15 change does not necessarily make UPI a paid service for consumers. Instead, it introduces a commercial layer on the merchant side. With a 0.4% MDR for regular P2M transactions above ₹2,000 and a ₹300 cap for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. The framework keeps P2P payments free, protects P2PM merchants from MDR and provides lower flat rates for sectors such as fuel, insurance and utilities. The broader shift is from an entirely zero-MDR merchant model towards a threshold-based system intended to create a more sustainable financial model for India's UPI infrastructure. Payments Council of India's chairman and AvenuesAI CEO Vishwas Patel believes that the introduction of the charges is a key step to build a viable economic model while keeping UPI free for consumers. "At the same time, sustainability must not come at the cost of financial inclusion. The continued zero-MDR protection for eligible small and micro merchants, along with support for expanding digital acceptance in Tier III, IV centres, will help preserve UPI’s accessibility," Patel said. So, what exactly changes next month and who will actually have to pay? UPI MDR: What Is Changing From October 15? The new MDR framework will come into effect on October 15, 2026. For regular P2M transactions above ₹2,000, merchants will pay 0.4% of the transaction value as MDR. Transactions of ₹2,000 or below will continue to attract zero MDR. For high-value payments, the MDR will be capped at ₹300. This cap applies to transactions of ₹75,000 and above. In practical terms, the structure will look like this: Transaction value ₹2,000 - ₹0 MDR Transaction value ₹3,000 - ₹12 MDR Transaction value ₹50,000 - ₹200 MDR Transaction value ₹75,000 - ₹300 MDR Transaction value ₹1 Lakh - ₹300 MDR The MDR is a charge on the merchant side. Consumers will continue to pay the listed price of the product or service. P2P transactions, including transfers to friends, family or between a user's own bank accounts, will continue to remain free. UPI apps won’t be allowed to charge a platform fee or any other fee for payments made through UPI. There are also no monthly quotas under the framework that would result in consumers being charged after a certain number of UPI transactions. The new MDR is a merchant-side charge and not a consumer-facing UPI fee. Merchants onboarded under the framework cannot pass the MDR on to customers while accepting UPI payments, the NPCI said. What About Small Merchants? Not every merchant will be subject to the 0.4% MDR. Small merchants operating under the Person-to-Person-Merchant (P2PM) framework will continue to enjoy zero MDR. The framework defines these as small vendors receiving up to ₹1 Lakh per month through UPI QR codes directly into their accounts. This means a small vendor does not automatically become liable for MDR simply because a customer makes a payment exceeding ₹2,000. Acquiring banks and payment service providers will monitor the monthly inward transaction threshold. Merchants receiving more than ₹1 Lakh through UPI for three consecutive months will be transitioned to the P2M category, effectively making the Existing QR codes will continue to work and small merchants will not have to replace their QR stands or soundboxes because of the MDR changes. How Are MDR Charges Bifurcated Among Sectors? Several sectors will not be charged the standard 0.4% MDR. Instead, they will have a flat MDR of ₹5 for transactions above ₹2,000. These include categories such as railways, telecom, insurance and fuel. For example, an insurance premium or fuel payment of ₹10,000 would attract a ₹5 MDR rather than the ₹40 charge that would apply under the standard 0.4% rate. Utility payments, including electricity, water and piped natural gas, will also fall under the designated industry programme category, with a ₹5 MDR for transactions above ₹2,000. Payments below ₹2,000 in these categories will continue to remain free of MDR. What About Mutual Funds And Stock Market Payments? Capital market transactions will have a separate MDR structure. Payments involving mutual funds, securities, stockbrokers and dealers will attract an MDR of 0.02%, with a maximum cap of ₹300. The category covers regulated capital-market entities, including asset management companies, SEBI-registered stockbrokers, securities dealers and investment platforms. The lower rate is intended to distinguish investment-related payments from routine retail and commercial transactions. Will Credit Card Payments On UPI Be Affected? The new MDR framework applies specifically to direct account-to-merchant UPI payments. Credit-linked UPI transactions, such as payments made using RuPay credit cards linked to UPI or pre-sanctioned bank credit lines, operate under separate credit product rules. As a result, the MDR won't apply to these transactions in the same manner as direct bank-account-to-merchant UPI payments. How Will The MDR Revenue Be Divided? The 0.4% MDR paid by the merchant will flow through different parts of the UPI ecosystem. In effect, the ₹0.40 MDR is split as 0.28% for the issuer bank, 0.08% for the TPAP and 0.04% for the acquiring bank. For every ₹100 eligible UPI transaction, the merchant will pay ₹0.40 as MDR to the acquiring bank, which is the bank handling the merchant’s UPI account. Of this ₹0.40, ₹0.28 (0.28%) will be paid by the acquiring bank to the customer’s issuing bank as interchange. A further ₹0.08 (0.08%) will go to the UPI app provider, paid by the payer-side payment service provider (PSP). This leaves ₹0.04 (0.04%) with the acquiring bank. Why Is UPI Introducing MDR Now? The move comes as UPI has scaled to become one of India's primary digital payment systems. UPI processed 24.51 Bn transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August 2026 alone. The policy framework argues that operating a payment system at this scale requires significant spending on server infrastructure, bandwidth, fraud prevention, cybersecurity and banking technology. Industry estimates cited in the framework put the annual cost of maintaining UPI operations at around ₹20,000 Cr. Until now, government incentives and subsidies have helped support the ecosystem. The new framework argues that these were intended as short-term support rather than a permanent mechanism for covering payment infrastructure costs. The MDR revenue will be retained within the UPI ecosystem and is intended to support infrastructure resilience, innovation, cybersecurity and customer service. It will also What Happens To The MDR Money? A dedicated fund for small merchants is also proposed under the framework. The fund will be used to support digital payment infrastructure in Tier III to Tier IV centres, including the northeastern states, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. It will also cover notified government schemes in Tier I and Tier II centres. The fund is expected to provide financial assistance to acquiring banks and payment aggregators for merchant onboarding and incentivise UPI transactions among small merchants. The detailed framework for the fund is expected to be finalised in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India within three months. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

General Motors is about to launch new versions of its bestselling Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra pickup trucks for model year 2027, and among the changes are new user interfaces for the trucks’ digital displays. The automaker has gone for a more minimalist approach than we’ve seen from it in the past, and after a demo yesterday, it seems like it has been listening to constructive feedback to improve the products. And yes, unlike GM’s electric vehicles, these trucks still let you cast your Apple or Android phone to the infotainment system.
Although GM showed us video of the main instrument cluster—the gauges and info that’s presented to the driver—we don’t have any screenshots we can show you. But I was impressed with the restraint and lack of visual noise; instead, the background is always black, which should be dark even at night thanks to local dimming technology.
There are a number of different views. One with simple half-moon dials for speed and engine rpm; on the right side of the display is a user-configurable zone, where you can browse your music or audio feeds, display trip info, or turn-by-turn directions. Another is a driver assist display, with green as the highlight color to show when Super Cruise is active; this shows you a representation of what the car’s fused sensors are seeing around it. A third is for off-road driving, with your various angles and diff settings, and a fourth is for towing.
Note the real controls for the HVAC.
Credit:
GM
Note the real controls for the HVAC.
Credit:
GM
But there’s also an even more minimalist version that simply shows the speed as big white digits and nothing else. This is similar to the night mode you’d find in Saabs, and it’s very useful for night driving.
At the base of the main instrument display is a strip of information that’s permanently displayed regardless of the view mode you choose—this includes things like your fuel level, the drive mode, and any warning lights that may appear.
Yes, it has CarPlay
The central infotainment screen still runs on Android Automotive OS, but now the home screen is a more useful split view showing the music and navigation apps, with a full map view rather than the limited map that GM previously showed in its split-screen view. “If you wanted to search something or provide feedback on road conditions or something like that, when you tapped on the screen, it took you out of the home screen and took you to the full-screen maps. Here, you can do everything that full-screen maps can do right inside this window,” said Colin McCormick, group product manager at GM.
A dedicated row at the bottom of the screen is for the climate controls, although, as you’ll note from the photos, there are physical dials to change the temperature, as well as physical buttons for fan speed and demisting.
GM has also integrated more Android-like notifications into the infotainment system and included the ability to create quick actions. It has also changed the behavior of some of its apps—now, if you accept a phone call, it won’t switch you out of whatever app was active to dump you into the dialer app anymore.

GM made the decision to drop Apple CarPlay and Android Auto phone casting from its newer EVs, and it’s one we’ve been pretty critical of. Although the automaker told us it made that decision in order to offer a better, more unified experience to its customers, that may well have changed: here, customers still have the choice to just cast their phone to the center screen.
And it has done a better job of integrating CarPlay and Android Auto into the experience, putting the casting apps in a large window or tile that takes up most but not all of the infotainment screen. To the left is another card that allows you to access other native apps, like towing or music (although you can still have CarPlay as the source for that native music app, should you start feeling a little Inceptionish). Porsche took a similar approach to working with, rather than against, users who enjoy CarPlay, and this looks like a welcome step from GM.
GM’s spokesperson wouldn’t be drawn on whether this means we’re going to see a corporate retreat from the previous stance on EVs, but I will note that the press release it sent Ars does say that the system was built “as a single scalable foundation across electric, gas and diesel-powered vehicles, it transforms time spent behind the wheel into an effortless, personalized journey,”—emphasis mine.
Passenger screens are here to stay
Complaining about the trend of OEMs putting an extra infotainment screen in the dash for the front passenger is evidently a losing battle now, because such a feature will be available on the Sierra and Silverado. The screen is coated in a polarized filter, so the driver can’t see what they’re doing or watch what they’re watching.
There are lots of native streaming apps now. The lower trim piece folds down to show more of the screen.

This can be streaming content or video piped in via HDMI from a port down by the passenger’s knee. And the passenger infotainment screen will pair with Bluetooth headphones so the driver doesn’t necessarily have to listen to whatever it is, either. (Some information will show up on the main infotainment screen, so the driver will have an idea of what content is playing on the screen and decide whether to pass through audio to the truck’s speakers, GM told us.) It’s not just for watching video, though—there’s even a full web browser, and you can use your smartphone as a keyboard or input device.

A Pennsylvania woman has died from complications associated with measles, the third death in the state this year involving the virus.
The 40-year-old woman died Saturday, Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong said in a Facebook post in which he called the death “measles-related.”
The post did not identify the woman other than as a resident of Jefferson County, a rural area about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northeast of Pittsburgh.
“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong said in the post.
The post did not say whether the woman was vaccinated against measles. No more information about the case would be released, it stated.
Pennsylvania’s two previous measles-related deaths involved infants. Both occurred in August and a coroner reported that the virus itself caused one of the deaths.
One infant, a boy, died shortly after birth of a ruptured spleen. The boy had measles that did not contribute to the rupture, according to Lancaster County Coroner Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.
Rather, measles was listed as a “significant condition” at the time of death.
The other infant, a 6-week-old girl with a genetic defect that left her highly vulnerable to infection, died due to measles, Diamantoni told The Associated Press.
The girl was born with a condition called Amish lethal microcephaly that causes an unusually small head and underdeveloped brain. Children with the condition typically live 6 months or less.
The first dose of measles vaccine is typically given to infants around 1 year old, meaning neither infant was old enough to be vaccinated.
As of Friday, Pennsylvania had 676 measles cases in 37 of the state’s 67 counties. Of those cases, 124 involved hospitalizations and four people who were vaccinated against measles, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health.
The three measles-related deaths reported by state and local officials as of Sunday did not square with figures of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which showed no such deaths this year.
“The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause,” read the CDC website Sunday.
Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and Republican President Donald Trump’s administration have clashed over details of the two previous deaths in the state.

Nick Reiner will not face death penalty if convicted of killing his parents, prosecutor says
Trial date unlikely before 2027, says Los Angeles County district attorney
U.S. prosecutors said Tuesday that they won't pursue the death penalty for Nick Reiner in the killings of his parents, actor-director Rob Reiner and his wife Michele Singer Reiner, who were stabbed at their Los Angeles home late last year.
Nick Reiner, 32, was charged with first-degree murder on Dec. 16, two days after the stunning killings of the couple. A grand jury allegation from this summer said he was lying in wait before killing the couple, ages 78 and 70. He has twice pleaded not guilty in the case.
Special circumstances in the allegations against Nick Reiner made him eligible for the death penalty, but Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said the issue would be deferred while his office decided whether to pursue it. Those circumstances include multiple killings and the use of a dangerous weapon, a knife.
Hochman said his office did a thorough review, including speaking Rob and Michele Reiner's families and evaluating mitigating factors in Nick Reiner's favour, before reaching its decision.
Hochman said the maximum sentence Reiner will be eligible to receive if convicted will be life without the possibility of parole.
Reiner's former defence attorney, Alan Jackson, said adamantly after resigning from the case that "pursuant to the laws of California, Nick Reiner is not guilty of murder."
Jackson had to withdraw for undisclosed reasons that he said were beyond his and the client's control, and a public defender took over for him.
Honoured at the Emmys
Rob Reiner received an emotional tribute at the Emmy Awards on Monday night. He won a posthumous Emmy at an earlier ceremony for best guest actor in a comedy series for his role on The Bear, and was honoured by his friend and The Bear co-star Jamie Lee Curtis.
"He was generous, kind and funny as hell, and a friend to all," Curtis said Monday. "And we all miss Rob and Michele and all those we lost this year."
Rob Reiner began as an actor, starring in the TV sitcom, All in the Family, as Michael (Meathead) Stivic, the liberal son-in-law to a much more conservative and bigoted Archie Bunker, played by Carroll O'Connor. Reiner won two Emmy Awards for that role.
He became a prolific director whose work included some of the most memorable and endlessly watchable movies of the 1980s and '90s. His credits included This is Spinal Tap, Stand By Me, A Few Good Men and When Harry Met Sally…, during the production of which he met photographer Michele Singer. They wed soon after and were married for 36 years.
Nick Reiner was the second of the three children they had together. Nick and Rob Reiner co-wrote the script for the 2015 film Being Charlie, which was partly based on the son's teenage struggles with addiction and homelessness.

The man in his 50s, identified as Mel Ismail, was surfing north of Geraldton when he was attacked at around 9.45am on Monday. He was roughly 40m offshore when he was bitten, local media reported.
Mr Ismail was taken to Geraldton Health Campus under priority one conditions, St John Ambulance said, after suffering serious leg injuries.
Ms Ismail is a staff member of the state’s fire and emergency services department, according to acting commissioner Melissa Pexton.
Authorities removed a badly damaged surfboard from the scene and sent it for testing to help identify the shark species involved.
The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development said that officials were working with local authorities to respond and that no shark activity had been reported to the City of Geraldton in the 30 days before the attack.
The beach, roughly 430km north of Perth, was closed in the wake of the attack, with residents asked to avoid the area.
Cadeyn Catto, a local resident and regular beach visitor, said the incident had shaken the community.
"My kids have grown up there and we spend most weekends on that beach and to this point it felt very safe," he told ABC News.
"I know over time we've had one or two little incidents, but nothing to this calibre."
He said the injured man was a well-known regular surfer.
Geraldton MP and shadow fisheries minister Kirrilee Warr said she was seeking further details from authorities.
"I do understand the victim is a well-known surfer amongst the community," she added. "We are really close-knit and when something like this happens, it does ripple. Those first responders, they would have been confronted with quite a scene, so I do hope that they are also receiving some support in and after this event."
She renewed calls for the state government to review its shark mitigation strategy. "We know millions of dollars is being poured into this mitigation strategy,” the MP said, “but it simply isn’t good enough to stand there and say, 'we have this strategy', but not know if it works.”
Fisheries minister Jackie Jarvis defended the state's protocols. "Western Australia has one of the most comprehensive shark hazard mitigation strategies in the country, using a range of measures to help keep people as safe as possible while they enjoy our coastline," she said. "My thoughts are with the person injured in today's incident, their family and everyone involved."
The attack is the latest in a series of serious shark incidents in Western Australia this year.
Steven Mattaboni, 38, was killed, while spearfishing off Rottnest Island in May, and diver Daniel Turpin, 35, was killed by a suspected 4.5m shark near Michaelmas Island, off Albany, in early June.

Legendary costume designer Bob Mackie dies aged 87
- Published
Bob Mackie, who designed dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner, Dolly Parton and Elton John has died, aged 87.
The US fashion designer, known as the "Sultan of Sequins" for his sparkling creations, won a Tony Award, nine Emmys and received three Oscar nominations during his career.
"It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr Bob Mackie passed away today," a statement on his Instagram account announced on Monday.
"He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," it added. "His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."
- From Marilyn Monroe to Sabrina Carpenter - Bob Mackie's designs in pictures 
  - Published4 hours ago
Mackie was particularly influential in Cher's career and designed her iconic Mohawk outfit, which she wore to the Oscars in 1986. It became known as her "revenge" outfit, because she wasn't nominated for anything.
The showgirl-inspired costume featured a plumed mohawk headdress and showed Cher's bare midriff - a very new, and very shocking look at the time.
The costume has gone down in fashion history as one of the most outrageous and extravagant ever to appear at the awards.
"I didn't get nominated for a movie that everyone thought I would actually win for [Mask] - so was dressing that night for a kind of revenge," Cher explained in the 2024 documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion.
Mackie told the BBC in 2010 that when Cher started out she "looked like no-one else in the entertainment business at the time".
"Everybody just went crazy over this woman as she could wear anything," he added.
Cher was widely reported to be the first woman to show her belly button on US television - and Mackie's designs were pivotal to that.
Mackie was also the creative genius behind several of Sir Elton John's costumes, including his now-iconic Dodgers baseball outfit - bedazzled of course - that he wore during his performances at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in 1975.
"Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special," Sir John wrote on Instagram. "His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood."
Singer Pink wore many of his designs over the years. Sharing several of the outfits she wore on stage during her Funhouse tour in 2009, she wrote "I was so lucky to be dressed by him for so long. He was loving, wickedly funny and an absolute genius."
"There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels."
Mackie was still designing up until recently - Sabrina Carpenter wore one of his designs at the MTV Video Music Awards last year.
He also designed the dress Miley Cyrus wore during her performance at the 2024 Grammy Awards. She won a Grammy that year for her break-up anthem, Flowers - perhaps it was her own version of a "revenge" dress.
Robert Gordon Mackie was born in Monterey Park, California, in 1939.
His design career started as a sketch artist for Jean Louis, a French-American costume designer. One of Mackie's early assignments saw him sketch the dress that Marilyn Monroe wore when she delivered her breathy rendition of "Happy Birthday Mr President" to John F Kennedy in 1962.
He married Hollywood singer and actress Lulu Porter in 1960, but they divorced three years later. They had a son together, Robin, who died in his early thirties from an Aids related illness.
Mackie was in a relationship with Iranian fashion designer, Ray Aghayan, from 1963 until Aghayan's death in 2011.
"I think I'm the oldest living designer in Hollywood," Mackie told The Guardian in 2018. When asked if he'd ever retire, his answer was simple - "I hope not."

Iran war has led to US munitions shortfalls, Pentagon inspector confirms
- Published
The US defence department's inspector general says the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump who has repeatly denied the US is facing shortages.
Trump has claimed US munitions supplies are "virtually unlimited" and said reporting otherwise is "fake news".
But the independent watchdog said the US spent more than $22 billion on munitions from February through June, leading to "strategic inventory shortfalls".
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment about the discrepancy.
The new report provides a first-of-its-kind, independent glimpse into US weapons stockpiles, data that is typically classified.
Previous estimates have painted a dire picture of the US shortages.
Over the course of the war, US forces have expended vast quantities of both long-range ground attack systems and the air and missile defences used to intercept incoming Iranian attacks.
A late July estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, found that stocks of some interceptors - such as the Patriot missile and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD - were significantly depleted, in some cases by more than half.
The inspector general's report did not disclose exactly how many of the weapons remain.
It did, however, note the inventory shortfalls and reveal "industrial base bottlenecks" for munitions resupply.
The report added that the defence department is now working to "streamline procurement processes and production lead times" to address the shortages and "respond rapidly to a contingency".
Trump and other administration officials have sought to cast reports of shortages as false and "treasonous".
In a 4 August X post, for example, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth described news reporting on the shortages as "not true".
And in a lengthy Truth Social post on 3 September, Trump claimed that the US had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition and is "stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen".
The watchdog's report also notes that equipment losses have totaled $3.7bn, with other $7.4bn in other expenditures. Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war from 28 Feb to 30 Jun.
Among the losses have been four F-15e fighter jets, a highly advanced F-35 Joint Strike Fighter and 30 MQ-9 drones destroyed in "various circumstances".
When US and Israeli strikes began, Trump repeatedly said that the conflict would be over within weeks.
More recently, he said the conflict might not end until "right after" the November midterm elections in the US.
Polls show that the war is unpopular among Americans.
One Reuters/Ipsos poll released in early September found that only 23% of Americans - and only half of Republicans - believe the US to be in a stronger position with Iran compared with before hostilities broke out.

Rs 11 product, Rs 325 MRP: Tukaram Mundhe flags huge hospital pricing gap
Tukaram Mundhe said hospital consumables can carry steep mark-ups long before reaching patients. He said weak monitoring leaves patients paying costs they cannot meaningfully assess.
Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) chief Tukaram Mundhe has flagged huge margins on hospital products and medicines, saying patients could be paying hundreds or even thousands of per cent more than the trade price of products used during treatment, without knowing their actual cost.
In a social media post, Mundhe, under whom a massive FDA crackdown is underway in the state, said the most expensive part of a hospital bill may never touch the hospital at all.
"The most expensive part of a hospital bill may never touch the hospital at all. A patient admitted for care has no way of knowing whether the price on a medical consumable reflects its actual cost or a markup fixed long before it ever reached the ward. That gap in information is, at its core, a public health issue," the IAS officer wrote.
He cited findings from a survey of hospital consumables in Maharashtra, which found significant differences between the trade prices of certain products and their printed maximum retail prices (MRP), resulting in massive markups.
According to the figures shared by Mundhe, an IV infusion set with a trade price of Rs 11.05 carried an MRP of Rs 325, representing a markup of 2,841 per cent. A syringe procured at Rs 6.75 had an MRP of Rs 57.20, while a catheter bought for Rs 29.41 carried an MRP of Rs 310.
"These are not elective purchases," Mundhe said, pointing out that patients receiving medical care often cannot compare prices, seek alternatives or question the price printed on a medical product.
He said the MRP is often fixed upstream by manufacturers and distributors and can remain disconnected from the trade price, creating what he described as an “unexplained margin”.
“The result is a system where the party bearing the cost has the least information to evaluate it,” Mundhe, under whose remit drug pricing and medicine-related regulation fall as FDA Commissioner, said.
The officer also pointed to what he described as a structural regulatory gap in medical consumable pricing. He said scheduled medicines are subject to price ceilings under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, while most medical devices and consumables are not subject to similar controls.
He said this leaves both their pricing and the information available to patients "almost entirely unmonitored".
Explaining the action taken, Mundhe said a review of the findings, along with clear guidelines on the permissible gap between the trade procurement price and the declared MRP, has been recommended to the Department of Pharmaceuticals and the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA).
He said such measures could help address not only the pricing gap but also the information gap patients are left to bear alone.
Under Mundhe, the FDA has been conducting a widespread food safety crackdown across Maharashtra. Several hotels, restaurants, clubs and other facilities have been raided and issued notices, while some have been shut down over violations. The strict enforcement has earned him widespread applause from several quarters.

FIDE, on Monday, confirmed the venue, format, prize fund and schedule for the World Championship match between reigning world champion D Gukesh and challenger Javokhir Sindarov.
Both Gukesh and Sindarov will be 20 when their duel begins, making it the youngest World Championship match in chess history.
India’s Gukesh had claimed the World Championship title in 2024 after he beat China’s Ding Liren. Uzbek GM Sindarov earned the challenger spot by winning the Candidates tournament earlier this year.
Here is all you need to know about the Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match:
Where will the Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match happen?
The Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match will take place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, Geneva, Switzerland.
Fondation Martin Bodmer is a heritage library and museum. The Fondation holds around 150,000 documents in around 120 languages, making it one of the finest private collections in the world.
When will the Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match happen?
The opening ceremony will take place on November 22. The first classical game is scheduled for November 24 and the final one on December 11. If a tiebreaker is needed, it will be played on December 12.
What is the tournament format for the Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match?
The Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match will consist of a maximum of 14 classical games. The winner of each game wins 1 point, while a draw would result in 0.5 points. The first player to reach 7.5 points wins the match and the title. If the score is 7-7 after all classical games, the title will be decided through tiebreaks.
What is the time control for Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match?
Each player will have 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 minutes for the rest of the game. A 30-second increment is added from move 41. A draw offer would not be permitted before Black’s 40th move. But before that point, a draw may be claimed through the Chief Arbiter or Deputy Chief Arbiter only in cases of threefold repetition or stalemate.
What is the prize fund for Gukesh vs Sindarov World Championship match?
The total prize fund is USD 2.5 million. Each player receives USD 200,000 for every game won and the remaining balance is divided equally between the two players at the end of the match.

For over a month and a half, residents of Chitpur Jyotinagar Colony in Cossipore, North Kolkata, have been without regular water supply after five public taps serving the colony ran dry following pipeline work in the area. Home to around 5,000 people, the 200-metre-long stretch is largely inhabited by people belonging to the Muslim community, and from lower-income backgrounds.
Residents, whose daily lives and livelihoods have been disrupted, alleged that water supply has been deliberately cut off by the state’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government to target them on the basis of their identities and force them out of the slum.
It is worth noting days after the election results were declared, local BJP MLA Ritesh Tiwari had pledged not to do anything for Muslims in his constituency. “Today, in front of Baba Bholenath, I swear, I will not do one job for them (Muslims) in the next five years. Will not issue any certificate for them. I am saying this live. I do not care about what anyone else says or thinks,” he had said.
Residents of Jyotinagar this colony, around 95% of them Muslims, depend on informal jobs for their sustenance. While women manage household chores in the morning before working at nearby factories in the afternoon, where they clean glass bottles and break glass panels into shards, most men work as daily wage labourers, masons, drivers, rickshaw pullers, or at factories.
How Did Water Supply Stop?
Alt News visited the water-deprived area, located a few meters from the over 200-years-old Cossipore Gun and Shell factory. The colony has five taps, which used to supply water from 5 am to 11 pm daily. Since July 29, after water supply was cut off, all five taps have been dry, locals said.
Locals said that water supply was perfectly normal and no complaints from the neighbourhood was made to the local civic body or any authorities, and yet, pipeline work was carried out in the area by the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) from July 26-28.
“Pipeline work was happening, they had dug two pits, one at the beginning of the slum and another at the end, marking the slum. On July 28, the water supply stopped around 11 pm. The next morning, we were waiting for the water supply to return. It has not been restored since,” said a resident, Mohinudeen Sheikh.
Sheikh, along with other residents, alleged that the pipelines were shut during the night while the roads were being repaired. “They used the cover of midnight to close the pipelines and mend the streets. We had no water from the early morning onwards,” he claimed.
‘They Also Took Away Electricity’
Residents said the water crisis was accompanied by a disruption in electricity supply as well. “They took away both water and electricity,” one youth said.
“They thought we were drawing electricity illegally from the main line, so they stopped the supply,” said a resident, Pinki Bibi. “All our houses have separate electricity connections and we receive separate bills. Then how can they say we are drawing electricity illegally?”
Residents claimed that electricity was restored after more than a week, following an incident during the Kanwar Yatra when poor visibility allegedly led some Kanwariyas to fall into the pothole-ridden lane. Alamgir Biswas, secretary of the Jyotinagar Colony, said that the supply was restored 10-15 days after the Basti Unnayan Samiti protested against the disruption.
Locals alleged that Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation (CESC) said the main-road connection had been shut to verify whether allegations of illegal electricity tapping were true. However, electricity supply remained available in the lanes branching off the main road. After seven days, CESC was able to verify that no illegal tapping was taking place and restored the connection, they added.
‘They are Trying to Evict Us’
Residents alleged that the disruption of these essential services was a part of a concerted attempt to evict the slum dwellers. Alamgir alleged: “The plan was to cut off the basic needs of water and electricity so that we leave the area. In this area, there is absolute communal harmony. Hindus and Muslims live harmoniously together. However, this government is trying to create a rift between us.”
Morjina Begum, who works at the glass factory, also alleged, “They are trying to evict us from this colony and therefore employing these tricks of cutting off the water supply. We are not new to this place. I was born here. My grandfather had settled here years ago,” while asserting, “We are not going to leave this place so easily. We will fight.”
Begum said residents had also approached the local councillor, Suman Singh, but has received no meaningful assistance as of yet. Alt News tried to speak to Singh, but he did not answer our calls till press time.
Saraswati Biswas, a 60-year-old Hindu resident, alleged that Tiwari, the newly elected MLA, had referred to the residents as “Bangladeshis and encroachers”. “He is calling us Bangladeshis and encroachers. How am I a Bangladeshi? My forefathers used to live here. I have proper documents proving that I am an Indian. I voted this year,” she said.
Legal Entanglement With Kolkata Port
While investigating the possible reason behind the elongated water supply disruption, Alt News found an intricate legal entanglement between the residents of the colony and the authorities of the Kolkata port.
As per legal records, the entire colony is built on a parcel of land measuring approximately 3478 square metres officially belonging to the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata. On February 23, the estate officer of the port issued an eviction order for the colony.
Alt News accessed the order, and found that it was issued based on the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The notice terms the residents of Jyotinagar Colony as ‘unauthorised occupants and/or trespasser to the port property’. The estate officer ordered the residents to vacate the land within 15 days of date of publication of this notice. Before the eviction order was passed, a hearing took place, wherein, port authorities submitted that ‘there is potential threat to communal unrest’ due to the existence of the colony.
According to legal documents accessed by Alt News, the residents of the colony came to know about the existence of this eviction order on June 9. The residents alleged that after the change of government in West Bengal, local BJP supporters started to campaign for the demolition of the slum. The locals claimed that they began deeming the colony as “a den of illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators”.
In order to seek legal protection from the eviction drive, residents appealed before the chief judge of the city civil court, Calcutta, however, on August 18, the court declined to grant any immunity from eviction to them.
The Port authorities in their submission before the city civil court had mentioned that ‘unlawful activities’ were ongoing in the colony. They described the premises as congested and unsafe for human habitation, citing the presence of inflammable materials and several uninsulated electrical wires that could potentially cause a fire. They also lodged two police complaints at the North Port police station on September 9, 2020 and July 25, 2022.
On August 19, the residents appeared before the Calcutta high court, seeking protection from eviction. The court granted an interim stay order on the eviction process till September 18. In the meantime, the water and electricity disruptions happened, which residents believe was done to purposely disrupt their lives to expedite the eviction.
Nine residents of the colony: Alamgir Biswas, Pinki Bibi, Mafajel Gazi, Sk Mainuddin, Rahima Bibi, Saraswati Biswas, Anita Prasad, Lima Bibi and Bonani Bibi appeared as petitioners before the high court. In their appeal, the residents had informed the HC that although the proceedings recorded before the estate officer of Kolkata Port mentioned two persons: Hafizul and Tarcina Bibi as respondents from the colony, the order does not record that any notice for eviction, under section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, was issued publicly.
It was also submitted before the HC that the order issued by the Kolkata Port does not record that the petitioners were called upon to show cause against the proposed eviction, were afforded an opportunity to produce evidence or were given an opportunity of personal hearing.
According to Section 4 of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971, all concerned persons, that is all persons who are in occupation of the public premises, have to be given the opportunity to show cause why they wouldn’t be evicted.
Section 4(3) of the Act clearly mentions: The estate officer shall cause the notice to be served by having it affixed on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the public premises, and in such other manner as may be prescribed, whereupon the notice shall be deemed to have been duly given to all persons concerned. However, the order issued by the estate officer makes no mention of any such notice being issued or served. This issue was also raised in the petition before the high court.
A team of lawyers including Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya, Samim Ahammed, Md Nasirul Hoque and Ivi Banerjee represented the residents legally. Speaking to Alt News, Ahammed said, “The Port authorities are claiming that the land in question is their property. But in reality, it is public property. Therefore, a government body like the Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, must ensure the fundamental rights of the public, in this case, their right to shelter.”
The State has the power to regulate and make sure people follow the law and cannot occupy public property illegally. They are exercising this power through the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. But while doing this, the State cannot treat people unfairly or take away someone’s home and leave them without shelter. Having a place to live and being able to live with dignity are part of a person’s inalienable rights protected by the Constitution, he explained.
Simultaneously with the HC appeal, another appeal was submitted by the residents before the chief judge of the city civil court seeking the restoration of water connection. This prayer, however, is still pending.
According to the port authorities, the total damage incurred due to the existence of the colony, starting from 1990, has reached approximately over Rs 61 crore. As per the legal records, the estimated monthly damage amount is calculated to be more than Rs 19 lakh rupees, and the port is losing more than Rs 2 crore annually in terms of revenue due to the colony.
Questions Of ‘Communal Targeting’
The geographical location of the water disruption has become a point of contention for residents, who have alleged that this is a form of communal targeting.
When one walks along Khagendra Chatterjee Lane towards the Ganges, with the Gun and Shell Factory on the right, the road turns left towards the river after two temples, and becomes Chitpur Strand Road. The Cossipore Jetty is on the right, followed by Jyotinagar Colony.
Residents showed Alt News the two points where pipeline work had been carried out. They said the entire stretch between the two points had remained without water. They also alleged that the points where the road was dug up correspond to the boundaries of Jyotinagar Colony, which has a predominantly Muslim population. According to the residents, taps immediately before and after this stretch, located in predominantly Hindu residential areas, continue to receive water.
Alt News checked the taps inside the colony and found them dry. Taps located immediately before and after the stretch where the pipeline work had been carried out, however, had water supply. We found that the tap directly opposite a temple, just before the first point where the road had allegedly been dug up, had water supply. The tap at the other end, near the second point where digging had taken place, also had water. In between, however, an approximately 150-metre stretch, had no water supply.
‘A Basic Need’
For residents, the suspension of water has led to tremendous daily struggle. “Water is a basic need. There are so many people in our colony, and there is no water. People have to stand in queues to fetch water from the taps that are present in the nearby areas. Though people are sharing their taps, they prioritise their own needs. This affects our work,” a resident said.
A woman in her mid-twenties, while cleaning utensils, showed buckets filled with water fetched from the river. “Look at the condition of the water we are using to clean. It is so muddy and filthy. At this point, all we can hope is we don’t fall ill,” she said.
The monsoon season has made it more difficult. “The water level is very high in Ganga now, so it becomes dangerous to bathe in the river or fetch water. The river water is muddy and unfit for consumption. But we are left with no option,” an elderly woman said. “We are scared that our children will develop skin infections. There are already a few cases,” said a woman in her thirties, while standing in queue to bathe her children.
Residents have to walk some distance from their colony to a functioning tap to fill water, which they then transport back on vans.
Locals Allege Administrative Apathy
Alamgir elaborated that after water and electricity supply was cut off on July 29, the following day, locals reached the corporation office and complained. “They took my number and told us that they would look into the matter. But nothing happened. On the following day, we submitted a written complaint at the main corporation office in Hatibagan. They also told us they would try to look into it. However, as everyone can see, nothing has changed as of yet,” he said.
Several residents had approached the local police station, the councillor, and MLA Tiwari, seeking their intervention, but no official visited the colony to inspect the reality so far, they lamented. Residents also said that when a group of women approached Tiwari, he dismissed them stating he was not responsible for the disruption of water supply and refused to restore it.
Further, Pinki Bibi alleged that Tiwari had used communal slurs and threatened the locals with eviction. “While talking to the people, he threatened them, ‘If I want, I could demolish the mosque that was built in the colony. And evict the entire colony with it,’” she said.
Morjina Begum told Alt News that residents believe they are being purposely treated this way because of their Muslim identities. Asked why they felt this was the case, she referred to speeches by chief minister Suvendu Adhikari and the local MLA following their election victories, in which they said they would not work for Muslims because Muslims had not voted for them. “Where are we supposed to go? There are so many of us?” she asked.

Burdened by the uncertainties of their future in the colony, an elderly woman in her 70s, sitting on the threshold of her house, said, “I pray that in my next life I am not born as a Muslim in this country.”
On September 9, Minakshi Mukherjee, CPI(M)’s central committee member, visited the locality along with other workers and leaders, and expressed her solidarity with the residents and protested against the eviction drive. At the initiative of the party, a water tanker visits the colony every two to three days to provide residents with an alternative source of water.
MLA Ritesh Tiwari Responds
When Alt News asked Tiwari about the predicament of people in his constituency, he distanced himself from the issue, saying, “The plot belongs to the Port. The people have a feud with the Port. The Port had ordered them to vacate. Later, the high court ordered them to refrain from taking temporary coercive action. The water supply is provided by the KMC. So, what role do I play here? What can I say here? The matter is sub judice, and it is better for political leaders to refrain from making any comments.”
When asked whether he could stand by the people of his constituency and help restore their water supply, he said, “This is not my job…they [residents] have sought the assistance of established political leaders… so they should keep faith in the people they have called. Should they lose that faith so quickly?”
Upon being further prodded on why he was not helping people in his own constituency, the MLA replied (in Bengali), “Why don’t you do my part of the job!” (“Amar bhaag er kaaj ta apni kore deben”)
