How to get Spotify's best audio quality
A few tweaks here and there can make all the difference.
Some people complain that the quality of music streaming isn't good enough but then don't realise they can adjust settings to improve their audio output. While your speakers or headphones play a huge part in how you hear music through Spotify, options in the app and on your device are important too.
If you've never explored Spotify's audio settings, or it's been a while since you have, take some time to customize them. Spotify Premium users, in particular, have several ways to make their music sound even better.
The most important: adjusting audio quality
The most logical place to start is with the audio quality selector itself, since that directly controls what Spotify sends to your device. To find it on iPhone or Android, open the Spotify app, tap your profile picture at the top-left and choose Settings and privacy. Next, select Media Quality.
On desktop, click the three-dot button at the top-left and choose Edit > Preferences, then scroll down to the Audio quality section. On mobile, you can set the quality independently for both Wi-Fi and Cellular, but on desktop there's only one selector. You can't change the quality in Spotify's web player, so use the desktop app for best results.
All Spotify users can choose from Low, Normal and High, with Premium subscribers also having access to Very high and Lossless. You'll see the bitrate and approximate amount of data usage per hour for each. Automatic adjusts based on your connection strength; for the best quality, disable the separate Auto-adjust toggle so Spotify doesn't modify it as you listen.
Further down the page, you'll see a Download quality section that offers the same options for offline files. If you've previously downloaded music and have since changed the quality, tap Download here to re-download everything to match the new setting. If you have limited mobile data but ample space on your phone, downloading music at High or Very high quality is a great plan. Then, you can shuffle your downloaded Liked Songs to enjoy high-quality CarPlay audio while driving.
Understanding Lossless quality
Lossless delivers CD-quality audio using compression that doesn't delete any information. However, your listening setup could render this quality irrelevant. Bluetooth can't carry true lossless signals, so there's no point in selecting this quality while you're using earbuds or Bluetooth speakers.
On your phone, you'll need wired headphones to enjoy lossless music. In theory, your phone's built-in speakers can play lossless audio, but you won't be able to appreciate it that way. Any pair of USB-C earbuds can carry a lossless signal, though using a more powerful DAC (digital-to-analog converter) provides a better experience. Wired speakers connected to your computer will support lossless audio, and Spotify also works on other devices that support high-definition sound. If you have a Wi-Fi-enabled speaker that works with Spotify Connect, it should support lossless playback since Wi-Fi isn't subject to the same bandwidth limitations as Bluetooth.
Other options, like the Spotify app on your smart TV, may have lossless quality available depending on the model. If they don't offer a quality selector of their own, start playing music on them, then open the app on your phone to control the other device via Spotify Connect. At the bottom-left of the Now Playing screen, tap the name of your desired listening device, then hit it again at the top of the Connect list. This shows you the current quality; tap Change quality settings to adjust it. A LG C1 TV and PS5, for example, are able to play 16-bit lossless Spotify audio through the eARC connection to a soundbar. They can't play full 24-bit quality, but the difference is likely negligible in most cases.
This brings up an important point: even if your setup can transmit lossless audio, the rest of your hardware could prevent you from being able to tell the difference. A $10 pair of earbuds lacks the audio fidelity for you to distinguish between a high-quality lossy and lossless stream, so you'll need quality headphones or in-ear monitors.
Your environment matters, too. Even though CarPlay and Android Auto can transmit lossless audio, you can't appreciate the difference with stock car speakers and noise from the road.
Other Spotify settings that affect audio quality
Outside the direct quality settings, there are other options that can improve Spotify's sound output. Under Spotify's Settings, visit Playback > Equalizer to pick a preset or manually adjust the frequencies on your own. This can make a difference, though take care not to have multiple layers of EQ applied. Your phone might have its own EQ settings, plus Spotify's and then potentially a third for your speakers or headphones.
In the same menu, you might want to disable Volume normalization. This establishes a baseline volume for all music so you don't have to keep turning it up or down. Having it on shouldn't affect audio quality unless you choose Loud, though some people swear audio sounds better with this turned off. Try both and see what you think. While you're here, also make sure Mono audio is disabled unless you need it for accessibility.
While not directly related to audio quality, you might also want to change the Track transitions options on the same page. The Crossfade option will cut off song endings if it's set to a long mix period, for instance. Finally, if you aren't concerned about your mobile data plan, it's worth visiting the Data-saving and offline menu in Settings. For the best quality, make sure Data saver is turned off, as this lowers streaming quality when you're not on Wi-Fi.
Choosing the right audio quality balance in Spotify depends on your environment, audio equipment and the circumstances. When you're at home in a quiet room using high-end speakers, you can appreciate lossless quality. But when you're using Bluetooth earbuds walking around a loud city, a lower streaming quality saves mobile data by not wasting bandwidth on music you can't fully appreciate anyway.
Plus, everyone's hearing is different. Some people can't tell the difference between a high-quality lossy stream and lossless. Online resources like ABX's High Fidelity Test can illustrate if you're able to tell the difference.

Investment firm Novastar Partners has made its maiden India bet by investing an undisclosed sum in Aviral Bhatnagar-led venture capital fund A Junior VC (AJVC), becoming a limited partner (LP) for the firm. Founded in 2024 by Bhatnagar, AJVC is a pre-seed focused investment firm that closed its maiden fund at ₹200 Cr last year. It has made 32 investments to date, backing early-stage startups like Iztri, Handy Panda, Mindcase, among others. Backing startups at the pre-seed or idea stage, AJVC typically invests ₹1.5 Cr for 9% equity. The firm then works closely with founders to build out the business by helping refine product, optimising hiring and people strategy, assisting in sales and marketing, while also aiding in finance, legal and compliance operations. Investment firm Novastar, which is building a private equity fund-of-funds, intends to support AJVC and its portfolio companies by facilitating follow-on funding rounds and providing networking opportunities as well as direct operational assistance. AJVC’s investment strategy, its tech-led sourcing infrastructure, and Bhatnagar’s network in the early-stage investment ecosystem were the key reasons driving Novastar’s decision to back the firm, Novastar’s managing partner Dhruv Jhunjhunwala shared with Inc42. “We believe a programmatic approach, like the one that AJVC is pursuing, where you build a sufficiently broad portfolio of a number of companies while maintaining discipline around selection, can be one of the most effective ways of investing at the pre-seed stage,” he added. Founded by Jhunjhunwala in 2025, Novastar operates a SEBI-registered category II alternative investment fund (AIF) that aims to back leading venture capital funds as a LP, as well as making direct startup investments. The fund focuses on sectors like AI, consumer tech, financial services, healthcare, and deep tech. It also aims to diversify its bets across the startup life cycle with plans to allocate around 15% of its capital to early stage strategies, the majority towards growth stage strategies, and a small share towards late stage strategies including secondaries and continuation funds. Jhunjhunwala declined to share details around how much capital Novastar has raised till now or the capital it plans to deploy. “In the medium term, we would love to announce our next set of investments that would be across funds and companies. But right now, our focus is on continuing to build the right portfolio and partnering with the right set of fund managers,” he said.

AstraZeneca disclosed that a breast cancer pill failed in a pivotal trial testing it as a first-line therapy in advanced tumors, a result that could limit the use of the medicine, STAT notes. The drug, camizestrant, in combination with another medicine did not outperform standard treatment on a measure of how long patients went before their cancer progressed. The drug earlier this month won accelerated approval in the U.S. as a treatment for patients who develop a mutation in their tumors that’s a sign of emerging drug resistance. Had the trial been successful, it could have opened up a much larger market for the drug.
Scholar Rock received U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for the first-ever therapy that targets the loss of muscle in spinal muscle atrophy, raising hopes that patients with the rare neurological disorder might have a better chance of moving and walking independently, STAT writes. The FDA approved the drug, Isembyld, for use in adults and children 2 years and older who are currently receiving SMA therapies that target SMN2, a key gene for neurons that control movement. The approval marks another step forward for patients with spinal muscular atrophy, a rare and progressive disease that destroys nerve cells that control speaking, breathing, and walking. Babies who go untreated usually die by the age of 2.

As calls for artificial intelligence regulation intensify, US President Donald Trump’s team have made it clear that if lab leaders want to implement an industry-wide slowdown, they’re going to have to do it themselves.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called on the US government to regulate AI companies within a wider effort to slow the pace of the technology’s development in an essay published Saturday. The essay received rare endorsement from both OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns chatbot Grok, following a week of intense debate about the technology’s threats to human safety. Microsoft chief executive officer Satya Nadella also called for pacing development.
Calls for AI slowdown and regulation have intensified after a number of researchers voiced major concerns in the last week about the speed of the technology’s advance. “AI progress is increasing,” former DeepMind researcher Rishub Jain told WIRED. “And as AI becomes more capable, it poses more risks.”
But David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, wrote on X, “If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel … Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic.”
Amodei had requested the government enable competing AI companies to work together on standards without breaching antitrust law, either by participating in discussions or issuing a waiver for the companies involved. He also called for government assistance in establishing international coordination, including with the Chinese Communist Party, though critics wondered how effective this would be. “China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know,” Sacks wrote.
Concerns about the US ceding its lead in the technology to China have caused the US government to mostly push back against the notion of slowing the pace of its development. “You have a lot of very negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” Trump said during a visit to Ireland. “We’re leading China on AI,” he added, “and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."
The US largely views China’s AI ecosystem as an economic and national security threat, and has previously been caught short by the country’s advances in the technology. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American,” House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN on Sunday. “So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel.”
In the meantime, companies say they are going to start taking voluntary steps to reestablish public trust that they are acting responsibly. On Sunday night, OpenAI’s Altman committed to a proposal by Amodei to give embedded third party evaluators employee-level access to their firms to check practices and products were safe, and report incidents. While these measures will have “significant costs,” he wrote on X: “Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.”

I cannot overstate the importance of having an air purifier that not only has enough power to actually purify a room's air but also caters to your home's particular needs. Pollutants like wildfire smoke, pollen, unventilated gas stoves, pet allergens, and even litter box odors can be potentially harmful additions to the air you breathe in your home.
Air purifiers from Coway have been a consistent top pick in our guide to the Best Air Purifiers for years, including the Coway Airmega Mighty2, which was released in March this year. Its predecessor, the Coway Airmega Mighty, had been our reigning “Best Affordable Air Purifier” for many years as well. I was excited to test the newest mid-size option built for medium to large rooms in Coway's Airmega line, where it sits between the compact Airmega 50 or 100 and the higher-capacity 350 or 450 models.
Released at the end of August, Coway’s Airmega Halo is an affordable, lightweight air purifier that aims to deliver whole-room air purification at an accessible price point. Plus, its focus is on promoting a healthier night's sleep with smart sleep features and quiet noise levels when in sleep mode.
Overall, it delivers on most of its promises, but I ran into some problems during field-testing that made me question its sensor, and I wish it had more transparency with pollutant levels.
Simple Design That’s Maybe Too Simple
The Halo is only 9.7 pounds, making it lightweight and portable as far as air purifiers go, but it doesn't have accessibility features like a top handle or wheels for easier moving. It has a small cutout in the back to grip, but because I have an upper-limb disability, moving it was awkward—I essentially had to hug the purifier to maneuver it, since I don't have large hands that can easily grip the inlet.
The purifier's cylindrical design with a 360-degree air-intake structure draws in polluted air from all sides, making for fewer spatial constraints and more options for placement around the home. The inside of the machine uses Coway's HyperVortex filtration system, which is an aerodynamic fan and duct design that Coway states is “inspired by eagle wings and golf ball dimples.” It uses wing blades to stabilize airflow, along with aerodynamic blades for powerful airflow for the generator fan and dimples to reduce air resistance for smoother air intake.
Setup was extremely easy—I just needed to unscrew the bottom, remove the filter from the plastic protective covering, screw the bottom back on, and plug it in. There's no need for a Wi-Fi connection, no app, and no remote. I started testing air purifiers earlier this year, and I've found I actually like having a connected remote, or better yet, an app that allows me to monitor air quality and adjust settings from afar. This model had neither. I also appreciate getting transparent numbers of pollutant levels directly from the machine rather than relying on colored lights, but this machine had the latter.

Gender disparity in organ transplantation is a global problem affecting each step of the transplantation process, from organ donation, recipient listing, waiting times and access, to post-transplant outcomes. This inequality is most visibly expressed in the overrepresentation of women as living donors, while men continue to be the majority of transplant recipients.
What the data reveals
India’s case is a particularly striking example of this gender imbalance. Women constitute the majority of living organ donors, but men get the majority of transplants. As per recent data from the National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organization (NOTTO), between 2019 and 2023, 63.8% of living organ donors were women and 69.8% of transplant recipients were men.
This is not a new divide. In 2019 and 2020, roughly two-thirds of living donors were women, but only about a quarter of recipients were women. A 2025 analysis found that women accounted for 36,038 of the 56,509 living donations over the five-year period studied, also highlighting the scale of the imbalance. Of these, however, only 17,041 were transplanted into women, as against 39,447 transplanted into men.
This gendered pattern raises a fundamental question: why are women expected to give and men positioned to receive in disproportionate numbers? The answer goes far beyond biology.
Behind the donations
Women’s decisions to donate organs are shaped by a complicated interaction between sociocultural expectations, economic conditions and family structures. In many Indian homes, women, particularly wives and mothers, are still expected to put the needs of their families before their own. The expectation can be particularly sharp in the case of a life-saving transplant for a close family member.
Studies have noted the role of women in familial organ donation. Mothers are, on average, 73% of all parental donations, and wives are 91% of donations between married couples. These figures are suggestive of a long-standing social tendency to assign the bulk of care work to women, and perhaps even to the final act of bodily sacrifice.
Psychological and experiential reasons may also play a role in women’s higher willingness to donate. Past experiences with the health care system, such as pregnancy and delivery, may increase familiarity with medical settings and trust in health care providers. But these explanations have to be discussed in the light of the strong influence of social conditioning. What seems like a personal choice can sometimes be influenced by expectations, emotional duties or an unspoken belief that a woman should make sacrifices for her family.
Patriarchal attitudes can also be a disincentive for men to become donors. Men are generally considered the primary breadwinner and economic provider for their families. Thus, the prospect of a man needing major surgery, a long recovery period or a temporary loss of income might be seen as an unacceptable financial risk. Such pressure can transfer the burden of donation to women.
This dynamic is particularly problematic when financial dependency is a factor. The costs of evaluation, surgery, recovery and the potential loss of household income may make male donation seem less feasible. In such cases, women may be subtly, and in more troubling cases, explicitly encouraged to donate, because they are seen as more expendable in the family’s economic structure. Thus, the line between voluntary altruism and coercion can become perilously blurred.
It is, therefore, the duty of healthcare providers to fully discuss these issues at every stage of the process, explain the ramifications of a donation and t ensure that they are indeed personal choices of women, and not influenced by other factors.
What needs to change
This has implications for more than just transplant statistics. Essentially, it’s a question of equity, autonomy and justice in healthcare. An organ donation system cannot be truly equitable when it is based on social and familial pressures about who is supposed to donate, and on socioeconomic or structural barriers about who gets the transplant.
Interventions are required at several levels to address this gap. Awareness must be the starting point, but awareness is not enough. Transplant services and community-based initiatives should be extended to rural, underserved and marginalised regions and not be confined to major urban centres. In particular, women should have equal access to information, evaluation and transplantation services.
Equally important is strengthening psychosocial assessment of potential living donors. Pre-transplant evaluation should not only include medical suitability and financial considerations, but also explore the wider social environment in which the donation decision is being made. Healthcare professionals should be trained to recognise warning signs of coercion, domestic abuse, threats, violence, manipulation and financial dependence. Donors must be provided with real opportunities to make informed and voluntary decisions, including the opportunity to withdraw without fear of repercussions.
Better and more comprehensive data collection is also needed in India. Good, disaggregated data on donors and recipients – disaggregated by gender, age, socioeconomic status, geography, relationship to recipient and other relevant factors, would enable policymakers to better identify disparities and design evidence-based interventions. Grassroots research is important because national averages can hide significant inequalities at the regional and community level.
The challenge is to move beyond the financial transaction of organ donation, and to acknowledge the quieter pressures that can exist within families. Sometimes coercion doesn’t take the form of an explicit threat. It could be the expectations of a wife, the responsibilities of a mother or the assumption that a woman should sacrifice herself for the family’s survival.
The bigger message is hard to miss: gender inequality does not stop at the hospital door. It can influence who gives, who gets, who waits and ultimately who gets a chance to live.
(Dr Shivakumar S. Patil is consultant, renal transplant surgery, Manipal Hospital, Hebbal. shivakumar.patil@manipalhospitals.com)

In early September 2026, people shared an alleged screenshot of an X post from the platform's Twitter era purportedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump posting on his @realDonaldTrump account, "Don't let Obama buy the election by handing out unlimited free money to states."
Users shared the image after Trump's pledge to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult should the Republican Party win the 2026 midterm elections. The president announced the pledge during the GOP midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 10, calling the payments a "Trump dividend."
The screenshot of the alleged tweet spread on Bluesky, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and other platforms.
(Thomas Mohr accessed via Bluesky)
Some users drew direct comparisons between Trump's alleged remark in 2012 and the news of his $5,000 pledge. Others referred to the "dividend" as bribery and socialism.
(@mandyarthur accessed via X)
In sum, the 2012 Trump post is real. He tweeted (archived) it on Oct. 30 of that year, one week before the Nov. 6 elections.
Don't let Obama buy the election by handing out unlimited free money to states.
— Donald J. Trump (@realDonaldTrump) October 30, 2012
Snopes emailed the White House for its response to users comparing the 2012 post to the "Trump dividend." We will update this article if we receive further information.
The 2012 elections concluded with former President Barack Obama winning a second term. The Democratic Party picked up two seats to continue maintaining a majority in the Senate. Republicans lost eight House seats but continued their control of the legislative chamber.
For further reading, we previously published a collection of 24 things Trump actually posted on Truth Social, including, for example, an Easter Sunday post threatening Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz or be "living in hell," as well as a Memorial Day message addressing "scum" that spent years "trying to destroy our country."

Pennsylvania says an unvaccinated woman has died from measles-related complications
An official in Pennsylvania has confirmed the measles-related death of a 40-year-old woman. Jefferson County Coroner Greg Furlong told NPR that the woman, who died on Saturday, was unvaccinated.
"This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease," a statement from the coroner's office said.
Officials have not released the woman's identity, but said she was a resident of Jefferson County. This is the third death that Pennsylvania state officials have linked to measles this year. No other states have announced measles deaths in 2026.
On Friday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 676 measles cases so far this year. It also reported 52 new positive cases from Wednesday to Friday.
Pennsylvania officials and the federal government have clashed over the number of measles-associated deaths in the state in recent weeks, as the U.S. faces a nationwide resurgence of the illness. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared that the highly contagious virus had been eradicated from the U.S. in 2000.
Last week, the CDC reported more than 3,200 confirmed measles cases in the country.
The agency said it was reviewing whether to count two measles-related deaths involving infants in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. After Gov. Josh Shapiro announced the state's first two deaths, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said on X the announcement appeared to have been "premature" and "may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers."
This clash is notable, as NPR's Rob Stein has reported. "The CDC usually defers to the state's determination" of cause of death in this kind of outbreak, "so the agency can alert the public, doctors and health officials around the country."
The CDC lists the number of measles cases reported in each state for 2026, as well as the number of hospitalizations. The agency has not listed the number of deaths for this year. Instead of giving a figure, there is an asterisk that explains: "The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause."
Kennedy has said on X that NCHS "will update as it receives and reviews submitted records."
The Jefferson County Coroner's Office also emphasized measles can lead to severe complications at any age.
"While cases of severe illness remain uncommon, this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly," said Chief Deputy Coroner and Public Relations Officer Jason Stiver in a statement. "Public health measures, early recognition of symptoms, and consultation with healthcare providers are important tools in protecting our community."
The county coroner's office is working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on the case. Pennsylvania and South Carolina have the highest numbers of confirmed measles cases in the U.S., according to federal data.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
- Published
Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour.
The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey.
His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up.
In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill.
"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.
"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."
The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues.
"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.
"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."
He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.
"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.
"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.
"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."
Hind's Hall performance
The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."
He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.
Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online.
The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram.
The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.
"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.
Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.
The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
'Most successful tour'
After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up.
In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft - the billionaire owner of the Gilette Stadium in Massachusetts.
Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric".
"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.
However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour.
Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."
In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.
"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.
He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."

A phrase used by FBI Director Kash Patel in a recent post has left some social media users confused, particularly those unfamiliar with US legal terminology.
“Indian Country will NOT be forgotten,” Patel said while announcing increased FBI resources and personnel for communities covered by the term. He said the FBI was putting “more agents, more resources, and more attention” into the field to address crimes and help victims and families awaiting answers.
But what exactly does “Indian Country” mean?
‘Indian Country’ Has Nothing To Do With India
In the context of Patel’s statement, “Indian Country” does not refer to the Republic of India. It is a longstanding legal term in the United States used to describe certain lands and communities associated with Native American tribes.
Under Section 1151 of Title 18 of the US Code, the term includes land within the limits of federally recognised Indian reservations, certain dependent Indian communities and Indian allotments whose titles have not been extinguished. The law also covers rights-of-way running through such lands.
The term is therefore linked to Native American and tribal communities in the US and has implications for federal criminal jurisdiction. The Legal Information Institute notes that “Indian country” can include reservations, trust lands, restricted-fee lands and other areas associated with Native communities.
What Was Kash Patel Announcing?
Patel was referring to the FBI’s expanded focus on violent crime and public safety in tribal communities.
The FBI has described Operation Steadfast Promise as a major effort targeting violent crime on Tribal lands. The agency said a related operation, Trusted Trails, involved 11 field offices and resulted in 86 arrests, 50 subjects being charged, 62 drug seizures and the recovery of 156 weapons between May 1 and July 31, 2026.
The FBI has also said it has increased personnel and investigative resources working with Tribal, state, local and federal law-enforcement agencies.
FBI Raises Rewards For Missing Persons, Homicide Cases
Patel’s comments also referred to the FBI’s “Voices Not Forgotten” initiative, announced in August.
According to the FBI, the programme increases rewards for publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons suspected of being victims of homicide in “Indian country” where the FBI has jurisdiction. The agency said the new protocol provides rewards of up to $25,000 for qualifying cases.
The initiative includes cases involving Missing or Murdered Indigenous Persons, commonly referred to as MMIP cases, and features an interactive map highlighting investigations where authorities are seeking information from the public.
Why Did The Phrase Confuse Netizens?
The wording also triggered a wave of reactions online, particularly from people outside the US who interpreted “Indian Country” literally and initially assumed that Patel was referring to India.
Some users expressed confusion over the phrase, while others joked about the apparent reference to India before others explained that it is a recognised US legal term connected to Native American tribal lands.
Some reactions also questioned why the FBI did not simply use terms such as “Native American communities” or “Tribal communities”, while others welcomed the announcement of additional resources for cases involving missing people and violent crime.
The confusion largely stemmed from the different meanings of the word “Indian” in the US context. In Patel’s statement, the phrase refers to Native American communities and lands covered by US law, not India.
A Longstanding US Legal Term
“Indian Country” is therefore neither a reference to India nor a new phrase introduced by Patel. It has been part of US federal law for decades and continues to be used by federal agencies and courts when discussing jurisdiction and law enforcement involving Tribal lands and communities.
Patel’s remarks were made in the context of the FBI’s ongoing efforts involving violent crime, missing persons and other investigations affecting Native American and Alaska Native communities.

క్లెయిమ్: 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి ప్రతి రోజు రాత్రి 12:00 గంటల నుంచి ఉదయం 6:00 గంటల వరకు ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పనిచేయకుండా మెటా ఆంక్షలు విధించింది.
ఫాక్ట్ (నిజం): అమెరికాలో Meta, వివిధ రాష్ట్రాల 52 అటార్నీ జనరల్స్తో ఒక ఒప్పందానికి వచ్చింది. దీని ప్రకారం 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారుల కోసం Instagram, Facebookలో కొన్ని కొత్త పరిమితులు, భద్రతా చర్యలు అమలు చేయాల్సి ఉంటుంది. ఈ నిబంధనలు అమెరికాలోని ఈ ఒప్పందంలో పాల్గొన్న రాష్ట్రాలు, ప్రాంతాల్లోని 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారులకు వర్తిస్తాయి. ఈ ఒప్పందంలో 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి రాత్రి 12:00 గంటల నుంచి ఉదయం 6:00 గంటల వరకు ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తంగా ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ మూసివేయబడుతుందని ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు. పైగా మెటా ఇటువంటి నిబంధనలు ఇతర దేశాలకు వర్తిస్తాయని ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ క్లెయిమ్ గురించి తగిన కీ వర్డ్స్ ఉపయోగించి ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతికితే, మెటా ఇటువంటి విధులను ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తంగా విధిస్తున్నట్టు ఎటువంటి సమాచారం మాకు లభించలేదు.
అయితే, అమెరికాలో Meta, వివిధ రాష్ట్రాల 52 అటార్నీ జనరల్స్తో ఒక ఒప్పందానికి వచ్చింది. ఈ ఒప్పందానికి కోర్టు ఆమోదం కూడా లభించింది. దీని ప్రకారం 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారుల కోసం Instagram, Facebookలో కొన్ని కొత్త పరిమితులు, భద్రతా చర్యలు అమలు చేయాల్సి ఉంటుంది. ఈ నిబంధనలు అమెరికాలోని ఈ ఒప్పందంలో పాల్గొన్న రాష్ట్రాలు, ప్రాంతాల్లోని 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారులకు వర్తిస్తాయి. ఇవి USలో ఉన్న ఇతర మెటా వినియోగదారులందరికీ వర్తించవు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ).
Meta ఒప్పందంలో 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారుల కోసం అనేక భద్రతా చర్యలు ఉన్నాయి. టీనేజర్లు Facebook, Instagram రెండింటినీ కలిపి రోజుకు రెండు గంటలు ఉపయోగించేలా డిఫాల్ట్ పరిమితి ఉంటుంది. అలాగే అర్థరాత్రి నుంచి ఉదయం 6 గంటల వరకు పోస్టులు చేయడం, కంటెంట్ చూడడంపై పరిమితి ఉంటుంది. పాఠశాల సమయాల్లో నోటిఫికేషన్లు మ్యూట్ చేయడం, ఎక్కువసేపు యాప్ ఉపయోగించినప్పుడు రిమైండర్లు ఇవ్వడం వంటి చర్యలు కూడా ఉంటాయి. అదనంగా, సురక్షితమైన ఫీడ్ సెట్టింగులు, బలమైన వయస్సు నిర్ధారణ, అనుచితమైన కంటెంట్, అపరిచితుల నుంచి రక్షణ, అలాగే తల్లిదండ్రులు పిల్లల సోషల్ మీడియా వినియోగాన్ని పర్యవేక్షించేందుకు మరిన్ని నియంత్రణలను Meta అందిస్తుంది.
అమెరికాలో Meta కుదుర్చుకున్న ఒప్పందానికి ఇప్పటికే అంగీకారం లభించింది. ఈ ఒప్పందాన్ని కోర్టు కూడా ఆమోదించింది. దీంతో 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారుల కోసం ఒప్పందంలో పేర్కొన్న భద్రతా చర్యలను Meta దశలవారీగా అమలు చేయాల్సి ఉంటుంది అని నివేదికలు పేర్కొన్నాయి. ఈ ఒప్పందంలోని చాలా నిబంధనలు 10 సంవత్సరాల పాటు అమల్లో ఉంటాయని, ఈ కొత్త భద్రతా ప్రమాణాలను TikTok, YouTube కూడా అమలు చేయాలని Meta కోరింది.
అయితే, ఈ నిబంధనలు అమెరికాలోని కొన్ని రాష్ట్రాలు, ప్రాంతాల్లో 18 ఏళ్లలోపు వినియోగదారులకు మాత్రమే వర్తిస్తాయి. ఈ ఒప్పందంలో 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తంగా ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ మూసివేయబడుతుందని ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ).
చివరిగా, 10 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి ప్రతి రోజు రాత్రి 12:00 గంటల నుంచి ఉదయం 6:00 గంటల వరకు ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పనిచేయకుండా మెటా ఎటువంటి నిబంధనలను అమలు చేయలేదు.

Vladimir Putin has arrived in India’s capital of Delhi ahead of an 11-member Brics summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
The Russian president and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, were due to hold talks with India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, while Chinese leader Xi Jinping was also expected to attend the two-day meeting.
Putin arrived at Palam air force Station in Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s minister of state for external affairs, Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.
The summit will mark Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and is seen as the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
On Friday posters of a beaming Modi lined streets in Delhi, along with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
Brics was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the Brics summit,” said Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation. “What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of Brics – today looks like a big constraint on Brics”.
It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the [expanded] group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the Brics foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025 but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, visited Kyiv this month, when the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

Multiple staffers at a Trump-aligned policy think tank have burrowed their way into the US Census Bureau, where they have access to sensitive data and have contributed to a public report that bolsters conspiracy theories undermining trust in elections ahead of the midterms.
In August, the Census Bureau published an anonymously authored report titled “Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election: A Beginning Analysis,” claiming to show that thousands of noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. A WIRED investigation revealed that the report appeared to employ faulty methodology, casting its conclusions into doubt, and that two of its authors work for the America First Policy Institute, a right-wing think tank with deep ties to the Trump administration. Now WIRED has found that the two authors are part of a larger team, made up almost entirely of AFPI members, who have been detailed to the Census Bureau and given access to its data.
The Census Bureau is home to vast troves of sensitive data on nearly every person living in the country, which is used for apportioning and drawing congressional districts as well as allocating federal funding based on population sizes. Experts and Census employees who spoke to WIRED worry that the noncitizen voting report is the first salvo in Census data possibly being used to undermine the results of the upcoming midterms or the 2028 presidential election.
A Census employee who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity says that there has historically been “nothing close” to what AFPI is doing at the bureau. “Frankly, it's disrespectful to the institution,” they say.
The Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to cast doubt on the accuracy of Census data in order to reshape elections. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that the Department of Commerce, which oversees the bureau, was circulating a rule change that would eliminate noncitizens from being counted in the Census, a move that could drastically reshape how Congressional districts are drawn. Republicans also took aim at a little-known statistical method called differential privacy that is used to protect the privacy of individual respondents, alleging that it makes the Census count inaccurate in ways that favor Democrats in congressional apportionment.
AFPI, meanwhile, has been integral to shaping the Trump administration’s policies and makeup. Brooke Rollins, who served as the group’s first CEO, is now the secretary of agriculture, and Linda McMahon, now the secretary of education, used to sit on the organization’s board. Former AFPI staffers have found their way to some of the highest ranks of the Trump administration, including former attorney general Pam Bondi, secretary of Veterans Affairs Doug Collins, secretary of Housing and Urban Development Scott Turner, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin, US permanent representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, deputy director of White House Domestic Policy Council Heidi Overton, and National Economic Council of the United States director Kevin Hassett.
In addition to Matthew Jensen and Jeff McCrea, the two AFPI members previously identified by WIRED, at least five other AFPI members have been or are currently staffed at the Census Bureau, according to sources and documents reviewed by WIRED. Sources who spoke to WIRED confirmed that all the AFPI members are detailed to the agency through the Intergovernmental Personnel Act (IPA), which allows people with specialized skills from certain institutions, like nonprofits and universities, to work for the government for up to two years on a temporary appointment.
The Census Bureau and AFPI did not respond to requests for comment.
John Abowd, former associate director for research and methodology and chief scientist at the Census Bureau, says that having so many people from a single organization would be “unusual.”
Among the names viewed by WIRED are Max Kossek, a researcher at AFPI’s Office for Fiscal and Regulatory Analysis, and Ryan Montgomery, who the website lists as a program assistant with the same AFPI office. Montgomery’s LinkedIn profile, however, says that he is now a “research engineer” at AFPI.
AFPI’s director for secure elections policy, Thomas Lane, is also listed as one of the employees that has been detailed to the Census Bureau. Lane, a former Trump campaign staffer and election denier, was subpoenaed by the Department of Justice in 2022 as part of its investigation into the president’s attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 election. (Lane was not charged by law enforcement.) In a 2020 video posted by the Arizona Republican Party, where a group of fake electors attempted to deliver the state’s electoral votes to Donald Trump, Politico identified a man wearing a jacket with the name “Lane” on it passing out the documents for the electors to sign making them “duly elected” and “qualified.” In 2024, CNN reported that Lane was prepared to serve as a backup elector for that same group.
Earlier this year, Democracy Docket reported that Lane helped write part of an early version of the Save America Act, the law that would require voter ID to register to vote, while working for the Republican majority House Committee on House Administration. Parts of the Save Act have also been included in the separate Save America Act, which, if passed, would require proof of citizenship in order to vote, a move that experts say could disenfranchise more than 20 million people.
Kossek, Montgomery, and Lane did not respond to requests for comment.
David Peterson, who AFPI lists as a research engineer with expertise in “computing, machine learning, and advanced software architecture,” and Jackson Mejia, an AFPI fellow who is an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin with a PhD in economics from MIT focusing on tax policy, also appear to be detailed to the Census Bureau. Peterson and Mejia did not respond to requests for comment.
Another person, listed as an IPA from AFPI, Michael Corey, is also listed among the group at the bureau. AFPI does not list Corey as a staff member on its website, but an AFPI email with Corey’s name does appear to exist. AFPI did not confirm whether Corey was currently associated with the think tank.
Danah Boyd, a professor at Cornell University who studies the census, says that there are vehicles like the American Association for the Advancement of Science through which agencies like the Census Bureau might bring in multiple IPAs. But AFPI, Boyd says, “is not an institution that is set up to bring all the scientists in the world together or that has built this long-standing infrastructure of doing independent statistical research. This is a partisan group with an agenda,” she claims.
All of the AFPI members are listed under the same project, focused on “ad hoc data analyses” to answer questions from senior leaders at Census and the Department of Commerce, according to documentation viewed by WIRED. The project appears to be led by Michael Lachanski, the bureau’s recently appointed deputy director for data, policy, and science, and a former fellow at the Claremont Institute, a conservative think tank that also has connections to the Trump administration. Lachanski is a political appointee. All of the AFPI detailees appear to have the “special sworn status” necessary to access sensitive Census data.
Recent reporting from Talking Points Memo found that the Census Bureau’s Data Stewardship Executive Policy charter had been updated in July to remove stipulations that prevented political appointees from interfering with the bureau’s data.
Another Census employee, who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the press, says that access to Census data is only allowed through approved “projects,” where employees and researchers have to explain how they're going to use the data and what they're going to produce. The employee says that it’s not unheard of to have multiple people from the same outside institution on the same project, but there appears to be a lack of civil servants involved in this one. The project’s “explicit reference to answering questions of interest to political appointees” is concerning, the employee says.
Boyd says this kind of work is a clear departure from the bureau’s mandate, which does not include providing data to political appointees. “These are all part of culture norms and practices of how you make certain you run a transparent agency to ensure that you are doing good by the American people,” she says.
There is precedent for political pressure at the Census Bureau: In 2021, less than two weeks after the January 6 insurrection at the end of Trump’s first term, then US Census Bureau director Steven Dillingham announced his resignation after a letter from the Office of the Inspector General revealed that whistleblowers had come forward to allege Census workers had been pressured by political appointees to create a report showing the citizenship status of every US resident.

WASHINGTON — Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will give a keynote address at a Children’s Health Defense conference in the nation’s capital this week, embracing the anti-vaccine organization he once led.
“We couldn’t be more excited to welcome our founder back to the CHD stage,” the nonprofit said in an email announcing Kennedy as a speaker.
The conference, which will take place at the Grand Hyatt Washington on Thursday, marks an important full-circle moment for Kennedy, who joined Children’s Health Defense in 2015. The group questions the efficacy and safety of childhood vaccines. Kennedy chaired CHD until December 2024, earning a six-figure salary while helping file dozens of lawsuits targeting state-level vaccine policies, according to his financial disclosures.
He took leave from the group during his campaign for the presidency, and severed ties permanently shortly before President Trump took office.
Through Kennedy, CHD has gained unprecedented access to the political levers of power. Ideas that are central to the group’s beliefs, but were once considered fringe, such as the disproven theory that vaccines cause autism, have been echoed by Trump in the White House
The group’s leaders, including attorney Mary Holland, have attended high-profile MAHA gatherings in Washington, and gained positions within the Department of Health and Human Services.
The CHD conference will serve as the secretary’s first public embrace of the group since he took the helm of HHS — a marked shift from January 2025, when Kennedy promised senators he would not do anything to discourage Americans from getting vaccines.
During his confirmation hearings, Kennedy attempted to distance himself from Children’s Health Defense and his prior anti-vaccine activism in order to secure key Republican votes. During one memorable exchange, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) grilled Kennedy by pointing to images of “Unvaxxed, Unafraid” onesies sold by Children’s Health Defense.
“Are you supportive of these onesies?” Sanders asked several times.
“I am supportive of vaccines,” Kennedy responded, adding that he had “no power” over the nonprofit.

Ukraine's postal workers deliver lifeline under Russian fire
- Published
Every morning Igor Smelyansky looks at a vast map of Ukraine on his office wall and decides where he should put his people in harm's way.
His aides provide him with live intelligence about Russian attacks and he deploys his teams, balancing their potential operational success against risk to life or limb.
But Smelyansky is no military commander. He is the head of Ukraine's state postal service, Ukrposhta.
And every day he must decide how far to send his postmen and women into the deadly "kill zone" along the front lines where the threat of drone attack is ever present.
"If it's too dangerous to go today, we won't go," Smelyansky told us. "We'll go tomorrow, or we'll go somewhere else. The key is to be as agile as you can."
Ukrposhta does more than just collect letters and parcels. It pays out pensions in hard cash, it takes payment for utility bills. And it delivers vital food and medicine to people on the margins of society.
As such, it offers a lifeline to millions of poor and elderly Ukrainians living in remote villages where shops are rare and trips to the city are expensive and dangerous. In a vast rural nation wracked by war, Ukrposhta is part of the glue that holds the country together.
That has made the service a target for Russia - which in recent months has stepped up not only its attacks on postmen and women but also sorting offices and logistical hubs. The Kremlin has claimed strikes like this are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian online retailers like Wildberries.
Speaking in his imposing Soviet-era office building that overlooks Kyiv's famous Maidan square, Smelyansky said: "If we don't go [to a village], we don't have basic supply. We don't have food. We don't have medicine. People will struggle. If we do go, they may delay a decision to evacuate from the areas they probably should have evacuated."
There are many risks. If a post van turns up unannounced, a crowd can form, creating a target for an opportunistic Russian drone operator. But if they call ahead, information could leak.
"Is it a danger?" Smelyansky said. "Absolutely. Because there are Russian sympathisers who can give them the location of the truck that's coming."
By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in
If Smelyansky chooses not to send a van in, he faces criticism. "You get messages from people from those villages: 'You betrayed us. You didn't come...' But if I go, I may risk the life of the driver."
Smelyansky says Russia is deliberately targeting his staff because of the vital role they play shoring up Ukraine's resilience, helping people stay alive in their homes through the fighting and bitter winters.
"It's not an accident, it's deliberate," he said. "By attacking Ukrposhta, you put pressure on people… who are depending on the truck coming in." Russia denies targeting civilians.
Since 2022, hundreds of Ukrposhta branches and vehicles have been hit, and more than 50 staff have lost their lives, either on the frontline or on their rounds, according to Ukrposhta.
We travelled with Kateryna Marynych, a 38-year-old postmistress, near Zaporizhzhia - a city not too far from the southern frontlines.
She lost her home and her husband during the full-scale invasion, and came to the area to rebuild her life. She ran the post office in the village of Lukasheve for two years until it was destroyed in March by a Russian drone, targeting soldiers working nearby.
After her van drew up, a steady queue of elderly folk formed. She sat in the front passenger seat, window open, handing out cash, taking payments.
One customer, Nadiia, said she was grateful: "It's a long way for us to travel to Zaporizhzhia. Especially now, at a time when there are attacks all around us. The fact that they come here is really nice."
Oleksandrivna, 77, arrived wearing a purple dressing gown, walking with a crutch. When I asked her where she would be without Kateryna, she replied: "We would be stuffed! I am just out of hospital after a stroke. Where could I go for my medicine?"
But Mykola, 64, pointed to another service the post office provides to a largely elderly population. "It is very important," he said. "It's one of the few joys of the month: you come out, have a chat with people, collect your pension, and go home."
For many people in remote communities, Kateryna can be their last link with the Ukrainian state.
She says she hopes her customers are proud of her. "They love me, they need me," she said. "They are waiting for me. Sometimes they call me, especially after attacks on Zaporizhzhia and ask me how I am. We are like a big family. My attitude towards them is like a grandmother or grandfather."
The attacks on Ukrposhta form part of Russia's wider escalation of its war on Ukraine, stepping up fast drone attacks on civilian infrastructure including business infrastructure, energy facilities, transport networks and border posts. Analysts say that as Russia's invasion stagnates on the battlefield in the east, it is looking for other ways of putting pressure on Kyiv.
For safety, Kateryna always travels with her partner, Slava, who drives. While she sorts the cash, he works from the back of the van, taking and receiving parcels, delivering food and water. He also carries a side-arm in a holster, for personal protection; these vans carry a lot of cash.
Both wear body armour when close to the front line. And they have an antenna in the van that shows them the location of the small first-person-view drones that render the frontline so deadly. They have seen drones from the car but luckily have not yet been hit.
She accepted her job was dangerous but would never change it. "It is my work," she said. "If I can't, who will do my job?"
Ukraine's defence comes in many forms - and it's not always delivered at the barrel of a gun.
Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk

China leads the world in churning out humanoid robots and four-legged robot dogs that also happen to be the most affordable on the market—and Unitree Robotics’ founder Wang Xingxing is arguably one of the people most responsible for that Chinese lead.
The introverted founder, who prominently appeared at a 2025 business symposium hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, became phenomenally wealthy after Unitree launched an initial public offering on the Shanghai Stock Exchange STAR Market on August 19. But extensive reporting by Beijing-based Caijing Magazine suggests Unitree’s success so far has been driven by Wang’s extreme micromanagement leadership style—an approach that may be more suited to a small startup than a fast-growing robotics company.
Caijing’s interviews with Unitree employees and investors paint a picture of Wang as someone who personally decides nearly every aspect of corporate strategy or product design, including the colors of materials and lengths of individual screws. The Caijing Magazine feature published on August 31, titled “The King of Unitree,” was translated into English by ChinaTalk, a US-based think tank and media organization, on September 10.
The founder’s obsession with details, coupled with his cost-cutting focus, has driven Unitree to produce some of the cheapest walking robots on the market. Robotics hardware engineers told Caijing Magazine that Unitree achieved this cost advantage through design choices and structural engineering—and Ars has done a deep dive into the specific design decisions on hardware components that make Unitree robots so cheap.
For example, a baseline Unitree G1 humanoid robot designed for robot developers and researchers sells for $13,500, not including shipping costs, while the Unitree R1 robot intended for more casual consumers sells for $4,900.
However, this cost-cutting drive comes at the expense of quality control, according to Caijing Magazine. Unitree employees described the company’s robots as having an “extremely high” rate of returns for repairs in the early years, although that has supposedly improved to the point where the company’s robots can survive the one-year or six-month warranty periods without breaking down.

A federal judge on Monday issued a preliminary injunction blocking the Trump administration from upending a long-standing policy that allows foreign students and scholars to stay in the U.S. for the duration of their training, a decision that suggests that plaintiffs opposed to the policy change are likely to ultimately succeed.
The ruling halts plans by the Department of Homeland Security to place a four-year cap on the kinds of visas used by graduate students and postdoctoral researchers while a judge hears full arguments in a lawsuit over the new policy. Experts warn the outcome of the case could have a dramatic impact on the nation’s biomedical preeminence given that international researchers make up a large share of the U.S. life science workforce. The new policy had been set to take effect on Tuesday.
In his ruling, Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts wrote that “the promulgation of the rule clearly failed to comply with the [Administrative Procedure Act].” Saylor added that the administration’s argument that the new visa policy is needed to safeguard national security was weak and “raises legitimate questions as to whether its real purpose is not to safeguard national security and protect our borders, but to achieve other, undisclosed, goals — such as, for example, asserting greater government control over academic institutions.”
While Saylor said that the plaintiffs have a “substantial likelihood of success” in the case, he declined to issue a summary judgment definitively striking down the DHS rule.
In a Sept. 3 hearing, an attorney for the coalition of academic groups that challenged the visa restrictions, Paul Hughes from the firm McDermott, Will & Schulte, argued the government did not conduct a sufficient analysis of the fallout of the new policy. Without a delay in its implementation or throwing out the change, he said schools would experience “irreparable harm.”
Michael Celone, a Department of Justice lawyer, in turn, argued that the government had done its due diligence and that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated tangible harm that would result from the policy. Celone said students who are impacted by the policy could either apply for extensions or easily apply elsewhere, comparing students choosing schools to taking a book out of the library.
Saylor seemed skeptical of the government’s reasoning, questioning how the policy would diminish any national security risks posed by international students. “I am struggling to see any real, rational connection between national security issues identified, which is not even half of a dozen incidents over 50 years, and this change,” he said to Celone during the hearing.
The judge also took issue with the relatively short time the policy was open for public comments: “Can I say it’s illegal? Probably not. But it is part of the mix here to what extent the government was taking its duty seriously in weighing costs and benefits.”
Academic groups, including the nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators and the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, have joined the suit. DHS; Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the department; U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement; and David Venturella, acting director of ICE, are named as defendants.
The case centers around a long-standing policy known as duration of status, which for more than 40 years has allowed international students and scholars to remain in the U.S. for however long it took them to complete their training.
The federal government implemented the policy in 1979 to streamline international students’ admission into the country. But the Trump administration has argued duration of status has led to the creation of “forever students,” whom they allege cheat the system by perpetually enrolling in courses to avoid leaving the U.S.
In mid-July, DHS announced that, going forward, foreign students and postdocs won’t be allowed to stay in the U.S. for more than four years on nonimmigrant visas unless they apply for and receive an extension. Students and postdocs already in the U.S. wouldn’t need to apply for extensions if their training will end before September 2030.
But in a suit filed in mid-August, the academic groups alleged that the new rules violate the Administrative Procedure Act, a law that governs how agencies implement new regulations. The plaintiffs alleged that DHS didn’t give interested parties enough time to comment on the new rule, didn’t respond substantively to comments, and hasn’t clearly explained why the new policy is a rational and necessary response to alleged visa fraud.
The academic coalition warned in the suit that uncertainty around whether foreign researchers will be able to stay in the U.S. for the length of their training could prevent them from coming here in the first place. A NAFSA poll of more than 1,000 current students and postdocs found that nearly half of them would not have come to the U.S. under a fixed period of admission.
In its response, the Trump administration dismissed the findings of the poll as “uncertain and speculative.” The government also argued that the new rule was necessary to safeguard national security and would have minimal downside, and that if international enrollment does decline, it could be for reasons unrelated to the end of duration of status.
International researchers make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates and around 60% of postdoctoral researchers. The new policy would mean many of them would need to apply for a visa extension; the average biomedical Ph.D. takes five to six years to complete, and National Science Foundation data indicate that about a fifth of postdocs have worked in that role for more than six years.
