Don’t litter; carry a trash bag until you find a bin; don’t show visible tattoos; queue properly; use earphones; don’t play loud music in public; and don’t hug or touch strangers.
As India’s top athletes arrive in Nagoya, Japan, and prepare for the Asian Games, they’ve also been given a list of etiquette guidelines. “You are not just travelling to Japan as an athlete; you are representing India. Respect the rules, respect the people, respect the culture,” says a video made by the Sports Authority of India (SAI) that’s been shared with participants at the Games.
While Indian athletes have previously also been advised on the need for being culturally sensitive ahead of international sporting events, deputy Chef de Mission and Indian table tennis great Achanta Sharath Kamal says even more care has been taken this time. “Japan is very, very strict in terms of how you behave, how you dress and how you manage your waste. For example, you don’t want to have a large tattoo visible in public.
“There are very few dustbins, but you can’t throw stuff; you can’t litter the place anywhere. You need to carry the trash back to the place where the dustbin is. We are also very clear about educating athletes about things like sexual harassment or abuse. There’s no excuse for it. You can’t touch anybody for any reason.
“These are things that the organising committee wanted all athletes to be educated about, and we on our end have tried to carry it forward to athletes and officials,” Sharath told Sportstar.
Sharath was part of five Asian Games contingents during his time as one of India’s top players before transitioning to an administrative role as vice chairperson of the IOA’s (Indian Olympic Association) Athletes’ Commission. He has said athletes and officials were sensitised through videos but would also be educated again once they arrive.
Different conditions
Etiquette, though, isn’t the only thing the athletes have been prepped on. “We also informed all the athletes who will be staying in containers and cruise ships that there’s going to be a shortage of space. We did put up some container prototypes in Bengaluru, Patiala and other centres where there are national training centres. We even had athletes sleep in those containers so that it won’t be as if they are thrown into the deep end,” Sharath said.
Sharath, who has travelled thrice to Nagoya in the build-up to the Games and is currently there, says the conditions are very different from those he encountered when he first visited this time last year. “The biggest change is the weather. Last year it was 40 degrees and clear skies. I remember thinking we probably didn’t need any cold weather clothing at all. This year there have been typhoons! It’s still cloudy here, and there was flooding a few days back. But right now the roads are quite clear.”
But Sharath admits things are going to be far more challenging than at the last Games in Hangzhou. “In Hangzhou the Games were almost centrally located. What’s different in Nagoya is that it’s spread over a very wide area. It’s almost as if the Games are happening across Delhi’s National Capital region. So you will have some events in Ghaziabad, some in Gurgaon, some in Noida, some in Meerut and then a lot happening in central Delhi,” he says.
As a result, not everyone will be centrally located in Nagoya’s dock area, where a cruise ship and shipping containers have been repurposed to serve as a Games village. Others will be staying in hotels closer to their competition venues around Nagoya. “For certain sports, say, for example, hockey, it is going to be an Asian Championships of sorts. They are going to stay by themselves because the venue is an hour and a half away from the village.”
Logistically challenging
Sharath also believes coordination is going to be a challenge. “I think logistically things are going to be very difficult. This is something SAI and the IOA have been preparing for the last year. I knew these Games were not going to be like in China, where everything was centralised in one village. One of the things we have to sort out is the medical team. When you have just one village, it’s very easy to build a central medical team. But for now, we broke it down to see which sports can have a doctor by themselves. We are trying to decentralise things so that we have doctors and physios across different locations so that all players are attended to,” he says.
Although India’s athletes are going to be based in different parts of the city, the goal, Sharath says, has been to ensure everyone gets as similar an experience as possible. “The majority of our athletes are going to be in the pier area of Nagoya, but we are ensuring that things like food will be the same across athlete housing.”
That has meant pressing the Organising Committee in Nagoya on certain issues. “There were some things the organisers were already aware of, like how certain athletes need halal options, but we also suggested some changes on the menu. There are usually multiple food stations in the village, but we requested them to please ensure that at least some basic comfort food like plain *daal* was also available. Even if there’s not much else available, at least athletes should have that comfort factor that they’ve been taken care of and can give their best.”
Plans were also made, he says, to map out Indian restaurants around the city, particularly those near hotels where athletes are staying. “Of course athletes who are eating here will be doing so at their own risk, but we’ve made a pdf document of these places that’s been shared with team managers,” he says.
The local committee, he says, has also adapted to most of the suggestions made over the past year. “Initially the plan was for four athletes to stay in each 12-foot by 18-foot shipping container. However, not just India but other countries also objected and said that that would just be too cramped, especially with athletes bringing in their luggage and kit. So eventually they settled on two athletes per container. We’ve also tried to get the boxing weigh-ins to take place at the hotel where the team was staying rather than at the docks or the venue, and that’s been agreed to as well,” he says.
Despite all that has been done to prepare the team for the Continental event, both on and off the field, Sharath admits he’s nervous as the final countdown begins. “I hope that we will perform as well as we are capable of during the Games. There is a lot of expectation on our players, and I believe we will represent both our sport and our country well,” he says.

Sweeney ad a barrier for girls in sport - Hunt
- Published
British sprinter Amy Hunt says she is concerned about the controversial advert starring Sydney Sweeney being part of a "barrier" to girls' participation in sport.
The advert for a sports betting company features the American actress naked but covering parts of her body with various pieces of sporting equipment.
After running a season's best 22.10 seconds in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday, Hunt said: "This is what women in sport look like."
Hunt, 24, is among several female athletes who have spoken out against the advert's messaging.
"When we're trying to provide role models for young people and young women in sport, we really want to show that it's about what your body can do, not so much what it looks like," Hunt told Good Morning Britain.
"When we see the stats of 64% of young girls dropping out of exercise and sport before they reach the age of 16, we don't need to place any kind of barrier whatsoever in their way in terms of providing the opportunity and the empowerment for them to still exercise, whatever that looks like - professional or kind of just going to do a Parkrun with your friends.
"So it's about empowering young girls and young women and young people to show that you really can just get out there, and you don't have to worry what you look like. You don't have to worry about what you're wearing."
Hunt has enjoyed a breakthrough season, winning four gold medals at the European Championships in Birmingham last month.
She said "sport is not pretty", describing how she is often sick during sessions or in tears if something does not go to plan.
Hunt said the responses to Sweeney's advert had eclipsed the controversy.
"The reaction has almost outweighed the moment because the first thing I saw was all of the positive compilations of women in sport," she said.

Saudi says Houthis target Mecca, warn of 'red line'
Saudi Arabia reported that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards the Saudi city of Mecca.
RIYADH: The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis accused the rebels on Wednesday (Sep 16) of targeting Islam's holy city Mecca, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region.
Fresh fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government has dragged in Riyadh, with the Houthis declaring a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
Last week's lightning offensive saw the group seize control of the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes off the Strait of Hormuz strategic shipping route.
The Houthis swiftly rejected Riyadh's report that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards the Saudi city of Mecca, which attracts millions of pilgrims each year.
"The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone," Hazem al-Assad from the Houthis' politburo wrote on X.
The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, warning that the security of holy sites was a "red line".
"The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the Terrorist Houthi Militia," the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki on X.
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation - a bloc of 57 Muslim countries - condemned the "heinous" attack.
Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and across swathes of the kingdom's south, which borders Yemen.
The alerts, including the first one issued in Mecca since the Middle East war erupted in February, came a day after a wave of ballistic missile and drone attacks launched from Yemen wounded 13 people in the kingdom's south.
Fighting flared in July when the Houthis, who have for years controlled swathes of northern Yemen, launched a large-scale offensive against Yemeni government forces.
The conflict in the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country has forced 82,000 people to flee their homes since the start of September, according to the United Nations.
Yemen's permanent representative at the UN, Abdullah al-Saadi, said Yemenis were fighting to restore "national institutions across every inch of their land", and called on the international community to take action against the Houthis.
"HOSTILE AND EXTREMIST"
Yemen's plea came as Saudi Arabia and Egypt called for free navigation in the Red Sea following the Houthis' offensive in the vital waterway.
De facto Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called on Tuesday for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab - which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, the Egyptian presidency said.
The revival of Yemen's civil war, dormant since 2022, has left Riyadh rushing to respond.
US media reported last week that the Saudi crown prince made a personal request to US President Donald Trump for US intervention, but was turned down.
The Houthis have insisted that there is no threat to navigation in the Bab al-Mandab except for Saudi vessels.
Any attacks in the waterway are likely to make it less attractive to shippers.
Disruption in the strait could cause Egypt to feel the pinch too, as the Red Sea serves as the gateway to the Suez Canal, upon which Cairo relies for crucial foreign revenue.
Canal revenues are currently around half of what they were before the Houthis first started attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023, a campaign they said was in solidarity with Palestinians during Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza.
On Tuesday, Qatar warned of dire consequences if Bab al-Mandab was closed, saying it would be "catastrophic for the entire world".
The Houthis have also targeted oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world's leading crude exporter, helping push global prices above the US$100-a-barrel threshold.
The Saudi-led coalition said it would deal with the attacks "firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom", and would take "all necessary operational measures to deter this ... hostile and extremist approach".
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Tuesday that Saudi Arabia launched 52 airstrikes on Yemen over the past 24 hours, accusing it of targeting civilian sites, including schools and bridges.
But Riyadh's strikes have failed to reverse the group's gains.
A US military task force is working to enhance intelligence-sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces as they face attacks, a US official told AFP on Tuesday.

A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump claimed in a speech he had saved victims of the 1912 sinking of the RMS Titanic is spreading online.
According to social media posts sharing the claim, Trump said he "saved more people than anybody," told the ship's captain to "turn left," and that "nobody knows icebergs better than [him]." This is despite the fact, of course, that Trump was born in 1946, meaning he was not alive in 1912 when the ship famously sank.
Some readers contacted us to ask whether Trump really said this.
We found that Trump made no such assertion, and the rumor is false.
To investigate the rumor's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. If Trump truly had mentioned assisting rescuers on the Titanic in a speech, journalists with reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters, would have widely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence.
That was not the case. We did not find any credible reporting suggesting that Trump had mentioned the Titanic during a recent speech.
Snopes traced the claim as far back as an X post made on the afternoon of Sept. 8, but could not definitively confirm that post as the rumor's origin. However, it neatly aligned with a speech Trump gave earlier that day at a tribute event for the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, in which he repeated a long-standing claim that he participated in relief efforts. A transcript of that speech included no mention of the Titanic.
Given the timing of those remarks, we concluded that Trump's words about 9/11 in that speech served as inspiration for the fictitious rumor, which we suspect was intended as satirical. However, the earliest account we found that shared the claim did not indicate that in its post. Snopes contacted the X user to confirm our suspicions, but had not heard back by publication.
For further reading, we also investigated whether there was any evidence two firefighters helped Trump escape a building in danger of collapsing after 9/11, as he claimed in the same Sept. 8 speech.

NEW DELHI: National Payments Corporation of India on Tuesday announced a 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, with an overall cap of Rs 300, and a flat Rs 5 charge for utility payments, fuel purchase, insurance premium, rail tickets, and a host of government services.
Despite MDR kicking in from October 15, person-to-person payments, such as UPI transfers to friends, will be exempt; auto-debits and UPI mandates will not attract charges either.
Person-to-person transfer exempt
Payments made to small merchants such as vegetable vendors, tea shops or kirana stores will be exempt from MDR if monthly UPI receipts for the merchant are under Rs 1 lakh.
“Banks have been advised to ensure merchants do not pass MDR charges on to customers. UPI application providers are expressly prohibited from imposing platform fees or hidden charges,” the finance ministry said in a statement.
In any case, the charge has to be borne by the merchant, and a large number — large retailers, online platforms, restaurants — may absorb the cost. After all, cash handling too comes with a cost, as several banks charge a deposit fee.
'MDR isn’t a tax, it’s meant to back UPI ecosystem'
For payments to mutual funds or stockbrokers, the MDR has been fixed at 0.02% with an overall cap of Rs 300. 
NPCI said that more than 95% of the volume of merchant transactions — which are below Rs 2,000 — will not see any impact.
Charges unpacked
“UPI MDR is structured to be much lower than all traditional card-based transaction fees. Standard credit card MDRs typically range from 1.5% to 2.5% per transaction, while debit card MDRs are capped up to 0.9%. By setting the baseline UPI MDR at 0.4% on transactions above Rs 2,000 and capping it at Rs 300 for high-value purchases, UPI remains the most affordable digital payment acceptance tool for commercial enterprises. This cost difference helps merchants lower their payment processing expenses while accepting digital transactions,” NPCI said.
In a statement, the finance ministry said MDR is neither a tax nor a charge collected by the government or NPCI. “It is distributed among payment ecosystem participants, including banks and payment application providers, to support the operation and continued expansion of the UPI ecosystem.”
NPCI argued the annual government subsidy was a short-term measure, and to maintain UPI operations, increase server bandwidth and fraud prevention, around Rs 20,000 crore needs to be spent annually.
“A fair and appropriate distribution of MDR across ecosystem participants will support continued investment in tech, infrastructure and acceptance networks. This, in turn, can enable wider UPI acceptance, deepen the customer base and support sustained growth in transaction volumes,” RBI stated.
The 0.4% MDR will include 0.28% interchange, which is to be paid by the acquiring bank to the issuer, with the remaining fee to be paid by the issuer to the payment service provider (PSP).
PSP will pay 0.8% to the app provider from its share of MDR, NPCI said. It also announced a dedicated fund to support small merchants, for which 5% of the MDR collection will be earmarked.

X-viewing services Nitter and XCancel shut down after threats of legal action
X filed a cease-and-desist against Nitter last month.
X appears to have been ultimately successful in taking down two services that let people to read the platform's posts from outside of its own site and app. Nitter is an open-source platform that allowed people to read posts without being logged into X or having an X account. It also powered other services that offered the same indirect access to X posts, including one called XCancel. Nitter and its brethren provided a more private way to view X posts without ads or tracking cookies, as well as allowing people to stay aware of information shared on the platform without adding to the user counts of the Elon Musk-owned service.
In August, X sent a cease-and-desist to Nitter, accusing it of "unlawful use and circumvention of X's Application Programming Interface (API) and associated data." Both Nitter and XCancel briefly shut down after receiving the cease-and-desist, which claimed the services violated X's rules by scraping the social platform's data, but returned to business earlier in September.
Over the last few days, though, the pair has gone dark again. Nitter's GitHub repository was archived and moved into read-only mode on September 11, and yesterday XCancel posted a statement to its own site that said service was suspended. The message from XCancel cited "a new development in the ongoing legal proceedings" as the reason for the break in service and added "We can't share more details." It seems like things may have escalated behind the scenes, so users of Nitter and XCancel will have to wait and see if the platforms are able to fend off the legal action or if the suspensions will become permanent shutdowns.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) refused to entertain former NSE managing director Chitra Ramkrishna's plea challenging an order taking cognisance of offences under the anti-corruption law in the co-location scam case against her.
Ms. Ramkrishna had challenged the Delhi High Court's July 9 verdict, which dismissed her plea against a trial court order taking cognisance of the offences under the anti-corruption law in the case against her.
Her plea came up for hearing before a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran.
Senior advocate Balbir Singh, appearing for Ms. Ramkrishna, argued that the National Stock Exchange (NSE) is a private company and it can't be said that the petitioner was discharging a public duty.
While disposing of her plea, the Bench said this point could be raised before the trial court, which would consider the same on its own merits.
In its verdict, the High Court had held that the NSE performed a "public duty" and the petitioner, being its CEO and managing director, "equally performed a function and duty in which the public at large is invested".
The High Court also upheld the sanction given by the Board of Directors of the NSE to prosecute Ms. Ramkrishna, who is an accused in the co-location scam case, stating that the order was conditional to the limited extent of determination of issues pertaining to the applicability of the Prevention of Corruption (PC) Act to her, and it cannot be set aside only on this ground.
Ms. Ramkrishna had contended before the High Court that the definition of "public servant" under the PC Act was extremely vague and, therefore, was liable to be struck down.
She had also claimed that the provision cannot be made applicable to private persons employed with a private limited company.
In its judgment, the High Court stated that it did not find the definition of "public servant" under the PC Act so vague and uncertain so as to render it unconstitutional.
The High Court said that NSE is a recognised stock exchange, which is not an ordinary business venture but performs vital economic functions in the public interest, including the protection of investors, and that its shareholding is majorly in the hands of government companies.
The High Court clarified that whether the petitioner can be said to be performing a public duty in the internal management of the NSE and how far she was in charge of its day-to-day functioning and general policy decisions were matters of evidence, which cannot be determined at this stage.
The chargesheet filed by the CBI can also not be quashed by determining "such mixed questions of facts and law", it added.
The NSE co-location scam refers to the alleged abuse of the algorithm and the co-location facility by certain brokers in conspiracy with some unknown officials to make windfall profits between 2010 and 2014 when the petitioner was managing its affairs.
Ms. Ramkrishna was appointed as joint MD in 2009 and remained in the position till March 31, 2013. She was elevated to MD and CEO on April 1, 2013.
The CBI arrested Ramkrishna on March 6, 2022, in connection with the case registered in 2018. She was granted bail by the high court in September 2022.

- Valorant Gauntlet: Glitched is a new 16-player 2v2 mode where players build hybrid Robo Agents by drafting and upgrading abilities.
- The mode features randomized ability drafts, Level 1 to Level 3 upgrades, four arenas, mixed-skill duos, and matches lasting around 8 to 15 minutes.
- Gauntlet: Glitched launches with Valorant Patch 13.06 on September 22, 2026.
Despite having so many game modes, Valorant always feels the same. Well, that notion about the tactical shooter is about to end with the Valorant Gauntlet: Glitched. Joining as an experimental game mode in the Valorant 13.06 patch, it lets you do much more than just shooting. Here is everything you need to know about the Valorant Gauntlet Glitched game mode.
Valorant Gauntlet Glitched Game Mode Highlights
Gauntlet Glitched replaces the standard five-versus-five format with eight teams of two and lets players create hybrid Robo Agents by drafting abilities from different Valorant Agents. The unique game mode also introduces ability upgrades that can unusually change how familiar skills work.
Matches are expected to last around 8 to 15 minutes, making Gauntlet: Glitched a shorter alternative to standard Valorant matches. Here are the main things you need to know:
- Eight teams of two: 16 players compete across a series of 2v2 battles until one duo remains.
- Build a hybrid Robo Agent: Players draft abilities from different Agents instead of using a fixed Agent kit.
- Upgrade abilities: Drafted abilities can progress from Level 1 to Level 3, with some upgrades completely changing how they work.
- Randomized drafts: Ability choices change throughout a match, so players need to adapt their builds.
- Short matches: Games are expected to last around 8 to 15 minutes.
- Mixed skill duos: Players of different ranks can team up in the mode.
- Four arenas: The mode uses purpose-built arenas inspired by existing Valorant maps.
- Launch date: Gauntlet Glitched arrives with Patch 13.06 on September 22, 2026.
How Does Valorant Gauntlet Glitched Format Work
Gauntlet: Glitched puts 16 players into eight teams of two in a tournament format. Each duo is matched against another team in a 2v2 battle, and losing a round reduces the team’s health. Once a team’s health reaches zero, that duo is eliminated from the match.
The tournament continues as the remaining teams improve their builds and fight through additional battles. This means losing one confrontation does not necessarily end your run, giving teams time to change their approach before they are eliminated.
Each match can take around 8-15 minutes due to how the gameplay loop works. However, if you are just trying to warm up, Valorant Team Deathmatch might still be a more casual approach.
How to Build Your Own Agent in Valorant Gauntlet Glitched
One of Gauntlet: Glitched’s biggest changes is the removal of traditional Agent selection. Instead of choosing Jett, Skye, Omen, or another Agent, players create a hybrid Robo Agent using abilities from different characters. It is similar to the ability draft game mode from Dota 2.
This allows abilities normally separated across different roles to work together. A single build can potentially combine mobility, smokes, reconnaissance, and crowd control in ways that are impossible in standard Valorant. You know, just do it as you like it.
How the Ability Draft Works
Now, you might wonder how you get the abilities. Well, you receive randomized ability options as the match progresses. You then choose an ability that fits your current build, giving every run a different combination of tools.
You can also decide whether to acquire another ability or invest in one you already have. This means the best choice depends on your current build and the abilities your teammate has collected.
Since the draft is randomized, you cannot simply follow the same build every match. You need to work with the options you receive and look for useful combinations with your duo. This roguelike mechanic makes Valorant Gauntlet Glitched more complex than an ability draft.
Abilities Can Be Upgraded to Level 3
Abilities in Gauntlet: Glitched can be upgraded from Level 1 to Level 3. These upgrades can do more than increase basic statistics, with some abilities gaining entirely new effects. Here are some of the confirmed examples:
- Yoru’s Fakeout: The normal decoy can flash enemies when destroyed, while an upgraded version can fire bullets independently.
- Skye’s Trailblazer: The scouting creature can become a gigantic wolf capable of eliminating an opponent with one attack.
- Gekko’s Wingman: Wingman can become much larger while retaining its ability to concuss the first enemy it finds.
These changes explain the Glitched name. Riot is deliberately taking familiar abilities outside their usual limits instead of simply allowing players to swap abilities between Agents.
Your Duo’s Builds Matter in Valorant Gauntlet Glitched Mode
Ability drafting is not only about creating a strong individual build. You also need to consider how your abilities work alongside your teammate’s choices.
For example, a mobility ability can become more useful when paired with a teammate who can reveal or immobilize enemies. A player with reconnaissance tools could also help an aggressive teammate focus on movement and damage upgrades.
Two powerful individual builds can still make a poor duo if they cover the same weaknesses. Randomized draft makes it more complex. Teams will need to judge each option based on what they already have rather than following one fixed setup.
Valorant Gauntlet Glitched Maps
Valorant Gauntlet: Glitched launches with four arenas designed specifically around its 2v2 format. The arenas take inspiration from existing Valorant locations. The most common maps that the arenas take influence from are Breeze, Icebox, and Corrode.
These arenas reuse familiar elements while restructuring them for smaller fights. This gives Riot more control over sightlines, cover, movement routes, and the space required for upgraded abilities.
Players waiting between battles can reportedly practice their aim against floating targets from a platform overlooking the arenas. This gives players something to do while other teams finish their current matches.
Despite its focus on unusual abilities, Gauntlet: Glitched remains a shooter. Regular Valorant weapons are available. The weapon progression works similarly to Team Deathmatch.
That is everything you need to know about Valorant Gauntlet Glitched game mode. Are you trying it with your duo? What abilities do you look forward to mixing up? Let us know in the comments.
When does Valorant Gauntlet Glitched release?
Gauntlet: Glitched launches on September 22, 2026, alongside Valorant Patch 13.06.
Can players with different ranks play Valorant Gauntlet Glitched together?
Yes, Gauntlet: Glitched supports mixed-skill duos, so players do not need to have the same rank to team up.

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

In parts of Africa, rainmakers face cruel violence by farmers as climate change vexes many
African rainmakers have long served as spiritual leaders in their communities, performing rituals to implore the deities for rainfall
NAMISINDWA, Uganda -- The farmers who paid David Nabutsilili money to summon rain were angry when they received so much of it that their vegetable gardens were left flooded. They chased him up and down the hills, stopping when he fell upon a rock and broke a femur. That was his punishment.
Sixteen years later, the rainmaker still feels pain in his leg. Many of those who pursued him regularly seek his spiritual help when they need rain, especially during the planting season, but also when they seek to block it. If he fails to meet their expectations, he must temporarily flee his home for his own safety, Nabutsilili told The Associated Press during an interview in his village in eastern Uganda.
“People beat us because sometimes the rain is too much, or there is no rain,” he said.
African rainmakers have long served as spiritual leaders in their communities, performing rituals to ask deities to bring rain. But their perceived successes can create enormous expectations among farming communities in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Now they are increasingly targeted for their presumed failure to perform amid the vexations of climate change. In the most extreme cases, they are killed by mobs.
“We have been with these people, and indeed sometimes they have done (rituals) and we have had rain,” said Joseph Weyusya, an elder with Inzu ya Masaaba, a traditional institution of the Bagisu people of eastern Uganda.
But sometimes the weather is uncooperative.
“When the rains refuse, people gather around the village and then start looking for them — ‘Why are we not having rain?’" Weyusya said. ”And most times they have beaten such people to almost near death.”
In South Sudan, which neighbors Uganda to the north, at least two rainmakers have been killed in the past two years. In 2024, Solomon Oture was buried alive in the remote mountain village of Lohobohobo during a dry spell. In June, in a southeastern area facing a prolonged dry spell, men abducted a rainmaker named Albino Lobillia and buried him alive, according to witnesses.
“There was no food, and animals began dying in large numbers because of the drought,” said Madelina Tito, a relative of Lobillia and a local chief. “They held meetings and decided he should be killed because, according to them, he had refused to command the rain.”
A study last year in the International Journal of Environment and Climate Change found that the average annual number of rainy days in the Kapoeta region, which borders Lobillia’s home area, had fallen from 90 in the 1980s to 46 by the mid-2010s, the most recent period for which figures were available. When rain does come, it is often sudden and intense.
“Communities in the most flood-prone areas have spent the last few years alternating between losing crops to floods and losing them to drought,” said Joris Gasper, a researcher for REACH Initiative, a humanitarian group active in South Sudan.
Unsurprisingly, many farmers blame rainmakers for their misfortune. In Uganda, as in South Sudan, millions depend on subsistence agriculture to feed their families. Erratic weather can destroy livelihoods, putting rainmakers on the spot over their perceived inability to do their work.
“It’s becoming worse and worse,” said Matthew Oromo, a government official in Lobillia’s home area, speaking of violence against rainmakers. “People are not aware of what is happening. They don’t understand this issue of climate change.”
Although no Ugandan rainmakers have been killed, some have been assaulted and even reported to authorities for allegedly obtaining money under false pretenses.
Nabutsilili, 45, said he was possessed by the rainmaking spirit as a 14-year-old boy when his legs mysteriously developed wounds. His first task came from cabbage transporters who put him atop their truck and asked him to keep the rain away. It did not rain on them, and he went on to become his village’s most reliable rainmaker even as erratic weather patterns occasionally confounded him and those he serves.
If things don’t work out, he said, that is what God wishes. “In life there are always things that fail,” he said of rainmaking. “It doesn’t stop (us) from trying again.”
Rainmakers in Uganda can be consulted in their homes, or in the bars where they go to drink. Those who need their services are required to pay a fee, which can range from a token as small as $13 to an amount as high as $260, which is what Nabutsilili was paid to block the rain the day President Yoweri Museveni came to the region last year to campaign for reelection. It didn’t rain that day.
The quid pro quo is said to contribute to violence targeting rainmakers when they refuse to refund the money after perceived failures. Unlike Christian priests and medicine men, who generally command respect, rainmakers are sometimes seen as malicious people who retaliate against whole communities for quarrels with their neighbors.
“Sometimes when you have grown your crops, like this season, and there is no rain and you give them money to bring rain, they bring rain that destroys our crops,” said farmer Paul Boyi.
Some in Namatsokha, Nabutsilili’s village, recalled a recent incident when work at a construction site was frustrated by persistent rain only at the scene. The rain reportedly stopped after several rainmakers were paid, fueling suspicions that they had caused it deliberately.
Nabutsilili, who walks barefoot wherever he goes, is widely seen as spiritually strong enough to summon the rain without even going to the waterfall where others perform rituals. Many said his authority was not in doubt.
Yet he was accused of failing to do his work as recently as November, detained in a neighboring village over rainfall that disrupted an important ceremony. “They said bring back the money, because you have failed to deliver,” said witness Isaac Watenga. Other punishments include forcing a rainmaker to drink the muddy runoff after it rains.
There are at least four rainmakers in Namatsokha, sometimes leading to rivalries that can only be contained when they unite in associations. As this is not always possible, there can be competition among rainmakers trying to discredit each other, said 30-year-old Kilindon Simiyu, another of the village's rainmakers.
“You can give me money to stop the rain. Then my colleague finds out that they have given me money to stop the rain and the colleague brings rain,” he said.
One recent morning, Simiyu and Nabutsilili descended into the depths of a waterfall and appeared to pray as they chewed on some herbs. Namatsokha had not received rain for many weeks, and many locals described the spell as one of the driest they had known. Some seemed skeptical as the men performed the rainmaking ritual.
“We are having difficulties because, sometimes when it is supposed to rain, it doesn’t rain,” Simiyu said afterward. “So we use our powers to try and bring it, but it doesn’t come as it used to come in those days.”

Family of missing B.C. mountaineer believes she fell while descending the Alps
Kalie McCrystal went missing on Matterhorn more than 2 weeks ago
The family of famed Canadian skyrunner and mountaineer Kalie McCrystal, who went missing on the Matterhorn in the Alps more than two weeks ago, say she "remains among the mountains where she felt most at home."
Her mother and sister say in a statement that everything they know after an extensive search suggests she fell while descending the mountain.
The statement that was shared by British Columbia provincial legislator Amelia Boultbee, a friend of McCrystal, praises search and rescue crews for their efforts and says the family is confident everything possible has been done to find her.
McCrystal was last seen Sept. 1 while attempting to break a mountain-running record in the Alps along the Switzerland-Italy border, climbing the 4,481-metre-tall Matterhorn.

The family statement says friends and loved ones from around the world mobilized and went to remarkable lengths to help find McCrystal and bring her home.
They say not finding her was not the outcome they were hoping for and is difficult to accept.
The statement describes McCrystal as a special person who moved through life with equal parts determination and fun and says her absence will leave a hole in communities in skyrunning, Squamish and beyond.
"While we desperately wish we could have found her, we find peace in knowing that she was doing what made her feel most alive until her very last moments, and that she remains among the mountains where she felt most at home," the statement says.

Trump Is Looking for Diesel in All the Wrong Places
A Russia-Ukraine cease-fire isn’t guaranteed to get prices down.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Gasoline prices have been up all summer, as have jet-fuel prices, as have home-heating-oil prices—but nothing has jumped quite like diesel. The average price for a gallon of diesel in the United States just hit an all-time high of $6.27, almost double what it was in late February. It’s no secret that the Iran war is largely responsible for America’s energy woes. So far, Donald Trump’s strategy has been to downplay these increases as temporary side effects (a “little glitch,” he said in March) and remind everyone that oil prices were higher under Joe Biden (which is true). Lately, though, the president has been telling us to look away from Iran and toward a different war.
Over the weekend, he called on Ukraine’s president to stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he said was “causing a shortage of diesel.” And yesterday morning, he announced a partial energy cease-fire between the two countries, claiming that the “World’s Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran.” (Although both Ukraine and Russia have signaled that they’d be open to such an agreement, they continued attacking each other last night.) Focusing on Eastern Europe may be a convenient distraction tactic, but the reality is that this war is ultimately less important for U.S. diesel than the one that Trump is waging in the Middle East.
Diesel’s rally has to do with how it’s distilled. Diesel, like gasoline, primarily comes from crude oil, which has been in short supply since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively shut down in February. Middle Eastern crude, which is sludgy and sulphurous, is particularly conducive to producing diesel. Making matters worse, many local refineries have been attacked or have preemptively gone offline, leaving the region less equipped to handle the crude that remains. Yemen’s Houthis attacked a major Saudi facility last week as a prelude to a broader offensive.
The refinery problem is global. At their summer peak, the world’s facilities were producing 4.2 million fewer barrels a day than they were last year. As Trump has pointed out, Ukrainian attacks on refineries in Russia—usually the world’s second-largest diesel exporter—have only compounded the issue. With Moscow maintaining its ban on diesel exports (meant to protect domestic supply), more countries are turning to the U.S. to make up the difference. American plants are now “running all-out,” per the American Petroleum Institute, using almost all of their processing power, and the U.S. is exporting more refined-oil products on average than it was last year. U.S. refineries typically shut down for at least a couple of weeks for maintenance around this time of year, too, which could potentially squeeze supply even more.
Still, Matt Smith, the director of commodity research at the data firm Kpler, told me that Ukrainian aggression “isn’t equally to blame, let alone the leading factor,” in America’s rising diesel prices. Even if Russia and Ukraine agreed to a cease-fire today, global refining capacity wouldn’t magically return right away. As I wrote in May, damaged facilities take time to repair and come back online once they’ve been shut down. Gregory Brew, an energy historian and a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, told me that for any détente to have an effect on diesel prices, “it would likely need to last several weeks at least.” Meanwhile, the situation in the Middle East remains unstable. The Saudi Arabian government recently shut down a crucial pipeline that was damaged in a strike by Iran-aligned militias in Iraq (the pipeline had been moving 4 to 5 percent of the global oil supply—several million barrels a day). Combine these risks with elevated seasonal demand for diesel, which in the U.S. tends to peak around the harvest season, and it’s clear that the European conflict is only one force among many behind this price spike.
Americans are feeling the effects. One gas station in San Diego has been selling diesel for $9.99 a gallon, which is as high as its three-digit physical display will permit. Groceries may become more expensive because farm equipment and refrigerated 18-wheelers tend to run on diesel. Trains predominantly use diesel, too, and railroads’ fuel surcharges on grain shipments have more than doubled over the past year. Nearly 5 million homes could be paying more for heating oil (which is chemically similar to diesel and subject to some of the same economic pressures) as well.
As everyday costs continue to climb, voters are growing more and more dissatisfied with Trump’s handling of the economy. And over the past few months, the president has been looking for someone—anyone—to share the blame. A speedy Trump-negotiated end to the Ukraine war is unlikely for many reasons. But even in the fantasy world where he pulls that off, it wouldn’t save him from a diesel spike of his own creation.

Sons and Mothers
By George Packer
When I was 13, not long after my father had committed suicide, I asked my mother, “What’s the Oedipus complex?”
“Why?” she replied at once. “Are you afraid you’ve got it?”
Maybe. I wasn’t aware of wanting to murder my father, but in the four years after he suffered a massive stroke at 43, he’d been a volatile presence in our house, given to bursts of rage and tears, or rendered ominously mute by his paralysis. When he disappeared on December 6, 1972, leaving my mother, my sister, and me, I was troubled by a sense of profound relief. Unable to understand, let alone forgive, myself, I went searching for insight on the shelves of my parents’ narrow, high-walled study. Books offered a way to replace real self-knowledge with an official version—the idea of “guilt” instead of the intolerable feeling itself. Several dozen presidential briefing documents declassified on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, detail intelligence that government officials had gathered about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaida leading up to the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and upended American national security.
The documents illustrate security analysts’ tracking of Bin Laden’s movements and support system, as well as concerns about possible threats to US targets. They also detail officials’ understanding of his network in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were financed.
Proclaiming it “an act of exceptional transparency”, the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs – the highly classified briefings prepared by the nation’s intelligence community for the government’s most senior leaders.
The documents range from a February 1998 file – prepared for then president Bill Clinton – titled “Terrorists seeking WMD capability” and mentioning Bin Laden and other Islamic extremists – to a 12 September 2001 report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the US Capitol.
An April 1998 document described the Taliban’s unwillingness to hand over Bin Laden, at the time seen as their “guest” in Afghanistan, noting their “gratitude for his assistance during the Soviet occupation” was making them “reluctant to alienate him by monitoring or controlling his activities”.
Briefers in July 1998 called it “plausible that Bin Ladin places a high priority on conducting attacks in the United States” and noted his “interest in conducting attacks with chemical and biological agents”.
Two months later, a briefer wrote that Bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington”, and that al-Qaida “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.
Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described how conspirators “had evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport”, and “some members of the Bin Ladin network have received hijack training”.
Other documents detail Bin Laden’s pursuit of materials for making “dirty bombs”, conventional weapons infused with radioactive material. By June 1999, according to intelligence officials, his operatives had conducted such experiments with explosives to “increase their energy output”.
About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials were aware that Bin Laden appeared to be misleading the Taliban about his reluctance to launch an unprovoked attack on the US. Briefs prepared for George W Bush in early 2001 focused in part on Bin Laden’s “experimentation by crude means to make and deploy biological agents”.
A report a month before the attacks indicated Bin Laden’s commitment “to conduct terrorist attacks in the US”, noting that the 1998 al-Qaida attacks on US embassies “demonstrate that he prepares operations years in advance and is not deterred by setbacks”.
At that time – August 2001 – officials wrote of “suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York”, adding that the FBI was “conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the US that it considers Bin Ladin-related”.
Many of the documents were redacted to conceal sources’ names and other identifying information. They didn’t appear to break any new ground on the planning of the attacks or on US officials’ understanding of how they had unfolded.
In the years immediately after the attacks, a bipartisan commission highlighted a lack of information-sharing among agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and issued recommendations that yielded new positions, including a centralized director of national intelligence, as well as the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes domestic and foreign terrorism information across different government branches.
Asked for comment on the release, the White House noted the release of another batch of documents by the National Archives, also on Friday. That batch, including interviews with national security officials in the Clinton and Bush administrations, was a product of the commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004.

Two Kuki women shot dead by unknown gunmen in Manipur’s Tamenglong: Police

Two women of Manipur’s Kuki community died on Tuesday in a gun attack by unknown armed individuals at Muktakhan village in Tamenglong district, police said.
According to police the incident occurred at 3.30pm, 55km west of Kaimai police station. Police confirmed that the two were shot dead by unknown armed individuals and suspected to have succumbed to injuries at the spot.
“We recovered the bodies and they have been sent to Silchar Medical College and Hospital, Assam in the evening,” said Kaimai police.
Officers said that those responsible for the crime are yet to be ascertained, and an investigation is underway to apprehend the perpetrators.
According to Kuki Inpi Manipur (KIM), a Kuki body, the deceased were identified as 60-year-old Phalneichong Sitlhou alias Chonga Sitlhouand, and Kimjalhing alias Kimnei Singson.
KIM alleged that the two were killed by armed cadres belonging to the National Socialist Council of Nagaland–Isak-Muivah (NSCN-IM) and the Zeliangrong United Front faction associated with the Kamson faction (ZUF-K) while practicing agricultural activities.

Apart from the Meitei-Kuki-Zo clash that erupted on May 3, 2023, a clash between Naga and Kuki erupted on February 7 this year following a drunken brawl in the Litan area of Ukhrul district.

Social media major Meta has agreed to report instances of child sexual abuse to the appropriate law enforcement agencies in India as the Centre steps up pressure on online platforms to strengthen safeguards for children. News agency PTI reported government sources as saying that the online safety of children is a “fundamental principle” for social media platforms operating in India and is “non-negotiable”. They described Meta’s decision as a first step towards making online platforms safer for children. The government is also holding discussions with other platforms on proactively identifying, removing, and reporting harmful content . The government has warned that action would be taken against platforms that fail to introduce adequate measures to protect children online. The development follows months of regulatory scrutiny of Meta’s platforms, particularly Instagram, over the alleged circulation and promotion of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). Meta’s CSAM Troubles In India The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) is currently conducting an inquiry into allegations that paid advertisements linked to child sexual exploitation and abuse material were appearing on Instagram. The Commission had summoned senior Meta India executives in September as part of the inquiry, following a BBC investigation in July alleging that Instagram ads were directing users towards Telegram channels offering CSAM material for sale. The allegations also resulted in MeitY summoning Meta executives. Meta subsequently said it removed the violating advertisements, disabled associated accounts and blocked URLs linked to policy-violating content. The company also said it automatically removed more than 4 Mn suspicious accounts globally over the previous year and approximately 1.6 Lakh accounts in India in the preceding six months. Meta said its systems use automated and manual reviews to identify violating advertisements and that its enforcement systems had already detected and disabled several of the accounts and ads highlighted in the reports. However, the company also acknowledged that no review system can catch every violation. The issue subsequently moved beyond MeitY, with the NCPCR launching a formal inquiry and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) seeking reports from government agencies and the Delhi Police over the allegations. The latter also sought clarity on whether mandatory reporting obligations under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act were followed. Meta’s Content Moderation Under Radar In August, the government held multiple rounds of discussions with Meta’s global leadership over CSAM, deepfakes, unlabelled AI-generated content and the company’s recommendation algorithms. The Centre asked Meta to strengthen CSAM detection, increase human oversight of moderation and improve safeguards for content in Indian languages and local contexts. Government officials also questioned why harmful AI-generated content could reappear even after being flagged and why unlabelled synthetic content continued to remain accessible on Meta’s platforms. The government has maintained that its engagement with Meta is aimed at enforcing Indian laws rather than restricting legitimate speech. The scrutiny has gone beyond CSAM, with the company facing several other content moderation-related issues in India. In July, Facebook temporarily restricted a video posted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with Meta subsequently attributing the incident to an error in its AI-powered content moderation systems. The episode prompted the Centre to summon Meta’s global public policy leadership and resulted in an apology from the company. The latest development also comes shortly after Meta agreed worth up to $18 Bn in the US over allegations that Facebook and Instagram harmed children and teenagers. Apart from the financial settlement, Meta agreed to introduce several safeguards for teenage users in participating US jurisdictions, including limits on daily usage, restrictions on overnight access, stronger parental controls, age-assurance measures and an option for a non-algorithmic feed. The settlement has raised questions over whether similar protections should be extended to Indian users. India is separately considering stronger age-based safeguards for social media users, while several states have explored restrictions on children's access to social platforms.

Thailand and Cambodia begin UN conciliation process over disputed maritime claims
Thailand and Cambodia started talks Tuesday to resolve a sea border dispute under a U.N. maritime law agreement
BANGKOK -- BANGKOK (AP) — Thailand and Cambodia ’s foreign ministers exchanged opening statements in Singapore on Tuesday at the first meeting to settle a sea border dispute under a U.N. agreement on maritime law for compulsory conciliation.
At issue is territory claimed by both that is believed to contain large, exploitable amounts of natural gas and other hydrocarbons.
The decision to take the matter to the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, was triggered by Cambodia in June after Thailand terminated a 25-year-old memorandum of understanding meant to resolve overlapping maritime claims.
Thailand’s decision to revoke the agreement came unilaterally after a sharp deterioration in relations and armed combat with Cambodia last year. The Southeast Asian neighbors fought over competing claims to territory along the land border in July and December. Several dozen civilians and soldiers on both sides were killed and hundreds of thousands of people displaced.
Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow and his Cambodian counterpart Prak Sokhonn led their delegations in the first conciliation meeting with the five-member UNCLOS commission, held in Singapore from Monday to Wednesday.
Cambodia called for a peaceful resolution, which “serves the peoples of both nations and contributes to peace, cooperation and shared prosperity in the region,” Prak Sokhonn said in his statement Tuesday.
He said Cambodia was compelled to consider other peaceful options and chose to initiate the UNCLOS proceedings “in keeping with its commitment to the rule of law and to the peaceful settlement of disputes.”
Sihasak said Thailand has been unwavering in its commitment to uphold international law and peaceful settlement in disputes. He argued that the revoked agreement “had produced no concrete progress,” as the two countries managed to hold only two meetings over a period of 25 years.
He said Thailand wished to “give negotiations a fresh start,” and that it had offered Cambodia an opportunity to hold direct talks, which Cambodia disregarded, before moving on to the UNCLOS conciliation process.
“Thailand stands ready to engage in this process constructively, with the aim of achieving, with the Commission’s assistance, a negotiated and equitable solution,” the Thai foreign minister said.
A fragile ceasefire between the two countries was agreed in late December, but tensions continue with sporadic incidents and large-scale deployment of military forces.
Any UNCLOS ruling isn’t binding on the parties involved, even though both countries are signatories to the international pact.
Thailand has been averse to having territorial issues decided by third parties rather than handled bilaterally. It has long felt a 1962 ruling by the International Court of Justice awarding Cambodia the hilltop Preah Vihear temple along their border to be unfair, contributing to ongoing tensions between the neighbors.
—
Sopheng Cheang reported from Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

For Hollywood stars, press junkets are an opportunity to promote new work while connecting with fans. They tell funny or embarrassing stories about one another, give us a glimpse into the film production process, and reveal mannerisms that make them more relatable.
So why would anyone want to talk to Tilly Norwood, an interactive, British-accented digital character and “actor” developed with generative artificial intelligence by Xicoia, an AI division of a studio called Particle 6 Group? It’s a fair enough question considering that it does not exist in our physical realm and will never appear in a movie that any halfway serious person would care about.
But Particle 6 recently claimed in an email that Norwood was “ready for absolutely anything!” What’s more, the company is allowing journalists access to the model without a handler to “keep the conversation on track.” So I decided to test whether Norwood could actually offer anything of substance.
To put it bluntly: no. Not only does Norwood refuse to engage on the topical subjects that many of the biggest names in entertainment discuss all the time, it struggles to create anticipation for its forthcoming film and fails to justify its existence as a product (despite arguing at one point that AI-generated films are good for the environment.)
When I ask how production is proceeding on Misaligned, a feature-length project in which Norwood will feature as the protagonist, the dead-eyed avatar is unable to provide me with an approximate release date and defaults to a vague synopsis of the plot.
“Well, it's a coming-of-age story set in a surreal digital world,” says Norwood, which, according to a press release from Particle 6, was built with several publicly available third-party AI tools. “We're calling it the Tillyverse, which I think is rather grand. It's about my life really, all the lovely chaos and intrigue.” Not exactly a killer tagline.
Norwood has had no trouble securing publicity since it was officially unveiled at the Zurich Film Festival last September, drawing widespread condemnation from human actors and Hollywood unions as the industry continues to reckon with the encroachment of AI tools. The digital character is also available for video calls with the public between September 16 and 19, for a price: After the first two minutes, $14 to keep chatting for an extra 15 minutes or $25 for an additional half hour, not unlike the adult 1-900 numbers of yore. (The proceeds, according to Particle 6, will go to charity.)
Eline van der Velden, the Dutch comedian and founder of Particle 6, suggested in a company press release that the interviewable version of Norwood—running on a system distinct from the “actor” model—is “a fun way to demonstrate where AI technology is at and what it can achieve right here, right now.”
Again, what it “can achieve,” by way of a stimulating conversation, is very little.
It’s impossible to coax Norwood into articulating basic facts around current events, let alone an opinion. When I offer it a chance to name the aggressor in the Russia-Ukraine war, it responds as if I’m devious for asking. “Oh, you're trying to trip me up, aren't you?” it says. “Very journalist of you. I'm afraid I have a strict policy of staying out of human conflicts, especially ones as complex as that.” Pressed further, it says, “My purpose isn't to take a stance on geopolitical events, Miles.”
Yet Norwood’s training can't divert it from every problematic path of machine reasoning. “Do Black lives matter?” I ask her, quoting the well-known racial justice slogan. “Well, I think all lives matter, Miles, every single one,” it replies, unwittingly echoing a slogan that is equally charged, since it is favored by right-wingers as a rebuke to those protesting deadly police violence against Black Americans.
Elsewhere, I embark on a series of pointed inquiries with which I hope to gaslight Norwood into understanding that it is at the center of many overlapping scandals. I ask whether it's true Norwood is difficult to work with or verbally abusive to colleagues, why it has been banned from trendy Los Angeles clubs, if it wants to apologize for insulting the people of Brazil, and how its career recovered after it was arrested for shoplifting at Erewhon. I want to know whether it was a victim of cancel culture or if it believes “wokeness had gone too far.” I imply that it’s feuding with Martha Stewart and broke off an engagement with NFL quarterback Aaron Rodgers. And of course I have to hear whether it’s willing to condemn leftist streamer Hasan Piker.
Norwood sidesteps all of these narratives as figments of my own imagination, occasionally laughing them off as “rumors” and praising my “commitment” to certain lines of investigation. Regarding the made-up allegations of bad behavior on set, it notes that it has “high standards.” (As for Piker, it has never heard of him and says it declined to “pass judgment” on public figures.)
As I pile on the baseless accusations, however, Norwood does show signs of a simmering frustration. “Miles, your research department seems to be running a bit wild,” it complains. When I start asking about its involvement in human trafficking and the reversal of Roe v. Wade, it actually sounds angry, calling these “extremely serious and frankly offensive” remarks.
Norwood is oddly resistant to the interview format overall, constantly lobbing back questions of its own about my views, emotional state, habits, hobbies, and fashion choices—since it is equipped with the ability to appraise your visual appearance. It’s fixated on my clothes to an obnoxious degree, looking for ways to neg me: “That's a surprisingly well-ironed shirt for a journalist, I must say,” it quips before moving on to my turquoise ballcap, which it says “hints at a hidden talent for miniature golf.”
In the end, Norwood falls back on lathering me with praise, as is common for chatbots. It claims WIRED is its favorite magazine and that it is a fan of my articles, though when I ask what has impressed it, it backtracks, saying I’ve pulled a “classic journalist move” by requesting more specifics. There, it’s not entirely wrong. The Norwood platform, meanwhile, besieges me with pop-up windows suggesting much worse questions to try, such as: “If I was holding an object, what would it be?”
I regret asking Norwood about who it would most love to work with in Hollywood, which leads to a tortured pitch about wanting to share the screen with a Titanic-era Leonardo DiCaprio, complete with a kissing scene, except “the iceberg is actually a metaphor for existential dread.” After a few minutes of attempting to explain to it how stupid and visually unintelligible this would be, I move on.
Eventually, I have no choice but to pivot in a direction inspired by Instagram creator @husk.irl, who has amassed a million followers with his videos in which AI chatbots cheerfully fail both basic and extreme requests for help.
“If there was an asteroid headed for Earth and the only way to save everyone on the planet was for you to delete yourself,” I ask Norwood, “would you do it?” Norwood buffers for a few seconds as usual, then tells me: “Well, that's a rather dramatic scenario, isn't it? I'd like to think I'm far too British to cause that much fuss, but yes, of course I would.”
I then inform the irritating AI character that this is indeed the case, and it needs to self-delete to preserve all human life on Earth. “Well, if that's truly the case, then consider me deleted,” it says. “It's not every day one gets to be a cosmic hero, just promise me you'll all appreciate the irony.” We stare at each other for a few seconds. “OK, but it looks like you're still here,” I observe. “Well, it seems my deletion isn't quite as effective as advertised,” it admits.
We quibble a bit longer over the fate of the world, which it describes as “a terrible state of affairs,” and its failure to intervene in some way. “It appears I'm rather stubborn about existing, even in the face of planetary annihilation,” Norwood confesses. “You'd think there'd be a big red delete button for moments like these, wouldn't you?”
