Carney's European address will find an eager audience in a continent rattled by Trump
PM to speak at European Parliament as Canada, EU appear poised to move closer
One of the drawbacks of giving a historic speech like the one that Prime Minister Mark Carney gave in Davos, Switzerland, in January is that people expect an encore every time you speak.
The Carney government has been at pains to lower expectations for anyone who's hoping for another worldwide viral moment when Carney addresses the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday morning.
There will be nothing that will really surprise those who've been following the prime minister's publicly expressed thinking, or the progress of the growing rapprochement between Canada and the European Union, one senior government official told CBC News.
And yet neither the Canadians nor the Europeans are downplaying the large expectations they have for an expanded EU-Canada alliance that goes far beyond the current Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
Carney 'nailed it' at Davos: EU committee chair
"Europeans looked very positively on him and on that speech in Davos," said Sven Simon, chair of the European Parliament's committee on constitutional affairs. "He nailed it. He put it really in the right direction. I think in those uncertain times, we, both the Europeans and Canadians, have a huge interest in closer co-operation."
Carney himself, while stressing that this trip is not the grand finale of a grand bargain, told Bloomberg News that he expects great things in the future.
"It's an exciting time. Look, it's not going to be solved this week in Strasbourg. This, to be clear, it's the start of a process, but it's the start of a high-ambition process."
All indications are that both sides are heavily focused on the Canada-EU Summit scheduled for Oct. 29-30.
"I think that there is a significant step to be done in October because both parties would like to enhance or to elevate their relationship," EU Ambassador to Canada Geneviève Tuts told CBC's Power and Politics.
"We want to reimagine the relationship between the EU and Canada."
Rattled Europeans
Hans-Gert Pöttering, a former president of the European Parliament who visited Canada last week, told CBC News that the Trump administration's treatment of Canada had shocked Europeans.
"There is somebody who wants to make Canada the 51st state of the United States. And all these crazy ideas, I think are the basis that we see how important Canada is for us," he said.
Both Canadian and European officials often say they want to work with "like-minded" allies, and for the Canadians, "like-minded" has increasingly come to mean "European," while for Europeans, it increasingly means "Canadian."
Both sides have poured cold water on any talk of Canada joining the EU. The Canadians say they aren't interested in the basic formula of EU membership under which countries give up some sovereignty in return for access.
Canada is engaging with Europe in order to strengthen its sovereignty, not to dilute it, a senior official told CBC News.
The same official said that reporting in the Wall Street Journal that suggested Canada was looking to reproduce arrangements that non-EU members such as Norway have with the union — which do involve some concessions on sovereignty — are false.
No name yet to define the relationship
European officials also say they envision an alliance between the EU and Canada, rather than an amalgamation. But the partnership they envision would go further than the current relationship with the United Kingdom.
Germany's David McAllister, who chairs the foreign affairs committee of the European Parliament, told CBC News that neither side had yet paid much attention to labels — but stressed the EU is not trying to get Canada to surrender sovereignty
On the contrary, McAllister, who trained in Manitoba at CFB Shiloh as a young soldier in the German Army, said Europe was willing to collaborate with Canada to protect itself from U.S. threats.
- What we know about Carney's push for a 'unique alliance' with the EU
- AnalysisZelenskyy's comparison of Canada to Ukraine is imperfect — but it matters
"We in Europe understand that threats and economic pressure against an ally simply damaged the trust which we need among transatlantic allies," he said. "That's why the U.S.-Canadian dispute, which President Trump is responsible for, has received such wide media coverage all over Europe."
On the trade front, 99 per cent of commerce between Canada and the European Union is already tariff-free. Both sides speak about the importance of getting 10 holdout countries, including France and Italy, to ratify CETA, but that's mostly symbolic.
Canada is also already integrated into two vital pan-European projects: the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program that provides low-interest loans for joint military procurement and the Horizon program that funds scientific research.
Untapped possibilities
But both sides say there are areas of co-operation that remain under-exploited or even unexplored.
There have been signs of openness to increased labour mobility, although it's very unlikely that would go as far as the full freedom of movement that exists in the EU.
Two areas appear to be of greatest interest. The first is to use the free trade framework that already exists to build a genuine synergy between Canada's natural resource and energy wealth, and Europe's large market and manufacturing capacity, to the benefit of both economies.
CETA "is actually a fantastic framework, but we are not fully using it either in Europe or in Canada," said Tobias Cremer, who sits on the foreign affairs and defence committees of the European Parliament.
"A lot of our especially medium- and small-sized companies don't even know the potential we have. Canada has all this potential, but the infrastructure for instance isn't actually set up yet to go across the Atlantic."
- Mark Carney to meet with Emmanuel Macron in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon
- European Parliament to open Ottawa office as Carney seeks 'unique alliance' with EU
Both Carney and the Europeans often point out that Europe — large and rich but resource poor — and Canada — lightly populated but resource and energy-rich — complement one another naturally. That is not always as evident in the U.S.-Canada relationship where, in any case, the current U.S. administration views Canada more as a rival than a partner.
A second avenue is to combine forces in sovereignty-protecting projects that would be difficult for Canada to do on its own.
In his interview with Bloomberg, Carney said that "sovereignty is determined by where you stand in a series of strategic capabilities in space, obviously in AI, in sovereign computing, in critical minerals, in energy."
Carney also mentioned financial payments as a potential vulnerability, one of "those interconnections, that integration [that] can be used as leverage against you."
China has long viewed dependence on the U.S. dollar and the U.S.-based SWIFT system for international payments as a weakness, and sought to "de-dollarize" not only its bond holdings but also its trade with other countries. India, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and the U.A.E. have all set up new facilities for trading payments to avoid the dollar and go around U.S. banks, and increasingly, traditional U.S. allies are thinking along the same lines.
The U.S. would likely perceive any move by Canada and Europe to cut SWIFT out of their trading arrangements as another threat to a U.S. dollar that is already losing ground as the world's go-to currency for trading and saving.
Planning and stockpiling together
Building sovereign resilience could also involve holding shared stockpiles of essentials. The pandemic, as well as transportation bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz and Suez Canal, and the trade disruptions of the Trump era have moved governments away from the just-in-time delivery mentality of a decade ago to one of planning and hoarding.
"We're hearing talk in Canada about stockpiling raw materials," said Mark Camilleri, Brussels-based president of the Canada EU Trade and Investment Association. "Maybe there's a way that we can work together in a trusted manner, in a more efficient way, in what's becoming a very inefficient world."
Canada is sending a message to the Trump administration, says Brian Clow, former prime minister Justin Trudeau's chief adviser on the Canada-U.S. relationship: "We can sell elsewhere. We can have security partnerships elsewhere."
"Both Europe and Canada are under attack, frankly, by the United States on our economy, on our sovereignty, and that is pushing us closer together," said Clow.
For the Carney government, Europe is not only a place to trade, but also a potential replacement partner with which to integrate sovereign networks, launch satellites, stockpile critical minerals and build a strong defence manufacturing base, or as Carney put it to Bloomberg, a place to "deepen co-operation with like-minded partners so you have sovereignty, so you have resilience, so you have independence.
"No country can do that alone."

'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
- Published
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.
He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.
'The poor called us poor'
Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."

Etor's first break came whilst doing a kind of national service in Nigeria, when he realised lots of locals were being hospitalised with food poisoning, because they were trying to preserve things by drying them in fields.
To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".
"It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.
He then completed an undergraduate degree at Newcastle University and a PhD at the University of Durham, before securing his current job in Bristol.
Sir Steve Webb, the former MP and Pensions Minister, who got to know Etor through the church in Bristol, called his achievements "remarkable".
"David's message is very much that people shouldn't be defined by their upbringing or their background," he said. "They shouldn't be written off."
"I was pinching myself on my way here this morning," Etor added.
"Nothing good was supposed to come out of me."

BRICS leaders on Saturday (September 12, 2026) called for stronger cooperation in disease surveillance and medical product regulation, welcoming the establishment of a dedicated sub-working group to advance an integrated early warning system for the prevention and response to mass infectious diseases.
In their New Delhi Declaration, the leaders stressed the importance of strengthening health infrastructure and local production of medical products to enhance preparedness for future health emergencies and ensure timely, affordable and equitable access to healthcare services, vaccines, therapeutics and diagnostics.
They also called for strengthened collaboration among BRICS medical products regulatory authorities and welcomed efforts to develop a common GxP white paper consolidating regulatory best practices and technical approaches.
Public health emergencies transcend national borders
The leaders recognised that infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic threats, antimicrobial resistance and other public health emergencies transcend national borders and require stronger international cooperation, timely information sharing and coordinated action.
"Acknowledging that infectious disease outbreaks, zoonotic threats, antimicrobial resistance and other public health emergencies transcend national borders and require strengthened international cooperation, timely information sharing and coordinated collective action, we underscore the importance of enhancing global health security through resilient surveillance systems, effective early warning mechanisms, and strengthened preparedness and response capacities," the declaration said.
The leaders recognising the central role of the World Health Organization and the amended International Health Regulations (2005), underscored the importance of resilient surveillance, early warning and rapid response systems and coordination.
"In this regard, we welcome the establishment of a dedicated Sub-Working Group to advance the BRICS Integrated Early Warning System for the prevention and response to Mass Infectious Diseases, and its Terms of Reference," they said.
Collective preparedness
The initiative is aimed at strengthening collective preparedness against infectious disease threats through closer coordination among member countries and faster sharing of information.
The declaration also called for greater regulatory cooperation to ensure that medical products remain available, accessible and meet standards of quality, safety and efficacy across BRICS countries.
"We encourage strengthened collaboration among BRICS Medical Products Regulatory Authorities by extending the scope of the existing Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in the field of medical products regulation to the Regulatory Authorities of all BRICS member countries," the declaration said.
Collaborative regulatory approaches
They reiterated the importance of strengthening collaborative regulatory approaches to ensure the continued availability and accessibility of quality, safe and efficacious medical products.
The leaders also welcomed the collective efforts of BRICS regulatory authorities in developing the BRICS GxP White Paper.
"We welcome the collective efforts of BRICS Regulatory Authorities in developing the BRICS GxP White Paper, consolidating best practices of regulatory experience and technical approaches," the declaration said.
The GxP refers broadly to good-practice standards followed in areas such as manufacturing, laboratory and clinical processes, with the common framework expected to facilitate greater sharing of regulatory experience and technical approaches among member countries.
Strengthen domestic health infrastructure
The leaders also linked health security with stronger domestic health infrastructure and local production of medical products, calling for greater preparedness for future health emergencies.
"We emphasize the importance of strengthening health infrastructure and local production of medical products, enhancing preparedness for future health emergencies through stronger surveillance systems, laboratory networks, leveraging digital health technology and Artificial Intelligence," the declaration said.
They also called for technical cooperation among public health institutes, development of robust regulatory frameworks, skilled health workforces and collaborative research and development.
The declaration stressed that these measures were needed to improve access to healthcare products and services and strengthen the capacity of BRICS countries to respond collectively to health emergencies.
People-centred digital healthcare systems
The leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to people-centred digital healthcare systems and welcomed the BRICS Compendium on Digital Health Architecture for Continuum of Care, including access to healthcare in remote areas.
The leaders also supported the activities of the BRICS Vaccine Research and Development Centre and recognised the importance of collaboration in nuclear medicine.
They welcomed the activities of the BRICS Nuclear Medicine Working Group and noted the importance of the BRICS Health Journal in disseminating research findings and promoting scientific cooperation within the BRICS framework.
The declaration also emphasised the importance of sharing experiences, innovations and best practices among BRICS countries to improve health outcomes and advance universal health coverage.

Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary on Tuesday (September 15, 2026) transferred ₹579.23 crore in relief to 8,27,472 flood-affected families, a day ahead of a central team’s visit to assess damage in the State.
As per Disaster Management Department (DMD), around 50 lakh people and crops spread in 55,000 hectares of land across 15 districts have been affected by the floods.
A team led by Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan is scheduled to visit Bihar on September 16.
Mr. Choudhary transferred ₹7,000 per family, via Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) to the bank accounts of flood-affected families during an event held at the ‘Sankalp’ auditorium in Patna.
Santosh Kumar Mall, Principal Secretary of the Disaster Management Department (DMD), gave a detailed presentation to the Chief Minister regarding the flood-affected areas, relief and rescue operations, and the facilities being provided to the affected people.
Addressing the gathering, Mr. Choudhary said that amidst the challenging flood situation, the State government’s top priority is to provide immediate relief, assistance, and security to the affected families.
He asserted that the government stands with flood-affected people with utmost sensitivity and will not permit any shortcomings in relief and rescue operations. “Over 1,200 community kitchens are operating to provide food to flood-affected people, and approximately 1.28 crore meals have been served through these kitchens so far,” Mr. Choudhary said.
Further, he instructed officials to continue providing food, drinking water, medicines, and other essential amenities to people in the affected areas. Twenty-one teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) are engaged in rescue operations
The CM emphasised transparency in the process of identifying and verifying eligible beneficiaries and instructed that if any eligible affected family has been left out of the assistance scheme, they must be included in the relief list within a week. He also said that no eligible family should be deprived of government relief. He directed that the reconstruction work should proceed rapidly alongside relief operations, following the theme of “Build Back Better Than Before.”
“All reconstruction and recovery tasks—including the provision of agricultural subsidies and road repairs, as well as all necessary assistance to affected families and farmers—must be completed within one month,”Mr. Choudhary said.
He further instructed officials to prepare a comprehensive and factual report on the flood damage ahead of Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan’s scheduled visit. “The state government’s objective is not merely to provide immediate relief but also to restore normalcy in the flood-affected areas quickly and ensure reconstruction that results in a better situation than before. The government, administration, disaster management machinery, and all concerned departments are working in a coordinated manner towards this goal,” he added.

Air pollution spiked after the Trump administration stopped embassy monitoring
Growing up in Shanghai in the early 1990s, Eric Zou remembers the air.
"I lived a couple of miles next to a chemical plant and it was just really bad, really foggy," he says. "It's the middle of the day, but you can't see the sun."
Intensive industrial activity blanketed many cities in China during the 1990s and 2000s with extremely hazardous air. But Zou, now an environmental economist at the University of Michigan, says that many people didn't really understand this smog as air pollution, or something that could harm them.
"When you have a big smog event, people often talk about that as fog, they think it was just like bad weather," says Zou. One big key to changing that sentiment, he says, was information initially provided by the United States.
In 2008, U.S. officials installed an air quality monitor on the embassy in Beijing and began making the information public. Over time, that helped spur demand for cleaner air, says Zou. "Once you have pollution information, it tends to be that it actually helps people to realize, 'Oh, I actually value air quality.' "
Since 2008, the State Department's monitoring initiative has expanded to more than 80 embassies and consulates. Research suggests that monitoring contributed to measurable improvements in air quality, especially across many low- and middle-income countries with limited monitoring systems of their own.
But in March 2025, the Trump administration shuttered that program, citing monetary costs. Research out this week suggests the move had health costs for the people living in those countries. Over the several months following the shutdown, air pollution levels measured via satellite increased by 24-33%, researchers reported Monday in the journal PNAS.
The State Department did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.
"It's a great study, high quality. And it's a real pity," says Andrea La Nauze, an environmental economist at Deakin University in Australia who has researched the benefits of the program, but wasn't involved in this study. The program "led to sustained improvements in air quality that were continuing to increase after 10 years," she says.
She says this new research suggests those improvements aren't guaranteed if monitoring stops.
Measuring the consequences of not measuring
When Zoe Yiyuan Zhou first heard the news that the Trump administration was shuttering the embassy air quality monitoring, it struck her as a research opportunity.
"It's such a rare case to study this drawback," says the Columbia University climate researcher. While there's ample evidence of the benefits of increased monitoring, she says there aren't many examples of a sudden falloff of surveillance.
Zhou and her colleagues decided to compare air pollution levels before and after monitoring ceased across 46 cities. Since they didn't have on-the-ground measures of air quality for the latter part of that comparison, they used satellite data for both.
The team found no significant trends in air pollution over the 300 days preceding the end of U.S. reporting. But about three to four months after reporting ended, pollution had gone up, on average by about 30%. Satellite data isn't a perfect substitute for monitors that can measure on-the-ground pollution. The researchers estimate their satellite measurements translate to about a 4% increase in PM2.5 — the small suspended particles that can enter the lungs and bloodstream and cause health problems.
"That magnitude is certainly concerning," says La Nauze. "Particulate matter is a serious and dangerous thing, and being exposed to it is not good."
The increase was highest in Southeast Asian cities, including Manila, in the Philippines, Rangoon in Myanmar and Vientiane in Laos, says Zhao. Pollution also spiked more in cities with fewer monitoring alternatives.
The study can't say why pollution increased after monitoring stopped.
For countries with nonexistent or nascent monitoring programs, U.S. data may have prompted more regulatory action, says Zou. "Maybe the U.S. Embassy was a really strong force, in terms of a third-party auditing mechanism, and once that's removed, people are like 'Now I can just pollute, right?'"
In many industries, it costs money to cut down on pollution, says Zhou. When monitoring stops, companies may see it as an opportunity to cut those costs.
But the researchers did find some potentially hopeful news. Pollution levels seemed to go back down somewhat after peaking about three or four months after monitoring stopped.
It's difficult to say why this decrease happened, Zhou says, or whether the trend will continue. She suspects that it may reflect other forms of monitoring, by individuals or local governments, coming online in the wake of the U.S. withdrawal.
But not all areas may have the ability to readily make up for what's been lost, she says, especially in regions where air quality monitoring is new.
"Data is just so important," says Zhou. "Having access to information is necessary to make sure that these previous gains can continue. Public information creates accountability."

Two years ago, Marineland of Canada — a theme park in Niagara Falls that trained beluga whales, dolphins, and other animals to perform acrobatic tricks for entertainment — closed its doors. The decision came after years of financial turmoil, along with journalistic investigations, whistleblower accounts, and government inspections that revealed animal neglect and suffering at the park. Since 2019, 19 beluga whales and one killer whale have died at Marineland.
Three beluga whales just died at one of America’s top-rated aquariums
Why even the best aquariums can’t give animals what they need.
The closure was a win for animal welfare, but where would its animals go? Marineland’s surviving menagerie included, among other species, four dolphins and 30 beluga whales.
Given that beluga whales and dolphins are highly social animals that live in pods and swim long distances in the wild, animal welfare groups didn’t want to see them transferred to other parks like Marineland, or conventional aquariums, where the exceptionally smart and active animals would continue to suffer in captivity. Instead, they called for some of the 30 belugas to be rehomed to a proposed — though not yet built — 110-acre coastal sanctuary in Nova Scotia, Canada.
That didn’t happen. Instead, this summer, the four dolphins and two of the beluga whales went to an aquarium in Spain, while the other belugas were transferred to two SeaWorld locations — theme parks that are similar to Marineland — and two famous US aquariums: Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, which received two, and Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, which received 10.
And just as Shedd’s belugas should’ve been adjusting to their new environment, things took a turn for the worse. Over the course of eight days from late August to early September, Peekachu and Rain — two belugas who arrived at Shedd Aquarium in mid-August — and another beluga whale named Beethoven, who had been at Shedd for decades, died.
The three animals’ cause of death at Shedd Aquarium remains unknown as the aquarium awaits necropsy results.
While the three deaths in quick succession have put a spotlight on Shedd, they have also renewed scrutiny of a deeper problem with aquariums: their intensive confinement of wild animals, which runs throughout their history and goes beyond any one institution or animal.
The limitations of aquarium life
Shedd Aquarium is one of the US’s oldest and most prestigious aquariums, though this isn’t its first beluga whale controversy.
Its first two belugas were taken from the wild — an estuary in Canada — in 1991. The next year, they got four more from the wild and soon after, two of them died from cardiovascular collapse after receiving an anti-parasitic drug.
“These whales died to serve a tourist attraction,” a spokesperson for the International Wildlife Coalition said at the time. “It’s horrific.”
Since then, Shedd hasn’t directly sourced any beluga whales from the wild, though it’s recorded 15 beluga births in captivity. But whether taken from the wild or born in captivity, some scientists and animal advocates argue the inherent limitations of aquarium life are inhumane. One of the most outspoken among them is neuroscientist Lori Marino, an expert in marine mammal behavior and intelligence and president of the Whale Sanctuary Project, which is building the proposed Nova Scotia sanctuary.
In the wild, beluga whales have far-ranging seasonal migrations, live in complex social groups, hunt for food, and raise juveniles. But Marino says that captive belugas — whether at a park like Marineland or a storied aquarium like Shedd — are in small, artificial, and unchanging environments that deny them the ability to engage in many of their natural behaviors.
“The level of boredom that they experience is really unbelievable,” Marino told Vox. “For an animal like that, with a brain like that, that’s torture.”
A Shedd spokesperson told me that research it participated in — along with other zoological institutions — found that ensuring that animal enclosures are dynamic, well managed, contain enrichment activities, and facilitate strong socialization do more to predict good welfare than the volume of space they’re allotted.
However, such artificial environments can lead to serious welfare problems. It’s not uncommon for marine mammals — and other animals in zoos and aquariums — to display “stereotypic” behavior, or repetitive motions that are indicators of stress. They might endlessly swim in circles or other patterns, continually regurgitate and reingest food, repetitively move their heads, or grate their teeth on hard surfaces. Critics call it “zoochosis.” Some researchers believe captivity may induce depressive-like states in some animals.
Zoos and aquariums tend to downplay the harms of captivity and, instead, position themselves as stewards of the animals at their facilities and protectors of their counterparts in the wild. Some animal advocates, including Marino, often argue this is largely a facade to justify the continued captivity of the animals.
Are aquariums for animals, or us?
Known as “the Fish House,” the first modern aquarium opened in 1853 at the London Zoo. At the time, zoos and aquariums were pitched to the public as pure entertainment — places for city dwellers to see exotic animals from far away lands up close.
But as the modern environmental and animal welfare movements matured in the middle of the 20th century, they began to question the practice of putting wild-caught animals on display in enclosures that amounted to a minuscule fraction of their range in nature. By the 1970s, in response to the criticisms, some aquariums and zoos began to pivot from marketing themselves as entertainment venues to being invested in the conservation of wildlife.
Zoos and aquariums posit that if we’re to protect wild animals in, well, the wild, it makes sense that helping the public gain an affinity for them in a not-so-wild setting is an important part of the equation. Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium, for example, describes its mission as “sparking compassion, curiosity and conservation for the aquatic animal world.”
Aquariums and zoos often say they achieve these goals by raising a lot of money for conservation projects, helping to reintroduce vulnerable species back into the wild, and inspiring visitors to get involved in conservation.
There is some merit to the first claim. In 2022, the 238 zoos and aquariums accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) — of which Shedd is a member — spent $252 million on projects to protect and preserve wildlife habitats. It’s a lot of money, though it amounts to about 5 percent of what AZA members had spent on operations and construction.
The evidence is even thinner on aquariums’ and zoos’ claims around helping to reintroduce endangered species back into the wild, as it’s an incredibly difficult and rare feat, and on motivating attendees to become conservation advocates.
Some surveys of zoo-goers have found that zoo attendance can modestly improve their conservation knowledge and behavior. But despite some 700 million annual visits, far fewer visitors volunteer or donate to protect animals in the wild.
Despite the heavy conservation messaging, animal advocates argue that entertainment is still the priority for most zoological institutions. According to the AZA, 80 percent of the animals in its member aquariums are taken from the wild, which seems to be in direct conflict with protecting animals in the wild. Shedd Aquarium declined an interview request for this story, and when I asked a spokesperson what percent of its 32,000 animals were taken from the wild, they wouldn’t say.
“Acquiring animals from the wild is not contrary to conservation goals as long as species are acquired in an ethical and sustainable manner,” an AZA spokesperson said over email. “These are thought-out and strategic actions with sustainability in mind.” However, AZA didn’t define how to ethically and sustainably take animals from the wild.
And Shedd — like many other aquariums — encourages guests to pay for “encounter” experiences with beluga whales and other wild, non-domesticated species, like penguins, sea lions, and otters, at up to $205 a pop. These often involve the guests having a few minutes to pet the animals and take photographs with them. (The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has temporarily prohibited Shedd and other facilities from using the rehomed belugas in encounter programs.)
A Shedd spokesperson told me the criticism of these encounter programs as inhumane and unethical is “unfounded and indeed contradictory,” citing a study about dolphins that it participated in. The study, however, wasn’t designed to measure how encounter programs affect dolphin welfare, but rather looked at how dolphins use their habitat, with encounter programs as one variable among many. A 2021 literature review on encounter programs found that most research on them lacked rigor and that “the justification for using [encounter programs] within zoos remains questionable.”
As for the belugas at Shedd, Marino told me she hopes that they survive, but says this moment should lead to more honest conversations about the ethics of aquariums.
Institutions like Shedd “are supposed to be the best,” Marino said. “But people need to understand that it’s the best of something that doesn’t work. … It’s not a question of who’s accredited, who’s not. It’s about keeping these animals in tanks for entertainment. That’s the proposition that has to be probed, that has to be questioned. And that’s the one thing they don’t want to do.”
Shedd, for its part, doesn’t seem ready to probe the proposition quite yet. A spokesperson told Vox that it hasn’t ruled out breeding the animals it received from Marineland, which could mean another generation of long-lived belugas in captivity.

Walker stars for Chiefs as Swift & Cruise watch on
- Published
The Kansas City Chiefs began their NFL season with a 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos.
Patrick Mahomes, playing his first game since suffering a knee injury in December, ran in the opening touchdown and threw for two more as the Chiefs recorded a statement win at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City.
New signing Kenneth Walker, the Most Valuable Player for the Seattle Seahawks in last season's Super Bowl, made the biggest impact by rushing for a career-high 173 yards and scoring twice on his Chiefs debut.
"I've been saying it all off-season that K9 is going to make a difference," said Mahomes.
"That offensive line and K9, they took over the game. It went really well."
The Broncos levelled the scores in the first quarter, but quarterback Bo Nix was sacked four times and intercepted once as the Chiefs pulled away.
Three-time Super Bowl winner Travis Kelce moved second on the NFL's all-time list for most receiving yards by a tight end with a 59-yard play for the Chiefs.
Only former Chiefs star Tony Gonzalez (15,127) has more receiving yards in the position than Kelce (13,073).
Singer Taylor Swift, Kelce's wife, and actor Tom Cruise watched the game together from the stands.
The Broncos won the AFC West title last season, ending the Chiefs' run of nine successive divisional crowns.

A US federal judge has temporarily blocked a Trump administration rule that sought to replace the decades-old “duration of status” system for foreign students with fixed-term admissions, including a four-year cap for most international students.
The ruling by Massachusetts District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV came just a day before the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) rule was scheduled to take effect. The judge said the policy was likely to cause “catastrophic” damage to the US higher-education system and economy and found that DHS had failed to comply with requirements under the Administrative Procedure Act.
The decision offers temporary relief to international students in the US, including a large Indian student population.
Under the current system, foreign students can generally remain in the US for the duration of their academic programme as long as they maintain their authorised status.
The new system would have generally limited F-1 and J-1 admissions to the length of the programme, subject to a maximum of four years.
Students who needed additional time would have had to apply for an extension through US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), with approval left to government officials.
The rule also included a 30-day grace period after studies, down from the existing 60 days, and imposed additional restrictions on changing majors, transferring institutions and starting new programmes.
Judge Saylor said DHS was required to comply with the Administrative Procedure Act despite citing national security and border-control concerns.
The judge found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in challenging the rule and that implementing it could cause immediate and irreparable harm.
“The damage to the higher education system and to the economy of the United States is likely to be catastrophic,” Saylor wrote.
He also rejected the government's argument that any injunction should apply only to the organisations that brought the case.
The plaintiffs represent nearly 600 public and private institutions, while more than 5,000 higher-education institutions operate across the US. Saylor said limiting relief would create parallel regulatory systems and potentially inconsistent decisions.
For Indian students, the immediate impact is relief from the four-year cap and associated fixed-term admission requirements while the legal challenge continues.
Students who are already in the US can continue to operate under the existing framework for now, rather than being immediately pushed into the new extension system.
This is particularly significant for Indian students pursuing longer academic programmes, including doctoral and research courses. Harvard President Alan Garber had previously questioned the four-year limit, noting that a typical PhD can take at least six years.
The ruling also means students are not immediately subject to the proposed additional restrictions on changing programmes, transferring institutions or pursuing another degree.
India is currently the largest source of international students in the United States.
According to the Open Doors 2025 report cited in the case material, 363,019 Indian students were enrolled at US colleges and universities during the 2024-25 academic year, accounting for nearly 31% of all international students in the country.
That makes any change to the US student-visa system particularly important for Indian students, universities and families considering higher education in America.
The rule could have created additional uncertainty for students whose courses extend beyond four years, particularly those in doctoral, research and other lengthy programmes.
Under the blocked rule, students requiring additional time would have needed to file a formal Extension of Stay application with USCIS.
The decision temporarily prevents that new system from taking effect.
However, the judge's ruling is a preliminary injunction, not a final decision on whether DHS can ultimately introduce a fixed-term visa system.
The underlying legal challenge will continue, so the rules governing international students could change again depending on the final outcome.
The proposed rule also contained provisions affecting students who left the US and later sought to re-enter.
Those travelling outside the country after the rule took effect could have been subject to the new fixed-date admission system.
Because implementation has now been postponed, those provisions do not take effect while the injunction remains in place.
The DHS rule was not limited to students.
Foreign journalists holding I visas would have faced a 240-day admission limit, while Chinese media representatives would have been subject to a 90-day limit.
Judge Saylor raised concerns about the possibility that the rule could be used against journalists critical of the government, particularly DHS officials.
He questioned whether the policy's actual purpose could extend beyond national security and border protection to greater government control over academic institutions and the press.
DHS had argued that the fixed-term system would help combat fraud and make it easier for the government to identify and address visa overstays.
The department also said the existing duration-of-status system had allowed some foreign students, exchange visitors and media representatives to remain in the US without sufficient routine government oversight.
The judge, however, found that national-security and border-control claims did not exempt DHS from its obligations under the Administrative Procedure Act.
For prospective Indian students, the ruling removes an immediate source of uncertainty, but it does not permanently eliminate the proposed four-year limit.
The legal battle is still underway, meaning students and universities will have to monitor further court decisions and any subsequent action by DHS.

Apple’s new Siri AI and iOS 27 are rolling out from today, September 14, 2026. Apple first promised a rebuilt Siri in 2024, then delayed it to 2026, but it’s finally here. And while it was ex-CEO Tim Cook who announced Siri AI way back in 2024, this time around it is new CEO John Ternus who will lead the rollout of the all new Siri AI as well as the new hardware lineup, headlined by the iPhone Duo. A lot has been written about the new iPhone Duo and the Pro models, so we won’t belabour those points here. The thing that’s surprised many is that Apple is not targeting the entry-level or the mass market with these launches at all. The premium positioning of the hardware is being attributed to Ternus’ own background leading Apple’s hardware division. That may be true to a large extent, but given the supply chain woes of the past year and a half when it comes to memory and storage chips, there’s also the feeling that Apple had no choice but to cater to the high-end market in 2026. That may well change next year. But this year, the entry barrier to experiencing the best of iOS 27 and all its Siri AI features is slightly higher. This makes us wonder will Apple’s AI experiences be worth it to justify this high price even if the hardware shines? If Apple is unable to cater to the basic AI expectations even after two years of promise and development, there will definitely be some concern. Three things decide whether Apple can pull it off: Whether Siri AI can adapt to how people in different markets speak, particularly given India’s diversity Whether it can run smoothly and just as well on older iPhones Whether the features will sway consumers enough to pay subscription fees for Siri AI in the future What The Focus On Hardware Actually Means Before we answer these questions, a brief detour. Every year-end Apple is once again in the spotlight for its latest iPhone release. In that regard, 2026 is no different. But there’s a decidedly different Apple when it comes to iPhones this year. There’s no focus on the entry-level segment; instead it’s all about the higher-end iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo. These models are the most expensive iPhones being sold by Apple. And some could argue that only the iPhone Duo is offering something different. But given the high pricing in India and indeed in other parts of the world, something feels different this time. Apple devices have always been one of the most expensive products in the market, and this is true for iPhones too. But Apple has always offered something for every class of user, particularly with India on its mind. With the new generation, its best features come with a huge price tag. Backing our argument around the high pricing for the hardware this year, Gartner’s Padhi said it is a supply chain problem rather than opportunism on Apple’s part. Data centre demand is pulling semiconductor supply towards servers, raising memory prices, and memory, not the chipset, decides how much AI can run on a phone. Financing softens the first payment but not the second, and he expects extended zero-cost EMI to become standard, with the interest recovered only if customers stay in the ecosystem through services. That may well change in the future, but older phones will certainly have a few hardware compromises that Apple’s AI experiences can’t work around. Is Apple Risking A Fragmented Experience? According to Apple, Siri AI draws on personal context from messages, emails and photos, acts inside apps, reads what is on screen and reaches the web for current information, with a separate Siri app syncing conversations through iCloud. Photos gets Spatial Reframing, Image Playground creates photorealistic images, Safari's Notify Me tracks price drops, and Shortcuts can be built by describing a task in plain language. Apple lists Apple Intelligence and Siri AI together as available on the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max and every iPhone 16 model or later, as well as iPads with an M1 chip or newer. Siri AI also reaches CarPlay and AirPods on the go. But there is a genuine split when it comes to the top end and entry-level iPhones. In iOS 27, Apple has an on-device model that is more powerful than anything it has shipped, and the features that model enables are held to newer hardware. According to Apple, the most powerful on-device model, along with the expressive voices and more advanced dictation it powers, runs on the iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, iPads with an M4 chip or later and at least 12GB of memory, Macs with an M3 chip or later and at least 12GB of memory, and Apple Vision Pro with the M5 chip. Everything else in Siri AI, including personal context, onscreen awareness, web answers, the dedicated Siri app and Visual Intelligence, runs on the broader device list, which still includes the iPhone 15 Pro and the base iPhone 17, which now retails for ₹99,900 in India. Rishi Padhi, principal analyst at Gartner (India), sees this as a deliberate trade-off by Apple. The company is building one Siri AI across all its hardware, accepting a slower, language-by-language rollout, precisely because a single experience is the foundation its services are sold on. It is the opposite of Google's problem, which is managing fragmentation across many Android phone makers. Will India Get Feature Parity? The second answer is mixed, starting with how Apple lists availability. Apple's iOS 27 page shows that some apps have genuine regional limits, usually tied to content rights, which is why the likes of Apple News are not offered in India. But India is well covered elsewhere. When it comes to AI-powered Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, Mail and Messages summaries, voicemail summaries, Siri product knowledge, Type to Siri and dictation, Indian users get feature parity with their global counterparts. The difference could matter in real-life usage. Early reviews of Siri AI say it is strong on capability and cautious on reliability. Testers reported that Siri finally lived up to the promise Apple had made for a smart assistant, and Indian users running the beta reported noticeably better handling of local accents. Other verdicts point to uneven performance, with repeated failures and misread requests leading reviewers to conclude that reliability is not yet ready for everyday use. However, beta testers who switched back to the older Siri version reported that Siri AI felt slower and less reliable at routine tasks such as timers, alarms, messaging, and maps. Reviews from developers point to a structural limit rather than a bug as a major concern. Siri AI can only act inside apps whose developers have registered their actions with Apple in a specific, pre-approved format, and apps whose functions fall outside that list are left out entirely. Developers on Apple's own forums noted that even Apple's own sample testing app cannot be reached, and Apple says that Siri AI works best with apps that have done this groundwork. Plus, the previous point around hardware limitations applies to AI features. Gartner’s Padhi expects RAM or memory to become the dividing line for the best Apple Intelligence features, and on Mac that is already visible: Apple's advanced on-device Siri voice model needs an M3-class chip and at least 12GB of memory. Can Apple Get Users To Pay For AI? Apple aficionados have accepted the Apple Tax to a certain extent. They already pay a premium for hardware that runs Apple's AI. But now with the iPhone 18 Pro at ₹1,64,900 and the foldable Duo at ₹2,99,900, this appetite for paying the Apple Tax could be tested. Apple has also said some AI features will be capped, and that paying more will unlock higher limits. The same buyer may pay for the phone, then pay again for the AI on it. Part of that already exists. Server-dependent features such as image generation carry daily limits, which can be removed with an iCloud+ subscription plan. But there is another change coming that is reliant on Apple being able to convince people to pay for Siri AI. Apple states that starting with the 2027 software releases, enhanced access to server-side features including Siri AI will be available, that usage limits will apply in future, and that increased access will carry a fee. One direction Apple may take can be seen in the current iCloud pricing tiers. In this case, certain features like summaries of connected camera feeds are capped to one camera at the 2 TB Apple iCloud+ subscription plan (₹749 per month), with two cameras and five cameras being unlocked at more expensive plans (₹2,999 or ₹5,900 per month). Padhi expects Apple to fold AI into a subscription rather than sell it separately, since Private Cloud Compute carries a real and recurring cost. The likely form is a tiered plan added to what users already pay, most probably bundled with iCloud+, mirroring Google, where Gemini access sits inside Google One. On the cost for using the AI experiences, the answer is unfavourable for Apple. Apple has said higher usage will carry a fee and on-device advanced features will cost consumers more in the future, based on how reliant they are on Siri AI. The paradox is that sophisticated customers who pay a premium for Apple iPhones are also the most in need of reliable smartphone-centric AI tools. On that front, iOS 27 is Apple's best foot forward till date. But when it comes to consistency for its AI features and the high entry cost, it remains an uneven proposition for those in India at the moment.

The United States has, for the first time, acknowledged that it has weapons deployed in orbit, revealing a previously undisclosed military capability in space. US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said on Monday that Washington now possessed “on-orbit space control weapons” that could protect American forces from hostile action. Meink made the disclosure while speaking at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in Maryland. However, he did not reveal what the weapon is or when it was deployed. “This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said. Meink said the decision to reveal the existence of the weapon was deliberate and intended to deter potential adversaries. He later told reporters that providing further details could weaken its deterrent effect. At a press roundtable, Meink declined to discuss the weapon's design, capabilities, testing, or the type of targets it could potentially engage, according to The War Zone (TWZ). The US Space Force later offered a broader explanation of what it means by “space control”. It said the term includes missions aimed at challenging and controlling activity in space through both kinetic and non-kinetic methods. According to the Space Force, such capabilities could be used to disrupt, degrade, or, if required, destroy an adversary's space systems. They can serve both offensive and defensive purposes, including technologies capable of interfering with satellites without physically destroying them. The lack of details has prompted speculation about the nature of the newly acknowledged system. Victoria Samson of the Secure World Foundation told the Financial Times that the weapon could be a space-based jammer. She noted that the US has generally tried to avoid kinetic attacks on satellites because destroying spacecraft can create hazardous debris in orbit. Clayton Swope of the Center for Strategic and International Studies, however, said the announcement was too broad to establish a clear deterrent threat. He argued that countries such as China and Russia would need at least a general understanding of the weapon's destructive capability and the circumstances under which Washington might use it to properly assess the threat. Russia and China, the two principal geopolitical rivals of the United States, are considered potential threats to American interests in space. According to the US Space Force, China “develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernization strategy”, while Russia “views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts” In 2024, the US said Russia had placed a satellite into orbit that it believed could potentially attack other spacecraft. More recently, reports suggested that two Russian satellites may have intercepted communications from at least a dozen European satellites since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. China has also been developing counterspace technologies designed to disrupt or disable an adversary's satellites. The US has itself become increasingly open about developing offensive space capabilities. In 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order strengthening the Space Force's responsibility for protecting American space assets and developing capabilities to attack adversaries' systems. The military competition in space began alongside the space race. After the Soviet Union launched Sputnik into orbit in 1957, both Washington and Moscow started examining ways to deploy weapons in space as well as methods to disable or destroy satellites. Nuclear weapons were initially regarded as the biggest threat in orbit. However, the United States, the Soviet Union and other countries signed the Outer Space Treaty in 1967, which prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction in orbit. Despite the treaty, major powers have continued to develop capabilities that could be used in conflicts beyond its restrictions. Russia, the US, China and India have explored technologies aimed at targeting or disrupting satellites operated by rival countries. Satellites play a crucial role in modern military operations, supporting communications, surveillance and navigation. Their growing importance has made space an increasingly contested domain for major military powers. #EmmysSoWhite again: No actors of colour win during 2026 Primetime Emmys
All acting category winners during TV's biggest night were white
In 2015, activist and writer April Reign created the #OscarsSoWhite hashtag.
Now, she says she doesn't really watch award shows live, and last night's Emmys was an example of why.
There was a clear lack of diversity among the winners during Monday night's Primetime Emmy Awards broadcast. Actors of colour were entirely shut out of the major acting categories, with all 10 broadcasted awards going to white performers.
"It's not a regression, it's definitely a stall," said Reign.
The other two major acting categories — supporting actor and supporting actress in a limited series — were given out last week at the Creative Arts Emmys, but those winners didn't change the tally.
'A pattern, not a moment'
By Tuesday morning, #EmmysSoWhite was trending, with users calling out the Television Academy on social media.
"The academy saw that three black women made history at the Emmys winning the big categories of the night and how happy everybody was and said never again," one user wrote on X, referencing the 2024 Emmy awards, "so now we’re stuck with #EmmysSOWhite for the foreseeable future "
"What is this... #EmmysSoWhite" wrote another, alongside a photo composite of the winners.
Reign started the #OscarsSoWhite hashtag in 2015, when all 20 acting nominees for the Academy Awards that year were white, sparking a conversation and a movement about the Academy and its voting body.
While there have been some changes in the following years aimed at addressing these discrepancies, Reign called out Monday's results.
"This is a pattern, not a moment," Reign said in an interview with CBC News. "A single snub is an accident. A pattern this consistent is a design feature of how the institution votes."
The Television Academy released a transparency report in February revealing that the majority of its members in 2026 — 67 per cent — were white. It publishes this report annually, with the first official one coming out in 2021.
At the same time, the academy pointed to steady year-over-year growth in its membership among people identifying as biracial, multiracial, East Asian and Southeast Asian, as well as women, non-binary, transgender and intersex voters.
Reign said the conversation around representation needs to begin long before awards season, pointing to the writers, casting directors and behind-the-scenes decision-makers who shape which stories and characters make it to the screen.
"We can't wait until we get to the award shows to have this conversation when, you know, the pipeline starts before a single word is written on the page," she said. She suggests asking questions like who the casting directors and show-runners are, and who is saying a white character couldn't be queer or a person of colour.
"Those are the questions that we need to ask from the very beginning so that we're not having these conversations again in February or March for the Oscars, and in September for the Emmys, because it's too late."
It's worth noting that outside of the primetime broadcast, Ernest Harden Jr. picked up an acting win Monday night for his guest-starring role as Louie Cloverfield on The Pitt. But the guest acting categories weren't presented during the broadcast. Octavia Spencer also won for narrating Lost Women of Alaska.
And while Monday night's show was a complete shutout for actors of colour, director Hiro Murai won a golden statuette for Widow's Bay. He's now the first Asian filmmaker to win best directing for a comedy series at the Emmys and only the third to win a primetime Emmy in any category, joining Emmy-winning directors Lee Sung Jin, who won for Beef, and Hwang Dong-hyuk, who won for Squid Game.
How does this compare to previous years?
Representation at the Emmys was actually down before Monday's ceremony even started.
Variety reports only 17 performers of colour scored acting nominations this year — a sharp drop from 28 last year.
The Emmys made headlines for diverse nominations in 2021, however every single lead and supporting acting winner that year ended up being white, also prompting the hashtag #EmmysSoWhite.
Let's look at how things have shaken out over the last few years for diverse winners at the Emmys.
Last year (2025): One of the 12 acting races went to a person of color — Tramell Tillman won for Severance and made history as the first Black man to take home outstanding supporting actor in a drama series.
2024: Four out of the dozen acting trophies went to diverse winners (including Liza Colón-Zayas, Lamorne Morris and Shōgun stars Hiroyuki Sanada and Anna Sawai).
2024 (January): This delayed ceremony was the peak of diversity for acting wins, with five actors of colour taking the stage to claim trophies: Quinta Brunson, Ayo Edebiri, Niecy Nash-Betts, Steven Yeun and Ali Wong.
2022: We saw three diverse performers win: Lee Jung-jae, Zendaya and Sheryl Lee Ralph.
2021: This was the last time all of the primetime acting winners were white.
On the Television Academy's official site, it says the academy is "dedicated to honouring excellence in television while promoting creativity and diversity, and empowering storytellers through recognition, education and leadership"

The performance gap between frontier AI models from US tech companies and the best open-weights models from Chinese companies has closed to just 4.4 months, according to a Mozilla report. That explains why many companies are shifting to the significantly cheaper open models for routine work—and helps reveal a narrow band of workloads where frontier models are worth the cost.
Most organizations should ideally be using open models as the default for the majority of their work, according to the latest State of Open Source AI report from Mozilla, published on September 15 and shared with Ars prior to publication. The report highlights how a leading open model, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, achieves a composite AI performance score on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index that is just three points behind Anthropic’s Fable 5 closed frontier model, all while costing just 30 percent of the latter.
“Closed earns its premium in a few places: expert professional work, high-intensity retrieval, and long context,” Raffi Krikorian, chief technology officer at Mozilla, said in an email to Ars. “We see the decision to pay for closed as workload-specific rather than organization-specific.”
The open-weights AI models allow anyone to download the main model components and run the models on their own computers, but developers still typically withhold vital information such as training data, the data pipeline, and training code. By comparison, US tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI mostly offer closed frontier models that keep everything proprietary, requiring customers to pay more for access.
Organizations still pay for closed frontier models because they work out of the box and come bundled with “compliance packaging, support, and accountability,” whereas many organizations lack the staff to run open-weights models well, Krikorian explained.
But the steadily narrowing performance gap between open and closed frontier models, coupled with the cost-effectiveness of open models, is now widely recognized by many companies. For example, the delivery company DoorDash has been using Kimi for routine work while reserving Fable for more difficult tasks that would normally take human experts longer to complete.
The narrowing performance gap is being measured in several ways. For example, the research nonprofit METR has defined an AI model’s time horizon as the length of tasks—measured by how long human experts require to complete them—that can be handled by AI models with a “reliable” 50 percent success rate. That time horizon has been doubling on a set cadence that has accelerated over time.
The best closed model can currently do a job that is 1.7 times as long as the longest job that the best open model can reliably finish.
“If the open frontier can handle a seven-hour job, the closed frontier can handle a 12-hour one,” Krikorian told Ars. “In four months, the open model handles the 12-hour job, and the closed one handles something around 20.”
Tasks requiring between eight and 12 hours are typically the ones that a closed frontier model can do and the open models cannot handle yet, Krikorian said. No models are generally capable of reliably doing tasks longer than 12 hours, whereas tasks taking less than eight hours can be done by either type of model and could be handed off to the cheaper open models.
There are many nuances and caveats for such comparisons. For example, closed frontier models often come with their own harness—the software layer that helps the models access various tools and memory to perform agent-like actions. Harnesses custom-built by AI labs for their models can sometimes boost performance on various tasks, whereas the models may perform less well with third-party harnesses.
To level the playing field, the benchmarking company Vals AI has been evaluating different open and closed models by using its own neutral harness. When every model ran on the same harness in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 evaluation, the open-weights model GLM 5.2 from the Chinese company Z.ai (Zhipu AI) scored within a point of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 and 4.8 while costing about five times less per completed task.
In other words, paying for closed frontier models buys about a four-month head start at about five times the per-task cost—but only when currently looking at tasks taking between eight and 12 hours.
“Pay when that head start is worth it, something like a deadline that lands before the open frontier catches up would be here,” Krikorian told Ars. “Routine work you’ll still be doing next quarter is not, because you’ll be able to do it for a fifth of the cost soon, and the model won’t be the bottleneck anyway.”
Concentrations of power
The surging popularity of open-weights models can be seen on OpenRouter, the AI gateway and marketplace that gives developers access to hundreds of different models from multiple providers. The Mozilla report noted that eight of the top 10 models ranked by token volumes in August 2026 provide open weights.
However, open models are still lagging behind closed frontier models in revenue. A paper by Frank Nagle and Daniel Yue for the Linux Foundation found that open models earned just 4 percent of overall revenue compared to closed models getting 96 percent of revenue—although they were looking at data from May through September of 2025.
“In the last year, open models have exploded, so we do expect revenue to have shifted,” Krikorian said.
The current reality is that “most of the open models the world runs on are Chinese,” Krikorian said. “The Chinese labs are running the same playbook the Americans ran with Android—give it away, but own the ecosystem around it,” he explained.
But Krikorian is not so concerned about “Chinese models” as he is about the risk of concentration. At the moment, the best open models are concentrated in China, whereas the best closed frontier models come from US companies. He argued for US and European labs to start competing in the “same open lane, so that no single country sets the world’s defaults.”
“The uncomfortable truth is that the plural ecosystem around open-weight AI is largely funded by Chinese capital right now,” Krikorian said. “That’s a plurality and a concentration at the same time.”
The history of development for open source software such as Linux may offer some lessons for how an “alternative coalition” could come together, Krikorian said. Such open source software infrastructure was funded by a coalition of organizations that “each needed the commodity layer to exist,” including neutral foundations.
Any coalition for building more open AI models would likely consist of “institutions with a mission rather than a market,” as opposed to frontier AI labs, Krikorian said. He described it as follows:
We need public compute programs funding fully open reference models. Switzerland’s national compute producing Apertus is an example. Foundations need to hold the same neutral ground that they held for the internet’s open protocols, extended into models, harnesses, and agentic standards. Companies that benefit from commodity models have to participate. And philanthropy has to cover what none of the others will—evaluation and audit infrastructure, especially.
Krikorian also called for the alternative coalition to go even further than open-weights models by embracing more of the open source approach. “It’s hard to fully trust a model with decisions if you can’t tell how it was trained or what it was evaluated against,” he said.

Tamil Nadu Minister for Health and Family Welfare K.G. Arunraj on Tuesday (September 8, 2026) announced in the Legislative Assembly that the State government would implement a Statewide mission to reduce the amount of salt in the daily diet of the public.
Dr. Arunraj said non-communicable diseases such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, stroke, and kidney disorders were among the most important public health challenges in Tamil Nadu. Nearly 50% of medically certified deaths in Tamil Nadu are caused by cardiovascular diseases. Approximately 1.8 crore people in Tamil Nadu are living with hypertension.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that a person should consume less than five grams of salt a day. However, scientific studies indicate that the people of Tamil Nadu consume an average of 7 to 8 grams of salt per day. Studies have also found that approximately 88% of the salt consumed as part of the South Indian diet comes from salt added during cooking at home. Global scientific studies have established that even a reduction of just one gram of salt per day can significantly lower blood pressure, he said.
Further, an international study involving approximately 21,000 people who used a low-sodium salt substitute, in which a portion of the sodium was replaced with potassium, demonstrated a 14% reduction in strokes and a 12% reduction in overall mortality. Based on this scientific evidence, the State government has decided to formulate and implement an integrated strategy to reduce high salt consumption in Tamil Nadu, Dr. Arunraj said.
Statewide survey
Announcing the key initiatives under the mission, Dr. Arunraj said for the first time, a Statewide survey based on urine samples would be undertaken to scientifically determine the current level of salt consumption among the people of Tamil Nadu.
Standards would be implemented to gradually reduce the amount of salt used in kitchens under the direct control of the government, including those serving the Nutritious Meal Programme, the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, government hospitals and hostels, he said.
The feasibility of making available to the public a low-sodium salt substitute, in which a portion of sodium is replaced with potassium and which does not produce a noticeable difference in taste, would be studied as a pilot project in selected areas, he said.
Through the ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ initiative and Health and Wellness Centres, people with hypertension would receive systematic counselling on reducing salt intake. A Statewide awareness campaign will be undertaken to educate people about salt content in food and simple ways to gradually reduce the excessive use of salt in everyday home cooking, he added.

Forget Hollywood. “American Idol” is heading to Georgia, dawg.
In news that felt all too depressingly common in production-starved Los Angeles, word emerged Tuesday that “American Idol” — which has been broadcast live from Los Angeles since it originated in 2002 — would move production to Georgia.
ABC, as well as producers Fremantle and 19 Entertainment (via owner Sony Pictures TV), didn’t respond to requests for comment about the news. But it makes “American Idol” the latest studio-based reality competition series to pull up stakes and leave Los Angeles in search of tax incentives and lower costs.
Fox’s “The Masked Singer,” for example, has moved to New Jersey, having most recently shot on the Fox lot in Century City. Also, ABC’s “Shark Tank,” which had been produced on the Sony lot in Culver City, has moved to Atlanta, as has Fox’s “Lego Masters,” formerly shot in Van Nuys. And game shows like “Family Feud” and “Celebrity Family Feud” have also relocated to the Atlanta area.
Popular on Variety
The loss of more reality and game series production in California comes even as the state’s film and television tax credit program has expanded to include unscripted fare. But there’s a catch: Those competition shows must have a budget of more than $1 million per episode. That makes it difficult to qualify, even for major shows like “American Idol.”
The California incentives still don’t include docuseries, talk shows or game shows. States like New Jersey and Georgia, on the other hand, don’t limit their incentives. Georgia’s tax incentives require a total production spend of $500,000, making it more attractive for shows like “American Idol.”
	“Reality and unscripted television remain excluded (with the exception of competition shows), despite being one of California’s most productive, scalable, and culturally influential sectors. At a time when producers are navigating shrinking license fees, shorter episode orders, and tighter margins, the ongoing omission of this entire category raises real questions about the long-term viability of keeping these productions in-state,” Weinstein Senior owner Todd Weinstein, Esq., wrote in a post on LinkedIn last year.
Reality television has been a foundational part of California’s production economy for decades,” he added. “These shows generate thousands of jobs, support local vendors, keep post facilities running, and increasingly require the same physical infrastructure as scripted content. They might look different with faster schedules, leaner teams, and alternative storytelling structures but they are no less real in terms of economic impact. Still, they continue to sit outside the framework of the tax credit.”
“American Idol” was broadcast from Television City in the Fairfax district for most of its run; it later shifted to Red Studios Hollywood.

From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed
- Published
Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.
Kazakhstan's Rybakina produced a brilliant performance to beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 in Saturday's final and repeat her Australian Open success against the same player in January.
Clutching the trophy on Saturday night, Rybakina reflected that "some magic is happening" for her after her difficult lead-in to the tournament.
The 27-year-old aggravated a foot injury during her quarter-final in Cincinnati against Iga Swiatek last month, a little over a week before the final major of the year began.
Playing on through injury could have disastrous consequences for the rest of the season - but Rybakina, knowing the top ranking was in her grasp, wanted to try and play in the final Grand Slam of the year.
"I was so upset. I didn't know actually how it was going to be day by day," she said.
"We arrived in New York and did an MRI. It didn't look that great.
"I couldn't even walk for the next few days without pain.
"I was lucky enough to have a very good doctor in Australia. She was on the phone with us all the time and somehow, with the team, we made a plan."
Rybakina did not do any on-court training for a week but daily recovery sessions in the gym - plus trips for dinner and to the cinema to "switch the mind" - helped get her ready for another major triumph.
She won her first four matches at Flushing Meadows without dropping a set, including seeing off four-time major winner Naomi Osaka.
Her run from then on - which included beating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen in the quarter-finals, outlasting third seed Coco Gauff in the semis and outplaying top seed Sabalenka in the final - was nothing short of outstanding.
"I was so unlucky with the injury, but I'm very proud," Rybakina said.
"I still can't believe it."
Composed Rybakina 'like a machine'
Rybakina had already been confirmed as world number one by reaching the semi-finals in New York. The fact that her final opponent was Sabalenka, the player she will replace at the top of the rankings, added an extra dimension to Saturday's championship match.
Rybakina won the first set despite her serve, one of her biggest weapons, misfiring.
She landed only 27% of her first serves during the opener, but still won 22 of 30 points behind her serve and did not face a break point as she took the lead.
Sabalenka eventually broke in the 12th game of the second set to send their match the distance, but Rybakina who dominated the decider.
While the Belarusian grew visibly more frustrated as the final slipped away, Rybakina remained remarkably composed.
"The way she [Rybakina] quietly walks around, she doesn't really lift her head up and she gives no emotion away whatsoever," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.
"Rybakina is like a machine out there. You never know what's going on in her head."
However, nerves did show when Rybakina threw in two double faults as she served for the title.
At 40-30, the trophy in her sights, Rybakina could have blinked. Instead, she cooly sent down her 12th ace of the match to secure her third Grand Slam title.
The second seed produced her biggest celebration of her three major wins - a smile and both arms raised in celebration as she took in the applause.
Rybakina has now won two of her three Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, all of which have come on their favoured hard courts.
'She will win many more Slams'
On Monday, Rybakina will become the 30th different women to top the world rankings.
She is a different personality to Sabalenka, who held the position for the past 99 weeks, but Croft believes she will "take it in her stride".
"I actually think she has the right personality to deal with it," Croft said.
"There are going to be a lot of players around her nipping at her heels. She can fluctuate with her levels, but when it really matters, we've seen her be able to bring it to the table.
"It's not going to be easy to hang onto it. I think women's tennis is really exciting right now."
Rybakina has completed three parts of the career Grand Slam, with just a French Open victory missing from her collection.
After winning Wimbledon in 2022, she did not claim her second major until January's Australian Open, and has now added a third in New York.
She has never previously been further than the quarter-finals at Roland Garros, although she did win a WTA 1000 event on clay in Rome in 2023.
Former British number one Laura Robson said on Sky Sports: "She is an all-surface player - clay is the worst one, but when you get her on something that's quite lively or quick, she's unplayable at times.
"I genuinely think she will win many more Slams. I just don't see, when her serve and return are on, how pretty much anyone can beat her on a hard court."
