Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”

European football players’ union FIFPRO Europe demanded reforms to FIFA’s decision-making structures on Monday, arguing that the world body’s now-abandoned investment proposal exposed dangerous flaws in how global football is governed.
The union released a study claiming FIFA’s shelved Forward Enterprise (FFE) initiative would have converted the game’s flagship competitions into assets for private capital without proper consultation with key stakeholders.
FIFA President Gianni Infantino unveiled the FFE proposal earlier this year before withdrawing it amid widespread opposition. FIFPRO Europe said the governance shortcomings that enabled its development remain unresolved.
“FFE was an attempt to convert the game’s core competitions into an investable, tradeable and undervalued financial asset for private capital,” the report stated, produced with Player IQ and Football Benchmark.
The study comes amid a wider debate over the balance of power in the global game. In court filings related to challenges from European football body UEFA, FIFA argued that opposition to its proposals is driven by efforts to preserve Europe’s dominant position in the sport.
The union said it supported efforts to increase development funding for smaller federations, but argued that any solidarity mechanism should be shaped jointly by stakeholders across the game.
“Any future proposal to grow solidarity funding should be built together, through trusted governance, not advanced unilaterally,” it said.
ALSO READ | UEFA urges US court to deny FIFA subsidiaries’ bid to join Infantino discovery fight
According to the report, European clubs employed 856 players at the expanded FIFA World Cup 2026 and released players worth about 16.9 billion euros (USD 19.8 billion), representing 94 per cent of the tournament’s total player value.
It added that all 20 individual award winners across the last five World Cup editions were employed by European clubs.
FIFPRO Europe said the findings underscored the need to protect what it described as football’s “critical infrastructure” and called for an independent review of FIFA Council executive decision making to ensure major changes could not be advanced by a single office acting alone.
The report noted that the share of World Cup revenue distributed as prize money to participating countries had fallen to about 7.7 per cent in 2026 from 10.5 per cent in 2006, despite strong growth in tournament revenue.
“Players receive only a fraction of that return, while participating federations rely on it as FIFA’s only performance-based revenue stream,” the report said.
The union also urged the formal inclusion of players, clubs and leagues in football governance alongside national associations.
Reuters has contacted FIFA for comment on the report’s findings.

Wired vs wireless speakers: What are the pros and cons?
Bluetooth and Wi-Fi make different compromises, and a wired connection alone doesn't guarantee better sound.
Wireless speakers are often treated as the convenient option, while wired systems get cast as the choice for better sound. The connection alone doesn't settle this question, though. Speaker design, amplification, source material and room acoustics all affect what you hear.
It also helps to separate the connection from the way the speaker is powered. Traditional passive speakers need a separate amplifier, which sends the amplified signal through speaker wire. Powered, or active, speakers have amplification built in. A wireless speaker receives audio over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or another wireless connection, but that doesn't necessarily make it cable-free. Many home models still plug into an outlet, while portable speakers run on batteries.
What wired speakers still do better
One clear advantage of passive wired systems is modularity. Because the amplifier and speakers are separate, you can replace or upgrade one without rebuilding the whole setup. That matters when you're putting together a stereo or home theater system you expect to keep for years.
A wired connection also removes Bluetooth transmission from the latency chain. Bluetooth can introduce a delay between the source and the sound reaching the speaker, with the amount varying between devices. Video playback can often compensate by delaying the picture to keep it in sync, but it's harder to mask in video games since the sound needs to react to what you're doing. The Bluetooth Special Interest Group's explanation of LE Audio describes buffering in Bluetooth Classic Audio as one source of that lag and explains how LE Audio can reduce it.
That doesn't mean a cable automatically makes music sound better, though. If the source is a lossy audio file, some information has already been removed during compression. Switching to a wired connection can't put that information back. The quality of the speaker, amplifier and recording still matters, as does the room you're listening in.
Cables are the obvious trade-off. A basic stereo pair is usually easy enough to wire, but setting up surround sound can mean running speaker cables to several points around a room. That can limit placement or leave you figuring out how to hide wires along walls, under rugs or behind furniture.
Where wireless speakers have the advantage
Wireless speakers are easier to place when you don't want to run audio cables across a room. Bluetooth models connect directly to a phone, tablet or laptop without relying on home Wi-Fi, which makes them especially useful for portable listening. That's the core appeal behind the models in our best portable Bluetooth speakers guide: flexible options you can easily carry anywhere you need them.
Wi-Fi speakers are better suited to a permanent home setup. Compatible models can use the same network for synchronized playback across several rooms, often through a companion app. The Denon Home 200, 400 and 600 speakers we reviewed, for example, use the HEOS app to group speakers or control rooms separately.
The trade-off is that wireless systems replace some cable management with network and software dependence. Wi-Fi speakers still need power, and multi-room platforms can work best when you stay within one ecosystem. Bluetooth range and reliability can also vary with distance, interference and the devices involved.
Bluetooth doesn't automatically mean poor audio quality, either. Many codecs use lossy compression, but Qualcomm's aptX Lossless is designed to deliver CD-quality lossless audio with compatible hardware, a lossless source and suitable wireless conditions. Wi-Fi systems can support lossless and high-resolution streaming too, so the connection type alone doesn't determine how good a speaker will sound.
Some portable models support Wi-Fi, as well. As our Sonos Play review notes, that device can use Wi-Fi at home or Bluetooth for a direct connection while you're out.
Which setup makes more sense for you?
Wired speakers are the stronger fit for a permanent stereo or home theater system if you don't mind running cables. Passive models give you more freedom to replace the amplifier or speakers later, and the wired connection avoids Bluetooth latency.
Wireless speakers make more sense when portability, easier placement or multi-room playback matters more than component-level upgrades. Bluetooth is best-suited for speakers you want to move around, while Wi-Fi works better for several speakers spread through a home.
Sound quality alone shouldn't decide it. Start with where the speakers will live and whether you care more about upgradeability, portability or multi-room playback. Then compare the actual speakers that fit that setup to get the best audio quality for your situation.

Does BJP's Rajasthan urban poll results show a shift in its loyal voter base?
The BJP emerged as the top party in Rajasthan's urban local body polls. But it was just one percentage point ahead of the Congress in vote share. Setbacks in BJP strongholds have exposed cracks in its traditional urban base. This is why this rings warning bells for the BJP.
The BJP has won Rajasthan's urban local body elections, securing 4,179 of the 10,235 declared wards, against the Congress's 3,613. The BJP's seat share also rose from 35.7% in the previous election cycle (2019 to 2021) to 40.8%, while the Congress slipped from 40.7% to 35.3%. PM Narendra Modi called it "proof of the victory of truth over the echo of falsehood." However, the BJP's victory in the cities and towns in Rajasthan might be masking deeper trouble for the saffron party.
The win also exposes discontent within sections of the BJP's traditionally loyal urban electorate. This was not the kind of sweeping civic victory that an incumbent government backed by a formidable urban organisation would have expected.
While the BJP's victory lies in its victories in a large number of wards and its lead over the Congress, the warning signs are clearly visible in the municipal corporations in the districts of Bharatpur, Pali, Ajmer, Bikaner, Jodhpur and Alwar, where the party failed to secure a majority.
All the seven corresponding Lok Sabha seats went to the BJP in the 2024 General Elections. Several of them are BJP strongholds and are associated with the party's most prominent leaders, including that of Rajasthan CM Bhajan Lal Sharma, state BJP president Madan Rathore, former CM and BJP national vice-president Vasundhara Raje and Union ministers Arjun Ram Meghwal, Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Bhupender Yadav and Bhagirath Choudhary.
Independents, meanwhile, won 2,273 wards, but their share remained virtually unchanged at 22.2%, compared with 22.4% in the 2019-21 election cycle.
So, the poll results point not to an abandonment of the BJP by its traditionally loyal urban voter base, but to worrying cracks in it.
The BJP's urban constituency, built from the Jana Sangh era and consolidated by the BJP from the 1980s onward, has included traders, shopkeepers, Bania-Vaishya and Jain communities, sections of the salaried middle class and voters connected to the RSS network in Rajasthan. Their support has helped make Rajasthan's cities BJP strongholds, even when the party has faced attacks in rural constituencies.
Polling for 309 urban local bodies in Rajasthan was conducted on September 9 and 11. The previous cycle stretched over four rounds between November 2019 and January 2021. A direct comparison of the two contests is complicated as delimitation before the 2026 polls added 2,770 wards. Nevertheless, the BJP's rise from 2,666 of 7,474 wards to 4,179 of 10,235 declared wards represents a five-percentage-point improvement in seat share. The Congress's seat share fell by approximately the same number.
BJP WON, BUT IT'S NOT AN USUAL SWEEP
Urban Rajasthan has traditionally provided the BJP with a dependable political base. Traders, shopkeepers, the salaried middle-class and sections of the Bania-Vaishya, Jain and other "upper-caste" communities. The BJP's organisational network, ideological appeal and reputation as the natural party of urban Hindu voters have generally helped it withstand local dissatisfaction.
There is, however, no caste-wise post-poll survey establishing that these communities shifted away from the BJP in 2026. A defensible conclusion is that loyalties have weakened selectively, depending on the candidate, performance of local administration, conditions of civic infrastructure and equations concerning factional.
The BJP secured 40.8% of the declared wards, but its vote-share lead over Congress was just 0.94 percentage points. It won clear majorities in urban local bodies in Jaipur, Kota, Udaipur and Bhilwara, but only four of the 10 municipal corporations. Meanwhile, the Congress won Bikaner, which saw a massive mobilisation against the BJP, led by Shri Karni Sena, over the now-stayed UGC caste-equity norms.
REBELLION IN BJP, CONG LED TO INDEPENDENTS CONTESTING
Independents have captured Bharatpur (Rajasthan CM Bhajan Lal's home turf) while Municipal Corporation polls in major cities like Ajmer, Alwar, Jodhpur and Pali produced fractured verdicts. The picture becomes clearer when the results of these politically significant corporations are examined individually.
In Bharatpur, Independents won 36 of 65 wards, securing an outright majority, while the BJP managed 20 and Congress seven. The result points to a powerful local rebellion, and, because of the optics involved, a BJP defeat here appears to be politically more damaging than an ordinary setback in a municipal election.
"Bharatpur is one region where people often do not take the Congress or BJP symbol and contest as Independents. Therefore, Bharatpur should not be assessed strictly through the Congress-BJP binary," said Sharat Kumar, Rajasthan Bureau Chief of the India Today Group, in a YouTube broadcast.
Congress was in power in Bharatpur. In 2019, after it had won only 18 of 65 wards, it managed to form the board with support from Independents and BSP councillors.
It must be noted that news agency PTI, before the polls, reported widespread unrest in both the BJP and Congress over ticket distribution. Several aspirants denied tickets by the two parties, entered the contest as Independents.
BJP LOSS BASTIONS OF STATE CHIEF, FORMER CM VASUNDHARA RAJE
In Pali, the Congress won 29 wards, the BJP 21 and the Independents 15. Pali is associated with BJP state president Madan Rathore. The party's inability to emerge as the largest force here raises questions about ticket distribution, local leadership and organisational cohesion.
In Jhalawar, the Congress won 29 of the 45 Municipal Council wards, against the BJP's 13. Jhalawar is the political stronghold of former CM Vasundhara Raje, although the BJP retained the separate Jhalrapatan municipality. The result suggests that the BJP label alone could not overcome local anti-incumbency.
"Vasundhara Raje's supporters are influential in several constituencies, and the BJP lost in some urban areas where leaders connected to her on caste or personal grounds held sway...," said Sharat Kumar of Rajasthan Tak, India Today Digital's sister portal.
In Ajmer too, the Congress emerged as the largest party with 37 of 80 wards, followed by BJP with 32 and Independents with 11. Ajmer has long had a strong BJP-RSS presence and was controlled by the BJP previously. The loss in Ajmer could also be attributed to former BJP mayor Dharmendra Gehlot's rebellion, which might have hit the party's local calculations. Rajasthan Tak's Sharat Kumar also said that "the BJP performed poorly in areas associated with women and child development minister and South Ajmer MLA, Anita Bhadel, who is considered close to Vasundhara Raje."
In Jodhpur, the BJP and Congress finished level with 44 wards each, leaving Independents decisive in board formation. The BJP emerged as the largest party in Alwar but fell short of a majority. The inconclusive verdicts carry wider political significance because Jodhpur and Alwar are associated with Union ministers Gajendra Singh Shekhawat and Bhupender Yadav, respectively, making them notable setbacks for the BJP in the strongholds of its senior leaders.
Rajasthan Tak's Kumar linked the BJP's underwhelming performances in Jodhpur and Alwar to dissatisfaction with the Union ministers associated with the two seats. He, however, stressed that the Congress failed to capitalise on it.
"Gajendra Singh Shekhawat worked hard, but could neither secure a clear majority in Pokhran nor settle the contest in Jodhpur. There is considerable resentment against Bhupender Yadav in Alwar, but why did Independents benefit from it and not Congress? That is something Congress must think about," said Sharat Kumar.
DID KARNI SENA'S PROTEST AGAINST UGC EQUITY NORMS DENY BJP VOTES?
In Bikaner, the Congress secured a majority with 42 of 80 wards, while the BJP remained far behind. The city is associated with Union minister Arjun Ram Meghwal and has had a BJP-controlled corporation. It must be noted that the Rajput-centric Shri Rajput Karni Sena had mobilised against the UGC's 2026 caste-equity regulations. The group had also vowed not to vote for the BJP.
After the poll results, Karni Sena chief Mahipal Singh Makrana claimed that its Swarna Nyay Manch had supported more than 1,500 Independents and that the campaign contributed to the BJP's Bikaner setback, according to a report in The Times of India. However, the BJP has disputed this interpretation, and argued that Independents have traditionally performed strongly in Rajasthan's municipal elections and that their success could not be attributed to the Sena campaign.
ROADS, DRAINS AND REBELS MATTERED TOO. CJP ALSO A FACTOR?
The urban elections came amid mounting complaints over Rajasthan's civic mess, repeatedly highlighted by whistle-blowers such as Khurpench and reflected in reports of broken roads, waterlogging, overflowing drains, garbage piles and unreliable municipal services.
The timing of the polls added to the BJP's challenge. The polls took place during the monsoon, when these failures were difficult to conceal. Unlike Assembly or Lok Sabha elections, civic contests are local, and voters can judge a party by the councillor, the drain and street outside their homes before considering its ideological message.
"The BJP went into the election when roads in the big cities were broken, drains were overflowing and garbage had accumulated," said Sharat Kumar. He argued that the party survived the discontent because its cadre, senior leaders and organisation worked collectively.
Ticket denial also produced many rebels. Many ran as Independents and offered traditional BJP voters a way to punish the official candidate without voting for Congress. This helps explain Bharatpur and several other hung civic bodies. This, however, does not establish a statewide independence wave. Independents won 22.21% of declared wards this time, almost identical to their 22.36% share during the 2019-21 urban body poll cycle.
While the CJP's "School Theek Karo" campaign amplified youth anger over crumbling government schools before polling, with the Rajasthan government subsequently announcing a three-year, Rs 12,500-crore infrastructure plan.
After the results, the CJP cited the BJP's setback in Bharatpur, CM Bhajan Lal Sharma's home district, while warning that neglecting education and employment could further hurt the party.
Sharat Kumar also pointed to frustration among sections of the OBC electorate, including Kumawat candidates who contested and won as Independents. The Kumawats, often grouped with Kumhar-Prajapats, are an OBC community, with a notable presence in Jaipur and across the Ajmer, Bhilwara, Nagaur, Sikar and Pali belts.
Kumar also warned that the BJP could not treat "original OBC" communities as a permanent vote bank without providing political representation.
Before the polls, the Rajasthan OBC Commission's survey triggered pushback from Jat and Gurjar organisations, which alleged that the government had released selective data while withholding the full report on political representation. The controversy, coupled with complaints of inadequate representation among communities such as the Kumawats, could have weakened the BJP's hold over sections of its OBC base.
RISE OF AAP, RLP AT CONGRESS'S EXPENSE?
Interestingly, the BJP's setbacks did not translate into decisive gains for Congress. Instead, smaller parties and Independents captured the space created by dissatisfaction with the ruling party in several pockets. The AAP won 42 wards, including 31 of 60 in Baran Municipal Council, ending Congress's 15-year control of the body. The CPI(M), meanwhile, captured 29 of Nokha's 45 wards, while the Nagaur MP Hanuman Beniwal-led RLP increased its tally from 14 wards in the 2019-21 cycle to 63 this time.
The RLP's gains were largely in central-western Rajasthan, where its leader Hanuman Beniwal commands support among sections of the Jat electorate. While this aided in the RLP's win in the region, the factor could have adversely affected the BJP.
One must remember that Rajasthan's Jats had joined the community from Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh in farmers' protests. They have also demanded a central OBC status. A demand for a separate Jat Regiment has also sustained political discontent within sections of the community in Rajasthan. These factors and the emergence of Beniwal and the RLP could have impacted the BJP's performance in the region.
"Jats are not a fixed vote bank. They look at who will stand with them and support the strongest local leader," said Sharat Kumar of Rajasthan Tak.
The verdict from Rajasthan's cities and towns may not yet amount to a realignment of voters. But the BJP's handling of civic failures, unpopular candidates, internal factionalism and demands for representation from caste groups appear to have made sections of its support base more willing to consider alternatives. The Congress, however, failed to harness that unease, allowing AAP, the RLP, CPI(M) and Independents to gain ground in several important pockets that are politically important to the BJP.

You may not know it, but minivans are making a comeback in the US. Look around, and you’ll start to notice an uptick in these breadboxes on wheels. Sales were up 21 percent in 2025, suggesting that the humble minivan is shaking off its “uncool” stigma and finding new fans among an SUV-weary public. I’m here for it.
Kia’s electric van lineup is getting more interesting with reveal of PV7
The PV7 is longer than Kia’s previous electric van and comes in two versions: one for passengers and one for cargo.
One of the companies currently carrying the torch for minivans is Kia, which has sold its popular Carnival minivan here since 2021. Kia is also one of the few automakers making all-electric vans. This week, the Korean automaker rolled out its new PV7 at IAA Transportation in Germany. This is the second electric van from Kia’s Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup, following the PV5 “people mover,” which went on sale in 2025. The PV7 is longer than the PV5 by about 2 feet and comes in two variants, one for passengers and one for cargo.
All of which is to say that Kia should bring its increasingly interesting electric vans to the US. If they are attractively priced — and this is Kia, so it’s safe to assume that’s possible — I really think these vans would do numbers. The people yearn for a moderately priced electric van!
The PBV vans are technically impressive on several levels. They’re built on Kia’s dedicated PBV architecture (E-GMP.S) that features a flat-floor layout for easy loading and unloading. The PV7 will come with a 71.5kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack or a 96.2kWh one. Kia claims the Cargo Long-Range version will get 460km (285.8 miles) on the generous WLTP cycle (which tends to be around 10–20 percent more generous than the EPA’s estimates). It’s built on an 800-volt architecture, which enables 10—80 percent charging in under 25 minutes using a 350kW DC fast charger. And it supports vehicle-to-load outlets to power external tools and equipment. The infotainment runs on Kia’s Android Automotive-based Pleos Connect OS, which includes its Gleo AI natural-language voice controls.
This all sounds great! And the design is just forward-looking enough to erase any concerns about the typical clunkiness of van ownership. The front end features a distinctive two-tone design with a dark upper section that wraps around the windshield, giving it a visor-like appearance. The upright look and tall, flat roof suggests a large interior space perfect for vanlife compartmentalization. The low front bumper and plastic body cladding around the base add a rugged, practical border. Both the passenger and cargo versions feature distinctive wheels with a squarish multi-spoke design. It’s not boring, but it’s not so in your face as to challenge your worldview.
While Kia’s not saying whether the PV7 will be making its way to the US anytime soon, a version has been spotted testing in the US, according to Electrek. Officially, the van will be launched in Europe and Korea in the second half of 2027, with “additional markets, derivatives and conversion models to follow.”
PBV was introduced during CES 2024 as a family of EVs built on a flexible vehicle architecture with different swappable body types. The vehicle can be transformed from a minivan to a full-size van to a small truck, depending on the specific need. The driver cab remains fixed, while the rest of the vehicle is interchangeable, like a real-life Duplo set. Of course, that was a concept from a different era. We’ve now veered into a darker timeline, at least for EVs.
I get why Kia would hesitate to name the US as a future market, what with our well-documented history of cutting off our nose to spite our face. The minivan market may not be as red-hot as, say, the one for lifted trucks that roll coal and grind up spandex-wearing cyclists for breakfast. But the times, they are a-changing. Gas prices are going up and up. And an electric van could just be thing that finally heals our broken nation.

The Indian men’s and women’s Kabaddi squads bound for the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 were given a warm send-off at the Sports Authority of India (SAI) National Centre of Excellence (NCOE), Gandhinagar, on Tuesday.
The men’s squad is led by Head Coach Balwan Singh, with BC Ramesh and Anup Kumar as Assistant Coaches, while the women’s team is coached by Neeta Dadwe, with Mamtha Poojari as Assistant Coach. Both squads comprise 12 players, coaches and support staff.
The two teams underwent their final preparatory camp at SAI NCOE Gandhinagar from September 5 to 14, 2026, in the run-up to the Asian Games.

Women’s team captain Pushpa Rana highlighted how the growing league culture in India is contributing not only to the development of Indian Kabaddi but also to the strengthening of the sport internationally. “The league culture in our country is not only helping develop our own team and our players, but is also strengthening Kabaddi in other countries. Players and coaches from different countries are getting exposure through our leagues and taking that experience back to their respective countries. This is helping the standard of the sport grow internationally. The dedicated Kabaddi facilities here at SAI NCOE Gandhinagar have also provided us with a very good environment for our preparations,” she said.
India has the hugely popular Pro Kabaddi League which has been running for over a decade, bringing kabaddi talent from all over the world to India for a 12-team franchise tournament. This is a men’s event. Apart from exhibition games, there has been no women’s equivalent of the league.
Men’s team captain Sunil Kumar spoke about the changing nature of the sport and the increasingly competitive environment at the international level.
“Kabaddi has evolved significantly. The game is becoming faster and more tactical, and the competition at the international level is increasing. The training environment here has been very good, particularly the Strength and Conditioning facilities, which have supported our physical preparation. We are prepared for the challenge and will give our best at the Asian Games,” he said.
Women’s team Head Coach Neeta Dadwe expressed confidence in the team’s preparations and highlighted the extensive training undertaken by the squad ahead of the Asian Games.

“We are very well prepared. We had a 15-day training camp in May, followed by a month-long camp in June, then another month-long camp at JSW Bellare and finally the camp here at SAI, Gandhinagar. We are looking forward to the Games,” she said.
“We received very good support during our training camps here. The management was very receptive to our requirements and all our requirements were addressed promptly, which helped our preparations. The arrangements, including the Mess and the overall support extended to the teams, have been excellent. We are confident of doing our best at the Games.”
Men’s team Head Coach Balwan Singh lauded the commitment and hard work put in by both the men’s and women’s squads in the lead-up to the Asian Games and expressed confidence in their performance.
“Both the men’s and women’s teams have worked extremely hard during the camp. The players have shown great commitment, discipline and dedication throughout the preparation, and the quality of training gives us confidence about our performance at the Games. We are grateful to SAI NCOE Gandhinagar and the management for the support extended to the teams during the camp,” he said.
The Indian women’s Kabaddi team won the gold medal at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, defeating Chinese Taipei 26-25 in a closely contested final, while the Indian men’s team also clinched gold, defeating Iran in a hugely controversial final that saw a nearly hour-long delay due to a dispute in point ruling.

A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.
“Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.
With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.
Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.
Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”
“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.
Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.
A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.
Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.
Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.
But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.
“Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.
“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.
Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.
Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there.
“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”
Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.
For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.
Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.
Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.
Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.
Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.
“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”
As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities.
César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”
A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

AI 'SpongeBob' parody of problems in Egypt draws scrutiny of authorities
- Published
An AI-generated version of the hit US cartoon character SpongeBob SquarePants has recently become the unlikely star of a controversial online trend by Egyptians criticising living conditions, amid strict rules about political dissent.
A wave of satirical postings began last month with a Facebook group dedicated to "Complaints of the Residents of al-Hamour Bottom" - the Arabic name used for SpongeBob's underwater home, Bikini Bottom.
Soon images were showing Egypt's President, Abdul Fattah al-Sisi, as the money-grabbing Mr Krabs, a seabed overcrowded by tuk-tuks (automated rickshaws), and schoolgirl fish being sexually harassed by sleazy, male fish.
Other posts prompted comments complaining about allegedly corrupt ministers, skyrocketing rent, and the poor state of health and education.
The manipulated images of the SpongeBob programme, originally produced by Nickelodeon, were created by users of the site.
Within a couple of weeks, the Facebook group had picked up 1.8m followers. One astute cartoon depicted ministry of interior staff underwater, warning: "Be careful", before the group was suspended, amid reports of official scrutiny.
A teenage girl who claimed she was the group's administrator put a video clip online saying that she and her fellow creators should not be held responsible for political posts that some members had posted in spin-off groups.
Pro-government media and TV presenters accused the outlawed Islamist Muslim Brotherhood, of exploiting the viral phenomenon. Egypt's military ousted the Brotherhood-backed President Mohammed Morsi in 2013, following mass protests against his one-year rule.
"The trend of al-Hamour Bottom belongs to the Brotherhood," insisted well-known talk show host Tamer Abdel Monaim in a programme dedicated to the topic. "Its aim is to sow confusion."
While many posts containing the most sensitive political comments have now been removed, some of the most popular content has continued to circulate widely on social media. Many Egyptian celebrities, social media influencers and brands adopted the theme, sharing AI-generated memes of al-Hamour Bottom.
"The laughter surrounding Bikini Bottom is not necessarily a sign of happiness," the Egyptian radio presenter Rabab Kamal told her thousands of Facebook followers. "People are laughing because circumstances have become so absurd that laughter feels like the only possible response."
Home to more than 110m people, Egypt is the most populated Arab country. Since the 2011 Arab Spring, it has been through years of social and economic upheaval. Ordinary Egyptians still struggle with high inflation from previous currency devaluations affecting their standard of living.
Regional instability has hit Suez Canal revenues, tourism and remittances from Egyptians working in the Gulf. Fuel costs have risen and this summer, the government raised some electricity tariffs by 12%.
At the same time, there is increased intolerance for public dissent in Egypt since the military, led by Sisi, returned to power. The government fears instability and challenges to its rule.
The surreal humour of SpongeBob and his aquatic friends - particularly popular with Millennials and Generation Z - became an unlikely way to work around this.
"The Egyptian government has long been cracking down on online expression. Thousands of people in Egypt languish for years in pretrial detention simply for expressing views online that are not sanctioned by the state," says Mahmoud Shalaby, a regional researcher at Amnesty International.
"This repression is not limited to political opponents. It extends to a wide range of people, including religious minorities, people who do not adhere to a religion, people perceived to be LGBTI, and female social media creators who are often prosecuted under vague morality laws."
Although Sisi insists he is committed to freedom of expression and that Egyptians are free to air any views, few are buying it. Late last month, the president appeared to obliquely reference the SpongeBob craze when he referred to "social media chaos" and how ongoing public discussions failed to grasp the magnitude of national challenges.
Egyptian state security encourages reporting on suspicious or anti-government behaviour.
It may not come as any surprise then that already a lawyer has reportedly submitted a legal complaint against "the administrators, operators, financiers and contributors behind the creation of online content, pages and social media accounts associated with al-Hamour Bottom".
The Cairo 24 news site says he has called for a review into "satirically depicting economic conditions and decisions in a manner that could disturb public security and social order".
The mounting pressure means that SpongeBob could soon be setting aside his new pharaonic costume and giving up the pyramids and his Egyptian home.

From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say.
The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers.
A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; £38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference.
Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday.
Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded.
Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas.
They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year.
Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations.
However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe.

Alberta NDP flies the anti-separatist flag to steal a UCP riding in Calgary
A surprise upset 5 weeks before referendum, and a whole year before next election
In among all the splashes of Alberta NDP orange and UCP blue, there was plenty of red adorning the front yards of many homes ahead of this week’s Calgary-Shaw byelection.
No, sorry, I’m not talking about Alberta Liberal Leader John Roggeveen and the 3.8 per cent vote share he snagged.
The red refers to the many Canadian flags homeowners have newly erected, and the pro-unity, anti-separatist lawn signs that have sprung up throughout Alberta.
The campaigning New Democrats sensed the kind of reception they’d get at those doors for their candidate Kyle Campbell, now the MLA-elect.
“If you were flying a Canadian flag or you had a forever Canadian sign … Yeah, we pretty much could mark you down as a supporter,” NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters on Tuesday, the day after his party’s victory in what was previously a UCP riding in Calgary’s deep suburbs.
It’s often too easy and too foolish to treat the results of a single byelection as a predictor of a general election a year away, although darned if the partisans like Nenshi won’t try.
We’re likely on firmer ground trying to discern what a byelection says about the mood heading into the referendum about Alberta separation that’s set for five weeks from now.
Polls have consistently indicated that Albertans, especially in big cities, resoundingly support the “stay” option and oppose holding a future referendum for independence.
Now, another indication, in the form of voting results. At least in Calgary-Shaw, the public mood has turned against Premier Danielle Smith and her United Conservatives, who thrust the province deeper into the unity debate by crafting and scheduling the Oct. 19 vote.
Shaw residents converted what was a 14-percentage-point UCP victory in the last election into a nearly four-point NDP byelection win. Of the 12 Calgary ridings that Smith’s party took in 2023, Shaw had the third-widest victory margin, a fact that might bring worry to UCP cabinet ministers and backbenchers in the city.
The win in Shaw was somewhat of a surprise to the NDP, judging by, among more publicly available factors, the fact Nenshi said his party’s relatively modest win margin “exceeded my wildest expectations.”
After all, the Opposition party had long been trailing the UCP in public opinion, and Nenshi lagged behind Smith, including in the city he formerly served as mayor. Most voters may have been squarely against separation or even the debate itself, but that dissatisfaction hadn’t been washing up on United Conservative shores. Not yet at least.
Smith and her Shaw candidate Mike Derry might have said repeatedly that they endorse staying in Canada, but Campbell and Nenshi spent much of the campaign trying to remind voters how responsible the UCP government is for the referendum — and that senior organizers in the party favour separation.
How thoroughly did the New Democrats wrap their campaign identity around federalism? After Campbell’s victory speech at a southwest Calgary bar, supporters spontaneously broke into a rendition of O Canada.
After the verdict that got his backers singing, a jubilant Nenshi called the byelection an “earthquake.”
“This means that 35 days from today, we send Danielle Smith and her separatist pals packing, and within a year from now, we give Albertans the NDP government they deserve,” he said.
Sure, Alberta would have a Premier Naheed Nenshi if Shaw’s 18-point swing from UCP to NDP gets translated to the rest of the province in the fall 2027 election.
In the same way that a stunner of a federal Conservative victory in a 2024 byelection in the Toronto riding of St. Paul’s led to Prime Minister Pierre Poilievre in 2025. Or didn’t.
In mid-2024, the Pierre Poilievre Conservatives stole a federal byelection in downtown Toronto, flipping a seat that had been Liberal for three decades. One year and one prime ministerial resignation later, the Liberals took the riding by 28 percentage points, and Mark Carney secured a fourth straight Liberal government term.
Ample time to interpret message
That Toronto byelection sent a political message of sorts that ultimately led to Justin Trudeau’s resignation. There’s ample time and opportunity for Alberta’s premier to interpret the message that voters sent her in the sort of suburban seat her party can’t afford to lose in a general election.
Barring another political “earthquake” on Oct. 19, independence referendums will be a distant memory come next fall. Alberta politics could change a lot before then; heavens knows they’re prone to turbulence.
Smith could pivot her agenda farther away from the independence question. She could give her Opposition less room to cast her as an agent of disunity, and themselves as the exclusive guardians of Alberta’s place within Canada.
It’s also possible United Conservative members give their federalist leader new marching orders on that same matter, and urge her at a November convention to get in line with many party activists and take a more pro-separatist stance.
The future could also be determined by what Calgary-Shaw and other ridings look like in the next election. Alberta’s electoral boundaries are getting revised by an unorthodox UCP-led advisory panel, with the prospect that the cities’ suburban ridings are spliced with more UCP-friendly rural areas.
The October referendum seems to have left its striking imprint in one riding. The boundary revisions will be but one of many factors that will colour in the map when all Albertans get to vote next year.

About 70% of the year-to-year variation in winter air pollution across northern India may be explained by the frequency of western disturbances, possibly providing warning of unusually polluted winter months in advance, researchers said.
Western disturbances are storm systems that travel eastwards from the Mediterranean region towards South Asia by strengthening vertical ventilation and bringing precipitation that helps clear accumulated pollution, including PM2.5, from the air.
The team said winters with more frequent western disturbances tend to experience lower air pollution levels, while winters with fewer of these storms are more susceptible to persistent severe pollution.
"Currently, many of the most disruptive air-pollution measures are taken only after severe pollution is already developing," lead author Yuanyu Xie, an associate research scholar at Princeton University's School of Public and International Affairs, U.S., said.
"If scientists can anticipate the overall severity of the coming winter months ahead of time, governments, businesses, and communities will have more time to prepare," Ms. Xie said.
They also found that the frequency of western disturbances is linked to ocean temperature patterns already evident during the preceding autumn.
The team said the overall severity of winter pollution in north India may thus be predicted about a season in advance. Air pollution levels across northern India, including Delhi-NCR, spike during the winter season, increasing residents' health risks.
A combination of vehicle emissions, stubble burning in the neighbouring states of Punjab, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh and weather patterns that trap pollutants close to the ground is attributed to the seasonal spike in pollution.
Emergency measures, including pausing construction, restricting industries and limiting traffic, are implemented on severe pollution days, but may be a challenge if put in place on short notice.
The researchers said seasonal forecasts could indicate whether the coming winter is likely to have relatively severe or mild pollution levels overall, rather than predicting pollution levels for a particular day months in advance, thereby offering a more practical approach.
The information could provide a lead time, allowing authorities to strengthen enforcement before the pollution season begins, coordinate responses across jurisdictions, and give businesses more time to prepare for potential restrictions, they said.
"Emission controls will remain of paramount importance," co-author Denise Mauzerall, a professor of public and international affairs and civil and environmental engineering at Princeton University, said.
"However, we show that forecasts of winter pollution based on observations from the previous autumn can allow additional pollution controls to be arranged in advance of extreme pollution periods. This could provide time to plan and implement cost-effective controls that mitigate peak pollution concentrations in winter in northern India," Ms. Mauzerall said.
The authors wrote, "Nearly 70% of the inter-annual variations in winter PM2.5 pollution across northern India are explained by western disturbances (WDs) — prevailing extratropical storms originating from the Mediterranean region — through PM2.5 removal via enhanced ventilation and precipitation."

Tiny krill are turning up in deep-sea hydrothermal vents. Scientists want to know why
Antarctic krill are the lifeblood of the South Pole.
These shrimp-like crustaceans serve as a crucial food source for penguins, seals, and whales. "Most of them feed on Antarctic krill," says Kim Bernard, a biological oceanographer at Oregon State University and a National Geographic explorer. "And if they don't, they feed on something else that feeds directly on Antarctic krill. So they are absolutely fundamental to the functioning and health of that ecosystem."
For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.
Krill also recycle nutrients that allow tiny algae called phytoplankton to grow. In addition, krill are fished in large numbers to produce aquaculture feed and omega-3 fatty acids as dietary supplements.
But experts say this rich habitat in the Southern Ocean at the bottom of the world is shifting rapidly due to climate change. "It's one of the most rapidly warming areas on the planet," says Bernard. "And that's cascading through the food web and affecting the Antarctic krill population."
Now, Bernard and her colleagues report in the journal Communications Biology the discovery of a surprising habitat for the krill — hydrothermal vents, which are basically hot springs on the ocean floor. Characterizing the importance of this habitat, especially for reproductive females, may help inform how to safeguard these crucial crustaceans.
Venting feelings
Antarctic krill tend to be located in the upper layer of the ocean. "They can be found forming swarms and layers at the surface," says Bernard. "You can photograph them from airplanes."
They can also be found at the sea floor at different depths, but she says these deeper observations have been sparse and anecdotal.
Then, in late 2024, Bernard was in Bransfield Strait off the Antarctic Peninsula while aboard the National Geographic and Rolex Perpetual Planet Southern Ocean Expedition in collaboration with the Schmidt Ocean Institute.
One of her colleagues, UCLA benthic ecologist Andrew Thurber, was using a remotely operated vehicle in a trough some 3,600 feet below the surface to study and video record a hydrothermal vent. Picture "extremely hot water coming from deep within the Earth's crust," says Bernard, "and it's bringing with it metals and sulfides and all sorts of other chemicals that form almost like a tower."
It's a seemingly inhospitable place. Bernard wasn't studying the vent but she was eager to observe the sampling nevertheless.
"While having a little tea break upstairs in the galley," she recalls, "I was watching the big screens showing in real time what was happening."
And that's when she saw a flicker of movement in the corner of the screen. It was, unmistakably, a krill.
"It's like underwater ballet," she says, describing the krill's backflips. "It just looks like pirouetting. I pretty much threw the tea in the air and ran down to the control room, screaming, 'There's krill, there's krill!'"
Krill had never been spotted at a hydrothermal vent before. The other research team had planned to sample the geology and microbiology of the vent, but they gave Bernard a precious 15 minutes to try to catch a few specimens.
"They have what they call a suction sampler, which is essentially a vacuum that slurps whatever you want to slurp up," she explains. The team managed to nab four individual krill, all reproductive females, "very heavily laden with eggs. Should be releasing them any moment."
"And to see something like that at a hydrothermal vent," Bernard continues, "is completely opposite to what we would have normally expected."
Researchers had thought that females probably released their eggs near the surface over deep water, but it had never been observed before. So Bernard found herself with a single basic question: "Why on earth are they down there?," she says. "I really wanted to just try and understand, what are they getting from that site?"
It takes a lot of energy for little krill to get down that deep. In addition, they're exposed to potentially toxic heavy metals like cadmium, barium and lead.
So whatever is bringing the krill to the hydrothermal vent, Bernard figured, it must be worth it.
"It's really critical that we put our efforts into trying to understand the role of the deep sea environment for reproductive krill," she says.
Four little krill, one big question
To get a better sense of what was going on, Bernard brought the handful of krill to the surface and compared their stomach contents to others she collected elsewhere on the seafloor in shallower, non-vent waters. The four females had clearly been feeding on microbes living down there. (And such a microbial food source would be available year-round rather than seasonal phytoplankton that rely on sunlight and photosynthesis.)
"The rest of the krill tissue," she says, "I dried up and literally carried in my backpack on the way home. I didn't want to put it anywhere out of my sight because it was so important."
That tissue later revealed that the krill had accumulated higher levels of metals released by the vent, like manganese. "That's an important nutrient or mineral for embryo development in crustaceans," says Bernard. "And it's very scarce in the Southern Ocean. So potentially that's a reason for them to go down there."
The warmer waters near the vent may also speed up embryo development.
All or some combination of these reasons may motivate the krill to journey downwards to the hydrothermal vent repeatedly and to then stay there for some time.
"The study shows that krill can make use of hydrothermal vent habitats, but it doesn't provide enough evidence to suggest that they are dependent on these habitats," says Simeon Hill, a marine ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey who didn't participate in the research.
Still, he's reassured that krill can flexibly use different parts of the ocean to live and feed as it demonstrates their resilience.
And he says that even though hydrothermal vents are reasonably well protected from destructive human activities, additional conservation measures may be needed.
"It makes me think it would be sensible to develop a marine protected area process that allows new vulnerable habitats to be added as they're discovered," says Hill.
That kind of protection may be especially necessary if those habitats are critical to the krill's reproductive cycle.
Two months after the original research cruise, the same vessel visited another Antarctic hydrothermal vent some 1,000 miles away. That vent also abounded with egg-laden female krill.
"It was incredible," says Bernard. "So I am sure that this is something that is not just a once-off, and there's more to this than we ever expected."

Data for 2024-25 reveals that 51,249 corneas were donated in India, which met just a quarter of the projected need of around 1,00,000 corneas annually. The reason for this is a utilisation rate of 50% at best, with actual transplants performed ranging only between 25,000 to 30,000.
Why does this happen? The cause for a significant proportion of this gift of vision not reaching an operating table is the donated corneal tissue not being tested or processed in time. Other causes include improper harvesting and storage, as well as the decrease in endothelial cell density, which comes with an increase in age of donors. While some of these factors may not have an immediate or implementable solution, what is fixable, is timing and logistics.
Understanding cornea retrival
Cornea retrieval after death is a race against the clock. First, is the six-hour window after death within which a cornea should ideally be retrieved. This can differ in different weathers. For instance, in winters and monsoon, it can be a time frame of 6-8 hours as well. The second, less-publicly known factor, is the clock that starts once the corneal tissue is in storage. Most Indian eye banks still preserve corneas in McCarey-Kaufman (MK) medium, which keeps tissue usable for about 72 hours. A few use newer intermediate media such as Optisol-GS or Cornisol, extending that window to between 10 and 14 days.
Doctors at the Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences (RPC), AIIMS Delhi, along with engineers from IIT Delhi, are testing a way to recycle discarded donor corneas using a bioengineered graft. Corneas that fail transplant standards, because of low cell counts or minor damage, can be stripped of living cells and turned into a reusable structural scaffold for patients with surface-level corneal damage. While the trials are still at a very early stage, it does point toward a future where less of what is donated ends up being discarded.
However, until we come up with a way to reuse corneas that miss the deadline, the window closes and the tissue has to be discarded. 72 hours, or even two weeks, is not much time to test a cornea, find a compatible patient, and move tissue from an eye bank to an operating theatre. The challenge is intensified because almost 70% of all corneal collection and use is concentrated in just six states - Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. A cornea retrieved in a smaller town, with no local surgeon waiting, can become unusable while it is in transit to a city that has one.
What can be done
Extending storage life is the first step. Eye banks must shift from using MK medium to intermediate media, and eventually to organ-culture storage, which some countries use to keep corneas viable for up to a month. This helps to buy precious time to find the right recipient instead of the nearest one. A national, real-time inventory linking every eye bank directly to surgeons in 50 cities, could let a cornea about to expire in Kozhikode be offered to a waiting list in Chennai before it is thrown away.
As fresher corneal tissue survives testing and transplant better, the next focus must be on reducing the time between death and retrieval, and retrieval and preservation. Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes, where hospitals proactively notify eye banks of deaths and trained counsellors approach grieving families, help to reduce this time factor and outperform voluntary home collections. Expanding that model into more hospitals, rather than relying on a push only during Eye Donation Fortnight, will help to increase the corneal utilisation rate.
Quality assurance (QA) programmes at eye banks will also help in effectively reducing the discard rate, even with an increase in the volume of donated corneas. A study showed that the discard rate came down from around 40% to 30% with better donor acquisition processes and improvement in tissue recovery due to effective compliance with quality assurance programmes.
While we address the donation aspect with awareness and educating the people on the benefits of organ donation, we must also take care of the delivery with better storage chemistry, faster hospital protocols, and a database that shows, in real time, exactly which cornea is about to run out of time, who needs it and where.
(Dr. Suvira Jain is medical director, ASG Hospital Limited, Worli, Mumbai. Suvira.Jain@asgeyehospital.com)
