A team in form - how Farke has turned Leeds around
- Published
As the nascent Premier League table takes shape, the sight of Leeds United in third place feels like a throwback to the turn of the century, when they secured five top-five finishes on the bounce.
Monday's 4-1 home win over Newcastle United means Daniel Farke's unbeaten side have made their best start to a top-flight season since 2001-02 under David O'Leary.
In truth, Leeds, with eight points from four games, have been playing well for some time, and it can all be traced back to a bold change of formation by Farke almost nine months ago.
The German switched from a back four to a back three at half-time against Manchester City on 29 November, a game in which his team battled back from 2-0 down at the break to level things at 2-2 before conceding in stoppage time at Etihad Stadium.
Starting with the subsequent home win over Chelsea on 3 December, Leeds have lost only five of their past 29 league games, results which would place them fifth in the hypothetical league table for that timeframe.
So how have they done it? And can they push for European football for the first time in 24 years?
Robust recruitment
In the 2025 summer transfer window Farke and the club's new sporting director Adam Underwood made a point of signing tall players who could "add a special physicality" to the squad they were building for the robust demands of the English top flight.
Of the 10 permanent arrivals, eight – Jaka Bijol, Sebastiaan Bornauw, Dominic Calvert-Lewin, James Justin, Lukas Nmecha, Noah Okafor, Lucas Perri and Anton Stach – stand more than 6ft tall.
Speaking in July 2025, Farke said: "I wouldn't say it's coincidence that they are all tall players but, of course, if you join the Premier League and you have one of the smallest groups, you expect that probably there is more pressure on you than there was in the Championship. You have to make sure that you're also good in defending crosses."
This summer, after losing centre-back Pascal Struijk to Brighton, Farke moved for two World Cup players - Bosnia-Herzegovina's Tarik Muharemovic and Switzerland's Nico Elvedi - to bolster his defence.
Despite an error leading to Bazoumana Toure's late consolation goal for Newcastle, Muharemovic has looked particularly impressive, playing every league minute in front of 6ft 5in England international James Trafford, who became the most expensive British goalkeeper in history for the second time when he joined for an initial £40m from City.
Throw in Harry Wilson, one of the league's standout players last season, who joined on a free transfer from Fulham, and Leeds' latest signings look to be particularly shrewd.
The tactical shift
Leeds lost eight of their first 13 league games in 2025-26, leaving them in 18th position and facing the very real prospect of relegation.
Reports at the time suggested Farke, whose side had pipped Burnley to the Championship title the previous season, was in real danger of losing his job.
While the rejig clearly had its intended effect on the Leeds defence – among the ever-present clubs in the division, only champions Arsenal, City and Nottingham Forest have conceded fewer goals since the switch – it has helped in other areas too.
The most notable beneficiary has been Dominic Calvert-Lewin. Since last December only Erling Haaland, Ollie Watkins and Joao Pedro have scored more top-flight goals than Calvert-Lewin's 14.
Having toiled as the lone centre-forward in a 4-3-3 formation, relying on infrequent support from out wide, Calvert-Lewin has thrived with a proper strike partner, often in the form of Nmecha or Okafor, who boasts seven goals and an assist in his past 11 league appearances.
Although Farke still finds himself alternating between 3-4-3 and 3-5-2, Calvert-Lewin himself has said: "I enjoy having bodies around me."
With Crystal Palace the visitors to Elland Road on Saturday, Calvert-Lewin is aiming to become the first Leeds player to score in six consecutive league home games since Arthur Hydes in 1932.
The former Everton forward missed out on a place in England's World Cup squad but, with three goals in all competitions this season, he is surely in with a chance of an international recall on Friday as Thomas Tuchel prepares for the Nations League quadruple-header.
The Elland Road effect
Elland Road was bouncing on Monday night as the vast majority of the 36,693 fans savoured Leeds' stunning performance.
The famous old ground has been something of a fortress under the lights in recent seasons. Before consecutive losses to City and Sunderland in February, Leeds had gone 25 evening kick-offs in league and play-off games without a home defeat, winning 20 and drawing five.
The thumping win over Newcastle meant their new manager, Matthias Jaissle, became the latest coach to be welcomed to what Leeds fans call 'Daniel Farke Penitentiary'.
The online meme – in which managers defeated by Farke are 'sentenced' to time in his fictional prison – flooded social media again after the game.
Farke enjoyed the adulation of the supporters at full-time and, while he has quite rightly played down early talk of European qualification, a continuation of this form will have the Elland Road faithful dreaming of a return to those famous Champions League nights of a quarter of a century ago.

A Nation of Strange, Idle Men
Jon Ronson’s The Castle argues that men are giving up on society because they have nothing better to do.
Like many Millennial men, I used to be pretty invested in Ye, the artist formerly known as Kanye West—primarily because of his music, but also because of his unique position as the one celebrity who seemed empowered to behave however he wanted. He interrupted Taylor Swift at the Video Music Awards; he said “George Bush doesn’t care about Black people” at a Hurricane Katrina fundraiser; he brought a Jesus look-alike onstage. I would shrug, and keep listening. Then his do what I want ethos went very bad. Ye called slavery “a choice”; he came out as a fan of Hitler; he wore a KKK-style hood.
With escalating horror, I questioned what had happened. Was it about having too much money? Untreated mental illness? I wondered when logic and shame might kick in—when someone might get him to stop. But the more he was rejected by his peers, the media, and some fans, the more Kanye seemed to act out. Eventually, I accepted, grimly, that I was watching someone who, feeling abandoned and misunderstood, was determined to ignore all of his critics and double down on pursuing his chosen path.
I thought about Ye while I was reading The Castle, a new nonfiction work by the journalist Jon Ronson that attempts to unpack the motivations of wayward men who no longer fit into traditional society. Ronson is probably best-known for his 2015 book, So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed, a journalistic account of the emotional incentives and historical context behind the social-media-fueled frenzy that became known as “cancel culture.” Like the people in that book, many of the subjects of The Castle have been shoved to the margins. But the forces at play in this new book are more disparate, and perhaps more stubborn, than an angry online mob. Ronson explores how men become alienated because they can’t achieve success in their chosen field, because they can’t pay their bills, because they have too much money, because the town around them went to hell. The book shows how their free will, coupled with a lot of free time on the internet, leads them to pursue their self-interest as best they can—which, eventually, begets more alienation.
The Castle opens with the story of a strange encounter with a strange man. One night in 2023, Ronson’s 20-something son, Joel, and three of his friends (two are women) are invited to a mysterious castle in the middle of nowhere—specifically, Woodstock, Connecticut—for what they believe is a party. There, the women are asked to participate in a bizarre dating show hosted by a man named Chris Mark. The idea is apparently that 101 women will dress up like princesses and vie to be Mark’s girlfriend; once the situation becomes predictably awkward, Mark seemingly deems the night a bust and kicks everyone out. Ronson, who wakes up to a slew of texts from Joel describing what happened, is alarmed by the whole episode—and decides he needs to meet Mark himself.
On their first meeting, Mark at first seems transparent about how he spends his time. He owns the castle, where he lives with several women who he met online. The entire scene strikes Ronson as reminiscent of Hugh Hefner’s grotto—an analogy they discuss at Ronson’s prompting. But Mark, in Ronson’s telling, quickly grows antagonistic, abruptly asking Ronson to sign an NDA, then later barraging him with suspicious texts and threatening him with a pair of goons. Ronson concludes that Mark has “nurtured a private fantasy of manhood” that the journalist has put at risk by asking questions. (Mark has contested many of the details and claims of The Castle, including that he sent anyone to threaten Ronson, and has said that Ronson “presented me and events involving me in a profoundly misleading manner.”)
The Castle is about both Ronson’s investigation into Mark and the bigger phenomenon Mark seems to represent: too-idle men, most of them less wealthy than Mark, littering the country, yearning for some kind of grander purpose. He’s especially interested in men ages 25 to 54 who are both unemployed and no longer looking for work—people he claims have “opted out of society,” choosing instead a “life of male nothingness.” In a moment of general anxiety about men—whom they vote for, what they’re reading, whether they share their feelings—his interest isn’t political. It’s empathic. He offers no prescriptive solutions, wags no fingers. Instead, he wants the reader to conceive of the scale of social anomie, and to envision the millions of other men chasing meaning in the wreckage of their former aspirations.
In particular, Ronson focuses on a demographic whose life expectancy has dropped in the 21st century: middle-aged white men without college degrees, many of whom suffer from what a pair of Princeton economists he speaks with define as “deaths of despair” brought on by “the erosion of a way of life.” Once upon a time, such men—who widely supported Donald Trump in all three of his runs for president—were sold on the American dream. Now some of them are characterized by “a kind of cowed, vaguely shocked hopelessness,” Ronson writes. Others, facing social rejection, have started to live “like separatists, creating worlds in which they didn’t have to live or interact with other people except on their own terms.” Women, too, suffer from deaths of despair—but it’s the men, Ronson indicates, who have been raised to envision themselves as heroes, a self-image that can drive them to dark places.
Ronson illustrates how easy it can be for these men to slide off the map. His most endearing subject is Greg Chism, a father of two daughters in small-town Illinois. Chism was a single parent with tons of medical debt living in a place without a lot of job opportunities when, in the 2010s, he discovered a YouTube channel encouraging viewers to “make a video and change your life.” A few of his early videos got some attention, after which Chism received coaching from the platform’s employees, and he eventually struck on a winning formula: bizarre sketches involving his two daughters that played like the output of a hallucinating LLM fed on Nickelodeon. These generated millions of views, and some of them got really weird; Chism and his kids dressed like babies, or pretended to eat cat food off pizza. Soon came the blowback: Chism was, the internet claimed, a bad father abusing his children by making them participate in these creepy videos. His channel was demonetized, then banned. He was shunned just as quickly as he’d been celebrated.
But Chism, whom Ronson tracks down, has not been radicalized by the wave of hatred that came his way. Nor does he seem to be a bad father; his (now teenage) kids express mostly fond memories of their channel. He admits making errors in judgment—see: cat food—but in the end, Ronson writes, Chism was “a single father juggling responsibilities while feeling foolishly idealistic about sharing his family’s lives on the internet.” Becoming a YouTuber had seemed like a way for Chism to stop sliding toward destitution. Instead, his entire life was put under a microscope. Ronson uses Chism’s guilelessness to show how unexpected and profound the pitfalls can be for anyone looking to find a foothold in the new world.
So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed examined a group of people whose lives were ruined by the internet in one particular way; The Castle flips the framing. In the latter book’s view, the internet allows its users to choose their own particular off-ramp from ennui. Seeking female companionship, Chris Mark turns to dating apps; eager to feel seen, Greg Chism becomes a YouTuber. One subject, the podcaster Andrew Gold, begins tailoring his content to anti-woke audiences, racking up huge numbers by playing to the preexisting grievances of his angry followers. Another chapter digs into Ronson’s rocky friendship with the comedy writer Graham Linehan, whose involvement in the gender-critical movement led him to act out online in ways that Ronson reads as self-destructive. (Linehan has disputed many of the details of Ronson’s depiction, and called it “an indictment of him and the cowardly, careerist, mendacious class of people who could roughly gather under the title ‘Graham Linehan’s old friends and colleagues.’”)
A swerve comes toward the end when Ronson wonders whether he has fallen into the same trap as some of those men. By treating Mark’s story as something only he can make sense of, Ronson has neglected his friends and his marriage. “Everyone I met for this book had, I thought, a similarly dysfunctional relationship with purpose, hunting too desperately for it,” he writes. “And now there was a generation of men, unanchored from society and going it alone—as content creators, culture war influencers, amateur sleuths.”
Ronson doesn’t build toward any prescriptive conclusions; he gives these men a platform to explain how they feel, and allows the reader to weigh the validity of those feelings. I remember the Chism pile-on well, and was slightly horrified to hear the story from his perspective—how confusing it must have felt to toggle so rapidly and randomly between being seen as heroic and villainous. Ronson’s empathy is not boundless; he draws hard lines around some of Mark’s behavior. But he seems to understand that his personal judgment is more or less meaningless. The factors shaping these men are external, but how they react comes from the inside—and many of them remain trapped in their own metaphorical castles, far from the light.

'How can anyone trust him?' SC raps Rajpal Yadav, extends time to pay ₹2 crore in cheque bounce cases
The court extended its earlier order exempting him from surrender until October 5, underlining that it is one last opportunity
The Supreme Court on Tuesday extended time for actor Rajpal Yadav to furnish ₹2 crore within two weeks in cheque bounce cases, even as it said it had no faith in him. It cited his past conduct in the Delhi high court, which sentenced Yadav to three months’ imprisonment.
“Knowing his past conduct, how can anybody on earth trust him?” a bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana observed as it took up Yadav’s application seeking more time to comply with the September 8 Supreme Court order exempting him from surrendering on the sole condition that he deposits money within 24 hours.
The bench extended its earlier order exempting him from surrender until October 5, underlining that it is a one “last opportunity” to prove his bona fides. It allowed his request for a two-week extension to deposit ₹2 crore.
The bench reminded Yadav of the opportunities the high court granted him to fulfil his commitment to repay the loan for production of a film in 2010. The high court on July 10 sentenced him and his wife to three months’ imprisonment.
Senior advocate PS Patwalia, who appeared for Yadav, told the bench that his client is in genuine financial distress. He added Yadav needs “some breathing time” to arrange the money. Patwalia requested two weeks to arrange ₹2 crore. He informed the bench that Yadav’s mother has some immovable property that will be used to arrange the money.
The bench told Patwalia that Yadav’s theatrical skills are well known in Bollywood. “Our only concern is that he does not perform such drama with the court, what he is known to do perfectly in Bollywood,” the bench said. “...we take a lenient view making it clear that as a last opportunity. Two weeks are granted to the petitioner to honour our September 8 order.”
Patwalia said the other side also is not going to get the money if Yadav is sent to jail. “For over four months, he has remained in jail until his fraternity came together to bail him out. If he does not honour now, the writing on the wall is very much clear.”
The complainant, Murli Projects, filed a criminal case against Yadav, saying he took a ₹5 crore loan in 2010 to produce the film ‘Ata Pata Lapata’ with a commitment to repay ₹8 crore but defaulted.
Senior advocate Ajit Kumar Sinha, who appeared for Murli Projects, said attempts to secure the money have failed. He added that the principal loan amount is ₹7.5 crore without interest. Sinha said the immovable property Yadav is talking about is under mortgage.
Yadav sought release on probation after the trial court sentenced him in May 2024. The high court upheld the trial court order after giving Yadav opportunities to honour his undertaking to repay the loan amount.
The high court noted that Yadav and his wife had paid ₹2.25 crore to the complainant during the pendency of proceedings.

IPO-bound NODWIN Gaming has launched NODWIN Sports, a mainstream sports vertical focused on developing sporting properties, mass-participation events, and commercial partnerships. The move expands NODWIN Gaming’s play beyond gaming and esports as it looks to build a broader youth media and entertainment business spanning live events, content, and intellectual property (IP). The vertical will develop original sports and fitness properties, advise sports federations and governing bodies, facilitate brand and media partnerships, and provide operational and production support for sporting events. India will serve as the base for NODWIN Sports’ expansion across markets in the Global South, the company said in a statement. The launch comes as NODWIN Gaming prepares for a potential IPO. In March, cofounder and MD Akshat Rathee told Inc42 that the company was looking to raise around $100 Mn in a pre-IPO funding round. Gurbaksh Virdi To Lead New Vertical Gurbaksh Singh Virdi has joined NODWIN Gaming as vice president to lead the new vertical. Virdi previously worked with Red Bull, U Sports, PUMA, Cornerstone, and Adidas India across sports marketing, athlete management, IP development, and commercial partnerships. He also worked on running initiatives for Virat Kohli’s One8 brand at Cornerstone. Most recently, as sports marketing lead at Adidas India, he managed the brand’s initiatives across cricket, running, training, football, and motorsport, including partnerships with the BCCI and the Indian Olympic Association. NODWIN Sports will draw on the company’s capabilities across content, production, partnerships, and community engagement to develop and operate sporting properties. The company said its experience building youth-focused properties such as the BGMI Masters Series, Comic Con India, NH7 Weekender, and VCSA would help it create sports IPs targeting younger audiences. Founded in 2014 by Rathee and Gautam Virk, NODWIN Gaming operates across gaming, esports, pop culture, music, live events, and content. It counts Nazara Technologies, KRAFTON, Sony Group Corporation, JetSynthesys, and Good Game Investments among its investors. The company operates in more than 20 countries and has been expanding through acquisitions and investments across gaming, esports, and youth entertainment. NODWIN Gaming is also taking a measured approach to its IPO timeline, with Rathee previously saying that the company would file its draft papers only after achieving financial, governance, investor, and internal readiness.

CBI books Arunachal anti-dam activist Bhanu Tatak over FCRA violations
According to the first information report (FIR), the CBI alleged that Tatak received more than ₹17.6 lakh from various foreign organisations
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) registered a case against Arunachal Pradesh-based lawyer and environmental activist Bhanu Tatak for allegedly receiving over ₹17.6 lakh from foreign organisations and individuals in violation of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA), officials said.
Tatak, legal adviser to the Siang Indigenous Farmers’ Forum (SIFF) and coordinator of civil society organisation Dibang Resistance, was associated with protests against major hydropower projects proposed in the northeastern state.
According to the first information report (FIR), the CBI alleged that Tatak received more than ₹17.6 lakh from various foreign organisations and individuals directly into her personal savings bank account without obtaining the registration or prior permission required under the FCRA.
The agency named several overseas entities as alleged sources of the funds, including Philippines-based Asia Indigenous Peoples Network on Extractive Industries and Energy and Indigenous Peoples Rights International, Ireland-based Front Line and UK-based Human Rights Resource Centre.
In September 2025, Tatak was stopped by immigration authorities at Delhi airport from boarding a flight to Ireland following a lookout circular issued against her by the Arunachal Pradesh police.
She was scheduled to attend a three-month academic programme at Dublin City University.
The CBI further alleged that Tatak did not file income tax returns and that the foreign contributions received by her were not reflected in official records.
The agency claimed that the funds were allegedly used to “organise and sustain anti-dam protests” in Arunachal Pradesh, which, according to it, were adversely affecting the country’s economic and strategic interests.
Responding to the allegations, Tatak said the matter was under investigation and that she was fully cooperating with the investigating authorities.
“I am a law-abiding citizen and have committed no violation of the law,” she told HT.
Tatak said she was a recipient of the Bhagirath Prayas Samman Award, India 2023, for her work in river conservation, besides educational and research scholarships. The award was presented to Tatak and Dibang Resistance at the 10th India Rivers Week function held at BAIF in Maharashtra in November 2023.
Tatak and the organisations she is associated with have been opposing the proposed 12,500-MW Siang Multipurpose Project on the Siang River. Dibang Resistance has also opposed the 2,880-MW hydropower project on the Dibang River.
Tatak joined the Indian National Congress (INC) in Itanagar on December 2, 2025.

Combining healthy dietary practices with regular physical activity is the most effective non-drug strategy for achieving sustained weight loss and improving key metabolic health indicators among adults with overweight or obesity, according to a major review by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) here.
The findings, published in the international journal Obesity Pillars, are based on an umbrella review that analysed evidence from 112 systematic reviews and meta-analyses covering 2,332 randomised controlled trials and more than 5.07 lakh participant observations across over 50 countries.
The review, led by ICMR-NIN scientists Mahesh Kumar Mummadi and Samarasimha Reddy, compared the impact of dietary interventions, physical activity, lifestyle changes and combined approaches on weight management and cardiometabolic health.
Researchers found that all major non-pharmacological interventions produced statistically significant, though generally modest, reductions in body weight and Body Mass Index (BMI). However, the combination of diet and physical activity delivered the most sustained results, with participants losing an average of 3.68 kg beyond 12 months compared with control groups.
Low-calorie diets were found to be the most effective for short-term weight loss, resulting in an average reduction of 2.64 kg within the first three months. Physical activity alone led to smaller reductions in body weight, but its benefits increased over longer follow-up periods.
Lifestyle interventions such as behavioural counselling, goal-setting, self-monitoring and health education also showed positive outcomes, with their effectiveness improving over time. Beyond weight loss, the study highlighted significant improvements in metabolic health. The combination of diet and physical activity produced the greatest benefits in blood sugar control, reducing fasting blood glucose levels and insulin resistance after 12 months.
Physical activity emerged as the most effective strategy for lowering blood pressure, reducing systolic blood pressure by about 6.1 mmHg between six and 12 months. Intermittent fasting showed the largest short-term reduction in diastolic blood pressure and supported weight loss for up to a year, although these benefits were not sustained beyond 12 months.
ICMR-NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the importance of an integrated approach to tackling obesity. “Healthy dietary practices, regular physical activity and behavioural support each have a role, but their combination can provide broader and more sustained benefits. This is particularly relevant for India, where scalable and sustainable approaches are needed to address the growing burden of overweight, obesity and related non-communicable diseases,” she said.
Mr.Mummadi noted that although the review drew evidence from more than 50 countries, most studies originated from high-income and upper-middle-income nations. India and other lower-middle-income countries remained under-represented, highlighting the need for more locally relevant research, said a press release on Saturday.

A Liberal factional figure has rejected a suggestion he gave “ridiculous” evidence that Dominic Perrottet’s sister-in-law shared in $660,999 for giving a “mum’s perspective” on lobbying clients, the New South Wales anti-corruption watchdog has heard.
Jeremy Greenwood told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Wednesday it was not relevant that Anita Perrottet’s children were under five at the time she provided advice on vaping among minors.
Greenwood also denied he gave false evidence about her coming up with the term “zero unnecessary euthanasia” several years after it appeared in a greyhound industry report.
Icac is investigating an allegation that Greenwood, Charles Perrottet and Christian Ellis shared in $2m in payments between 2020 and 2023 from fugitive developer Jean Nassif, or his company Toplace, in exchange for political outcomes.
Greenwood, who alongside Charles Perrottet has denied payments were political donations, returned to the commission on Wednesday after Nassif made an explosive video appearance from his Beirut bedroom on Monday and Tuesday. Nassif declared he was “not corrupt”.
Peggy Dwyer SC on Wednesday questioned Greenwood in relation to his previous evidence about advice he said Anita Perrottet gave to lobbying firms Beckington, controlled by Greenwood and Ellis, and JPG Advisory, controlled by Greenwood.
Dwyer has alleged invoices of $660,999 paid to Anita Perrottet’s company, Macquarie Consulting, over two and a half years were her husband, Charles Perrottet’s, share of the money from Nassif.
Anita Perrottet has told the watchdog payments were for “strategic and marketing advice” she provided; while Charles Perrottet has said they were “holistic” payments covering his advice to Nassif on his developments as well as his wife’s work.
Greenwood has previously told the commission Anita’s advice, for which the commission has no written evidence, provided a “mum’s perspective”. He said after first being contracted by Beckington in 2020, she may have come up with the term “zero unnecessary euthanasia” for greyhounds, and given advice about discouraging minors from vaping, including removing flavours such as bubble gum, as well as black market regulation.
On Wednesday, Dwyer took Greenwood to 2017 recommendations by the NSW greyhound industry reform panel, which included the phrase “zero unnecessary euthanasia”, suggesting to Greenwood he had “outsmarted [him]self by coming up with that false evidence when it’s clearly a term used in a document years earlier”.
“I disagree,” Greenwood replied. Dwyer showed Greenwood a submission by Philip Morris to a 2020 senate inquiry which referenced measures to regulate the illicit tobacco trade and a 2019 report committing to applying guidelines to prevent youth access to vapes.
Greenwood said he had read the submission by Philip Morris, a client of his, but rejected Dwyer’s suggestion it “makes a mockery” of his evidence about Anita Perrottet’s advice.
After Dwyer asked him how old Anita Perrottet’s children were at the time she provided advice on vaping, Greenwood said he did not know, and did not think it was relevant.
The presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened to tell Greenwood he was “not here to debate with counsel assisting” but to “answer the question”. Greenwood said: “I presume they’re under 10.”
Dwyer, telling Greenwood that Anita Perrottet’s children were around two and three at the time, asked: “Did she give you a mum’s perspective on deterring under-fives from vaping?
“No,” Greenwood replied.
Dwyer said: “Your evidence is ridiculous, can I suggest to you, that Anita Perrottet contributed to a debate that had been the subject of professional reports … for many years before you say you brought Anita Perrottet on board.” Greenwood disagreed.
At the inquiry last week, Greenwood acknowledged an arrangement under which payments to Macquarie Consulting would also remunerate Charles Perrottet for advice he gave to Nassif.
He rejected a suggestion he gave false evidence at private hearings with Icac every year between 2023 and 2026, in which he did not mention an arrangement. But on Wednesday, he said he had never been in a financial arrangement with Charles Perrottet for consulting work, but said they had previous arrangements “on a racehorse” and “an old Redfield [college] rugby fantasy football league”.
Dwyer said it was a “ridiculous response” given his previous acknowledgment “that an amount going to Macquarie Consulting was in effect to thank Charles or compensate him for the advice he had given to Jean Nassif”. Greenwood disagreed.
Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year and is not expected to appear. Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?
- Published
An oval ball, in September, in Melbourne usually means just one thing - the business end of the Australian rules football (AFL) season.
But on Friday, at the unsportingly early time of 7am, 100,000 people will begin filing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for a very un-Australian sporting spectacle - American football.
The LA Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers in their opening National Football League (NFL) fixture, the first time the country has hosted a meaningful, non-exhibition regular season game.
The match sold out months ago, with more than half the crowd expected to be people living outside the state of Victoria. On the official ticket resale site, a restricted view seat is priced at more than A$650 (£350/US$470).
"Walking down the street, it's AFL finals week and you wouldn't even know," says Thomas McMillan, host of the NFL podcast Any Given Sunday Australia.
"It's all NFL everywhere. There are bars that are nothing but 49ers bars or Rams bars. We have a Ram Tram getting around the district. When you're in Melbourne and AFL isn't visible, it shows how big this is at the moment."
Kickoff at 10.35am local time on Friday may not be typical for local fans, but meets the demands of prime time US television schedules and their advertisers.
The league held its first international match in 2007, and over the past two decades the overseas matches have become a long-term strategy to attract supporters and their dollars.
Nine games outside the US are scheduled for the upcoming season, including three in London. But Melbourne is the furthest that players and US-based fans will have to travel.
"Obviously there are question marks when you hear you are playing in Australia," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey told a press conference this week.
"But it has been so cool… the food's incredible, the coffee's great."
That caffeine reference was perhaps as much to the time zone, as nod to the city's famous café culture.
Melbourne is a mind-warping 17 hours ahead of California where both teams are based, and much of the pre-match attention has been on the two teams and their contrasting approaches to trying to "beat" the jet lag.
For the 49ers, who arrived late last week, their players have had time to get over the long journey, adjust to the time zone, acclimatise and practice at a nearby stadium.
Controversially, the LA Rams are taking things to the other extreme, planning to arrive on Thursday morning local time on a charted Qantas A380 superjumbo, play on Friday, and get back to the US west coast shortly afterwards, in theory to prepare for their next match with minimum disruption to the player's body clocks.
"Definitely it's a gamble," says McMillan. "If they don't quite get things right after the 16-hour flight, you still might have that jet lag, even though you're trying to avoid it."
"And not everyone can sleep on planes," says his co-host Danny Webb. "Whether you're in first class, business class, whatever it is, you're still on a plane."
"And", adds McMillan: "And they're six foot six most of them, so it's going to be even tighter seats".
Despite it technically being a "home" game for the Rams, who bid for NFL marketing rights in Australia under the leagues Global Markets programme, this all means it is the San Francisco 49ers that have more of a presence around Melbourne this week.
And while most practice sessions have been behind closed doors, there have been player appearances at a rally for fans and an AFL match, while ex-stars turned up at that most Australian of traditions, the weekly fundraising "sausage sizzle" at the country's most high-profile hardware chain.
American sports journalist Dontay Atkinson predicts this fan engagement will be reflected inside the stadium and that the MCG will be "heavily red" (the 49ers colour), accusing the Rams of doing "exactly jack squat to sell the NFL brand or connect with Australians".
Writing on X he added: "Fly in, fly out, no contact. I'm sure the Aussies feel great about that snub."
McMillan says he can understand the approach by the Rams, who are seen as contenders for the 2027 Superbowl.
"They're looking at this as a game they need to win," he says.
"We do feel a bit snubbed, and feel the 49ers are doing the right thing,
"But it is their job, so that's where the Rams coaching staff has gone 'nah, we're taking this approach'.
"I just worry that they have missed the boat of ingraining themselves as the Australian team. It leaves it open for others, and the 49ers have really jumped on that."
The LA Rams insist there has been no snub, though speaking to the BBC, the club's Head of International Stephanie Cheng dodged the question of whether she would have preferred her players to have been in town this week.
"It's really a culmination of more than four years of work," she said. "It's not just about game week. We have long term rights."
Cheng says the Rams are the only NFL team with a membership programme for Australian fans, and that it has sent coaches into schools and communities to promote "flag football" – the non-contact version of the sport which will feature in the LA 2028 Olympics.
She also points to regular earlier visits by star players including running back Kyren Williams in March. This week its cheerleaders have visited US military bases in Australia before coming to Melbourne, and the franchise has installed a 22-yard floating football field on Melbourne's Yarra River serving as a fan zone.
"From day one, when we've come to Australia, there's been incredible enthusiasm," Cheng said.
While no Australian players will be on the field on Friday, there are dozens playing US college football and a handful in the NFL.
Most are punters, kicking specialists tapped up after showing their prowess playing AFL or rugby league.
But it is the success of Jordan Mailata, an offensive left tackle with the Philadelphia Eagles, who in 2025 became the first Australian to play in, and win, a Superbowl that was a "major turning point in Australia's fandom of the NFL " says Webb.
"Seeing an Australian in what we'd called a skilled position and then winning a Superbowl. It doesn't get better than that".
Friday's game is the first of three matches in Melbourne to be held over four years, under a contract between the NFL and the state of Victoria.
The league's preference, says Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, is to have annual games in Australia similar, to the way the game has grown in the UK.
"We're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market," he told Reuters.
And while many US-based supporters are not fans of the international fixtures, these games are here to stay, says Webb, and the hype and the sell-out crowd in Australia augurs well for it to become a long-term fixture,
"I had mates four years ago asking why are you doing an NFL podcast? It's not a big sport here," he said.
"And now every single one of those mates are asking me for tickets for the game."

Most people associate heart disease with men, and generally elderly men. This, however, is far from the real picture. Heart disease is a serious health problem in women as well, but still remains underdiagnosed and sub-optimally managed in our country. One of the main reasons for this is that in many cases, women may not have the ‘classic’ symptoms of a heart attack. This can result in symptoms being overlooked or misdiagnosed as acidity, stress, tiredness or other minor health issues.
Warning signs in women
Chest pain or pressure is common in women, but they can also get other, more subtle, symptoms. These may occur suddenly or slowly.
The following signs should be watched out for:
- Unusual shortness of breath, even without much exertion
- Abnormally excessive fatigue
- Nausea, vomiting, dizziness or sweating
- Back pain or discomfort in the back, jaw, neck, shoulders or arms
- A sense of pressure, weight or unease in the chest
Sometimes, both women and healthcare providers may ignore these symptoms or dismiss them as fatigue or digestive issues, particularly when there is no severe chest pain. But continued or atypical symptoms should never be left to self-diagnosis.
Understanding heart disease in women
The risks of heart disease can vary for women of different ages. High blood pressure, diabetes, obesity and high cholesterol contribute to the risk. Heart health can also be impacted by smoking, inactivity, poor diet and chronic stress. Some conditions that can occur during pregnancy are also likely to be factors in heart risk, and should be discussed with a doctor, including high blood pressure and diabetes during pregnancy. Hormonal changes may also play a role. Once women reach menopause, the risk of cardiovascular disease rises, as there is less protective oestrogen in the body.
Also, coronary artery disease is not always obstructive: a normal angiogram does not necessarily exclude heart disease. as women have a higher incidence of microvascular angina, and so, it is important to not stop evaluations.
What is also of great concern is that women might not seek medical treatment if symptoms are atypical. During a heart attack this delay can be fatal, as every minute counts.
Steps to make a difference
Protecting your heart health does not always mean making big changes in your lifestyle. Simple daily practices and regular health checkups can make a big difference.
These are some steps that women can take:
Know your numbers: Be aware of blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol—especially if there is a family history of heart disease.
Diet : Follow a balanced, nutritious diet, preferably a Mediterranean/DASH diet.
Be physically active: Walk, exercise or do something you enjoy regularly, to help maintain your heart health.
Stop smoking completely: This protects the heart and the rest of the body as well
Do not ignore unusual symptoms: Sudden difficulty in breathing, sudden weakness, chest discomfort or pain in the jaw, back or arms should be promptly evaluated.
Women don’t always experience noticeable symptoms when they have a heart disease. Sometimes, symptoms may not be obvious. For women to own their heart health, it is crucial to be aware of these symptoms, understand their risk factors, and seek timely medical attention. Women’s heart health should be also given increased importance in healthcare settings because their symptoms may be less apparent at times, and early detection and prompt medical intervention can make a huge difference.
(Dr. Saurabh Juneja is director & head, CTVS, cardiac sciences, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital. dr.juneja@gmail.com)

China criticises idea it is in 'malicious competition' over AI
- Published
China has hit out against what it has called "threat narratives" over AI governance and warned against "engaging in confrontation and malicious competition".
It follows Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development - but in a way that prevents China from pulling ahead in the AI race.
Over the past week, industry insiders at the leading US artificial intelligence labs have been warning in extremely stark terms about the potential threat AI poses, with some saying it could wipe out humanity.
But US President Donald Trump has said that his priority is making sure the US develops the tech faster than China.
On Monday, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters that "narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition serve only to disrupt the process of global AI governance and are not in anyone's interest".
"All parties should work together to advance AI in a manner that is open, inclusive, beneficial to all, and oriented toward the good," he added.
His comments highlight the difficulties in getting an agreement between the world's two leading AI powers.
An agreement between the US and China to regulate AI development is "next to impossible", says Chang Jun Yan, an assistant professor with the military studies programme at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
"As part of each state's core national security interests, cooperation in taking things slower and more safely in relation to AI, is very, very unlikely."
Artificial intelligence now sits at the heart of the US-China rivalry as the world's two largest economies seek to gain an edge in advanced tech. Despite US export bans on critical chips, Chinese AI innovation has been expanding, driven by open-source technology and Beijing's backing.
Many experts believe the US is still ahead, and Chinese firms are trying to catch up as they struggle to raise the hundreds of billions of dollars that investors are ploughing into American AI.
But Beijing, including Chinese leader Xi Jinping himself, has also spoken about the risks posed by AI. China must "balance development and security", and introduce and improve relevant laws and ethical guidelines, and strengthen prevention of risks, to "safeguard the interests of the people and national security", state security minister Chen Yixin wrote on Sunday.
He warned of the dangers of "hostile forces" such as foreign intelligence using AI and called for international cooperation.
"There are strong signals that Washington and Beijing share an understanding of frontier risks," Kenton Thibaut, a senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote recently.
China has "technical reasons" to work with the US, she argues, because its developers would be able to see how their models are deployed outside China, and detect and understand vulnerabilities.
In July, China set up the World AI Cooperation Organisation, which aims to shape global AI governance. And speaking at the Brics summit in India on Sunday, Xi proposed creating a community for open-source AI.
All this comes as calls for AI regulation grow louder in the US, especially after a former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week that "there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future" if the current pace of development continued.
Since then top industry bosses, such as Dario Amodei, have called for a slowdown and more regulation.
"We need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities," Open AI's chief executive Sam Altman wrote on X on Monday, which was echoed by Microsoft boss Satya Nadella who said AI development "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities".
But US President Donald Trump downplayed the risks, saying that he wanted to keep the US's lead over China "because whoever wins AI, wins".
The competition is fierce.
The former Anthropic employee Coxon told the BBC that there needed to be "some sort of coordinated slowdown with China, if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale".
As Trump prepares to host Xi at the White House next week, the two sides are trying to include AI on the agenda, the South China Morning Post reports.
It is also likely to be part of the talks between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, who are trying to meet before next week's summit, the paper said. Vice-Premier He runs the agency that oversees the country's economic planning, including AI development.
While collaboration between the US and China is important, experts say the stakes are high for both countries.
"If China establishes a durable lead in frontier AI, this will not be viewed in Washington as losing a technology race," says Chasen Nevett, managing director at Hong Kong-based firm, Forani Investments.
"It will be viewed as losing part of the strategic infrastructure of the next industrial era."
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia
