Foodtech unicorn Rebel Foods managed to cut its net loss for the fiscal year FY26 by 16.3% to ₹281.8 Cr from ₹336.6 Cr in the previous fiscal. Operating revenue rose 20.7% to ₹1,951.6 Cr compared to ₹1,617.4 Cr in FY25. The rise in revenue was led by product sales. Revenue from the sale of food items rose 20.9% to ₹1,891.9 Cr in the year under review from ₹1,565.3 Cr in FY25, while service revenue — commission, storage and franchise income — stayed broadly flat at ₹32.7 Cr. Other operating revenues, which includes delivery services income, rose 38.5% to ₹27 Cr from ₹19.5 Cr last year. Meanwhile, international revenue jumped 38.8% YoY to ₹283.81 Cr, while revenue from India grew 18% to ₹1,667.75 Cr. Revenue from overseas contributed 14.5% to the startup’s top line in FY26, a slight improvement from 12.6% in FY25. Rebel Foods currently operates 45+ brands across India, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom. Including other income of ₹43.4 Cr, the total income stood at ₹1,995 Cr in FY26, up 20.3% from ₹1,658 Cr in the previous fiscal. EBITDA loss also narrowed about 50% to ₹62.4 Cr from ₹123.7 Cr in the previous fiscal. The startup said that a stronger consumer engagement and continued improvements across store operations, tech and supply chain contributed to higher productivity and margin expansion in the fiscal year. “FY26 marks an important step forward for Rebel Foods, with growth and profitability increasingly coming together. As our platform scales, we are seeing the benefits of stronger consumer engagement, higher store productivity and operating leverage flow through to the business. Our focus remains on building a predictable, sustainable and highly scalable food platform for the long term,” cofounder and global CEO Ankush Grover said. Founded in 2011 by Kallol Banerjee and Jaydeep Barman, Rebel Foods started as a delivery-only brand with ‘Faasos’. Over the years it has expanded the number of labels it operates. Its portfolio of quick service restaurant (QSR) brands includes names like Behrouz Biryani, Mandarin Oak, Oven Story Pizza, Sweet Truth, LunchBox, The Good Bowl, Firangi Bake, the Biryani Life and Wendy’s, serving across 120+ cities. The startup has raised $773 Mn in funding to date from the likes of KKR, Temasek, Lightbox, Evolvence, among others. The startup entered the unicorn club in 2021 after raising $175 Mn in its Series F round from investors Qatar Investment Authority, Coatue and Evolvence. Rebel Foods has been recalibrating its financial and operational strategy as it reportedly eyes a public listing in India. Earlier, it had launched QuickiES, a 15-minute food delivery service, and planned to expand its offline footprint through physical restaurants and food courts. However, the startup had to shut down the vertical earlier this year amid high cash burn. It has also been seeking to leverage its global presence and multi-brand portfolio, while improving unit economics and moving towards EBITDA breakeven. A leadership reshuffle, with Ankush Grover elevated to global CEO and Jaydeep Barman moving to chairman and group CEO, further aligned the organisation for its next phase ahead of a possible public listing. Magnifying Rebel Foods’ Spending The startup’s total expenses for the fiscal rose 14.1% to ₹2,265.9 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,986.6 Cr in the previous year. Here is a breakdown of where Rebel Foods spent the most: Cost of Raw Materials Consumed: Comprising 34.6% of the total expenses, the spend on raw materials, components and packing materials rose 15.6% to ₹784.4 Cr during the year under review from ₹678.5 Cr in FY25. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs, which includes salaries, wages, gratuity fund and provident fund, rose 6.3% to ₹412.3 Cr from ₹387.8 Cr in FY25. Brokerage And Commission: The biggest expense growth in FY26 was from this head, where it rose 30.6% to ₹317.7 Cr from ₹243.3 Cr in the previous fiscal.

The Kennedy Center Is Trump’s Hostage
The president berated a congresswoman during a board meeting, then posted that he would abandon the Kennedy Center if his name isn’t added to it.
Donald Trump has given the federal judiciary an ultimatum: Let him put his name on the Kennedy Center, or he won’t save it.
That threat came after a federal judge, Christopher Cooper, today blocked yet another effort to add the president’s name to the building. Moments later, Trump virtually joined a Kennedy Center board meeting, at which he slammed Cooper’s decision and lashed out at Representative Joyce Beatty—the ex officio board member challenging his overhaul of the institution in court—according to a person with knowledge of the meeting, who spoke with me on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal proceedings.
Later, Trump posted on Truth Social that the center’s “Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board’s approved name,” adding, “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.”
After months defined by empty theaters and canceled shows, the Kennedy Center has become a shadow of the premier performance venue it was just over a year ago. A Washington Post report this week revealed that the center’s finances are on the brink of collapse and that it could face bankruptcy. But while the institution has diminished, its leaders—and Trump’s allies on the board—have continued to push his plans forward, repackaging their oft-repeated claim that the only way to save it from financial ruin ahead of a two-year renovation is to emblazon it with Trump’s name. The crisis at the Kennedy Center is entangled in a larger effort by Trump to control what Washington looks like—a fight that has taken on higher stakes as his administration evades federal procedures designed to protect historic places from the whims of any one president.
The immediate outcome of today’s events adds more confusion. General trustees voted in favor of closing the center, and two staffers told me that leaders subsequently announced through the building’s broadcast system that the Kennedy Center was closed to the public. It was unclear if that announcement meant that employees would also be barred from the premises, according to one of the staffers, both of whom spoke with me on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. Cooper issued a preliminary injunction in May to temporarily block the center from closing; if he does not lift or amend that ruling, the announced closure will put the board in violation of the court’s orders.
“The Board’s decision today reflects sound judgment and a clear prioritization of safety above all else,” the center’s vice president for public relations, Roma Daravi, told me in a statement. “As the main building closes for urgent renovations—long overdue and desperately needed to protect the safety of patrons, artists and staff—the Center remains committed to pursuing a safe and efficient renovation through all legal means.” The White House referred me to Trump’s post when I asked for comment on this story.
Meanwhile, the latest evidence of trouble at the Kennedy Center is scattered on the velvet carpet in the Grand Foyer, after a portion of its ceiling collapsed during a storm on September 4. The incident, which did not result in any injuries, has become the primary example for leaders describing the building’s urgent needs—and, as Daravi put it, debate whether “decades of neglect and deferred maintenance” are to blame. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick doubled down last night, posting security footage of the moment the chunks of ceiling suddenly fell to the floor. “If a performance had been underway, patrons could have been killed,” he wrote. The rubble and the hole in the ceiling are still on full display, while signs, ropes, and a yellow cone caution people against entering the foyer.
The fallen ceiling has become a key image of the Kennedy Center’s crisis. Trump’s allies say it’s proof that the building’s troubles predate this administration, and can be resolved only by the appropriately recognized intervention of the president-as-master-builder. But to some who oppose his overhaul, the center’s loud publicization of the problem underscores the board’s eagerness—perhaps overeagerness—to shut down the building.
In a filing this week, Beatty’s team alleged that the center was citing the ceiling damage as justification for closure, but pointed out that a similar problem in 1977 was addressed without shutting down the center. (Beatty’s lawyers told the court that further discovery could show that mismanagement under Trump led to the institution’s insolvency.)
Either way, after the board’s latest vote to close, the next step is to wait and see if Cooper will allow it this time. It’s unclear if anything he heard today will persuade him—including a lengthy assessment of the building’s conditions that a real-estate firm prepared for the board—given his previous statement that the initial closure plans were “ill-informed and seemingly preordained.” But a crumbling ceiling might just do the trick: During the hearing today, Cooper indicated that he would consider amending his preliminary injunction to authorize closure for urgent circumstances.
The other emergency—the money—is even messier. The Washington Post reported on Sunday that Kennedy Center leaders are warning trustees of financial collapse within weeks, saying that the institution could soon be unable to make payroll or cover routine bills. The alarm follows an earlier Post report on internal financial records showing that the center could face a deficit of $23 million—even amid its drastic spending cuts this year.
To keep Trump’s plans for the center alive, the board has already appealed today’s ruling against adding his name to the facade, and Beatty revealed in a court filing to Cooper that leaders had been weighing 10 different ways in which Trump’s name could be added back to the center’s edifice. “The Board seeks to provide multiple options so that President Trump can be legally and appropriately recognized and acknowledged on the facade of the Kennedy Center so that he agrees to carry the burden of managing the renovation and provides the Center with a much required financial rescue,” a resolution that the board had prepared for this week read, though it was later dropped from the board’s agenda so trustees could focus exclusively on closure.
In his ruling today, Cooper reiterated the conclusion he had already reached four months ago. “Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” he wrote, adding that the latest renaming plan “bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted.”
Trump’s reaction today to Cooper’s decision—both online and before the board—underscores the bargain that has defined his stewardship of the Kennedy Center. Its leaders say that it is nearing financial and structural collapse, and that Trump is uniquely capable of raising the money and overseeing the work to turn the institution around. Today’s hearing brought up new questions about those claims, including what bankruptcy would even mean for a charitable trust organization created by Congress. If its finances are truly as bad as leaders and reports say, the court might eventually need to consider placing the center under the control of an independent receiver. For now, the venue is trapped between self-inflicted crises and the conditions that have been attached to solving them. But saving the Kennedy Center may ultimately require something its leadership has gone out of its way to resist: separating the future of the institution from the wishes of the president.

Harleen Deol is raring to go for the newest opportunity in her career: Women’s Caribbean Premier League (WCPL).
The India international became the fifth Indian to join the ongoing edition after a last-minute move saw her sign for defending champion Barbados Tridents.
She’ll share the dressing room with pace-bowling all-rounder Pooja Vastrakar and big-hitter Kiran Navgire. Meanwhile, wicketkeeper-batter Yastika Bhatia and pace ace Shikha Pandey have been drafted by the Trinbago Knight Riders.
“It’s been amazing. I’ve just attended one practice session, and then we went on a cruise for a team bonding activity. That was a really nice experience,” Harleen, for whom this is a maiden international franchise stint, told reporters on Friday.
The 28-year-old has been part of the Women’s Premier League since its inaugural edition in 2023, representing Gujarat Giants for three seasons. Most recently, she played for the UP Warriorz. She has amassed 653 runs in 28 innings overall, striking at 116.19.
“Shashank Shekhar Tapikar (Cricket Operations, Barbados Tridents) sir had approached me and asked whether I wanted to play in WCPL. I said ‘why not’. It’d be a different experience, different wickets, and different people. Franchise cricket is a bit different but it’s good for learning,” the 28-year-old batter revealed.
Harleen was part of India’s 2025 ODI World Cup-winning squad and travelled to England for the historic first-ever women’s Test at Lord’s, although she didn’t feature in the four-day fixture.
However, the Punjab player did not make the T20 World Cup 2026, Asia Cup, and the Asian Games squads. The last time she played a T20I for India was last December. Moreover, she was also left out of the India A squads for the ongoing multi-format home series against the visiting Australians after captaining One-Day A squad during the England tour in May. India won the 50-over leg 2-1, with Harleen registering a half century in the opening fixture too.
Missing out on action with the Indian setup, at A or senior level, doesn’t bother her.
“I don’t think a lot about these things. Wherever I am, it’s the same cricket that is to be played. I just want to play and enjoy, and give my best wherever I’m playing,” she explained.
“I don’t think as a player you change a lot in your technique. Yes, you can watch someone and learn something from them. But I don’t think you can change your technique through this method. I have not changed too much,” she said when asked whether she would use this WCPL stint to better her T20 game.
“If we talk about internationals, it’s not that I haven’t done well in T20Is. It’s about the combinations that fit in.”
For now, Harleen wants to bank on a tried and tested mantra during her stay in the Caribbean: going with the flow.
“ Ye sab plan karte karte banda fass jata hai (You get stuck as soon as you start planning what you want to achieve). I’m someone who takes it one day at a time. If you think too much ahead, it can disappoint you. In T20 cricket, I’m focussing on my process and not the result.”

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Charlotte Mandrier. It has been edited for length and clarity.
On Monday, September 14, I was cleaning up my inbox and deleting emails when I saw that Starbucks was collaborating with the Peanuts brand to sell merchandise inspired by "The Great Pumpkin."
I remembered last year when Starbucks released a small number of bear cups. My daughter, who is 9, had wanted one but hadn't managed to get hold of one. She was so disappointed.
She clearly hadn't known about the Snoopy cups that were going on sale, or I would have heard about it from her. She is obsessed with Peanuts, Snoopy, and "The Great Pumpkin."
She watches the movie all year long
As an autistic person, she has a special interest in Peanuts, specifically "The Great Pumpkin." She watches it all year long, even though it is a very fall movie. She listens to the music from the film's soundtrack. She was born in Santa Rosa, where the museum commemorating Charles Schulz — the cartoonist who created the Peanuts comic — is located. When she was little, she went to a camp at the museum and learned to ice skate at Snoopy's Home Ice next door. She even looks like Linus. She loves everything about this brand.
As it happened, her birthday is in two days. So when I saw that these limited-edition Snoopy cups and other merchandise celebrating the movie would be on sale, I told my husband I was going to try to get one for her.
I woke up in the middle of the night
I set my alarm for Tuesday morning at 3:30 a.m., quietly sneaking out of the house to arrive at our closest Starbucks in downtown Chevy Chase at 4 a.m., when it opens.
Walking six blocks to get there, I only saw one other woman on the street. It turned out she was going to the same Starbucks to wait in line, too.
When I got there, no one was in line yet, and I felt so relieved. I had imagined that there would already be a huge line, with people hoping to take all the stock to resell it later.
I suppose that since it was a fairly commercial area, rather than a residential area, people didn't think to go there to get the merchandise.
Slowly, others arrived. There were three of us waiting for the merchandise, and three regulars who were just there to get their coffee.
Although they were meant to open the doors at 4 a.m., apparently, there was a staffing issue, and they didn't open until 5 a.m. The regulars said that it wasn't normal for the shop to open late.
The lights were on, but we couldn't see anyone inside. We tried knocking because we weren't sure if someone was there, and just didn't know we were waiting. We were desperate to get the good stuff.
There were about 10 Snoopy cups
While we waited, I used my phone to take photos of the merchandise and count how many cups were available. I could see about 10.
Then someone finally unlocked and opened the doors for us. Once I got in, I bought a Snoopy cup, a tote bag, a keychain, a mug, and some pins. It came to about $200.
One of the regulars who was there got swept up in the hype and got a cup, even though it wasn't why she'd come.
It was incredibly exciting that I had managed to get the stuff. I was so excited, imagining my daughter's face in two days when she opens her birthday presents.
Sneaking back into the house at 5:30 a.m. and hiding it all away, I pretended I had just woken up.
As soon as she sees on YouTube that these cups were for sale, I know she'll be disappointed, thinking that, like last year, she missed out. I'll give an Oscar-winning performance, telling her I wish we could have gotten there sooner, and maybe we can look for Snoopy cups that people are selling online.
And then, in two days, I'll give her all the Peanuts presents. I really cannot wait.

Gen Z gets foot in Rajasthan local politics as 6 win Jaipur polls
Six Gen Z candidates won in Jaipur's civic polls, while 21-year-old Neha Sharma triumphed in Alwar. The results signalled a modest but visible generational shift in Rajasthan's local politics.
Rajasthan's urban local body election results have offered a glimpse of Gen Z's growing presence in grassroots politics, with six young candidates winning seats in the Jaipur Municipal Corporation after the BJP and the Congress fielded 18 candidates from the generation across 150 wards.
Of the 18 Gen Z candidates in the fray in Jaipur, four winners were from the Congress and two from the BJP. The six councillors will account for about 4% of the civic body's elected strength.
The Congress fielded 12 Gen Z candidates, twice as many as the BJP, which gave tickets to six.
Among the youngest winners was 21-year-old Congress candidate Faiz Hasan, who won Ward 71 by defeating 39-year-old Independent candidate Mohammad Salim. BJP's Palak Yadav, also 21, secured victory in Ward 10, defeating 39-year-old Congress candidate Vandana Jakhar.
Another closely watched contest was in Ward 115, where 29-year-old BJP candidate Suraj Godiwal defeated 67-year-old Congress candidate Suresh Biwal by 1,063 votes. The result underscored the generational shift visible in some contests, with Godiwal being 38 years younger than his rival.
The elections also produced notable victories outside Jaipur. In Alwar district's Thanagazi ward, 21-year-old journalist Neha Sharma won after making her electoral debut.
Speaking after her victory, Sharma said her years of reporting from rural Rajasthan inspired her to enter politics and work directly for people. "Kyun na shuruwaat khud se hi ki jaaye? (Why not start with myself?)" she said.
Sharma said she had often seen villagers and farmers travel to Jaipur and spend hours outside government offices or waiting to meet elected representatives to get their grievances addressed. She felt that merely reporting such issues was not enough, prompting her to take a more direct role in public life.
While young candidates remain a small minority in Rajasthan's urban local bodies, the results highlighted an emerging Gen Z presence in local politics, particularly in Jaipur, where six candidates from the generation secured victories.

On food labelling and misleading claims, weight loss drugs, climate change, rabies, cancer care, and more
(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
This past week, as with the previous week, the nation continues to be concerned with food labelling. With the Supreme Court bringing up the packaged food labelling issue up again, a couple of weeks ago, it has been surely and firmly dragged into the public platform. There has been a great deal of interest in the Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s recommendations on front-of-pack labels, and debate about the merits of the case.
What are these standards that FSSAI promises to hold the packaged food in India up to? We took a long,hard look.
For an idea of what the whole FSSAI submission on labelling was, initially, check out this conversation between Zubeda Hamid and I; we also indicate trends worldwide, in Sunday’s Health Wrap video. While appreciable that some standards have come to play in this entirely unregulated sector, there are questions about the caveats in the proposed recommendations. FSSAI has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages. Activists find the “two or more” classification problematic.
For a more detailed explanation on what the Red hexagon on your snack pack means, read what Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote. FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages. In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase. The FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat. The plan is to exempt single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey.
Meanwhile, Soibam Rocky Singh explains why the Central Consumer Protection Authority is cracking down on ‘100%’ claims on food products. Such claims can give consumers an impression of absolute purity or completeness that may not match what is actually inside the packet. The FSSAI has also asked food businesses to stop using “100%” claims on food labels, packaging and promotional material.
Here, Prabalika M. Borah examines the hype behind Proffee: protien+coffee, and here are the highlights of an ICMR-NIN study which shows that Vitamin D3 outperforms D2 in supporting muscles and heart.
Close on the nutrition topic is weight loss drugs. A recent study showed that GLP-1 weight loss drugs are effective even at low starter doses, with lower side effects. Yet another study in the United States showed that more children under 12 in U.S. are being prescribed weight-loss drugs. Prescriptions for GLP-1 weight-loss drugs among children under 12 in the U.S. have risen more than 300-fold since 2019.
Here is a supervised experiment of a fitness coaching putting himself through a GLP 1 course, recording minute observations through the course. Arvind Ashok writes: ‘I’m a fitness coach. I tried a GLP-1 drug for three weeks’, issuing a statutory warning to readers not to attempt the same at home without a prescription.
Climate change will also never be further than a beck and call away. It has dominated headlines periodically, and likely will be even more frequent in future. Jacob Koshy writes: Global warming will exceed limit, UN says in a report that maps path to get back below danger zone. UNEP’s detailed ‘overshoot, peak and decline’ pathway seeks to hold the peak as low as possible and then bring temperatures back down below the 1.5°C limit; report terms it ‘best remaining option’.
Yet another new study highlights the life-saving role of air conditioning, but indicates that it comes at a cost. Do check this story out, for the details: Keeping cool saves thousands of lives yearly, but at a cost of worsening global warming, experts say.
On the rabies front, there was some exciting news in the region. I record how Bhutan leads South-East Asia in eliminating rabies as public health problem. The WHO also validated Bhutan’s claim and explained that this was achieved through conscious of deployment of the One Health approach, affording some key lessons for neighbour India too.
Meanwhile, Authorities are probing ‘counterfeit’ rabies vaccine, and the counterfeit ‘Abhayrab’ rabies vaccine batch remains under investigation. Why is this important? With rabies, the margin for error is exceptionally small. A genuine, potent vaccine administered promptly can prevent a fatal disease; a counterfeit product can create the dangerous illusion that protection has been provided.
On dogs, segueing into cancer, we had an interesting article this week on whether dogs can sniff cancer? Bengaluru-based startup Dognosis is using AI to analyse dogs’ brain activity, respiration and body language, turning their reaction to scent into data. Click on the link to learn more.
Dr. Jayanth Reddy meanwhile wrote on how transplant oncology is rewriting the story of liver cancer, and why surgeons, instead of trying to cut the cancer out of the liver, remove the entire diseased liver and replace it with a healthy one.
In the In Focus podcast, there’s a discussion with Dr. Narayana Subramanian about cancer ‘vaccines’ and if will they revolutionise treatment. What are these new therapies and what cancer do they treat? Why are they called vaccines when they don’t actually prevent cancer? How does mRNA tech work and how is AI helpful in this? Will these personalised treatments be available in India any time soon and how expensive will they be?
And for that little bit extra, do take a look at this week’s links of health stories that moved the world in their own ways:

C. Maya highlights an important trend: Fading fear of HIV puts focus on rising STI risks among youth in Keralam

As we come to the close of eye donation awareness week, here is an article from Dr. Mohan Rajan and Dr. Sujatha Mohan on Eye donation in India: current scenario and way forward

Dr. C. Aravinda advises that In child sexual abuse, one needs to focus on healing the survivor

The US Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, a comprehensive cryptocurrency bill backed by President Donald Trump, Reuters reported. The procedural vote failed 49-50 on Tuesday, falling short of the 60 votes required to advance the bill. Four Republican senators, Jerry Moran, Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Thom Tillis, joined Democrats in voting against it. The bill's failure effectively puts it on ice as Congress is set to leave Washington this month ahead of the November midterm elections, when Republicans will seek to retain control of both chambers. Quick answers to key questions The Clarity Act is a proposed bill aiming to create a federal regulatory framework for digital assets. Its significance lies in providing legal certainty for crypto companies, which have lobbied extensively for clearer regulations to foster institutional participation and stability in the market. The Senate's rejection of the Clarity Act led to an immediate decline in Bitcoin's price, reflecting market sentiments that were hoping for regulatory clarity. This uncertainty contributed to increased volatility in the crypto market, as investors reacted to the setback. The failure of the Clarity Act may prompt the SEC and CFTC to set their own rules for crypto, but these could be less stable than legislative frameworks. This situation keeps regulatory ambiguity alive in the industry and affects long-term institutional investments. Some Democratic senators opposed the Clarity Act due to concerns about its ethics provisions, which sought to address potential conflicts of interest for public officials involved in the crypto industry, particularly regarding President Trump's financial interests. For Indian cryptocurrency investors, the failure of the Clarity Act has no direct impact on their operations, as they fall under Indian regulations. However, it signifies a missed opportunity for a potential regulatory model that could have influenced India's crypto framework. Tillis switched his vote from yes to no in a procedural move that preserves the possibility of bringing the bill back for reconsideration. The Clarity Act sought to establish a regulatory framework for digital assets, which crypto companies have argued would provide greater legal certainty for the industry. With the legislation stalled, the focus is now expected to shift to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), which could set rules for the crypto market using their existing authority. According to Shiv Ram Pande, Chief Business Officer, BitSave, there will be little day-to-day change for crypto companies and investors in the near term. Spot Bitcoin and other crypto ETFs will continue to trade, while banks and asset managers can continue offering custody and crypto-backed lending. "What stays open is the question Clarity was meant to settle. Which digital assets fall under the SEC, and which fall under the CFTC, and most importantly what protections do investors get?" Pande said while talking to Mint. He said the regulatory questions remain particularly relevant following the Terra-Luna and FTX collapses in 2022. Pande added that the failure of Congress to pass the legislation could push the SEC and CFTC to establish rules themselves. While that could help in the near term, such rules could be more easily rewritten under a change in administration than legislation, potentially making a material difference for institutions with a long-term investment horizon. The US regulatory setback has no direct impact on Indian crypto investors or platforms, Pande said, as they continue to operate under Indian regulations. India's existing tax treatment, including a 30% tax on gains and 1% TDS on transfers, remains unchanged. The indirect impact, however, could be significant because India loses a potential reference point for crypto regulation. "A US market-structure law would have been a tested template for classifying digital assets and splitting oversight between regulators," Pandey said. Bitcoin is also priced globally, meaning volatility in the US market can reach Indian investors on the same day, he added. Bitcoin fell from around $78,000 before the vote to about $76,000, according to the latest update. It had fallen more than 5% as the Senate vote appeared headed for failure, its biggest one-day percentage decline since June, according to Reuters. Shares of crypto exchange Coinbase and stablecoin issuer Circle also fell as much as 10%. The crypto industry spent hundreds of millions of dollars campaigning for the legislation, which would have created a regulatory framework for digital assets. Trump had urged Congress to pass the bill after courting support from the crypto industry during his 2024 presidential campaign and describing himself as a "crypto president". Trump has also earned more than $1.4 billion from his family's crypto ventures. Markets are also awaiting the US Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision, due at 11.30 pm IST on Wednesday. The latest update says markets have largely priced in a rate hike aimed at curbing inflation. Higher rates could weigh on risk assets, including cryptocurrencies, in the short term. The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 10, 2026) refused to entertain a PIL raising concerns over the government-run nationwide human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination campaign for adolescent girls to prevent cervical cancer.
A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana said whenever there is a case of incorrect vaccination, ordinary rules of compensation will apply.
"Would you like to withdraw? Do you want us to comment something?" the Bench observed.
"Don't ask us to make harsh observations. If petitioner members are doctors, it's a very very serious issue. It's a question of health of millions of our daughters. And you want to derail this," it said.
The top court orally said that the PIL was filed with an ulterior motive and lacked bonafide.
The lawyer appearing for the petitioner said that he was only pressing on adverse events and compensation, nothing on HPV.
"I am not at all anti-vaccine. My first contention is the way it is being implemented. Second, there is no adverse event mechanism. Whenever there is an adverse event, it must be monitored. There should also be a compensation scheme," the lawyer said.
When the apex court refused to entertain the plea, the counsel withdrew the plea and the matter was dismissed as withdrawn.
The top court was hearing a plea filed by the Universal Health Organisation challenging the manner in which the government-backed HPV vaccination programme is being implemented.
The plea alleged that it violates constitutional guarantees of informed consent, bodily autonomy, transparency and accountability.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for 14-year-old girls from Ajmer in Rajasthan on February 28.
A single-dose Gardasil 4 vaccine, a quadrivalent HPV vaccine, is being used under the campaign. The injection provides protection against HPV types 16 and 18, which are responsible for cervical cancer, as well as types 6 and 11.

Gates Foundation commits $1 billion to help build and deliver equitable AI
The Goalkeepers Report this year focuses on the urgent actions needed to ensure AI helps narrow gaps between the richest and poorest rather than widen them
The Gates Foundation has announced plans to spend at least US$1 billion over the next two years to expand access to artificial intelligence (AI) and AI-enabled solutions, opportunities, and knowledge.
The announcement came as the foundation launched its 10th annual Goalkeepers Report late Monday, which this year focuses on the urgent actions needed to ensure AI helps narrow gaps between the richest and poorest rather than widen them.
“The Gates Foundation was created in part to address a basic market failure: the people with the greatest needs often have the least power to shape where innovation and investment go,” said Bill Gates, chair of the Gates Foundation, in the report. “Much of our work has been about closing that gap. AI presents the same challenge, only at much greater speed. Left to the market alone, the most capable tools will be built first for the people and institutions most able to pay for them—not necessarily for those who could benefit most.”
The Goalkeepers Report identifies three areas where action now could help AI improve lives and livelihoods for more people in the years ahead: Make AI tools work in every language people speak. More than 90% of the data used to train early large language models came from English-language sources, leaving many communities that could benefit from AI poorly represented in data on which these tools were built.
Build AI tools for the contexts in which people will use them. Effective tools require data and expertise from the places and populations they are intended to serve, with countries and communities deciding how data is managed and protected.
Invest in people and access so communities can shape how AI works for them. Doctors, farmers, teachers, and developers need opportunities to learn how to evaluate AI tools and adapt what works to their own contexts. They also need affordable access to the technology, which will require action from technology companies as well as investment from governments and philanthropy.
“Equitable access to the benefits of AI will not happen on its own. But if AI tools are built with the expertise of the end users, they can put knowledge and advice in the hands of hundreds of millions of people who have not benefited from previous technology revolutions,” said the foundation in a statement.
According to the statement, over the next two years 40% will be allocated to support education, including AI tutoring to help individualise student learning and teaching tools for use in US classrooms and abroad; 40% will support health care, from diagnostics and clinical decision-making support for frontline health workers to maternal and newborn care tools and the discovery of new drugs and vaccines; 10% for agriculture, including to help smallholder farmers get AI-generated advice customised to their soil, weather, and crop conditions; and the remaining 10% will be used to build the digital foundation that equitable AI depends on, including datasets in languages the tools do not yet understand.
“We can harness AI for good. But it won’t happen by accident,” Gates said in the statement. “It requires a deliberate, specific commitment from government leaders and the companies developing the technology: to measure success not only by what AI can do for the most profitable users but by what it can do for the people who stand the most to gain.”

During a June 2026 congressional hearing, Steiner said a proposed rule would mean the Postal Service would not mail out ballots in states that failed to hand their absentee voter lists to the federal government. The service created the rule to comply with an executive order President Donald Trump signed in March, supposedly to ensure "citizenship verification and integrity in federal elections." Stipulations in the order included the use of secure envelopes with barcodes and a demand that states send their voter rolls to the service for eligibility verification purposes. However …
… The Postal Service confirmed the new rule pertained only to determining voter eligibility in the mailing out of blank ballots, not returning completed ballots. Also, Steiner didn't appear to provide multiple "ways" (plural) to block the delivery of mail-in ballots, as users alleged.
Snopes readers emailed us to ask about this rumor, with some of them attaching a screenshot of a Threads post. The screenshot, showing a partial profile image, read:
Postmaster General has already said there are ways he WILL block mail-in ballots, so… The minute you get your ballot, fill it our and take it to the nearest drop box, usually near libraries. Do NOT mail your ballot through USPS!
Find a BALLOT DROP BOX only !!!!
Please copy this and share on your feed.
(Received via Snopes reader email)
A reverse image search for the same screenshot located users sharing the same image on Facebook, Threads and X.
A Threads search found the original post (archived) matching the partial profile image from the above screenshot. That user presented the claim and the advice to avoid mailing completed ballots on Sept. 2:
(@kirkanthonyb2020 via Threads)
A search on X for similar text located a popular post (archived) from June 25 that contained a version of the claim about the postmaster general, without the advice to use designated drop boxes. That post read, "JUST IN: U.S. Postmaster General CONFIRMS he'll BLOCK mail-in ballots to states refusing to share citizenship and voter data with the Trump administration":
(@jackunheard via X)
On June 24, one day before that X post, Steiner was a witness in a televised hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee. During the hearing, Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., asked Steiner, "Yes or no: If a state refuses to turn their absentee voter list over to the federal government, will the Postal Service still mail their ballots under this proposed rule?"
Steiner answered, in part, "Under our proposed regulation, no." (The full hearing is available on YouTube, with pertinent remarks beginning at the 30:37 mark.)
In sum, this rumor about the postmaster general's alleged statements and guidance on voters delivering their completed ballots mixed truth and falsehood.
It's true that, during the June hearing, Steiner confirmed one way the Postal Service might block, or decline, the delivery of mail-in ballots. At the time, Steiner was referencing a proposed rule. The rule
That rule, which may restrict mail-in voting, stemmed from an executive order President Donald Trump — who has repeatedly promoted false claims of massive voter fraud — signed in March. Part of that order mentions of the use of secure envelopes with barcodes. It also stipulates that states that intend to use the Postal Service to deliver mail-in or absentee ballots should send their voter rolls to the service so that it can verify voters' citizenship and eligibility to vote in federal elections.
However, the claim that voters should avoid mailing their completed ballots through the Postal Service and instead directly deposit them into designated ballot drop boxes doesn't accurately reflect what the new rule means in practice. The Postal Service confirmed the new rule pertained only to determining voter eligibility before mailing out blank ballots — not when completed ballots are mailed back in — meaning that while there's nothing wrong with using drop boxes to ensure delivery of completed ballots, the reason some users recommended them was not reflected in the rule.
Additionally, Steiner didn't appear to provide multiple "ways" (plural) to block delivery of ballots, as users alleged.
On Sept. 14,
Snopes contacted the Postal Service to request comment about the rumor, and spokesperson Nikolaj Hagen shared the following statement in an email:
The Postal Service is committed to fulfilling our role in the electoral process when public policy makers choose to utilize us as a part of their election system. We rely on longstanding, robust and tested policies and procedures, which have proven successful in the secure and timely delivery of Election Mail. Through August 28, the Postal Service has delivered 233.3 million pieces of Election Mail nationwide during Fiscal Year 2026, with an on-time score of 97.94%.
White House spokesperson 
'Misinformation and speculation'
In a Sept. 4 news release, Steiner addressed what he called "misinformation and speculation" about the issuance of the Postal Service rule and defended the service's duty to comply with Trump's executive order.
The release also featured a recent whistleblower complaint that warned of "potentially catastrophic problems in the development of the United States Postal Service's new system for handling federal election ballot mail." The complaint specifically referenced the service's new rule establishing a voter verification system that officials would use to determine which voters receive blank ballots via mail.
One part of the complaint alleged that if one barcode on a single ballot in a bulk mailing of 10,000 blank ballots failed to properly scan during the verification process, the entire batch would be rejected and sent back to the state, meaning none of those voters would receive their ballots.
Steiner said the Postal Service "takes these concerns seriously," as well as that, "Regardless of political party or perspective, we share a common goal: ensuring that Americans can have confidence that their election mail will be handled securely and delivered reliably should their election officials choose to use the mail for ballot delivery."
For further reading, we previously reported about the many details of the new Postal Service rule, Trump's executive order and the beginning of the many legal challenges associated with the matter.

Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found.
Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year.
Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa.
The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning.
The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India.
Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”.
The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides.
The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990.
Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.”
The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure.
Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.”
Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s.
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers.
Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing.
Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands.
“Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said.
Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

Months after a fractured wrist had healed, a 42-year-old homemaker from Mysuru was still unable to cook or even tolerate the touch of clothing on her hand. Despite repeated investigations confirming that the fracture had healed, she continued to have severe burning pain, swelling, stiffness and changes in skin colour.
She was eventually referred to pain specialists and diagnosed with Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS), in which the nervous system continues to generate pain long after the original injury has healed. With specialised pain management, she gradually regained function and independence.
Pain specialists say such cases highlight the need to recognise chronic pain as a condition that may require specialised care.
At Victoria Hospital, attached to the Bangalore Medical College and Research Institute (BMCRI), more than 1,200 patients have undergone specialised pain-relieving procedures since its pain clinic was established in June 2023. The clinic, run by the Department of Anaesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine, has also provided outpatient consultation to over 4,000 patients.
Public awareness campaign
As September is observed as Pain Awareness month, the Karnataka Chapter of the Indian Society for Study of Pain (ISSP) has launched a public awareness campaign urging people not to accept chronic pain as an unavoidable part of life, but to seek specialised care when it persists beyond the normal healing period.
“Our team led by our head of the department Nethra S.S. has performed over 1,200 advanced pain intervention procedures and has seen over 4,000 patients in the outpatient department,” said Satish Kumar M.N., associate professor, Department of Anaesthesia and Pain Medicine, BMCRI, and treasurer of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
The clinical team, comprising associate professor Nethra H.N., assistant professor Harshavardhan H.S., Satish Kumar and Dr. Nethra, treats patients with cancer pain, neuropathic pain, musculoskeletal disorders, spine-related pain, knee and shoulder pain, trigeminal neuralgia and other chronic pain conditions.
Besides image-guided nerve blocks and joint injections, the clinic performs advanced procedures such as radiofrequency ablation, which interrupts pain signals from affected nerves.
Dr. Kumar said the acquisition of a radiofrequency ablation machine had enabled the BMCRI to offer procedures that were previously available largely in corporate hospitals.
Pain is more than a symptom
Sadasivan S. Iyer, consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Manipal Hospital, Old Airport Road, and vice-president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP, said a common misconception was that patients should simply learn to live with chronic pain.
“Many patients are told to simply live with pain because investigations do not reveal an obvious cause. But persistent pain can itself be a medical condition requiring specialised evaluation and treatment,” he said.
While acute pain serves as the body’s warning signal after an injury or illness, pain lasting beyond three months can become a condition in itself, he said. The nervous system can continue to transmit pain signals even after tissues have healed. Therefore, normal scans do not necessarily mean that the pain is imaginary, while abnormalities on imaging do not always explain the severity of symptoms.
Beyond painkillers
Pain medicine is not limited to prescribing stronger painkillers. Depending on the condition, treatment may include medication optimisation, physical rehabilitation, psychological support, lifestyle modification and minimally invasive, image-guided procedures such as nerve blocks, epidural injections and radiofrequency ablation.
“The goal is not simply to reduce a patient’s pain score. It is to help them sleep better, return to work, perform daily activities and regain independence. Pain relief is ultimately about restoring quality of life,” said Murali T.S., consultant and lead, Pain Medicine, Apollo Hospitals, Bengaluru, and president of the Karnataka Chapter of the ISSP.
When should patients seek help?
According to the ISSP, millions of Indians live with persistent back and neck pain, sciatica, diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, cancer pain and pain that continues after surgery.
Specialists advise people to seek evaluation if pain lasts for more than three months, repeatedly returns, interferes with sleep or daily activities, persists despite treatment of the original illness, or is accompanied by burning, shooting or electric shock-like sensations.

Japan’s average retail price of pork loin this month came to ¥293 per 100 grams, hitting the highest level since the survey began in August 2003, the agriculture ministry has said.
Prices for a pack of 10 eggs averaged ¥309 in the latest reporting month, matching a record high marked in March, May and June, according to the ministry data released Tuesday.
Demand for domestic pork is increasing amid higher prices of imported produce, reflecting the yen’s weakening and increasing pork demand worldwide.
The rise in egg prices was attributable to the lingering impact from the spread of avian influenza last year and the start of sales of seasonal products using eggs at fast food chains.
The monthly price survey covers a total of 470 stores — 10 each in the country’s 47 prefectures. The latest survey was conducted from Sept. 7 to 9.

A second season of HBO Max’s Harry Potter TV series is in the works, and the cast continues to grow.
The streamer has plans for an accelerated production of the series adaptation of J.K. Rowling’s book s, with Season 1 on the way and production looking to start soon for Season 2.
Read on for everything we know about Season 2 of HBO’s Harry Potter show:
When will Season 2 of HBO’s Harry Potter TV show come out?
No release date has yet been set for the second season of the series, but production is aiming to start this fall ahead of Season 1’s premiere.
Who will be new in the cast for Season 2 of HBO’s Harry Potter TV Show?
Watch on Deadline
Bonnie Hill will take over the role of Ginny Weasley, Ron’s younger sister and the youngest Weasley sibling, in Season 2 from Gracie Cochrane, who will portray her in Season 1. Cochrane stepped away from the series due to unforeseen circumstances, prompting the recasting of Harry’s eventual love interest as well as a key character in Rowling’s second book, The Chamber of Secrets.
Lenny Rush (Am I Being Unreasonable?) will portray Dobby, the loyal house-elf who serves the Malfoy family. Billy Barratt (Invasion), who holds the record as the youngest International Emmy winner, will portray Tom Riddle, the younger version of Lord Voldemort.
Deadline first broke the news of Nicholas Hoult’s casting as Professor Gilderoy Lockhart, who serves as Defense Against the Dark Arts teacher in Rowling’s book The Chamber of Secrets. We then first reported Kit Harrington stepping up to fill the role after Hoult departed due to scheduling issues. Harrington voices the character in the audiobooks.
The newest round of additions thus far include Molly Hewitt-Richards, who will portray Moaning Myrtle, Rafe Spall as patriarch Arthur Weasley and Jasper Ambrose as Colin Creevey. Rafe Spall is the son of Timothy Spall, who portrayed Peter Pettigrew aka Wormtail from the third Harry Potter film onwards. Deadline first reported that the casting search for Creevey was underway, whose camera comes in handy in Season 2, in June.
Who else is behind Season 2 of HBO’s Harry Potter TV show?
Jon Brown (Succession), who was a writer on the first season, has been elevated to co-showrunner for Season 2 alongside Season 1 showrunner Francesca Gardiner. The elevation lines up with the faster production schedule.
“As we have laid out our plans for the overlapping production schedules to finish Season 1 by Christmas and to return to production for Season 2 this autumn, it has become clear that bringing on a co-showrunner is the key to maintaining our momentum,” Gardiner said. “I’ve loved working with Jon from the very first day we met on Succession through to these recent times together on Harry Potter. Not only do I have huge admiration for his writing, but he’s also a brilliant collaborator and a lovely person. We are lucky to have him.”
Gardiner also executive produces. Mark Mylod serves as executive producer and directed multiple episodes. Rowling, Neil Blair, and Ruth Kenley-Letts of Brontë Film and TV, and David Heyman of Heyday Films also executive produce the series, produced by HBO in association with Brontë Film and TV and Warner Bros. Television. It will air on HBO and be available to stream exclusively on HBO Max.
When does Season 1 of HBO’s Harry Potter series come out?
Season 1 of the series premieres Christmas day 2026.
RELATED: ‘Harry Potter And The Philosopher’s Stone’: See First-Look Photos From Upcoming HBO Series
Will there be more seasons of the Harry Potter show on HBO?
The idea is one season per book, but the show has not yet been renewed for a third season. Chairman and CEO of HBO and Max Content Casey Bloys gave brief updates on the series post-Emmys 2026.
“Each book is a huge event. I’m right now thinking about season by season as far as what it all adds up to. But I can tell you, Christmas Day is going to be a great launch day for Harry Potter,” he said.
He also reinforced the idea of a tight production schedule.
“We’re trying as hard to bring it back as quickly as possible. It’s not going to be two years [between seasons], but we’re trying hard to keep it as compressed as possible,” he said.

Reading 1-2 Brentford: Bees book place in Carabao Cup fourth round with tense win at League One side
Report and free match highlights from the Carabao Cup third round tie between Reading and Brentford at the Select Car Leasing Stadium; Callum Wilson and Fabio Carvalho were on target in the first half for the Premier League club; Paudie O’Connor gave League One side hope of comeback
Tuesday 15 September 2026 23:34, UK
Brentford emerged from a tense finish against Reading to book their place in the Carabao Cup fourth round with a 2-1 victory at Select Car Leasing Stadium.
Callum Wilson and Fabio Carvalho were on target in the first half as the Premier League club showed a clinical touch against League One opposition, who produced a number of chances but lacked the firepower to finish them off.
Paudie O'Connor eventually pulled one back to revive Reading's challenge and Brentford could not rest easy in the remaining 18 minutes, although substitute Igor Thiago was among those who should have killed the match off.

It took just 136 seconds for Brentford to take the lead with Wilson finding the bottom left corner of the net after a slip in defence by O'Connor turned Dango Ouattara's pass into an opportunity.
A cross by Carvalho caused problems in the visiting box and Reading then had the ball in the net but referee Tom Nield ruled out O'Connor's bicycle kick for a high boot.
O'Connor was doing everything possible to make up for his earlier mistake as he headed a free-kick inches over the crossbar.
Reading had clearly recovered from the shock of going behind so early as they poured forward, with a double clearance by Michael Kayode saving Brentford before Jamie Reid went desperately close.
O'Connor slipped again as he fluffed a clearance, giving Wilson time to pick his spot only for keeper Joel Pereira to get his body in the way.
Brentford scrambled to keep out Reid as he closed in on goal and then Conor Masterson flashed narrowly wide, but the Premier League club then scored on the counter-attack.

Ellery Balcombe's sharp reflexes prevented Josh Stokes from pulling one back for Reading but Brentford should have extended the lead only for Kayode to send a close-range effort wide.
Liam Fraser reminded the visitors they could not relax as he drilled a shot past the left post but the better chances were now coming at the other end, with Ouattara this time at fault for not making the most of a great opportunity.
Reading deserved a goal and it arrived in the 72nd minute when a corner was met by O'Connor's header, with the Irish defender's finish setting up a nervy finale.
On came Thiago but he was unable to improve the standard of finishing by his team, which had declined noticeably in the second half.

Pulley, a software that startups rely on to track their funding, is shutting down after seven years.
The company said in a statement published on its website on Tuesday that it will cease operations after December 8.
Pulley had raised more than $50 million from investors, including Founders Fund, General Catalyst, Stripe, and 8VC. It previously tried to challenge its much larger rival, Carta, in the cap table management business — software that helps companies track who owns shares and issue new equity as they raise money.
As part of the wind-down, Carta has agreed to help move customers and is offering them a limited-time promotion, according to Pulley's statement.
Yin Wu started Pulley after she sold an Android app called Echo to Microsoft in 2015.
"Though this is the closing of one chapter I, along with many of our strongest team members, have no intention of riding off quietly into the night," Wu wrote in a LinkedIn post on Tuesday. "There has never been a better time to solve big problems. For the immediate future, we are focused on working with Carta's team to take care of our customers."
On Tuesday, founders posted screenshots of the email they received from Pulley.
"We have worked diligently to develop a transition plan that ensures you won't experience any disruptions as we cease operations," the company wrote in the email. Customers who move to Carta will be able to keep their current Pulley pricing for the first year, and Carta will credit any unused portion of their Pulley subscription.

National Park Service warns visitors to stay away from elk and black bears - or face the consequences
It’s illegal for parkgoers to get closer than 25 yard from an elk or 50 yards from a black bear
America’s national park lovers should get outside to view majestic wildlife this fall - as long as it’s from a safe distance, officials warned Monday.
There will be increased elk and black bear activity this season, officials at Tennessee’s Great Smoky National Park cautioned.
Wild animals are unpredictable and getting too close can lead to harmful human-wildlife encounters.
Deaths are extremely rare but a handful of park goers have been mauled by protective mama bears and gored by bison in the past few years.
“Enjoy wildlife responsibly by remaining at least 25 yards away from elk and 50 yards away from black bears,” the agency cautioned in a statement.
Part of the risk to humans is related to the time of year. Black bears are feeding on fall food sources ahead of hibernation, consuming up to 20,000 calories a day to build fat reserves that sustain them through the winter months.
That’s why they can be highly active during the autumn months, moving across the park as corns and other fall foods become abundant.
It’s also the annual elk breeding season, known as the rut. During this period, male elk experience elevated levels of the male hormone testosterone, which can lead to heightened aggression toward any perceived threats, including people, vehicles and pets.
Both elk and black bears are seen at parks across the U.S., including Wyoming, Montana and Idaho’s Yellowstone National Park, Washington state’s Olympic National Park and Wyoming’s Grand Teton National Park.
It’s illegal for park goers to get closer than 25 yard from an elk or 50 yards from a black bear, as well as any distance that causes an animal to change its behavior.
“Violations may result in fines or arrest,” the park noted. Fines can range from hundreds to several thousand dollars.
However, many people get too close to park wildlife each year, whether it’s their intent or not.
In July, a grandfather was hurled eight feet into the air by a male bison in Yellowstone, shattering the man’s femur. There have been multiple bear attacks in Glacier National Park including one which led to the death of a Florida man.
People who accidentally find themselves too close to an approaching elk or black bear should slowly back away, the park said.
“If a black bear continues to follow, stand your ground, be loud, throw rocks and continue to back away slowly. If an animal approaches you, it is your responsibility to safely and calmly maintain the legal distance,” officials advise.
Fight back if a black bear is attacking, but find shelter or a strong protective barrier if an elk attacks.
“If nearby shelter is not available, run away,” the park service says.

Banihal, Sep 16: The Education Department in Jammu and Kashmir's Ramban district has suspended a government school teacher following allegations of harassing a female student.
According to an official order issued by the Chief Education Officer (CEO) Ramban on September 15, 2026, the accused teacher was posted at Government High School Harroge in the Gool zone.
The action was taken under Rule 31 of the Jammu and Kashmir Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1956, following an inquiry report submitted by a committee previously constituted on September 14 to look into the matter.
The order stated the accused has been placed under suspension with immediate effect due to his involvement in the alleged harassment incident involving a student of the school. During the suspension period, the teacher will remain attached to the Government Primary School, Bhatta, in Zone Khari.
Copies of the order have been forwarded to top administration officials, including the Director of School Education Jammu, the District Development Commissioner Ramban, and relevant zonal education officers for necessary action and compliance.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

My husband and I have been traveling internationally with our boys since they were each 10 months old.
Now, they're 9 and 11 — and together, we've visited 35 countries and countless cities. Our favorites tend to have a few things in common: great food, fewer crowds, rich culture, and plenty of things to do as a family.
If you are looking to travel with kids and venture beyond the usual tourist hot spots, there are four cities I'd wholeheartedly recommend.
Lyon is considered France's food capital, and it didn't disappoint.
I believe that even the pickiest eaters will love Lyon's delicious pastries (especially brioche aux pralines roses, a buttery pastry studded with candied pink nuts) and shockingly affordable Michelin-level dining.
We had one of the best meals of our lives at Brocoli: The five-course vegetarian tasting menu was only 40 euros per person.
As much as we loved eating our way through Lyon, the city itself was just as much fun to explore. Old Lyon is beautiful and has a hidden network of covered passageways called traboules.
These passageways cut through Old Lyon's buildings, shops, and courtyards. We spent an afternoon knocking on random doors and cheering every time one opened up into a secret shortcut, quickly turning a walk into a full-blown scavenger hunt.
The Cinema and Miniature Museum was another highlight, with a massive collection of original movie props from blockbusters like "Batman," "Star Wars," and more. Standing inches away from the original Batmobile was definitely a core memory for my boys!
Beyond Lyon, an easy day trip to the beautiful Lake Annecy gave us a welcome break from the July heat. We rented a boat, swam in the sparkling blue lake, and made it back to Lyon in time for yet another delicious dinner.
Turin, Italy, brought us cars, mummies, and happy tummies.
If your kids love pasta, pizza, and gelato, Italy is an obvious choice. Rome, Florence, and Venice are popular with families, but I'd suggest skipping those hot spots for their less famous, equally impressive cousin: Turin.
Turin has excellent food, beautiful piazzas, and enough desserts to satisfy any kid.
Plus, it's home to several cool museums and attractions, including the historic Egyptian Museum. The kids were fascinated by rooms full of mummies, sarcophagi, and ancient everyday objects that offered a glimpse of life thousands of years ago.
Nearby, we rode a glass elevator up the Mole Antonelliana for 360-degree city views, then wandered the Royal Palace of Turin, a lavish 16th-century palace with an armory on full display. We felt like we'd stepped into a world of knights and kings.
My car-loving crew also loved the National Automobile Museum. We followed the evolution of cars from early, ginormous vehicles to sleek modern-day marvels. We spent several hours here and could've easily stayed longer.
And then there was the food: homemade pastas, nightly gelato, and gianduiotti, Turin's famous smooth chocolate-and-hazelnut treats. Pro tip for the grown-ups: Turin is the birthplace of vermouth, so be sure to get a glass before dinner!
Busan, South Korea, was colorful, coastal, and laid-back.
Busan is a coastal city with beautiful beaches, colorful neighborhoods, and serene temples.
It will always be especially memorable for our family because it was the first city where we let our boys take the lead in planning: They researched activities and food and planned our daily schedule. We simply followed along.
We got lucky and arrived on a Saturday. Hundreds of drones lit up the sky over Gwangalli Beach, with the illuminated Gwangan Bridge as the backdrop. We learned that this happens every Saturday, all year long, and it was a wonderful way to start our trip.
On other days, we rode the colorful Sky Capsule along the coast, explored Gamcheon Culture Village, and visited Haedong Yonggungsa, a beautiful Buddhist temple built into the rocky coastline.
Evenings were for Korean barbecue, street food, and bubble tea, with daily stops at Korea's famous video game arcades. The trip was planned by kids, after all!
Da Nang, Vietnam, is our favorite place we've ever visited as a family.
It's a bold claim, but I'll stand by it.
Our days here followed an easy rhythm: an enormous breakfast spread at our hotel, lazy pool afternoons, and evenings spent sightseeing.
At night, we wandered through bustling markets, sampling street food and shopping for souvenirs.
We hiked the Marble Mountains and spent a day at Ba Na Hills, where we walked across the famous Golden Bridge. We took day trips to two UNESCO World Heritage Sites: My Son Sanctuary, home to centuries-old Hindu temples, and the colorful city of Hoi An.
In Hoi An, we wandered lantern-filled streets before an evening boat ride along the river as the town came alive for the night. The kids were equally fascinated and amused by our tiny, squeaky boat.
I can't pinpoint exactly what made us fall so in love with Da Nang. Maybe it was the incredibly kind people, the beautiful beaches, or the amazing food. Whatever it was, we've been daydreaming about going back ever since.
